But given the confines of the project, Bonamici used cotton thread, which you can break by hand. For his apparel, he started by sewing a soft-brim hat. His hiking shorts are a dense but lightweight cotton lawn with a merino wool gusset in the crotch. For tops, he made a lightweight merino wool baselayer, a merino/silk sun hoodie, and a lightweight merino knit hoodie. For a rain layer, he sewed Ventile fabric into a simple anorak silhouette without closures, pockets, and seam tape. A student knit him two pairs of wool socks: one cozy pair for camp, one pair reinforced with mohair in the toe and heel. For insulation, he bought a sweater made from muskox wool, or qiviut, an exceptionally soft and warm fiber collected by Indigenous communities in the far north of Canada and Alaska in spring, when muskoxen shed their winter coats. Bonamici’s testing notes: “The clothing was all awesome, and super comfortable. It really didn’t feel like a compromise whatsoever. That qiviut sweater and beanie were incredibly warm, and the silk/merino hoodie was super comfortable while hiking in the 75-degree sunshine. Loved the cotton shorts, but we jumped in the river on the way home and I realized they’d take sooo long to dry … so I had to change out of them. I might look into a different material for the shorts long-term, maybe silk, as apparently silk dries faster than wool!” In addition to commissioning socks and buying a qiviut sweater, Bonamici decided to use some of his university budget on hiking shoes from the brand FEIT. This handmade footwear is built entirely from natural components, like vegetable-tanned leather uppers, cork footbeds, beeswax thread, and soles made from natural latex rubber. Bonamici’s testing notes: “The Feit shoes were pretty tough to walk in. Just so bulky and chonky, and the full leather lining was slippery inside! I didn’t get blisters, but felt some hot spots, and think that they’d need much more breaking in before being reasonable for a longer hike. The hand-knit socks were super nice though, no notes there!” After one night of testing the full kit—and a few more nights with certain pieces—Bonamici is pleased by how comfortable everything was (except the sleeping pad) and a bit surprised that nothing has broken. Great summer weather in the Pacific Northwest helped. “I feel confident that this suite of gear works really well for fair weather backpacking, so now I’m looking forward to more extensive material testing,” he says. Bonamici plans to bring the oiled-silk tarp back to his lab to test different combinations of fabric, oil, and seam construction for strength and hydrostatic-head water resistance. He’ll also reinforce the trekking-pole wrist straps and continue using them outside the project. He’s most excited, however, to return to his synthetic-based trail runners and beloved inflatable sleeping pad. As for the apparel, Bonamici will keep wearing every piece he made. “It was just so comfortable and friendly and perfectly well-performing,” he says.

item.title: What Three ER Doctors Wish Every Hiker Knew About Staying Safe Outside
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 5.50
(Photo: Douglas Sacha/Getty Images) How Backpacker reported this story: We spoke to three ER physicians who specialize in wilderness medicine and asked them to share the most common causes of serious injuries and illness in hikers. Most people don’t assume a blister will send them to the ER. Our fears on trail tend to be flashier, like violent changes in weather or a teeth-shattering fall. But according to ER doctors, the afflictions they most often see in hikers are much more understated. “Most backcountry emergencies don’t start as emergencies,” says Dr. Chris Williams, MD, an emergency physician and wilderness medicine educator in Tucson, Arizona. “They start as a hotspot on a foot, someone feeling a little too hot, a hiker feeling lousy at altitude, uncertainty about the route, or realizing you’re going through water faster than expected.” We asked emergency and wilderness medicine physicians what they see most commonly go wrong for hikers, and what they wish more people knew before heading into the backcountry. Turns out, it really is all about the little things. “The recurring mistakes in the backcountry are rarely dramatic,” says Dr. TJ Hartridge, DO, an emergency physician and assistant program director of the University of Utah’s Wilderness Medicine Fellowship. “It’s not typically snakebites or bear encounters. It’s the common stuff: musculoskeletal injuries, blisters, diarrhea illness, cold exposure.” Dr. Williams says more often than not, problems on trail start with the feet. “You can have tremendous cardiovascular fitness and still destroy your feet on a long hike,” he says. Dr. Williams recommends training specifically for backpacking in order to prevent injuries to the lower extremities. Running on its own can’t prepare your feet for the stress of hours in hiking boots under the weight of a heavy pack. Try walking around the neighborhood or training in the gym with a loaded pack and the shoes you’ll wear before heading out for something serious. Dr. Megan Eubank, MD, a University of Utah wilderness medicine fellow, says hikers also tend to be reactive, rather than proactive, when it comes to blisters. “Covering a hotspot before it develops into a blister can make a significant difference,” she says. “Everyone should carry an extra pair of dry socks. Wet socks are a major enemy when it comes to blisters, and wool or synthetic socks are generally preferable to cotton.” Ignore a hotspot long enough and the problem can start to snowball. Dr. Hartridge calls it a “decision cascade.” A blister goes ignored, becomes an open wound, then an infection, and eventually results in a call for help. Avoiding decision cascades might seem tedious, especially when it means stopping every time something feels a little off. But taking five minutes to deal with a hotspot is a lot easier than hiking out on an infected foot. In Tucson, where Dr. Williams is based, temperatures climbed to 107°F degrees during a weekend in August. The nearby Pima County Search and Rescue responded to 16 hikers in distress near Seven Falls, several of whom ran out of water or needed help cooling down. Heat illness cases are common in many areas during summer. Most hikers Dr. Williams treats in the ER come in with heat exhaustion. He’s also seen what happens when cases devolve into heat stroke, including a few that turned fatal. To avoid a trip to the hospital, plan carefully during hot weather. “Carry a reasonable safety margin of water, and don’t build an itinerary that assumes every water source will be available,” he said. Drinking too much water can also carry its own risk. Dr. Eubank says she often sees hyponatremia, or dangerously low sodium, among hikers during the summer. “One simple approach is to alternate water with an electrolyte solution rather than relying exclusively on plain water,” she says. In addition to staying hydrated, be sure to check the forecast and avoid hiking in the heat of the day, when temperatures are most extreme. Sometimes the most valuable piece of wilderness medicine isn’t any sort of treatment—it’s knowing when to turn around. The biggest killer? “Pride,” Dr. Williams says. He’s seen the consequences of that pitfall over the course of his career: A hiker feels a hotspot but doesn’t want to slow the group. Someone realizes they may be lost but keeps moving anyway. At altitude, the stakes get higher, but summit fever can cloud judgement. Dr. Hartridge calls these heuristic traps. A hiker can get so fixed on reaching an objective that daylight starts disappearing, for example, leaving them facing an unplanned night outside with whatever they happened to pack. Dr. Eubank understands the temptation. A big trip comes with months of planning and a hefty price tag. Still, “the mountains aren’t going anywhere,” she says. “Sometimes turning around is the smartest decision you can make.” You can’t plan around every injury, but you can prepare for them. Dr. Hartridge says wilderness patients can spend hours waiting for help, sometimes longer. A helicopter isn’t a guarantee, and it can take a long time for rescue teams to reach, stabilize, and transport injured hikers. By the time Dr. Hartridge sees someone in the ER, the original injury might not be the only thing he’s worried about. Even in summer, he watches for hypothermia. A hiker can spend the afternoon sweating, get hurt and stop moving, then still be waiting when the sun goes down and the temperature drops. It changes the math on what counts as a “minor injury” when you’re miles from the hospital. It’s a good reminder that even in the warmer months, you can plan for unpredictability. Packing extra layers and keeping an eye on the weather and your water supply is critical, even if it means hauling a little extra weight. “It’s much easier to solve a small problem in the wilderness than a big one,” Dr. Williams says.

item.title: 4 Sneaky Ways Experienced Hikers Get Lost on Trail and How to Avoid Them
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 4.88
Canyon country's topography can mess with GPS signals or even block them entirely. (Photo: Lauren Berger) You’re hiking along, minding your own business, when the trail you’ve been following suddenly disappears. You look behind you and the path is clear. You look forward, and it’s disintegrated into its true form: a game trail. Or perhaps you’re trucking along through a narrow canyon and pull out your GPS to make sure you take a left instead of a right, but your device can’t connect because, well, you’re in a canyon. We’ve all been there, and I’ve been there a lot. The miles I’ve hiked in the wrong direction, following a game trail, or taking a wrong turn probably add up to an impressively long backpacking trip on their own. I’ve even made the hiked-south-on-a-northbound hike error and had the gall to ask my hiking partner why he was going the wrong way after I emerged from a woodland bathroom break. All that to say, it can be hard to avoid getting lost on the trail. While we should all get better at reading a map, here are some ways to reduce your chances of making four common navigational mistakes. One of the greatest technological advancements for backcountry travel has to be the handheld GPS device. Whether you’re following a track on your watch, have the route downloaded to your phone, or are operating with a standalone backcountry unit, a reliable GPS track takes a lot of the guesswork out of knowing where you are on the trail or how to get back to it if you lose it. But GPS units have their limits, and one of these is when you’re hiking through deep canyons on the trail. GPS units track your location by receiving pings from orbiting satellites. When you travel through tall, narrow canyons, those walls can physically block the GPS unit from accessing the satellites and calculating your position. You can also encounter what’s called a “multipath error,” where the radio signal from the satellite bounces off the rock walls, resulting in delayed (or weak) signals. Avoid this: For routes that travel through deep canyons, you can often change settings on your GPS unit or watch to give it the best possible chance of connecting to satellites. First, enable multi-GNSS, which allows your unit to connect to networks outside of GPS, like GLONASS and Galileo, networks operated respectively by Russian and European Union space commissions. Some units allow you to switch to dual-frequency or multi-band tracking, which help filter out reflected signals from canyon walls and maintain a more accurate location. If your device doesn’t offer those options, take a few minutes to sit under the unobstructed sky before entering the canyon. This can help the device connect to additional satellites before the view is obstructed. And after all that, there will be some canyons where getting a satellite signal just isn’t possible. The best solution? Carry a map. Show me a hiker who claims to have never accidentally followed a game trail, and I’ll show you a liar. The game trail is an siren song to the distracted backpacker, starting out like a wide, clear path indistinguishable from the actual trail but petering out into a barely-there indentation amongst the undergrowth and brambles before ending at the edge of a cliff. Animals take the path of least resistance, which is often a nice, wide hiking trail following the contours of the landscape. When the animals inevitably veer off, they beat down an alluring pathway that looks exactly like the trail before, but fades as the animals disperse. If you find yourself staring at a blank expanse of forest or bushwhacking through the undergrowth after following what looked like a trail, congrats, you followed a game trail. Avoid this: Unlike technology failures, this one can be mitigated by paying better attention. Many developed trail intersections will have signage at the trail fork, and long trails often have specific blazes or markers indicating an upcoming turn. If the trail forks and you aren’t sure where to go (or what the actual trail is), take a few steps back, look for signage, or pull out the trusty GPS and look for your little dot before you take another step. Once you’ve incorrectly walked down the game trail, make sure you turn back in the correct direction instead of getting suckered by yet another game trail and getting lost even deeper in the woods. Remember that time I walked 50 yards off trail, got confused on the way back, and started heading south instead of north? Once you take even a few steps off trail, the woods can close in fast, and it can be easy to get even more confused about the direction to go, especially if you weren’t paying close attention when you walked off the trail toward your bathroom break. In dense trees, even 100 yards from the trail or a logging road can seem completely remote. Out of all of the casual ways you can get lost, this is the one that alarms me the most. It’s easy to get confused, start walking in the wrong direction, and wind up even more lost. Avoid this: It may seem like an overreaction, but I recommend bringing your navigation device with you if you step off the trail into the woods. At the very least, pay attention. If you walked 30 steps forward, turn around and walk 30 steps back in the same direction. If your path off the trail is blocked by deadfall, instead of taking turns and walking deeper into the woods, cut back through the trees until you can see the trail, then take another straight path back into the woods. You can also drop a pin where you left the trail if you’re seeking dispersed camping further back in the trees, or leave something bright on your pack at the edge of the trail where you stepped off, so you have a visual marker walking back. In my 15 years writing on the internet, the story that somehow got the most people arguing (and mad at me!) was this piece about how cairns are good, and I like them. Cairns have helped me find the correct route across boulder fields and blank expanses of sandstone more times than I can count. But I’ll also acknowledge that poorly placed cairns can draw hikers off the correct route, sometimes into dangerous territory. When hikers not affiliated with trail building make cairns as decorative objects, they run the very real risk of drawing hikers in the wrong direction, since so many of us (myself included) have internalized the rock stacks as a form of navigation. Avoid this: Have a backup method of navigation so you aren’t entirely relying on rock piles that may or may not have been created because someone thought the stack of stones looked pretty. If you think you’re heading off course or the cairn looks suspicious, make sure you can look back and see the cairn behind you, then check your map or GPS to ensure you’re heading in the right direction. It’s better to stay put and verify your course than follow errant rock piles into the abyss without knowing where the last correctly placed marker was.

item.title: ‘It Was Just Like a Monsoon’: Hiker Recounts Scramble to Evacuate During Grand Canyon Flood
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.94
Helicopter evacuation in the Grand Canyon, August 29, 2026 (Photo: David J. Gregory) When a ranger showed up at the door of David Gregory’s cabin in Phantom Ranch and told him to start getting his gear together, he wasn’t worried at first. “She says ‘you might want to just kind of gather your things. We may do a temporary evacuation,’” Gregory recounted in an interview with Backpacker. “What we were getting out of that was [that] we might move away from camp for a little bit until we got the all-clear, and then we could come back.” He was confident enough that he’d be able to return, he said, that he brought his cabin key with him. Less than an hour later, Gregory and his three hiking partners would be huddled in the stables at Phantom Ranch’s mule corral, sheltering from a lashing rain alongside several dozen other Grand Canyon National Park visitors and workers as rangers began to hash out the details of a helicopter evacuation. The hikers were among more than 80 people rescued from the canyon following a catastrophic flood on August 29 that killed at least 2 people so far and left more than a dozen missing. Gregory shared his story with Backpacker in a phone call from his home in Dallas, where he had returned after his group’s experience in the park. An avid backpacker, Gregory estimates that he’s visited the Grand Canyon between a half-dozen and 10 times over the years, including on river trips and on a rim-to-rim overnight. On his latest trip, he was joined by a college friend and the friend’s two teenage sons, neither of whom had visited the Grand Canyon before. The plan was to descend the South Kaibab Trail, spend the night at Phantom Ranch, then climb back out to the South Rim via the Bright Angel Trail. The weather forecast at the time looked “pretty good,” Gregory said. While there was a chance of thunderstorms, the estimated precipitation was just a fraction of an inch. “We didn’t have any reason to think we were going into a risky situation,” Gregory said. The group left their hotel early in the morning of August 29, arriving at the South Kaibab Trailhead around 6:30 a.m. As they ate breakfast, it began to storm. They waited out the weather under an overhang by the restrooms, counting the seconds between the lightning and thunder. The conditions soon cleared, and by 7:15, they were on their way into the canyon. About an hour in, another brief storm forced them to shelter under a rock overhang; after that, Gregory said, it was “sunny skies.” By the time they reached the Black Bridge across the Colorado River, it was hot, and the group was sweating. After checking into their cabins, Gregory and his partners still had time to kill before a 4 p.m. ranger talk. They decided to go on a short hike up the Clear Creek Trail, toward the North Rim of the canyon. About 30 to 45 minutes into the excursion, however, they spotted dark clouds massing over the South Rim and decided to turn around. “We didn’t have any packs, so we were walking pretty quickly back, but it started to rain on us,” Gregory said. “By the time before we even got to the [Phantom Ranch] canteen, it was just bucketing rain. It was just like a monsoon.” The hikers hustled to the canteen, where they and other hikers who had sought shelter from the storm watched the rain sheet off the nearby buildings’ roofs. After another half-hour, the storm petered out. With his clothes soaked, Gregory left to change in his cabin, where the ranger first warned him about a possible evacuation. About ten minutes later, the ranger reappeared. There was now a mandatory evacuation, she said, and he needed to grab his things and go immediately. Directed by staff, he and his companions crossed the bridge over Bright Angel Creek, by now running high and “chocolate black.” They headed first to the mule corrals, where they sheltered from the rain in the stables. As the rain picked up and water began to run down the walkway in front of the building, they left again, heading across the Colorado River on the Silver Bridge and gathering at a rock wall on the far bank. As the rangers did a headcount to make sure all the campers were accounted for, Gregory and his partners spotted their first clues that the flooding was worse than they had realized. “You could see the outflow from Bright Angel Creek, and we could see there was a tremendous amount of flow coming into the Colorado River,” he recounted. “There was some maintenance work that was going on, and we could see a bunch of the maintenance, I don’t know if it was a cabin, or, like, equipment, that was floating in the river.” Gregory estimated that about 30 to 35 people were gathered with them, a mix of visitors, park staff, and maintenance workers in high-viz vests who had been working on a water-treatment facility. On the other side of the river, he spotted a smaller group of hikers who had evacuated to higher ground. Finally, just before 6 p.m., the lead ranger told the group that they would be evacuated by helicopter, and led them back across the bridge to the water treatment facility. As they waited for rescue, Gregory said, he spoke with the maintenance workers, who told him that a “wall of water” had ripped the bridge they had used to cross Bright Angel Creek off its pylons. By about 6:20, Gregory was airborne and heading downriver in an Arizona Department of Public Safety helicopter. From the air, he said, the river looked “normal”, even peaceful. The water had churned into a milky brown, but there was no visible debris. A video Gregory posted to the Grand Canyon Hikers Facebook Group shows blue skies dotted with clouds, the walls of the canyon illuminated by the evening light. He landed at Grand Canyon Airport around 7 p.m., the rest of his group following shortly thereafter. The NPS managed the evacuation well, Gregory said, and he never worried about his group’s safety. Learning afterward about the hikers who died in the canyon, however, was a sobering experience. “Now I understand that not everybody got out,” he said. “I maybe lost a couple articles of clothing. No big deal. But other people lost their lives.“ When the debris is cleaned up and the damage repaired, Gregory said, he fully expects to return to the Grand Canyon. “I don’t think it changes my opinion,” he said. “I know there’s always risks in hiking and doing outdoorsy things.”

item.title: Will self-flying planes transform the skies?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.24
- Published Over an alfalfa field in California's San Joaquin Valley, a small crop-spraying plane is flying scarily low to the ground. There's little risk to humans though, as the plane is pilot-free. "We can actually go lower than a human pilot can," says Russ Marotzke, as the aircraft skims over the crop. Flying lower means less spray drift and therefore less chemicals are needed than in conventional manned crop-dusting, he says. The pilotless plane belongs to Pyka, where Marotzke works as a flight test engineer. Based in a converted Second World War hangar overlooking San Francisco Bay, the start-up makes self-flying aircraft without cockpits, designed either to spray crops or deliver cargo. It is among a small group of companies racing to bring autonomous fixed-wing aircraft into commercial service. Flying urban air taxis, so called electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, have captured much of the attention around autonomous aviation. But a quieter race is also under way to deploy self-flying planes, first for jobs like crop spraying and cargo delivery – and eventually, many of their makers hope, carrying passengers too. "A fully scaled, ubiquitous passenger operation is the holy grail," says Michael Norcia, Pyka's co-founder and CEO, who envisions a large fleet of minibus-capacity Pyka planes ferrying passengers up and down the US east and west coasts. "There's a decent chance we'll get to that point before the eVTOL industry." I've come to one of Pyka's crop-sprayer test sites, about 80km (50 miles) east of the company's factory and reached by a bumpy dirt road. Today, Marotzke and a colleague are trying out a software update on a demonstration aircraft. About a dozen Pyka aircraft are already in Brazil where they are used to spray crops such as cotton and soybeans, work previously carried out by human pilots. The crop-spraying plane is fully electric, with its battery in the nose. It can fly for about 35 minutes and carries up to 300L of spray in a tank in its middle. Pyka's planes are sometimes called large drones, but it seems an understatement: they all have 11.5m wingspans. Inside a shipping container beside the field, the engineers highlight on a computer the area they want the aircraft to spray. The software then plans the route, taking account of obstacles such as nearby power lines that have already been mapped. The take-off, down a runway beside the field, is seamless. About 15 minutes later, after sensing that it is running low on spray – water for today's purposes – the aircraft lands itself for a manual refill and demonstration battery swap. It then takes to the air again to resume spraying precisely where it left off. Autonomous flight is different from autopilot. Autopilot assists, much like cruise control and lane-keeping functions in a car. Autonomous systems aim to handle the entire flight, including take-off and landing, with little or no human intervention, using algorithms to process sensor data and control the aircraft. Self-flying planes have been slower to emerge than self-driving cars, despite operating in what is generally considered a more structured and predictable environment. That is partly because big tech companies "doubled down" on cars, pouring vast sums into the technology, says Mykel Kochenderfer, an expert in safe aviation autonomy at Stanford University. But it is also because aircraft are held to stricter safety standards than cars, creating a much higher bar for deployment. "The consequences for air accidents can just be so severe," says Kochenderfer. Military interest has been helping propel the technology. Many of the companies have defence contracts to demonstrate and trial their systems, often with fewer regulatory hurdles than on the civilian side, and some are even already supplying military customers, external. In the US, the largest autonomous fixed-wing aircraft approved for commercial civilian use so far is Pyka's crop sprayer, which won authorization last year. Though operations are limited to a tightly defined agricultural setting and require a ground operator and visual observer. It earlier secured similar approval in Brazil, where rules are more permissive. Pyka aims to scale up production from around two dozen planes a year currently to 1000 by 2030. Each sells for $550,000, with customers trained to operate them. The UK has yet to approve any such longer-term operations, though British firm Windracers is seeking permission to launch an autonomous cargo service in Shetland and Orkney. Its aircraft, designed to carry goods to remote areas, are also flying missions in Ukraine. "It would be the first heavy-lift air cargo service by drone certainly in the UK and probably anywhere," says Stephen Wright, Windracers founder and chairman. Supporters say autonomous aircraft could address pilot shortages, remove people from dangerous work such as crop spraying, improve efficiency – for example, by allowing aircraft to carry more cargo – and cut costs if one operator can oversee many planes. They also argue automation could make flying safer, pointing to past declines in accidents as more automated systems have been introduced. Pilots' groups remain wary. The US Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA) calls removing pilots "a serious gamble with safety and a step too far". The US National Agricultural Aviation Association, which represents crop dusting pilots, says small uncrewed aircraft can be hard for its aviators to see. Piloted planes, it adds, can spray a much larger area faster. Pyka and Windracers are building aircraft from scratch, arguing this allows autonomy to be designed in from the outset and the aircraft tailored to the job. Others are retrofitting existing larger planes. Backed by Boeing's investment arm, US-based Reliable Robotics is currently testing its system on the Cessna 208B Grand Caravan, a single-pilot cargo plane that can carry about 1360kg of payload over hundreds of kilometers. Retrofitting on certified aircraft lets the company focus exclusively on proving the autonomous system's safety rather than also having to seek approval for a new aircraft, says Robert Rose, its co-founder and CEO. Merlin Labs, also US-based, has been working its way up through progressively larger military aircraft and is now applying its system to the two-pilot Lockheed Martin C-130J military transport plane, with commercial multi-crew cargo planes next. "It is a common autonomy brain that can transition between different aircraft," explains Matt George, Merlin's founder and CEO. The companies also differ in their approach to AI. Reliable is avoiding it altogether, arguing it would complicate certification. Merlin, meanwhile, is taking a far more AI-centric approach. The divide is evident in so-called detect and avoid systems. One of autonomous flight's biggest challenges is replicating a pilot's ability to spot and maneuver safely around other aircraft and obstacles, and there is virtually no margin for error. With no perfect solution yet, companies are adding different sensor systems as well as duplicating those that already come as standard to provide extra back-up. Reliable has added forward-looking air-to-air radar to detect other aircraft more than eight kilometers ahead, with software that follows fixed rules to decide how the plane should respond. It is "better than a pilot's eyeballs" says Rose. Merlin, meanwhile, is using AI-powered cameras to detect and classify objects. Pyka has used lidar from the outset to detect trees, vehicles, large birds and terrain. But it's short range, so the company also plans to add AI-powered cameras, its first real use of AI onboard. "For a lot of things there's no need to use AI…but for figuring out that six pixels in the distance are an airplane versus some other smudge, it is perfect territory," says Norcia. The AI dilemma also extends to communicating with air traffic control. In shared airspace, aircraft must be able to receive, interpret and respond to radio instructions, typically from air traffic control. Reliable's solution is to have a remote pilot on the ground, initially fully trained, to handle communications and make safety-critical decisions. Merlin plans to use generative AI, trained on thousands of hours of recorded exchanges, to interpret instructions and respond itself. "Our problem is harder… but we want to move beyond remote piloting," says George. Merlin plans to reduce pilots in stages, from two to one and eventually none. Pyka, says Norcia, is content to let others "blaze the trail" in finding the best way to operate in shared airspace. Meanwhile, even if fully autonomous passenger flight remains elusive, many expect the technology being pioneered will inch into commercial aviation, potentially making piloted flying safer. That, notes ALPA, the US pilots' association, would be a welcome development.

item.title: The final minutes before floodwater crashed through Nepal-China border
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.80
- Published The video lasts only seconds. A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The CCTV footage, whose timestamp reads 10:59:53, went viral. For many, it was the first visual evidence of the sheer scale of the destruction that was unfolding. What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery show much of the border complex swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone. Electronic immigration records from Nepal's Rasuwagadhi border post are filling some gaps, as well as insights from its only surviving staff member. Tika Ram Pokharel, who happened to be in Kathmandu sitting an exam on the day, tells the BBC the crossing was unusually busy when floodwater hit. "This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet," explains Kathmandu-based hydrologist Ajay Dixit. "The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders." It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border. On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry. Nepal's immigration department has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster. Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal. The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 08:35:03 local time (10:52 Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong. Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing. Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy. Tika Ram Pokharel, the surviving senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning. The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure, a small trading settlement clustered around the crossing. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing. The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing. When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area. "Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel tells the BBC. Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together. That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck. At 08:37 - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood. China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes. People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear. And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices. It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day. "My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified. The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away. For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open. Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped. Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area. When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins." The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge. Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult. Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese. Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China. Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour. Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China. Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network. "Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. "We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port." Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing. The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck. "But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

item.title: Why did Modi urge Putin to end Ukraine war - and will he listen?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.75
- Published Russian President Vladimir Putin has been urged by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a close ally, to end Moscow's war against Ukraine. "Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said on Monday. Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. BBC correspondents in Delhi and Moscow look at what lies behind Modi's renewed appeal for peace, and Putin's response. Modi's comments on ending the war in Ukraine are not surprising and don't suggest any tactical change in India's foreign policy. In fact, speaking on the sidelines of a regional summit in 2022 - less than a year into the conflict - Modi told Putin publicly that "now is not the time for war". But it would be an oversimplification to suggest that Modi's current or past statements on the war can be seen as a rebuff to Putin or Russia's strategy. Western countries have pushed Modi hard to take a clear stand on the war - but Delhi has largely stayed neutral, urging dialogue to end the war instead. The stand hasn't made many Western capitals happy but they have continued to court Modi and India - it's just too big and too fast-growing an economy to be ignored. In this context, Modi's current statement cannot be seen as an attempt to please a third country. If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly? The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses. Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades. Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries. But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association. Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs. So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats. As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war. This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine. Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table. He didn't. And he hasn't. There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations. To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied: "Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path." Polite, but vague. And non-committal. After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long. And "moving forward" at what pace? And, crucially, on which path? All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success. Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on. Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory. And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country. In recent days Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine. "After [Russia] intensified its strikes on Ukraine's military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure," wrote the Kommersant newspaper this morning, "the Russian side is convinced that in the military confrontation time is working against Kyiv." While Putin believes that, he'll be reluctant to pause his so-called "special military operation".

item.title: US aircraft carrier docks near Thai beach resort Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.67
- Published After a record 250 days at sea without a port stop, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand, giving its nearly 5,000 crew members a much-needed break. The ship is docking close to the beach resort of Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife and for sex tourism. For the US it also carries strong historical echoes. When the weary sailors walk into the city's bars and restaurants, they will be treading in the footsteps of the hundreds of thousands of US troops who came here for R&R – rest and relaxation - during the Vietnam War. They transformed it from a sleepy fishing village to one of the world's most famous and frenetic party towns. Today the neon-lit alleys running down to the beach are much quieter than usual. The bars in the city's famous Walking Street still screen videos on their walls of pole-dancing women, trying to lure customers inside. But there are not many of those customers, and most seem to be family groups from the Middle East more interested in the Turkish ice-cream vendor than the go-go bars. The Iran War, which has affected tourism and consumer spending, has hit businesses hard here. The prospect of thousands of American sailors, with nine months of salary unspent while at sea, offers a rare opportunity to local businesses. The US carrier left San Diego last November on what was supposed to be a six-month assignment in the Pacific and South China Sea. However, the ship was diverted to the Gulf after the US and Israel began military operations against Iran in late February. Recently some members of Congress raised concern about reports of food shortages, broken toilets and mental stress among the crew. The US Navy acknowledged that working conditions have been tough, but said the crew were sufficiently well-supported. It would not, however, comment to the BBC on the carrier docking at Pattaya, citing operational security. Despite its close relationship with China, Thailand is a treaty ally of the US, and port visits by US Navy ships are a familiar occurrence. But this is probably the largest number of US military personnel coming straight from a war zone to Pattaya since the fall of Saigon in 1975. "This visit could be our best hope," said Anon Saiteer, who sells gems in a shop near Walking Street, which has put up a large sign welcoming the US sailors and marines and offering them a special discount. "We have nothing to lose – we just hope they will spend some money here." But US and Thai officials are trying to ensure this happens without any of the salacious headlines for which Pattaya has become known. The Thai authorities have said there are a few places where the US servicemen and women will not be allowed to go. One of them is Soi 6, which runs down to the main beach, and is known for its concentration of racy go-go bars. While the Thai police have reminded their US visitors that prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand, there are actually thought to be 25,000 to 50,000 sex workers in the city. Many of them work in Soi 6, where they stand outside the bars imploring men to come inside. The many cannabis shops in Pattaya are also off-limits to US crew members, along with sea-sports like paragliding and jet-skis. "It is their decision," Mayor Poramase Ngampiches told the BBC. "The US military have done their homework." US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson rebuffed questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing. Instead, he said the US troops would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand". "We're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can," he said. The US Navy has organised shuttle buses from the port into Pattaya running from 5am to 2am every day the carrier is here in Thailand. Two hotels have been designated suitable for those US crew members who want to splash out on a night onshore. The Thai authorities have deployed hundreds of police officers to keep an eye on the city's entertainment zones, and warned local businesses not to overcharge their American guests. "The visits of US military men 50-60 years ago introduced Pattaya to the world and turned it into a tourist attraction," says Mayor Poramase. "We have to be frank, the city has a reputation for bar girls. We understand the stereotypes. We can't stop that. "What we can do is to show that Pattaya has changed, that we now have other things, such as sports, seminars, wellness and family-friendly activities. It's a mixture of everything." Both countries hope that by the time the USS Abraham Lincoln begins the long journey home across the Pacific on 6 September, it will be with a refreshed and rested crew. With additional reporting from Nongnapat Patcham.

item.title: Iran attacks US bases in Middle East after reports US strike killed five at wedding party
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.66
- Published Iran has accused the US of a war crime after officials said a missile strike killed four people including two children at a wedding celebration. The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) said shrapnel from a missile hit a family wedding ceremony at a home in southern Iran, causing the deaths. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei called the incident a "war crime". A US Central Command (Centcom) spokesperson said it "never targets civilians", adding that it was aware of the reports. Iranian authorities said another 14 people were killed elsewhere. In response, Iran launched missiles and drones at US targets in Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Bahrain. Most of the drones and missiles Iran launched at neighbouring countries were reportedly intercepted. Kuwait said a drone started a fire in a residential complex but caused no casualties. Centcom said strikes on Iran followed "recent attempted attacks" by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against American forces and commercial shipping in the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway, through which around 20% of global oil and gas shipments usually pass. The Iranian military's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters warned that operations against American forces in the region would continue until the US "regrets" its crimes. US President Donald Trump described Tuesday's strikes on Iran as "large and powerful". Centcom said the targets included air defence sites, radar systems and maritime assets. Iranian media reported explosions across the southern provinces of Hormozgan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Kerman and Khuzestan. The IRCS said at least four people were killed and 67 others were injured when shrapnel from a missile hit a family wedding ceremony at a home in the coastal town of Kuhestak, in Sirik. Citing the Hormozgan Governorate, Iranian media named the dead as Zarkhatoon Taheri, 50; Kolsum Mallahi Nazhdnia, 43; Mohammad Mallahi, 16; and Amirali Karimi, four. Media outlets initially quoted the IRCS as saying that five people were killed. "Unfortunately, this is a residential building. And unfortunately, this happened during my daughter's wedding ceremony," Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building, said in a video broadcast by state TV. "It is a very saddening incident... Thank God the casualties were not higher." Iran's parliamentary speaker and top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said it was another attack showing the US was "Satan". BBC Verify confirmed that a video and two images taken on Tuesday near Kuhestak's coast showed the destruction of a telecommunications tower, and that other videos from Tuesday and Wednesday showed severely damaged houses about 130m (427ft) north of the tower. BBC Persian Forensics, by examining published videos and CCTV footage, found the telecommunications tower was about 112m (367 ft) from the house where the wedding was being held. Centcom spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins told the BBC it was aware of reports from Iranian state media of the attack in Sirik. He added: "The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC." Iranian state media reported that another seven people were killed in three separate US strikes around Ahvaz and Aqajari, in Khuzestan. The IRGC meanwhile said that four members of its aerospace force, which oversees Iran's ballistic missiles, were killed by US attacks in Kermanshah, and that three members of the paramilitary Basij Resistance Force were killed on Lavan island, in the Gulf. Early on Wednesday, the IRGC and the regular Iranian military announced that they had launched ballistic missiles and drones towards US bases in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates in retaliation for the US strikes. They said the attacks caused casualties and damage at the US Marine barracks at Camp Titin on Jordan's Gulf of Aqaba coast. Reuters news agency cited US officials as saying there were no casualties. The Jordanian Armed Forces said they engaged 13 ballistic missiles, 10 of which were destroyed and three of which fell in remote, uninhabited areas. The IRGC and the Iranian military also said that a maintenance centre, warehouses and equipment belonging to the US military were destroyed in Irbil, in Iraq's northern Kurdistan region, according to state media. Iraqi authorities did not comment on the attack, but local media reported that a US surveillance balloon was hit by drones. In Kuwait, the fire service said its crews put out a fire at a residential complex that was struck by a drone and that no casualties were reported. In a separate incident, the IRGC said two tankers caught fire after hitting mines while being guided through an "illegal route" in the Strait of Hormuz by the US military. Saudi Arabia's national shipping company said two Filipino sailors were killed "in a security incident" involving its crude oil tanker SIDR as the vessel transited the waterway on Monday. After about a month-long pause, the US resumed attacks on Iran on Sunday, when it announced it had struck two rocket launchers to prevent them being used to lay naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at air bases in Jordan and a drone at the UAE. The US and Israel launched a joint attack on Iran on 28 February, killing the country's supreme leader and other top officials at the start of a massive air campaign. Iran responded by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf with missiles and drones, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping. In June, the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) that called for an end to hostilities on all fronts and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. It also gave them two months to reach a final deal that covers Iran's nuclear programme, US sanctions and a permanent truce. However, the MoU collapsed within weeks, leading to a resumption of hostilities. Since then, both US and Iranian forces have fired on commercial shipping in the region, with Iran targeting vessels it says have sought to transit the Strait of Hormuz without its permission and the US enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports. Last week, the US had indicated that it was switching to economic sanctions on Iran, rather than military options, to try to win concessions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US economic measures. Additional reporting by BBC Persian Update: An earlier version of this story said weapons experts had identified the fragments shown on Iranian media as being from a US munition - AGM 84 Standoff Land Attack Missile (SLAM-ER). But after further analysis of imagery these experts think it is more likely to be a different US weapon, a JSOW, although there remains a possibility it is a SLAM-ER.

item.title: Norway's new king takes oath as mourners pay respects to his late father
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.58
Norway's new king takes oath as mourners pay respects to his late father Norway's Haakon VIII has sworn an oath before parliament in Oslo in the first major step of his reign as King. During Tuesday's ceremony, parliament also held a minute's silence for Haakon's father, the late King Harald V, who died on Friday. Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, was absent from the formalities as she continues to recover from a lung transplant. Following the ceremony, mourners began paying their respects at the late King's coffin, which is lying in state at the Royal Palace until 8 September.

item.title: South Korean police officer admits to closing missing person cases to avoid work
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.46
- Published A South Korean police officer has admitted to closing missing persons cases without investigating them in order to avoid additional work, according to authorities. The officer, surnamed Bu, was arrested earlier this month after he was accused of prematurely closing cases on the popular holiday island Jeju and lying to missing persons' families. Amid mounting public criticism, police embarked on belated searches for several missing persons on the island, and have since discovered four bodies in recent weeks. The scandal has prompted President Lee Jae Myung to vow to reform the police, as the government prepares to give the police more powers. On Tuesday, the Jeju Provincial Police said Bu had falsely closed at least two high-profile cases and had been charged with forgery of public electronic records, obstruction of official duties and dereliction of duty. In both cases, Bu had falsely claimed he had contacted the missing persons and then prematurely closed their cases without confirming their whereabouts and safety. A police statement said that during their investigations into Bu, he had "stated to the effect that 'the missing person was a typical adult so I thought about it carelessly. If the case was not closed, there would have been a lot to take care of, and out of a sense of pressure over the case handover, I falsely closed it'." One of the cases involved a 37-year-old woman named Jang Mi-ran who went missing in May and was reported missing by her boyfriend. At the time, Bu had told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to her and she did not want to meet the police nor be contacted by her boyfriend. Authorities later said that this was a complete fabrication by Bu. Bu had entered this false information into the system, and also logged that Jang had died in a traffic accident, before closing the case, according to authorities. Jang's body was found near a palm tree plantation on Jeju last week. In another case where a man in his 60s was reported missing in July, Bu similarly falsely claimed that he had spoken to the man and that the man did not want to be contacted. The man was eventually found dead earlier this month. Police also said that they believe Bu could have prematurely closed another 25 missing persons cases, though in some of those cases the people were eventually confirmed to be alive and safe. Violent crime is rare in South Korea, where suicide rates are among the highest in the world. While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month. This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for the country's police. The government had recently passed laws to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics. However, this move has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence. President Lee has vowed to reform the police in the wake of recent criticism. On Tuesday President Lee said that it was "regrettable" that because of a few "loach-like figures who muddy the well water", "the honour and pride of the majority of diligent police officers are being damaged".

item.title: Cup noodles made with cold water? BBC tries Japan's viral snack
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.17
Cup noodles made with cold water? BBC tries Japan's viral snack The BBC's Tokyo correspondent Kurumi Mori tries Japan's latest food trend, instant noodles made with cold water. The product has sold out in the country after going viral online. Unlike regular cup noodles, this version is designed to be a cooling summer snack, but does it really do the job? The BBC puts them to the taste test.

item.title: Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.13
- Published Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes. "We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous," Volodymyr Zelensky said. Ukraine has since formally notified the UN of the risks to civilian aviation. Russian President Vladimir Putin said the comments amounted to a "declaration of state terrorism". Most Western commercial airlines do not fly over Russia because of the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, but carriers in countries like Turkey and China do. Explaining the elevated airspace risk in his nightly video address on Tuesday, Zelensky said that "Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft" and did not want the loss of innocent lives. "There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said. Zelensky directed the warning to airlines continuing to operate flights to Russian airports, especially in major cities like St Petersburg and Moscow. In a statement on X, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Ukraine had officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace was not safe for civilian aviation. "We want to prevent unintended incidents," he said, adding: "The war is returning home to Russia." On Wednesday afternoon, flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed many planes flying over Russia, including arriving and departing from the two main airports, which had some delays, but few cancellations. Several airlines that fly through Russia told the BBC that they were carefully monitoring the situation. Qatar Airways, which flies into Moscow and travels through Russian airspace to get to the US west coast, said its flight planning was "guided by rigorous and continuous monitoring of airspace security, safety assessments, and geopolitical developments". Turkish low-cost airline Pegasus cancelled its flights to Russia on Tuesday and Wednesday, citing "technical and operational reasons", but said future flights "are operating as scheduled". FlyDubai, an Emirati government-owned carrier, told the BBC that it would "closely monitor the evolving situation in the region and adjust our flight schedules and routings as necessary". Ukraine has targeted energy facilities deep inside Russian territory and there have been repeated attacks on depots belonging to Russia's two biggest online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Its drone attacks have for months led to disruption at some of Russia's biggest airports, especially in Moscow where at times all four major airports have been forced to halt arrivals and departures. Several cancellations were reported on Wednesday. Ukraine does not have to target airports to cause disruption. Under Russia's air defence "Kovyor" (carpet) plan, flights are suspended if a drone is detected in the relevant area. Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were almost certain to continue this year. "There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert added. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict." Speaking to reporters at the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said: "They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists." His comments come as Russia's attacks on Ukraine continue, with heavy strikes killing 12 people on Tuesday and further attacks on Odesa, Sumy and Kyiv on Wednesday. Russia's military has said it is preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian power stations. The Ukrainian capital and its surrounding region have come under attack for seven days in a row. A few weeks ago, Zelensky said Russia was attacking Ukraine every day, and Ukraine's military had "begun the process of bringing the war back to Russia". At the weekend he said the same, that Russia had to feel the war was "returning to where it came from". Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes had damaged infrastructure inside Russia, while insisting that "only 10%" of oil refineries were left to repair. Chinese, Turkish and Gulf state airlines are among those using Russian airspace, with savings in time and fuel on routes between Asia and Europe. Other carriers have largely avoided the eastern European region since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February, 2022. Ukraine has closed its airspace to civilian aircraft throughout that period. The risks of civil aviation during a war are clear. A few months after war broke out in eastern Ukraine in 2014 between Russian-backed separatists and the Ukrainian military, a Russian-made missile brought down a passenger plane, killing all 298 people on board. Last year, the UN aviation agency ruled that Russia was responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014. The Kremlin has always denied any responsibility for the air disaster. In 2024, Putin apologised to the president of neighbouring Azerbaijan over the downing of a commercial airliner in Russian airspace, in which 38 people were killed. He said the "tragic incident" had occurred when Russian air defence systems were repelling Ukrainian drones.

item.title: River water smashed into tunnel and chased me for 20 minutes, Nepal worker tells BBC
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.92
- Published Nepalese hydropower workers have told the BBC about the catastrophic moment water from the Trishuli River crashed into their tunnel as the region was inundated by deadly flash floods last week. It started with a sudden, strong gust of air, says Pemba Dundu Tamang, whose team of about 30 was constructing the tunnel's concrete lining. The blast of wind sent plywood flying through the air and dislodged heavy machinery. Just outside, houses had already been swept away. "I ran towards the tunnel entrance," he said. "The water was chasing behind me and I was running ahead of it." Tamang lost several family members who were at home at the time. Nepal's death toll has exceeded 1,000 after last week's devastating floods, and officials say about 4,000 are missing. A number of the missing - potentially in the hundreds - are labourers like Tamang, working in a vast network of tunnels at hydropower sites along the river. Engineers have been pumping air into these tunnels as part of a huge rescue operation. "We are focused on search-and-rescue efforts at the tunnels, our work is continuing," Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP news agency. "Our soldiers are also deployed to collect bodies and prevent the spread of disease." The army said 119 people had been rescued on Tuesday. Tamang says he ran for about 20 minutes to flee the violent deluge, which followed him uphill. "I was almost unconscious with shock. I could not think clearly." His colleague, Itha Ghale, says the powerful gust of air almost blew them away as they sprinted. Over 99% of the electricity generated in Nepal comes from hydropower, and Tamang and Ghale had been working at a major production site helping to build the Upper Trishuli 3B Hydropower Project. The plant, which was due to open next year, was designed to re-use water from a hydroelectric plant further upstream to generate additional electricity for Nepal's national grid. There were several different teams operating there - and Tamang says the one operating the large tunnel-lining machine was the last to come out. But soon afterwards came a crushing realisation. "I could see where my house should have been. There was nothing left. That was when I realised everything was gone." Six of Tamang's relatives - his mother, elder brother and sister-in-law and three of their children - are gone, he said. They were at home on the riverside when the floods hit. Only his wife, son and one nephew survived. "I feel life is meaningless now. Surviving feels miserable. I do not know where to eat or where to go," Tamang says. "The dead are at peace. It is those of us who survived who suffer." Ghale, who lost eight members of his family, says he does not know why he survived. "Perhaps it was not my fate to die." The eight family members include his mother and eldest daughter. His three sons and wife survived. Tamang dreads what the future may bring, especially if these hydropower projects are shut down. "If things continue like this, we will go hungry. Sometimes I feel it would have been better not to survive." Tamang ultimately managed to take refuge with a few others in the village of Shanti Bazar for two days until the army came to rescue them. He estimates about 50 to 60 workers were able to escape the tunnel alongside him. He says more people could have been saved if proper resources had been in place. This is echoed by a new report which says there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the disaster - and that better early warning systems could have saved lives. Satellite images suggest the glacier surface was moving faster, meltwater was turning brown and a crack was developing in the surrounding rock, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment. These are all possible signs the mountainside was becoming unstable. The avalanche itself moved too fast for conventional warnings to help those closest to it, the scientists say. But further downstream, where the flood took 10 minutes or more to arrive, they say a comprehensive warning system could potentially have saved a significant number of lives. Right now, however, specialists from China, India and Nepal are continuing to use excavators and heavy machinery to blast through debris from the hydropower projects to try to reach workers still trapped at several hydropower sites. "There are probably still some survivors inside. I would be happy if they were rescued quickly," Tamang says. "I know many people who are still trapped there." Additional reporting by Justin Rowlatt, climate editor

item.title: Russian attack hits rail workers in new deadly strikes on Kyiv
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.66
- Published At least 12 people have been killed and 20 injured, including two children, in overnight Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukraine's capital Kyiv and the wider region, officials say. Six of the casualties were railway workers of the state Ukrzaliznytsia company after a depot was hit in Kyiv. Russia said its "massive strike using high-precision weapons" targeted Ukraine's military and energy facilities, and added that one person was also killed in Ukrainian strikes on Russia's western Belgorod region. This comes a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin was urged by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a close ally, to end the war. "Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said at a security summit in Kyrgyzstan. Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Overnight in Kyiv, eight people were killed and fires were reported in three city districts. Another four people were killed in the nearby town of Boryspil where a residential building was hit. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday morning that nearly 350 rescue workers had been working through the night in Kyiv and the surrounding region after the latest strikes. In a post on social media, he said Russia had fired a "significant number of jet drones and ballistic missiles". The strikes mark the sixth day of sustained Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv, in what appears to be a strategy aimed at exhausting Ukrainian air defences and undermining civilian morale. Russia's military warned over the weekend that its forces were preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities. Eight other Ukrainian regions were attacked, Zelensky said, adding that an Indian national was among the casualties. Ukraine's Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivsky later said the Indian man - who turned 26 on Tuesday - was killed in Boryspil. The overnight attacks come after 38 people were killed in Russian strikes on a weapons depot in the Kyiv region on Friday, causing shells, mines and drones to detonate. Separately, a drone attack hit a major Russian Baltic Sea port in Ust-Luga, triggering a fire, Leningrad regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said. Ukraine says targets like Ust-Luga - which handles millions of tons of petroleum products each year - are legitimate as they help finance Moscow's war effort.

item.title: Why US troops have a history in this raucous Thai city
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.48
Why US troops have a history in this raucous Thai city After a record 250 days at sea, the USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand close to the city of Pattaya. Known for its raucous nightlife and sex tourism, the BBC's South East Asia correspondent Jonathan Head explains the history between US troops and the beach resort.

item.title: Deadly strike on Kyiv warehouse prompts evacuations
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.18
Deadly strike on Kyiv warehouse prompts evacuations Nearly 400 people have been evacuated after a Russian strike on a warehouse near Kyiv killed at least 37 people, Ukrainian authorities have said. Videos showing the moment of a huge explosion and the plumes of smoke that followed have been shared online. The strike hit a depot storing weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area. An investigation into the "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosive right next to people" has begun, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson reports.

item.title: Vienna's great surprise: The Globe Museum
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 6.10
The museum charting how humans understand the world Beautiful, surreal and eerily empty, Vienna's Globe Museum the only public museum on Earth dedicated to globes, and it – quite literally – tells the story of our world. It's a chilly afternoon in Vienna, and the line for the Austrian National Library has already spilled out the door, curling like a ribbon around the grand Josefsplatz square. I'm not in the mood to wait – I've already struck out at several crowded nearby attractions where timed-entry tickets were sold out. Rather than join the queue, I walk down the street and stumble onto a smaller, somewhat hidden site: The Globe Museum. Tucked inside Vienna's 17th-Century Palais Mollard, it's the only public museum on Earth dedicated entirely to globes, and one of Vienna's greatest surprises. Different worlds I soon realise that I've wandered into another world – or more accurately, many of them. Just steps from some of the city's most celebrated, crowded attractions, Vienna's Globe Museum displays more than 220 rare and antique spheres, most created before 1850, ranging from towering Coronelli globes to tiny, foldable pocket orbs. Beautiful and surreal, the museum's extensive collection goes beyond geography to reveal how humanity has mapped and imagined the Earth and heavens above. It's a chronicle of human curiosity, and – quite literally – the story of our world. "Globes show the change in our imagination of our planet," says Nikolaus Schobesberger, the director of museum. "And this is the only place in the world where you can see so many of them at the same time." Visitors start by travelling through the Golden Cabinet, a lavish room with centuries-old frescoes depicting scenes from Greek mythology. It's the backdrop for a stunning array of globe-related instruments, like telluriums, which illustrate the Earth's orbit around the Sun, and armillary spheres, which use a framework of rings to visualise the movements of celestial bodies. As I reach the museum's four main galleries, I realise the whole place is pin-drop quiet. I shuffle slowly from one glass case to another, holding my breath to not disturb the stillness, even though I'm alone with centuries-old objects. I find myself marvelling at two spherical worlds suspended in time. One is terrestrial, with oceans awash in vivid blues and squiggly brown coastlines. The other is celestial, where mythological creatures and constellations spill across a tea stain-coloured backdrop. Barely bigger than beach balls, these two time capsules were made by the same craftsman 10 years apart in the mid-1500s and preserve a world as it was still coming into focus. In one, Europe, the Mediterranean and Africa's coasts are filled with place names, while North America fades into the uncharted Arctic. Asia is distorted, a hypothetical southern continent stands in for Australia and Antarctica and the Pacific is populated by sea monsters instead of islands. In the other, Renaissance astrological observations exist alongside Pegasus taking flight and Perseus brandishing Medusa's severed head. "They're some of the oldest globes we have in our collection," says Schobesberger. Moving from one globe to the next, I notice how these relics extend beyond geography and depict what people once believed.
