Many fill the space of unexplored oceans with dragons, while some confidently depict my home state of California as an island. Some pieces also preserve colonial-era prejudices with elaborately painted scenes depicting Indigenous people as cannibals. On one, African coastlines are dotted with Spanish and Portuguese flags, showing "ownership". "They're a part of this colonial thinking. And so, they're beautiful art, but you also have to think about the time they were created," Schobesberger says, explaining that every globe is as much a record of what people knew as what they didn't. That's why he believes the museum resonates with all types of people, not just historians or cartography enthusiasts. One of Schobesberger's favourite objects is a lunar globe from 1961. The front portion of the Moon is meticulously mapped. The back, however, is a stark white strip, intentionally left blank because the far side of the Moon had not yet been seen. An updated lunar globe made two years later, also on display, contains the missing portion. I can't help but circle back to a showstopper in the front hall, a replica of the Behaim Globe – completed by Martin Behaim in 1492, the year Christopher Columbus sailed west – which shows a world without the Americas. There's simply an expanse of ocean between Europe and Asia. "A globe is such a great thing because it's a small-scale model of our planet, so you can tell stories about the world on it," he says. "Climate, geology, topography, trade routes, everything." From curios to cultural cornerstones Walking through the museum, visitors can see the globe's own journey unfold. The earliest examples were luxury objects reserved for aristocrats and wealthy merchants. Over time, globes lost their exclusivity, shrunk in size and became more affordable and popular. They entered schools, appeared in living rooms and even became playthings for children. Today, they are so commonplace that my son even won his desktop globe in a classroom raffle. I entered the museum expecting to view globes as historic artefacts, but I'm surprised by how alive they still feel. Even with Google Earth at my fingertips, these tactile objects invite curiosity and imagination in a way that a screen doesn't. "It's not just that the globe is a scientific instrument. It's also an object which lets you dream of foreign countries," says Schobesberger. Globes in pop culture Beginning 24 September 2026, the museum's newest exhibition, Globes in Everyday Life, Art and Culture, will explore how globes evolved from a status symbol to a familiar fixture. It also showcases the globe's enduring place in pop culture, from architecture to art and film, like Charlie Chaplin's famous dance with an inflatable globe in The Great Dictator. "The main idea was to show that globes are almost everywhere as a part of everyday life," Schobesberger says. Schobesberger's own fascination began as a young child, when he became captivated by the ships, sea monsters and mythical creatures that filled the blank spaces of historical maps and globes. He began to draw his own world maps when he was just six years old. "You can think about what's possible on the other side of the world, even when you're sitting here in Europe," he says. "Nothing else can capture the imagination quite like it." More like this: That sentiment resonates with author JF Penn, who stumbled onto the Globe Museum while researching her novel Spear of Destiny, based on a relic housed in Vienna's Imperial Treasury. Like me, she ended up lingering far longer than planned. "I particularly loved the oversized antique globes with the patina of age and use," she says. "I considered how many fingertips have turned them over generations and wondered if they thought of travelling to these far-off places that I do." Even after visitors leave Palais Mollard, the search continues. Across Vienna, some 50 globes are perched on rooftops and facades, hidden in plain sight. The museum even charts them on a virtual map in its new exhibit, encouraging people to look upward as they wander the city. When I finally step back outside, the sky is dark and the streets are even more crowded. Earlier in the day, I had been seeking a quieter corner of Vienna. Instead, I was given a whole new way of seeing the world – a place that's constantly being redrawn and reimagined. --

item.title: The smoky plant goo that Finns can't stop eating
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.27
Pine tar: The surprising, smoky goo that Finns can't stop eating Once used to waterproof boats and treat infections, this smoky plant byproduct is now used to flavour everything from schnapps to bread. But how does it taste? I've been in the sub-Arctic city of Oulu, Finland for only a few hours when I'm caught under a torrent of late summer rain. I take refuge in a cafe and order a coffee and sugar-dusted pannukakku (a thick pancake). The waiter asks me, "What flavour? We have almond, tar, blueberry..." I'm certain I've misunderstood: "Did you say tar?" He nods nonchalantly. Welcome to Oulu, the northern Finnish city where terva (pine tar, usually translated in English simply as "tar") is on the menu. Produced by heating pine wood without oxygen, this thick, dark substance flavours everything from lager to ice cream, lending a distinct, rich smokiness. "It's an intense flavour, so a little goes a long way," says Matti Moller of the Arctic Food Lab, an initiative showcasing northern Finland's culinary culture. "But it's brilliant to experiment with in everything from fish to desserts." To Finns, pine tar's aroma has long been associated with wooden boats, summer cottages and sauna scents. So what's the recent culinary appeal? I've decided to find out. From sealant to meal Yet just two centuries ago, Oulu had a very different reputation. Encircled by dense pine forests and the winding channels of the Oulujoki delta, it was famed as the tar capital of the world. "Oulu has been a major trading hub since the 15th Century thanks to its position on the Oulu River," says local guide Sirpa Törmä. "By the 1860s, it had become the world's largest tar-exporting port." Essential for waterproofing wooden sailing ships, tar was produced by smouldering wood in tar pits across villages along the river, then transported in narrow boats to Oulu's harbour for global export. Thanks to its antibacterial properties, tar had also long been used as a natural wound treatment all over Finland. "As the well-known saying goes: 'If sauna, spirits and tar do not help, the disease is fatal,'" explains Ritva Kylli, a food historian at the University of Oulu. But how did it make its way to the Finnish palate? Tar-as-flavour made its debut on pharmacy shelves. Archives at the National Library of Finland reveal that tar-flavoured medicinal lozenges date back to the early 1900s, and Oulu's local papers advertised tervakaramellit ('tar sweets') as early as 1902. "These were medicinal lozenges sold in apothecary shops for coughs and respiratory diseases," says Kylli. Even if not every Finn enjoys the taste of tar, virtually everyone has tried the iconic black terva pastille. The nation's most famous brand is Terva Leijona (Tar Lion), sold to this day. Launched in 1933, the pastilles were created by Oulu pharmacist YW Jalander after watching locals inhale smoky tar fumes for their health. Facing low profits, he invented a tar essence (tervaessanssi) and infused it into liquorice pastilles, which he sold through his confectionary company, Merijal. Terva Leijona eventually changed hands, but it is still made using his recipe. As popular as they were, tar didn't make the leap from pastille to gourmet treat until the end of the 20th Century, says Kylli, as living standards rose and interest in regional heritage cuisine grew across the country: "[It] seems to be connected to a growing interest in the cultural memory of Oulu's tar economy, a trend spreading beyond northern historical trade routes to all of Finland," she says. "It was reimagined into a distinctive heritage flavour." 'It can be addictive' Matti tells me he buys tar chocolate and syrup a few times a year. "The taste is unique – sweet, smoky, medicinal and completely unmistakable," he says as we walk across the picturesque island of Pikisaari, connected to Oulu's city centre by a short bridge. "Why do we love it? Perhaps we're tasting our roots, the Finnish forest and our heritage." The Oulu region, as the historic heart of the pine tar culture, has also become the symbolic centre of pine tar cuisine, with a high concentration of restaurants, cafes and bakeries that produce terva foods. At Pekka Heikkinen, a family bakery in Kajaani founded in 1913, owner Kaisa Marin bakes traditional bread and pastries. "Tar boats used to sail right past our bakery to Oulu," she explains. "When pine tar food innovations emerged in the '90s, it was natural to start baking tar-flavoured bread." For Marin, the connection is deeply personal: "My grandmother washed my hair with tar shampoo in the sauna, and our cabin's boat was sealed with tar. To me, the scent is cosy, nostalgic and rooted in home. I love it!" She always keeps thinly sliced tar bread in the freezer, ready to fry in butter when guests arrive. Though not for everyone, she warns it can be addictive. "My uncle, a master confectioner, created a rich tar chocolate that we bake every Christmas. We've even made cakes with pine tar and spruce needles." Rina Hirviniemi, owner of the cosy Kahvila Kiikku, also bakes tar bread at least once a week, usually pairing it with gravlax. "In summer, I serve vanilla ice cream with tar syrup, and in winter, we grill with tar outside," she says. "I like keeping tar products on hand, though I don't put them on the menu – I have an eye for people I can recommend it to." So what does it taste like? Convinced, I decide to – literally – bite. According to Marin, ice cream is the best starting point for tar newcomers, so I head to Market Square's ice cream van. Cone in hand, I sit by Toripolliisi, the brawny bronze police statue keeping watch over the square, and take my first hesitant taste. A smoky-sweet aroma rushes from nose to palate – the unexpected whiff of bacon. Yet, it's surprisingly sweet. Intrigued, I can't stop eating. Bite by bite, it completely wins me over. Just as Marin predicted, I find myself becoming addicted. I head next to ChocoSomnia, an Oulu chocolate maker. "We make tar pralines, chocolate bars and tar coffee. We get curious first-timers, but also loyal regulars," says co-owner Mika Lähteenmäki. Sampling a square of dark chocolate infused with pine tar and cranberry, I'm struck by the balance of smoky depth, rich cocoa bitterness and soft berry sweetness; the very taste of a pine forest in midsummer. I can't stop there. My local friend leads me to a supermarket for Terva Leijona pastilles. Like impatient children, we tear open the box and pop the tiny black sweets. Instead of subtle sweetness, an intense, smoky rush clears my airways. My friend introduces me to two of his mates, and I discover that local usage varies widely: some drizzle tar syrup on bacon, others serve tar schnapps before nights out. For others still, tar candies reign supreme. While most Finns buy ready-made tar products, today's skilled chefs craft them from scratch. This is what brought me to Lasaretti, a restaurant tucked into the riverfront oasis of Oulu's Hupisaaret Park. Today, head chef Laurance Robinson is serving smoked whitefish pasta with tar pearls, pickled fennel and red onion. "I can't build a tar pit, so I buy flavouring from Kujala's farm to make my syrup for sweet and savoury dishes," he says. "Balancing its strong, pungent taste took time." Resembling caviar, the tar pearls burst in my mouth against the whitefish, sharp fennel, and sweet archipelago bread. It is pure umami with subtle smokiness. More like this: Originally from the Isle of Man, Robinson cooked across Europe before settling in Finland. "I'll never forget my first taste of tar in 2011 – a sauna soda from my future father-in-law. It tasted like an ashtray at first, but the smokiness mellowed. Later, when I had the freedom to experiment, I said, 'I want to be the tar chef.'" His tar pavlova recently won best dessert at an Oulu culinary contest. "I wonder how far I can push it." Watching passersby drift through the sunny park, I marvel at how tar shifted from a maritime necessity to the flavour of local identity. "You know what," says my friend. "I've had a horrible headache since morning, but after eating this dish, it's completely gone." I can't promise it cures headaches, but in every sense, tar remains a uniquely Finnish ingredient that still works its quiet magic. --

item.title: Classic Chicken Noodle Soup
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.97
There are plenty of shortcuts you could take with homemade chicken noodle soup, but this recipe isn’t interested in them. A whole chicken simmers with onion, carrots, celery, garlic, dill, and peppercorns to make its own deeply savory, golden broth. It takes a little time, but the result is about as classic and comforting as chicken noodle soup gets. The key to juicy chicken is treating the breasts and legs differently. Once the breast reaches 155°, you’ll pull the bird from the pot and remove the breast meat to keep it moist. The legs, wings, and carcass go back in, allowing the dark meat to become fall-apart tender while the bones and cartilage-rich wings impart richer body and flavor. A fresh round of carrots and celery goes into the strained broth along with the pasta, so the vegetables cook until tender without turning to mush. Ditalini is ideal here because the tiny rounds cook quickly right in the broth; other small shapes work too (more on that below). A generous handful of fresh dill added at the end keeps things bright, but parsley or chives make good substitutes. Chicken Noodle Soup FAQ What are the best noodles for chicken noodle soup? Ditalini is ideal because it cooks quickly enough to go directly into the chicken broth. Orzo, ABC pasta, or small macaroni work too. If using longer-cooking pasta, such as egg noodles, spaghetti, or fusilli, cook it separately. The extra starch and cooking time required by larger noodles can cause the broth to become too reduced. Can I use chicken breasts instead of a whole chicken? For this particular recipe, stick with a whole chicken. The breast provides tender shredded meat, while the legs, wings, bones, and cartilage give the homemade broth richness, flavor, and body. Removing the breast meat early prevents it from drying out while the rest of the chicken continues to simmer. Can I make chicken noodle soup ahead of time? Yes. The strained broth and shredded chicken can be made up to 3 days ahead; refrigerate them separately. The carrots and celery can also be cut up to 3 days ahead and refrigerated. To finish the soup, bring the broth to a boil over medium-high heat, then proceed with the recipe, adding the pasta, chicken, and fresh vegetables as directed. Can you freeze chicken noodle soup? Yes. Freeze the broth and shredded chicken, separately or combined, for up to 3 months. Add the pasta, fresh carrots and celery, and dill when reheating and finishing the soup. You can also freeze leftover chicken noodle soup in portions for up to 3 months, though the pasta will soften somewhat after thawing and reheating. Watch Molly make chicken noodle soup: - Fork Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 40 minutes - Yield 6 servings Ingredients 1 1 2 4 4 2 ½ 1 6 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Season one 3½–4-lb. whole chicken all over with 1 Tbsp. plus 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 2¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and place in a large pot. (For even better-tasting meat, season chicken up to 24 hours ahead and refrigerate until ready to cook.) Step 2Cut 2 medium onions into quarters. (No need to remove the onion skins; leaving them on helps the broth develop its golden color.) Trim and coarsely chop 2 medium carrots, peeled, and 2 celery stalks. Cut 2 heads of garlic in half crosswise. (These will eventually be strained out, so there’s no reason to be precious with your cuts here.) Step 3Place chopped vegetables, 2 sprigs dill, and 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns in pot with chicken. Pour in 14 cups cold water (or just enough to barely cover chicken) and bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Cook, reducing heat as needed to maintain a simmer, adding water as needed to keep the chicken submerged, and skimming off any foam from surface with a large spoon, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of breast registers 155°, 20–25 minutes. Step 4Using tongs, carefully lift chicken out of pot and transfer to a cutting board. Let sit until cool enough to handle. Step 5Arrange chicken breast side up. Grab a wing and pull it outward so you can see where it attaches to the body. Using a sharp boning or chef’s knife, cut through the joint to separate wing from breast (if you hit bone, you’re in the wrong spot; pull the wing out farther to help you get to the place where the joint meets the socket). Repeat with wing on other side. Step 6Cut through skin connecting 1 leg to carcass. Pull leg back until ball joint pops out of its socket; cut through joint to separate leg. Repeat with leg on other side. Cut along left side of breastbone (which runs right down the center of the breast). Angling your knife, cut breast meat away from carcass on left side. Repeat process on right side. Step 7Pull off and discard any skin from legs and breasts (removing this skin prevents excess fat from rendering into the broth; no need to discard skin on the wings). Return legs, wings, and what remains of the carcass to pot. (You should now have only the chicken breasts remaining on your cutting board.) Return soup to a simmer and cook, occasionally skimming fat from surface with spoon, until reduced by 1–2", very flavorful, and leg meat is very tender and pulls apart easily, about 40 minutes. Step 8Meanwhile, shred cooled chicken breasts with 2 forks into bite-size pieces. Step 9Cut remaining 2 medium carrots, peeled, on a diagonal into ½" pieces. Thinly slice remaining 2 celery stalks, then finely chop enough dill to yield ¼ cup. Step 10Using tongs, transfer 2 chicken legs to cutting board and let cool slightly before shredding. Set a large fine-mesh sieve over another large pot. Strain broth into second pot; discard bones, carcass, wings, and vegetables. Do Ahead: Broth and shredded chicken can be made 3 days ahead; refrigerate separately. Carrots and celery can be cut 3 days ahead; refrigerate. Broth and chicken can also be frozen, separately or combined, for up to 3 months. Step 11Bring broth to a boil over medium-high heat. Add 6 oz. ditalini and stir once. Cook 5 minutes. (If using a larger or longer-cooking pasta, cook it separately according to package directions rather than in the broth.) Add carrots, celery, and all of the shredded chicken meat to pot and cook until pasta is cooked through and carrots and celery are tender but not mushy, about 5 minutes. Step 12Remove pot from heat and stir in dill so it stays bright and fresh; season very generously with salt and freshly ground black pepper. Ladle chicken soup into bowls and season with more pepper. Editor’s note: This chicken noodle soup recipe was first published in January 2020; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite noodle soup recipes →

item.title: Pear Tarta De Santiago
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.00
I’m fascinated by the North African influence on Spanish cuisine. Take this traditional flourless almond cake, or Tarta de Santiago, which was a by-product of increased almond cultivation and culinary traditions during Spain’s Moorish era. The dense cake is perfectly suited for a relaxed breakfast, morning coffee break, or afternoon tea. This seasonal version includes chopped pears, though apples (or no fruit) work just as well. After the cake has cooled, I like to rest it in the fridge; then bring it back to room temperature for a soft and fluffy texture. The oldest recorded recipe for Tarta de Santiago dates back to the 1830s, via Luis Bartolomé de Leybar; written references to a similar almond cake, “Torta Real,” imply it has existed for centuries longer. A popular option at bakeries and cafés throughout Spain, particularly in the Galicia region, during the Feast of St. James, it was—and still is—served to travelers of the Camino de Santiago as a traditional reward when they reach Santiago de Compostela. More bakes for almond lovers here: Extremadura Almond Pie; Anytime Almond Cake; and Almond Croissant Galette. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour - Yield 6–8 servings Ingredients 5 1¼ 1 1 2 2½ 1–2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Lightly coat a 9"-diameter cake pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Using an electric mixer on medium-high speed, beat 5 large eggs and 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar in a large bowl until aerated and very pale yellow, about 5 minutes. Reduce mixer speed to medium-low and beat in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, 1 Tbsp. finely grated orange zest, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Add 2½ cups (250 g) almond flour or meal and beat just to combine. Using a rubber spatula, fold in 1–2 Bartlett pears, cored, cut into ¼" pieces (about 2 cups). Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Step 2Bake tarta until golden brown and it springs back when gently pressed, 35–40 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack; let tarta cool in pan 10 minutes. Run an offset spatula or small knife around sides of pan to loosen cake. Turn out onto rack, carefully turn right side up, and let cool completely. Step 3Just before serving, transfer tarta to a large plate and dust with powdered sugar. Do Ahead: Tarta can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature (or chill if you prefer a softer texture).

item.title: What Do Pro Chefs Cook at Home?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.33
You don’t need to watch The Bear to know that working in a restaurant is different than cooking at home. Chefs order ingredients at a (much!) larger scale than the average supermarket carries. They’ll fire the same dish again and again, no matter how much they might crave something new. A team of line cooks and dishwashers assist them with every step from prep to cleanup. But at the end of the day, chefs go home—where they need to feed themselves, of course, and maybe a kid or partner too. So we asked them: What do you cook when you’re not on the line? For breakfast: Korean Street Toast Breakfast Sandwich The first time I visited South Korea as an adult, in 2006, I became obsessed with the toast sandwiches sold from street carts in the mornings. Watching vendors work quickly over portable griddles, crisping buttery bread while simultaneously cooking a thin vegetable-packed omelet, was mesmerizing. What surprised me most was how distinct the breakfast sandwich tasted, despite using ingredients like American cheese, ketchup, and white bread. The cabbage, onion, carrot, and tiny sprinkle of sugar make it unmistakably Korean. Using bagged coleslaw mix will cut down on slicing time—an invaluable gift on my busiest mornings. —Beverly Kim, chef and co-owner of Parachute and Anelya, Chicago For the kids: Buckwheat Crepes With Banana-Sesame Jam Buckwheat crepes are one of those rare items that are both practical to make and feel like a flex. Tell another parent that you cook crepes for your kids on school days and just watch the confusion rise in their eyes. It sounds fancy, but they really do make sense for the busy parent who loves to cook. You don’t need a special pan—any nonstick will do—and each pancake takes just a couple minutes. Like many parents, I’m always looking for ways to boost nutrition for my family. Buckwheat is high in fiber and nutrient-dense, and has a low glycemic index. I love its earthy flavor, especially paired with butter browning in the pan. You can make the batter up to 3 days in advance, or if you’re in a rush, even 5 minutes is enough to hydrate the buckwheat. Because they’re barely sweetened, the crepes can cover multiple meals, skewing savory with a filling of melty cheese or cooked vegetables; or sweet, like this one, with jammy fruit. —Julia Sherman, chef, New York City, and author of Arty Parties and Salad for President For date night: Mussels Dijonnaise We find mussels to be a romantic dish. Eating them with your hands adds to the experience, and soaking up the broth with a charred and crusty baguette—well, there’s nothing better. Early on in our relationship, when we wanted to have a “date,” we’d squeeze it in right before the end of service at our restaurant. We’d sit at the bar and order mussels, a beet salad (we always have beets on the menu), and sparkling wine. The combination was quite enchanting. This version of classic steamed mussels, adorned with Pernod-infused butter and a Dijon-enriched broth, briefly transports us back to those corner stools, no matter where we make it. —Claire Wadsworth and Nikki Hill, chefs and co-owners of La Copine, Yucca Valley, CA, and authors of La Copine: New California Cooking from an Oasis in the Desert For entertaining: Creole Sausage Roll-Ups When I was at Kith/Kin, my former restaurant in DC, I saw first hand how much public policy is decided over hors d’oeuvres. Everyone’s favorite party snack—on the left, on the right, young, old—is pigs in a blanket. The flakiness of the crust, the juicy snap of the hot dog, it’s what unites us. That’s why these roll-ups are a staple at my own parties, plus some sort of chips with dip and, of course, drinks (a tequila neat is my go-to). When I host, I like to keep things simple. I channel the joy of cocktail weenies with the rich, spicy, smoky flavors of andouille sausage—way more flavor than regular hot dogs—wrapped in puff pastry. Instead of ketchup, I serve them with homemade hot honey mustard. I like to save any excess puff pastry and make my own version of a Hot Pocket with extra sausages and mustard sauce. —Kwame Onwuachi, chef and co-owner Dōgon, Washington, DC, and Tatiana, New York City, and author of All Hours: Crazy Good Food for Whatever, Whenever For dessert: Pear Tarta De Santiago I’m fascinated by the North African influence on Spanish cuisine. Take traditional flourless almond cake, or Tarta de Santiago, which some lore claims is a by-product of increased almond cultivation and culinary traditions during Spain’s Moorish era. It’s a popular option at bakeries and cafés throughout Spain, particularly in the Galicia region, during the Feast of St. James. And it was—and still is—ordered by travelers of the Camino de Santiago as a traditional reward when they reach Santiago de Compostela. A slice is perfectly suited for a relaxed breakfast, afternoon tea, or evening treat. At the restaurant I would spread the batter into a sheet pan, but at home a round cake pan works perfectly. After the cake has cooled, I like to rest it in the fridge to let it develop a softer, fluffier texture. There it waits, ready to be enjoyed at my leisure. —James Martin, chef and and co-owner of Bocadillo Market, Chicago

item.title: Korean Street Toast Breakfast Sandwich
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.18
The first time I visited South Korea as an adult cook in 2006, I became obsessed with the toast sandwiches sold from street carts in the mornings. Watching vendors work quickly over portable griddles, crisping buttery bread while simultaneously cooking a thin vegetable-packed omelet, was mesmerizing. What surprised me most was how distinctly Korean the breakfast sandwich tasted despite using ingredients like American cheese, ketchup, and white bread. The cabbage, onion, carrot, and tiny sprinkle of sugar are what make it unmistakably Korean street toast. This version stays true to the sandwiches I remember eating hot off the griddle: fluffy eggs, lightly crunchy vegetables, a sweet-savory balance, and golden toasted bread. Japanese milk bread gives the sandwich its signature pillowy texture, but soft white bread or Texas toast work beautifully too. Using bagged coleslaw mix will cut down on slicing time (valuable in the morning!), but note that if it contains red cabbage, it can tinge the eggs slightly blue as it cooks; if preferred, swap in a heaping ⅓ cup thinly sliced green cabbage and a 2" chunk of carrot, julienned. More great sammies here: Make-Ahead Breakfast Sandwiches; Veggie Club Sandwich; and Healthyish Breakfast Sandwiches. Recipe information - Total Time 25 minutes - Yield Makes 1 Ingredients 2 ¼ ½ ½ ¼ 3 2 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Whisk 2 large eggs in a medium bowl until homogenous and no streaks remain; add ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and season with freshly ground pepper. Add ½ small onion, thinly sliced, ½ cup store-bought coleslaw mix, and ¼ cup (scant) julienned sliced ham; mix to combine. Step 2Melt ½ Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large nonstick skillet over medium-low. Cook one ¾"–1"-thick slice Japanese milk bread, Texas toast, or other soft white sandwich bread until light golden underneath, about 2 minutes. Turn, add ½ Tbsp. unsalted butter to pan, and lift bread to allow butter to stream underneath. Cook until barely golden on bottom side, about 2 minutes. Transfer to a cutting board. Repeat with another 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and remaining one ¾"–1"-thick slice Japanese milk bread, Texas toast, or other soft white sandwich bread. Place 1 slice American cheese on top of 1 toast. Step 3Melt remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Pour in egg mixture and, using chopsticks or a heatproof rubber spatula, evenly distribute vegetables throughout egg. Cook, undisturbed, to let egg set slightly, about 1 minute. Using spatula, push into a thin rectangle about twice the length of bread, then cut in half crosswise with spatula to make 2 squares. Turn and cook until eggs are set but vegetables still maintain some crunch, about 1 minute. Sprinkle omelet with pinch of Korean brown sugar or raw sugar. Step 4Transfer omelet squares to cheese-covered toast, stacking on top of each other; leave pan over heat. Squeeze some ketchup over omelet. Close up sandwich with remaining toast. Return sandwich to pan and cook, turning halfway through, until bread is just golden brown and cheese is melted, about 2 minutes. Transfer to a plate and slice in half.

item.title: Buckwheat Crepes With Banana-Sesame Jam
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.34
Buckwheat crepes are one of those rare items that are both practical to make and feel like a flex. Tell another parent that you make crepes for your kids on school days (morning or night!) and just watch the confusion rise behind their eyes. It sounds fancy, but in practice, crepes really do make sense for the busy parent who loves to cook. You don’t need a special pan to make crepes—any nonstick pan will do; and each pancake cooks in barely a couple minutes. No need to make the batter ahead of time either: Just a 5-minute rest allows the buckwheat time to hydrate, but it lasts for 3 days in the fridge. It’s barely sweetened, so the crepes can cover multiple meals, skewing savory with a filling of melty cheese or cooked vegetables, or sweet, like this one, with jammy fruit. Like many parents, I am always looking for ways to optimize nutrition when cooking for my family. Buckwheat is high in fiber, nutrient-dense, and has a low glycemic index. I love its earthy flavor, especially when paired with butter browning in the pan. My crepe batter uses a mix of buckwheat and all-purpose flour (just enough gluten to hold them together), but keeps the ratio of the former higher, making them darker and more richly flavored than an all-wheat crepe. This recipe became such a household staple that my kids insisted I put it on the brunch menu at Oberon, the restaurant in Manhattan’s New Museum, where I am the Executive Chef. More breakfast winners here: Crispy Crepes With Dark Maple Syrup; Perfectly Fluffy Pancakes; and Hash Brown Breakfast Casserole. Recipe information - Total Time 45 minutes - Yield Makes 10–12 Ingredients 2 1⅓ ½ ⅓ 2 1½ 3 ½ 3 1–2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Blend 2 large eggs, 1⅓ cups whole milk, ½ cup (63 g) buckwheat flour, ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1½ tsp. dark brown sugar, and a pinch of kosher salt in a blender, scraping down sides halfway through, until smooth, about 2 minutes. Let batter sit at room temperature while you make the jam. Step 2Cook 3 very ripe bananas, peeled, cut into 1" pieces, ½ tsp. ground cardamom or cinnamon, a pinch of kosher salt, remaining 1 Tbsp. dark brown sugar, and 2 Tbsp. water in a medium skillet over medium-low heat, smashing bananas and stirring often with a heatproof rubber spatula, until darkened in color and jammy, 10–15 minutes. Remove banana mixture from heat. Step 3Whisk 3 Tbsp. tahini and ¼ cup water in a medium bowl until smooth. Add banana mixture and 1 tsp. fresh lemon juice (if using) and stir well. Taste banana jam and add remaining 1 tsp. fresh lemon juice if desired. Step 4Give batter a good stir, scraping bottom of blender jar to reincorporate any flour that has settled. Heat a 10"-diameter nonstick skillet over medium 2 minutes. Using a pastry brush, lightly coat pan with melted butter. Lift up pan from burner and pour ¼ cup batter onto one side, then immediately tilt pan and swirl batter to coat surface evenly. (Pan should be hot enough that bubbles begin to form in batter within a few seconds; if not, increase heat slightly.) Cook crepe until edges begin to brown and surface looks matte, about 45 seconds. Run spatula around edges to loosen and flip. Cook crepe until just set underneath, about 15 seconds; transfer to a large plate. Repeat with more butter and remaining batter, stirring between pours. Stack cooked crepes on top of each other. Step 5To serve, place a crepe on a plate, lighter side up. Spread about 2 Tbsp. banana jam over and fold in half, then in half again to create a wedge shape. Repeat with remaining crepes and more jam. Top with banana slices and/or black sesame seeds if desired. Do Ahead: Batter can be made 3 days ahead. Cover and chill. Bring to room temperature before cooking.

item.title: Creole Sausage Roll-Ups
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.34
Washington, DC is a cocktail-party town. When I was at Kith/Kin I saw firsthand how much public policy is decided over hors d’oeuvres. Everyone’s favorite—on the left, on the right, young, old—is pigs in a blanket, the little cocktail hot dogs wrapped in pastry. The flakiness of the crust, the juicy crunch of the hot dog within, it’s what unites us. Now when I host parties, I channel the joy of those cocktail weenies with the rich, spicy, smoky flavors of andouille sausage—more flavor than regular hot dogs!—wrapped in puff pastry. Instead of yellow mustard or ketchup, I serve them with an athletically spiced homemade honey mustard. I like to save any excess puff pastry and make my own version of a Hot Pocket. (Or if you have another package of sausages, make a few more roll-ups.) When I'm entertaining I like to keep snacks simple, like these roll-ups and some sort of chips with dip. And of course, we cannot forget about cocktails: A tequila neat is my go-to. Recipe adapted from All Hours, by Kwame Onwuachi and Joshua David Stein. Copyright 2026. Excerpted by permission of Alfred A. Knopf, a division of Penguin Random House LLC. All rights reserved. No part of this excerpt may be reproduced or reprinted without permission in writing from the publisher. More great party food here: Chicago-Style Pigs in a Blanket; Pork Adobo Pull-Apart Sliders; and Warm 7-Layer Skillet Dip. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 45 minutes - Yield 4–6 servings Ingredients 1 4 1 2 ¼ ¼ 3 2 1 1 1 1 ½ ½ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Working one at a time, cut one 17.3-oz. package frozen puff pastry sheets, thawed, in half lengthwise on a lightly floured surface. Place one of four 6"-long andouille sausages (12 oz.) on each rectangle ¼"–½" from a short end. Step 2Whisk 1 Tbsp. whole milk and 1 large egg in a small bowl. Working one at a time, brush egg wash along edge of pastry opposite sausage. Tightly roll up pastry around sausage, stopping as soon as it starts to overlap slightly; press gently to seal. Trim excess dough and pinch ends of pastry around sausage to enclose. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze until chilled through but not frozen solid, 1–2 hours. Step 3Whisk together ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. Creole or Dijon mustard, ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, 3 Tbsp. honey, 2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. cayenne pepper, 1 tsp. freshly ground black pepper, 1 tsp. granulated garlic or garlic powder, 1 tsp. granulated onion or onion powder, ½ tsp. Hungarian paprika, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl. Taste mustard sauce and season with more kosher salt if needed. Cover and chill until ready to serve. Step 4Preheat oven to 425°. Whisk remaining 1 large egg in a small bowl. Slice frozen sausage logs into 1"-thick pieces; arrange, seam side down, on baking sheet. Brush each piece with egg and sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Bake sausage roll-ups until golden brown, 15–20 minutes. Let cool slightly. Serve with mustard sauce for dipping. Do Ahead: Sauce can be made 3 days ahead. Keep chilled.

item.title: MrBeast's new challenge: Convincing fans to buy his first book
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.83
MrBeast is the king of stunts. His next big challenge? Convincing his more than 500 million YouTube subscribers to log off and read a book. On Tuesday, the content creator released his first novel, "The Most Dangerous Games," coauthored with bestselling writer James Patterson. As of Tuesday morning, the book was available for sale and sitting at No. 12 on Amazon's new releases list. It was No. 73 on Amazon's overall book list. "Having the name MrBeast attached to any book is going to get it a ton of immediate awareness and interest," said Matt Kaye, cofounder and CEO of Bindery Books, a book publisher that works with creators and other tastemakers to launch imprints tailored to their fans. "We'll see if the people in his audience who give it a shot love it enough to recommend it to other people," Kaye said. "However big the name is, the long-term success of a book lies in how much readers love it and recommend it to each other." To draw in readers, MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, is turning to one of his reliable marketing tactics: dangling a cash prize. Fans who buy the book can enter a competition he's hosting in September for a chance to win a $1 million prize. The novel contains clues and hidden easter eggs meant to help players compete in weekly elimination challenges, a company spokesperson said. Book publishing is one of many business ventures the MrBeast team is testing as it looks to expand beyond YouTube. The company's various bets include the "Beast Games" Amazon Prime Video competition show, selling chocolate bars via its Feastables candy brand, and offering financial services after acquiring the Step banking app. Influencer books have flittered in and out of popularity. During the 2010s, a wave of content creators like PewDiePie (Felix Kjellberg), Lilly Singh, Shane Dawson, and Zoella (Zoe Sugg) published chart-topping works. The creator-to-author pipeline has since calmed down, though the emergence of BookTok, a social-media community of readers and book recommenders, has rekindled creators' interest in publishing. "Books are having a moment again," said Jeff Speich, an executive who oversees Range Media Partners' publishing arm, Range Literary Publishing. "Anyone with a profile is thinking about if they have something to add to the space." While MrBeast has demonstrated he can promote just about anything to his fans, "The Most Dangerous Games" could also get a boost from its other famous author, Patterson, who over the last decade has helped books by Dolly Parton and former president Bill Clinton reach the top of The New York Times best-sellers list. "Publishers are looking for people who already have established audiences, whether that's authors or celebrities or massive creators, to break through the noise," Kaye said. "Most books that get published fall into the void."

item.title: A new plane is changing how airlines think about long-haul flights. Here's everywhere you can fly on the Airbus A321XLR.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.24
The world's newest airplane has changed the game by opening new routes to dozens of international destinations. The Airbus A321XLR is a single-aisle jet, but it can fly 800 miles further than the Airbus A321neo. This lets airlines fly it across the Atlantic to cities that wouldn't be popular enough to fill a wide-body airplane. Most XLRs also have lie-flat seats in business class to make the longer journeys comfortable. Plus, as part of the Airbus A320 family, the world's most popular aircraft type, the jet is easy for pilots and flight attendants to adapt to. It has very similar controls to the standard A320, with only a few changes in systems related to long-haul flights and an extra fuel tank. That's ideal for airlines because it means their pilots only need a short training session to fly it, rather than a whole new type rating. Last week, United Airlines and American Airlines unveiled a combined nine new international routes using the XLR. These are set to launch next year, but tickets can be booked now. In addition to compiling airline announcements, Business Insider tracked 32 XLRs on Flightradar24 to see where they have been flying this month. While there are another six in service with Wizz Air, the airline has been excluded from this list because it changed its strategy and now uses them on the same routes as typical narrow-body airplanes. The Airbus A321XLR has opened routes to dozens of new cities, mostly between Europe and North America. Not pictured here are another seven transcontinental or cross-country routes in the US, Canada, and Australia. For the routes closest to you, try this interactive map. Hover over each icon to see the destinations available from different cities around the world. Aer Lingus The Irish flag carrier was the second airline to start flying the XLR. All six that Aer Lingus ordered have been delivered. From Dublin, it flies to Cleveland, Hartford, Indianapolis, Minneapolis, Nashville, New York JFK, Philadelphia, Raleigh-Durham, and Washington, DC. In addition to these nine routes, Aer Lingus sometimes uses the XLR for short-haul flights around Europe. That lets the airline get the most out of them, keeping them in frequent use, while also showing their versatility. Air Canada Canada's national airline started flying the XLR in June. Three of the 30 it has ordered are currently operating. It flies them from Montreal to Calgary and Berlin, though the seasonal Berlin service will end early, on September 5, rather than in October. Air Canada also flies the jet to the French cities of Nantes and Toulouse; Airbus is headquartered in the latter. American Airlines American Airlines is one of two US carriers on this list, but it started flying the XLR first, beginning last December. It ordered 40, and seven of those are flying today. As of September 2026, it flies from New York JFK to Edinburgh and Los Angeles, and between Boston and Los Angeles. However, in late August, American Airlines announced four new XLR routes for 2027, which are now open for booking: - JFK to Amsterdam, starts March 28 - Philadelphia to Porto, Portugal, starts March 28 - JFK to Nice, France, starts May 6 - Philadelphia to Vienna, starts May 6 Iberia Spain's flag carrier was the first airline to receive an XLR and started flying it in November 2024. All eight that Iberia ordered have now been delivered. From Madrid, it flies to Boston, the Dominican Republic, Newark, Puerto Rico, Toronto, Washington DC, and the Brazilian cities of Recife and Fortaleza. Like Aer Lingus, Iberia occasionally uses its A321XLRs on short hops around Europe. Qantas The Australian airline operates seven XLRs and has another 41 on order. At the moment, they are used for flights between Australia's major cities, which could be operated by a regular narrow-body jet. It plans to use the XLR for longer flights: Manila was supposed to be its first international use in October, but this has been postponed. The first of its 16 configured with new business-class suites is scheduled to arrive in 2028. United Airlines United Airlines is set to become the largest operator of the XLR as things stand: It has ordered 50. However, only one has been delivered so far. After Business Insider toured the jet at July's Farnborough Airshow, it has flown a few times, mostly around the US. United will launch the XLR in earnest on December 1, when it is scheduled to fly from Washington Dulles Airport to Amsterdam and Dublin. Last week, it also announced a handful of new routes for 2027 that are open for booking: - Newark to Luxembourg, starts April 2 - Washington, DC, to Toulouse, starts April 26 - Newark to Ibiza, Spain, starts May 31 - Newark to Valencia, Spain, starts June 2 - Newark to Marseille, France, starts June 4

item.title: OpenAI's entanglements with a data center company go on display in a new filing
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.75
Every company in tech watches out for OpenAI. SB Energy can't look away. The data center developer filed its prospectus to go public on Monday, and it's uniquely intertwined with the AI lab behind ChatGPT, according to figures from the new filing. Everywhere SB Energy turns, there's OpenAI: leasing data center capacity, owning billions of dollars in warrants, even locking in an OpenAI software deal through 2028. OpenAI, should it get a 5% ownership stake in SB Energy, will also get to pick a member of the company's board. SB Energy's decision to go public signals the incredible expense in building new data centers and the rapacious demand for compute that OpenAI and its peers have generated over the last few years. SB Energy is building its first two data center sites, both in Texas. One will be allotted to OpenAI, the other to the Japanese conglomerate SoftBank, which owns more than half of SB Energy. The developer has also planning to build a giant new data center in Southern Ohio, with help from OpenAI and Nvidia. That data center site, at a planned 8 gigawatts of capacity, is set to be among the world's largest and serve OpenAI. In the filing, the developer warns about the depth of its relationship with OpenAI, which has confidentially filed its own initial public offering prospectus and is expected to go public next year. "We are dependent on OpenAI as our anchor data center tenant, representing a significant portion of our signed lease capacity, and any adverse change in OpenAI's financial condition, competitive position or willingness to perform its contractual obligations could materially and adversely affect our business," SB Energy wrote. SB Energy declined to comment. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. OpenAI will have a stake of up to $5.5 billion SB Energy is handing a chunk of itself to its biggest customer. The IPO prospectus says the company granted OpenAI stock warrants in early 2026, when the lab invested in SB Energy and signed on as a data center tenant. The deal will deliver pieces of SB Energy in various tranches, tied to the public offering and future valuation milestones. When the warrants were issued, they were worth $3.6 billion, and that value has grown to an estimated $5.5 billion as of June 30, according to the filing. The filing also says that, provided that OpenAI owns at least 5% of SB Energy's stock, it can nominate a candidate to SB Energy's board. This style of arrangement is growing more common in the era of high-expense infrastructure buildouts, where OpenAI is rallying billions of dollars toward getting as much computing power online as possible. The company has struck deals with Nvidia, Google, Amazon, Oracle, AMD, and other tech giants, sometimes committing to spend with the same companies it's taking investment from. SB Energy and OpenAI have a batch of other commitments A deal between SB Energy and OpenAI also gives the AI lab some other sweet perks, including rights to intellectual property. SB Energy has committed to spending at least $50 million on OpenAI's services, including ChatGPT Enterprise, through 2028. OpenAI's myriad ties to SB Energy could be a conflict of interest, the filing said. It says that SB Energy's board might find it difficult to enforce lease obligations against such a significant investor, and that OpenAI's interests as a tenant may "diverge" from its interests as a warrant holder. In a section about the company's risks, SB Energy writes, "any disruption in our relationship with OpenAI could impair our financing arrangements, limit our development flexibility, and materially and adversely affect our liquidity and the value of our common stock." item.title: Anthropic's Tom Blomfield says his new coworkers are a 'hyper-earnest group of meganerds' with a 'lack of ego'
item.description:

Tom Blomfield has shared a candid assessment of his new Anthropic colleagues: "often weird" but with a "surprising lack of ego or politics." Blomfield, one of the biggest names in UK tech, took a leave of absence from Y Combinator to join Anthropic's compute team in July. He wrote in a Tuesday X post that although Anthropic is "not perfect by any means," it has the "most powerful sense of mission of any company I've ever encountered." He included Monzo, the British fintech company he cofounded, in that assessment, writing that he "thought it was an outlier." "Overall impression of @anthropicAI after 2 months; hyper-earnest group of meganerds who are very very focussed on ensuring this AI thing goes well for humans," Blomfield wrote in the X post. Anthropic would likely agree with at least half of that statement: the startup has positioned itself as a company prioritizing AI safety. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In July, Anthropic's head of growth, Amol Avasare, gave another insight into the company's culture, sharing on a podcast that employees can openly challenge the CEO — even on Slack. The company behind the AI model Claude has also become one of the hottest career destinations in Silicon Valley — alongside rival OpenAI — as tech talent looks to participate in the AI boom and potentially cash in on one of the biggest ever tech IPOs. Overall impression of @anthropicAI after 2 months; hyper-earnest group of meganerds who are very very focussed on ensuring this AI thing goes well for humans. — Tom Blomfield (@t_blom) September 1, 2026 Blomfield became one of Anthropic's big-name summer hires as the AI talent wars have continued to heat up.
