item.title: Western training manuals update too slowly to properly prepare Ukrainian troops for a fast-changing battlefield, commander says
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.08
Western militaries training Ukrainian troops for war with Russia can't rely on the usual cycle of periodically updated manuals because battlefield lessons are changing too quickly, a NATO commander told Business Insider. Norway is leading multinational training for Ukrainian troops at Camp Jomsborg, a purpose-built camp in eastern Poland, as part of Operation Legio. The training needs constant updates about the tactics and weaponry that work on the rapidly changing battlefield, Brigadier Atle Molde, the commander of Task Force Legio, told Business Insider. "You cannot do that based on bureaucratic training manuals issued once a year or stuff like that," Molde said. "It's just too slow." The work happening in Poland "all comes down to being relevant for the sake of saving lives and helping the Ukrainians win this war," he said. That means making the training as accurate to the battlefield as possible, where weapons and tactics are evolving and becoming obsolete far faster than Western militaries are accustomed to. Operation Legio strives to impart Western doctrine and best practices to Ukrainian soldiers, who can then combine them with their hard-won battlefield knowledge. To do that effectively, trainers try to recreate the realities of the fight as much as possible, including the terrain, tech, and tactics. The challenge is that the battlefield changes quickly. Ukrainian soldiers say that tactics change every week, and cutting-edge battlefield tech can shift into obsolescence within a few weeks. That makes Ukrainian experience, not training manuals, central to keeping the training current. Instructors listen to feedback from experienced Ukrainian soldiers and integrate it, and Ukrainian instructors and leaders are also present. Maj. John, the S3 Operations Officer in charge of synchronizing the overall training operation, said Camp Jomsborg is defined "as a Ukrainian training center." If the Ukrainians tell their instructors that their armed forces don't do something anymore, then the training changes, Molde said. Molde said it's critical that the training keep pace with the battlefield. "You have to adapt to the situation, or you become irrelevant," he said. If "the training is not relevant, then more Ukrainians will die," Molde added. The war, as is, has already come with significant casualties on both sides. Jørgen, a Norwegian Army instructor for Legio's platoon leader course, told Business Insider that "we make a lot of changes, and we try to evaluate on a day-to-day basis, and we're bringing the flexibility to be able to change tomorrow or tonight." The Ukrainians regularly update their own training on very tight timelines as well. Drone school leaders previously told Business Insider that they need to constantly update the lessons they teach, sometimes every other week. Technology in the war is "moving forward at a very fast pace," Tetyana, a Ukrainian veteran who goes by the call sign "Ruda" and the head of R&D for drone school Dronarium, said. This means the school has "to be very fast in our adaptability." The rapid battlefield changes mean the kind of tech that's relevant shifts quickly too, complicating Operation Legio's efforts to mirror the battlefield as closely as possible. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in January that success in the war depends on who is "the fastest" at applying and adapting technology. Ukraine's tech companies work with this speed and the need for constant adaptation in mind. Ukrainian drone and weapons maker Frontline Robotics, for example, told Business Insider that it makes up to 20 changes to its products a month, while the CEO of Ukrainian arms maker Ark Robotics said that the company gets continuous requests for updates from soldiers. Companies stay up to date by messaging and FaceTiming soldiers, as well as by sending employees to dangerous positions near the fighting to test and make changes. Ukraine's experience has been a wake-up call for NATO, with the West worried that its militaries can't adapt their tactics and technology as quickly as Ukraine does. NATO in July said that "Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has highlighted how quickly warfare is evolving — with innovation cycles compressed from years into months." The alliance said "innovation on the battlefield is moving faster than ever." Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO's supreme allied commander for transformation, said in May that "adaptation is maybe the most important lesson" from Ukraine.

item.title: Sam Altman says fears that AI data centers guzzle water are overblown — but hard to dispel
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.83
Sam Altman says concern about AI water usage is a "meme" that doesn't actually hold any water. The OpenAI CEO was asked to respond to resistance to AI, including concerns about water consumption, on the premiere episode of the Sources podcast with Alex Heath, published Tuesday. Altman said that while they have a reputation for being water guzzlers, modern data centers use about as much water as an office building. "That has been a robust meme and difficult to disprove, but I don't think holds up to any scrutiny," he said. A 2024 report from a state government commission in Virginia — a hot spot for data centers — found that while some facilities used significantly more water than others, most data centers used the same amount or less than an average large office building. Water consumption has been a central concern in the backlash against data centers. A Gallup report published in May found 71% of Americans said they opposed the construction of a data center in their area, with 70% saying they worried specifically about the environmental impact. Half of the respondents cited the effect on resources, with 18% naming water specifically. A Business Insider investigation published last year found data centers were contributing to the water crisis in the West, in part because of water-intensive evaporative cooling techniques. The Data Center Coalition, an industry trade group, says data center developers use various cooling methods, including some closed-loop or waterless systems, and that they prioritize efficient water practices that account for local water availability. Altman also compared the water used by ChatGPT to that used in growing California almonds, a water-intensive crop. He said growing a single almond in California requires more water than is used in thousands of ChatGPT queries, adding "the people that are scarfing down 12 almonds at a time don't feel like they're doing something horrible from a water perspective, for the most part." Business Insider could not independently verify Altman's comparison, but the claim that water consumption from growing a single almond is orders of magnitude higher than an AI chatbot prompt generally lines up with available figures. Altman has said the average ChatGPT query uses about 0.32 milliliters of water, while Google has said the average Gemini app text prompt uses 0.26 milliliters. A 2019 study by researchers affiliated with the US Geological Survey found that growing a single almond in California requires an average of 3.56 liters, a little less than a gallon of water per nut. While he said the water concerns around AI are overblown, he said he thinks it's up to the industry to change the public's minds. "I think the right way to get people to like something is to deliver them value," Altman said, adding, "The industry has got work to do in terms of how we make these products easy to use and easy for people to get a lot of value out of."

item.title: Meta bricked the cameras on thousands of its AI glasses
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.61
Thousands of Meta's AI glasses no longer have functioning cameras after the company detected people tampering with the recording indicator lights. Meta announced new efforts in recent weeks to crack down on people who drill out or cover up the tiny lights on their Meta glasses, which can make it easier to surreptitiously record people. On Tuesday, Meta confirmed it's already shut down the cameras on thousands of devices following a software update intended to combat bad actors. The company said the enforcement action impacted the newest update affected less than one tenth of a percent of all Meta AI glasses sold. Semafor first reported the news. Meta has not released information on how many total devices have been sold since they were launched in 2021, but 7 million were sold in 2025 alone (at the .1% number, that would account for 7,000 pairs of glasses that were physically tampered with). Meta glasses have gained a somewhat fraught reputation lately, with some people referring to them as "pervert glasses." Business Insider has previously reported on Instagram's bumpy attempts to remove harassing content filmed on Meta glasses in public spaces. The glasses have always had an indicator light to show when they're recording, but people have found ways to hide or disable the light. The company is responding to that criticism with several new lines of defense, including a new PR blitz. On Monday, Meta's CTO, Andrew Bosworth, said in an Instagram ask-me-anything story post that the glasses are "the most privacy-forward camera" for consumers. "You haven't had a camera that put a light on when it took a photo or video of somebody since you had like a VHS tape recorder in the 90s," he said, referencing the light that flashes when the glasses are recording. "Your phone doesn't have that, and it's the most commonly held camera on earth." The company also put up billboards in Los Angeles, saying the eyewear is "designed for everyone" and "not just the people wearing them." A recent update would stop the device from recording if the light was tampered with, but people found a way around it: it only detected a blockage at the start of filming, so they'd start recording, wait a few seconds, then cover it up. The newest update closes that loophole. But not all people who had been trying to sneak around without the lights are going to have their cameras permanently disabled. If you drilled out your LED light, your camera function will never work again. However, if you had been using the popular method of just covering it with a sticker; the camera will work again once you remove the sticker. In a Thursday post on Threads, Meta's vice president of wearables, Alex Himel, wrote that only a "tiny minority of people" were tampering with the hardware, and said Meta will "keep rolling out updates like this to make sure the capture LED can reliably alert bystanders when photos or videos are being captured."

item.title: Tim Cook is out as Apple CEO. He gave a 15-year masterclass in succeeding a legend.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.55
Tim Cook has stepped down as Apple CEO, marking the end of one of the greatest tenures in business history. Cook took on the daunting task of succeeding Steve Jobs, just weeks before his premature death in October 2011. Vanishingly few people would have dared follow Jobs, Apple's iconic cofounder who reshaped how the world works with revolutionary devices such as the iPod and iPhone. Yet Cook pulled off what few thought possible: taking Apple to the next level. During his 15 years in charge, Apple roughly quadrupled its annual net sales and net income to over $400 billion and $100 billion, respectively, catapulting its market capitalization from around $350 billion to $4.6 trillion. Adjusted for stock splits, Apple's stock price rose by nearly 2,300% during his tenure, from about $13 to $317 at the close of Cook's last day as CEO on Monday. Now that Cook has made way for his own successor — Apple's hardware chief John Ternus — there are clear lessons to be learned from his success in following a legendary CEO. 1. Keep what works Cook safeguarded the core values that Jobs instilled at Apple. He told "CBS Sunday Morning" earlier this year that he protected principles such as focus, collaboration, obsession with the user experience, "insanely great" execution, and creating "magic" by owning the intersection of hardware, software, and services. Cook said he always saw Apple as Jobs' baby. "His DNA is deep in this company," he said. "We revere him." The now-departed CEO also said of Jobs that his "greatest invention wasn't a product — it was Apple itself." Read more about Apple's transition 2. Blaze your own trail Cook wasn't cowed by Jobs' remarkable legacy, but instead ran Apple as he saw fit. He told "CBS Sunday Morning" that when Jobs informed him that he would be Apple's next CEO, he also advised him: "Never ask what I would do. Just do the right thing." Jobs told Cook that he'd witnessed Disney become frozen by indecision after founder Walt Disney died, and he didn't want Apple to suffer the same "paralysis." "I'll never forget that," Cook said. "It was such a gift for me because he took off of my shoulder this question of 'What would Steve do?'" "I just put my head down and thought, 'I'm going to be the best version of myself,'" he added. While Jobs was in charge, he "made every major decision" at Apple, Tripp Mickle, the author of "After Steve," a book about the decade at Apple after Jobs' death, told Business Insider in April after Cook revealed he was stepping down. Cook restructured Apple to be "more democratic," with Apple executives making collective decisions and team leaders developing products instead of individuals reporting to Jobs, Mickle said. He also placed greater emphasis on operations and financials. Cook's Apple expanded into China to scale up manufacturing and cater to the country's rapidly growing middle class. The strategy allowed him to "make the iPhone ubiquitous," Mickle said. Cook grew services into a $100 billion business, and created a wearables category with products such as AirPods and Apple Watch. He also introduced Apple-designed silicon, which "breathed new life into its Mac business," Mickle said. His approach was "method over magic," Mickle said. "Where Jobs became regarded as a great innovator, who introduced products that upended industries, Cook became known for steering Apple's business success, as it became the world's largest company for a decade." On the other hand, Apple's reputation for innovation took a hit under Cook, Mickle said. He pointed to disappointing product launches such as the HomePod and the Vision Pro headset, and the canceled plan to build a self-driving car. 3. Play to your strengths Instead of trying to be Jobs, Cook applied his different skillset at Apple with great effect. "Cook's genius wasn't in designing the next iPhone; it was in building the most efficient supply chain on the planet and turning a hardware company into a recurring-service juggernaut," Chris Ballard, the managing director of Check Capital Management, told Business Insider. "There is a very small club of people who are able to successfully take over for a business legend without the company missing a beat," Kevin Carpenter, the author of an investing Substack named Kingswell, told Business Insider. "Cook certainly did so for Apple — in large part because he embraced his own strengths rather than trying to be a poor imitation of Steve Jobs."

item.title: Smile! You're on Dyson's $500 toothbrush camera
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.23
Are you ready to stick a $500 camera toothbrush in your mouth? Dyson just launched an electric toothbrush and "precision flosser" that blasts water into the gaps between your teeth. How does it find those gaps? Great question — it uses a tiny camera to spot them and power wash away plaque or bits of broccoli stuck in there. Behold: Honestly, it looks very cool. Dyson has a good track record of creating personal care devices with big price tags that totally revolutionize the category. People are nuts for their ultra-expensive hair dryers and styling tools. So if they can pull this off for oral hygiene? Hey, sounds good. Dyson is aiming to market this to people who aren't good at keeping up with flossing ("Few of us do it even though we know we should," the company says) since it makes it all a one-step thing. I'm all for gum health (who isn't?), but does it seem a little, uh, strange to have a camera on your toothbrush? The Great Camera-fication of Household Items We're already inviting cameras into our homes in more and more normalized ways. Video doorbells are more and more common. Robot vacuums have cameras and sensors that can map out your home. High-end fridges can peer into your shelves. There's even a fancy new AI toilet with a camera that tracks your health via your, uh, output. Dyson addresses the elephant in the room of bringing a camera-enabled device into the sanctity of your bathroom on its website, in an only-in-2026 Q&A section titled: "Are there privacy risks with an in-mouth camera?" The company says that the camera is "optimized for short-range vision and detection only" — basically, only when right up against your teeth, and not, say, taking video while getting out of the shower. It also says images are deleted from the app immediately after viewing, and not stored or shared. (I asked Dyson for more details on the privacy aspects of the camera and didn't immediately hear back). To be fair, monitoring your gum line isn't exactly the surveillance state; it's a very limited use item with potential for huge upside (oral health is serious stuff!). But our potential willingness to stick a camera in our mouth twice a day falls somewhere on The Great Camera-fication spectrum that leads to Meta glasses and Flock cameras. After all, remember when someone managed to remotely access a fleet of camera-equipped DJI robot vacuums? Dyson is testing our acceptance of cameras in everyday items. They might be onto something. Or, you know, you could save $500 and just remember to floss.

item.title: Is $155,600 a working-class salary? More and more Americans say yes.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.09
A majority of Americans hear themselves in Dolly Parton's "9-to-5." Sixty percent of Americans identify as working class, according to a Pew Research analysis of a January 2026 survey. That's up from 54% in 2024. And the label, historically applied to lower-earning workers, resonates across earnings levels. Middle-income families, who make between $51,900 to $155,600 depending on family size and location, identify especially with the term "working class." More surprisingly, half of high-income families, who earn more than $155,600, identify that way. That could be because the term itself is ambiguous: As the analysis notes, there's no one clear definition of working class. Some equate the working class with lower earners, while others see them as workers without a bachelor's degree, or those explicitly working in blue-collar fields like construction and agriculture. The Pew findings come as middle-earning or financially comfortable Americans don't feel well-off, even while their pay has grown. Median weekly earnings increased 8.4% from the first quarter of 2024 through the first quarter of 2026, outpacing the 5.5% inflation in prices over that time. The middle third of earners used to feel similarly about their savings and spending as higher-earners did. Those two groups have increasingly drifted apart, with sentiment among the middle earners tracking more closely with the lowest earners. That's reflected in how they're spending, too: In 2024, Morning Consult found that middle-income consumers were spending more like their lower-income counterparts. The increased identification with the working class also dovetails with a shrinking middle class, which has fallen from 61% of the population in 1971 to 51% in 2023. Some of the growing disconnect might be because of inflation. High prices generally make people feel bad about their economic prospects, and over the past few months, inflation has outpaced wage growth. Financial stress also correlates with identifying as working-class. Even still, half of those who reported a baseline of financial comfort — bills paid, expenses met, months of emergency savings — identified with the term working-class. Your political leanings might also play a role in working-class identification, especially as affordability messaging takes center stage in America. Steven Shepard, the associate director of political research at Pew and one of the report's authors, said, "If you hold most of these other things equal, that Republicans are just more likely to say that that term describes them than Democrats." Upper-income Republicans are far more likely to see themselves as working class than their Democratic counterparts. On the other side of the political spectrum, progressive politicians have homed in on this newly expanded working class. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani campaigned on an affordability platform meant to ease costs for the working class, which he told The New York Times is the "one majority in this country." "If you have to work to pay your bills, I think that that is one definition of being a part of the working class," Mamdani said.

item.title: Ukraine's ousted pro-tech defense minister is launching a new company backed by Palantir's Alex Karp
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.99
Mykhailo Fedorov, who helped drive rapid innovation in battlefield technology, particularly drones, before being ousted as Ukraine's defense minister this summer, is launching a defense tech company. The new company will focus on developing defense technologies intended to strengthen Ukraine and support partners, Fedorov said in a release, promising "more details to come." While much remains unclear about what the company will do, its first lead investor will be Alex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, an American AI, data, and operational intelligence company. In a statement, Fedorov said Ukraine would be the company's priority. "During the full-scale war, our team gained unique experience working with defense technologies in Ukraine and seeing firsthand how technology is transforming modern warfare," he said. Now, he and his team intend to leverage that in a new venture. In a video made with Fedorov at Palantir's Washington office, Karp said of Fedorov and his team that "you and your colleagues are launching a company that I think will be defining for the world, bringing your knowledge and acumen about the art of war." Before becoming defense minister in January, Fedorov served as minister for digital transformation, a role in which he was celebrated for a Silicon Valley-style approach to delivering major changes intended to better prepare Ukraine for an evolving fight. His time in Ukraine's defense ministry coincided with tech-driven successes in combat, including a mid-range drone strike campaign that has devastated Russian logistics and the expansion of its deep-strike campaign targeting Russia's military and industry. Fedorov's sudden departure in July, six months into the job, came as a shock to Ukrainian service members and industry figures alike. His push for radical changes within the armed forces, he said at the time, created significant friction with senior military leaders. After his dismissal, Fedorov spoke critically about Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi, Kyiv's commander in chief at the time, accusing him of blocking every initiative he and his team put forward, creating a rift. "Instead of figuring out how to defeat Russia asymmetrically, he figured out how to split the country," he said of Syrskyi. In public statements following Fedorov's departure, Syrskyi thanked him for his work and said he hoped that he would see "continued success as part of the Ukrainian team." Ukraine replaced Fedorov with Yevhenii Khmara, and later, it replaced Syrskyi with Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi, whom Ukrainian troops rallied around as a strong choice for the role.

item.title: The US Army's sweeping transformation for future wars has lost some of its biggest champions
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.49
With the resignation of Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll, the US Army has lost another top leader who was driving its sweeping transformation for future wars. As the service secretary, Dan Driscoll was a leading figure in reshaping the Army's relationship with industry and accelerating its focus on drone warfare. His departure, along with the dismissal of the service's top general earlier this year, has left the Army's modernization efforts in question. The Army did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment on how leadership changes will affect these efforts. Driscoll, a former military officer and investment banker, submitted his resignation on Monday. A US official told Business Insider that the secretary spoke to President Donald Trump about the state of the Army prior to that decision. Multiple news reports have indicated that Driscoll had concerns about the Army transformation initiative amid Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's removal of top generals. Earlier reporting had identified frictions between Driscoll and Hegseth. Hegseth fired Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George in April, dismissing him roughly a year and a half before the end of what is usually a four-year term. George's firing came as a shock, with reports indicating that his removal came after disagreements between the general and Hegseth. The shifts in the service leave elements of its leadership and its transformation up in the air. Early last year, Hegseth issued a memo ordering sweeping changes in the Army; at the time, it was described as the largest shift in force structure and priorities since the Cold War. The memo directed Driscoll to "transform the Army now for future warfare," with changes ranging from flooding divisions with drones to shedding older legacy systems and reforming the acquisitions process. The total cost of the transformation was estimated to be around $36 billion over the next five years. George and Driscoll became two of the most visible leaders carrying out that transformation. Driscoll, who Trump had previously identified as a "change agent" and "disruptor," spoke publicly about which weapons programs hadn't been successful, pushed for significantly greater investments in uncrewed capabilities, and pressed the Army to work differently with industry and adopt a more commercially driven mindset. Early in his tenure as the Army secretary, Driscoll told Business Insider that there was a need for the Army to modernize ahead of a future fight. "We feel a large enough existential threat, and it is important enough that we can no longer make decisions simply based off where jobs might exist or what private companies may benefit from our decisions," he said. "Instead, we have to optimize for soldier lethality in the fight ahead." One of Driscoll's latest transformation efforts was the Right to Integrate initiative, an attempt to break down walls between weapons from different suppliers and integrate them so that soldiers can more easily connect and use different systems. In May, he told reporters he had an "aha" moment about the idea after seeing how Ukraine had successfully connected drones, sensors, and weapons into its battle management program. George was also influential in service transformation efforts. He was involved in several efforts to speed up the Army's modernization, including helping drive the Next Generation Command and Control experimentation initiative to develop a prototype for the Army's new command and control system. Another of his signature initiatives was the creation of the Army's Unmanned Assault Battalion, an experimental unit in the 173rd Airborne Brigade launched last fall to apply lessons in drone warfare from Ukraine. The idea was that the battalion would specialize in drone tactics and help spread those lessons across the force. But last month, George's acting replacement, Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army's vice chief of staff, disbanded the battalion. The battalion is participating in an exercise that will conclude this month, an Army official told Business Insider. And then it "will deliver what it learned there, together with the past year's findings, to the Army to inform force design and future experimentation." After the exercise, it will refocus as airborne infantry. The decision confused defense analysts. "This decision is quite puzzling, given the Pentagon's Drone dominance initiative and the push for the US military to integrate drones into their formations and operations," Stacie Pettyjohn, a defense expert at the Center for a New American Security, told Business Insider. "They have asked to spend billions of dollars on drones," she continued, "and forgoing an opportunity to learn from Ukraine, a partner nation that is the most experienced in the world at using drones, does not make any sense," she said. The Department of Defense has continued to signal that technological innovation and uncrewed systems are priorities, as has LaNeve, who said in a written post that "the work of change continues." At the same time, he said that the Army also needs to prioritize warfighting fundamentals and soldier readiness. The Army's broader transformation is on uncertain footing. The push for change is still there, but it is unclear whether the initiatives put forward under Driscoll and George will continue. If they do, it's unclear who will be moving them forward.

item.title: Meta is switching to Slack because it says it's better for AI agents
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.45
Get ready to hear Slack notifications if you work at Meta. The tech giant is switching over from Google Chat to Slack for internal communications, according to a memo its AI chief, Alexandr Wang, sent out this week. Meta is making the move because it says Slack is better for handling AI agents, the memo reads. "Slack is the strongest platform available today for agents, which is why we're deciding to make the switch," it says. "Slack has a rich conversational interface for agents, mature developer tooling and strong 3P integrations. While not all of us are building agents today, everyone at the company will benefit from a robust and useful agent ecosystem." Wang's comment about "strong 3P integrations" refers to third-party integrations, meaning Slack is not only attractive because of the tool itself but because it already has a large range of external tools and AI agents that can plug directly into it. The move is a major win for Slack owner Salesforce, which has been investing heavily in AI features and products. Salesforce bought Slack for $27.7 billion in 2021. Meta and Salesforce declined to comment. Google didn't respond to a request for comment. The migration also shows how Slack has capitalized on the current craze for AI agents. The product has made it easy for users to integrate AI agents into it to automate tasks, request data, and provide teams with updates. Salesforce's stock has fallen over the past year amid concerns about whether those AI agents will eventually replace the software that many workers use. The company's stock surged nearly 23% in a single day last week following an expanded partnership with Anthropic and an earnings release reporting strong results, including new annual order growth and rising subscription and support revenue. "This is not the SaaSpocalypse," Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said. "We've been hearing about this for the last two quarters, these dire predictions about the end of software, and how the models eat everything, but none of them have come true for us." Have a tip? item.title: Apple's new CEO faces an early test
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.29
It's day one for John Ternus. He has eight days to settle in as Apple's new CEO. On September 9, Apple will stage its annual iPhone pageant. The reported headliner: its first foldable iPhone. No pressure, then. Further out, reports point to an AI home hub, camera-equipped AirPods, smart glasses, and a robotic assistant. It seems Apple has no shortage of places to put AI. It still has to make AI worth putting there, though. That is Ternus' problem. Apple had a head start in the AI-assistants race. Now it is playing catch-up. Apple delayed its AI overhaul of Siri, then turned to Google's Gemini for the next generation of Apple Intelligence. You can read that as a way to avoid paying Google-sized bills for research and development. You can also read it as an admission of weakness. Then there is the people problem. Apple has suffered a talent exodus. Foundation-models leader Ruoming Pang, engineering head Frank Chu, and design VP Alan Dye all left Apple for the same rival. Yes, Meta has become something of an Apple alumni association. Ternus needs to convince Apple's best people that the future is still being built in Cupertino. He also inherits one of Tim Cook's specialties: the tightrope walk between China, tariffs, and Washington. Cook was pivotal in expanding Apple's presence in China and helping the company navigate tariffs and supply chain challenges by getting on President Donald Trump's good side. Ternus won't have to handle it alone. Cook is staying on at Apple as executive chairman, a role that includes "engaging with policymakers around the world," the company said. Still, for Ternus, a hardware man, diplomacy is a rather different type of engineering.

item.title: The mystery of a 'little red book' about insurance startup Corgi
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.20
When investor Alex Ren visited the office of AI insurance upstart Corgi early last year, he was given a copy of a little red book emblazoned with a portrait of the company's namesake dog wearing a Mao-like red hat with a yellow star. It was called: "The Mission at Corgi." Business Insider viewed images of a book with the same name and cover. Inside, it contained a series of statements — some braggy, some bellicose, all of them blunt. "Boomers are slow and bad," the 17-page hardcover declares in reference to hiring. When Business Insider asked the company about the book, it said in a statement that it was not "Corgi material." "The unapproved version currently circulating was neither created nor produced by Corgi," it said. "It was created externally and given to Corgi as a gift by an investor. The thoughts and opinions expressed in that book are those of the author and do not reflect the position or views of Corgi, unless Corgi itself has affirmed them." In a later statement, Corgi said the book did include some material produced by the company two years ago — but "nothing to do with age, for example" or the cover image. "The book you have sent and referenced is third party material that Corgi did not create or endorse," it added. The company declined to name the investor who it says made the book or how many copies it was gifted. Corgi is one of Silicon Valley's buzziest startups, viewed as a brash newcomer in an industry often stereotyped as staid. It was valued at $4 billion in a July funding round, Forbes reported, and says it has raised over $378 million since its founding in 2024. It's also achieved internet virality, thanks to its X-posting employees, its all-night cafés, and a four-legged mascot. In a January LinkedIn post, Ren, a founding member of the venture capital firm Fellows Fund, said that after Corgi CEO Nico Laqua pitched him, he visited their office in early 2025 for an hourlong meeting. "At the end, we were handed a little red book titled 'The Mission at Corgi.' It opened with a line we won't forget: 'We work hard and sleep in the office because Corgi is producing some of the most meaningful work happening on planet Earth right now,'" Ren wrote. "That level of passion, ambition, and conviction immediately stood out. We were obsessed with the mission and the belief that insurance — one of fintech's hardest categories — could be rebuilt from first principles." Ren, who said Fellows Fund later invested in Corgi, confirmed the account by phone on Monday, before telling a reporter to contact Corgi for more information. Corgi declined to comment on how or why the book was given to Ren. Two former employees said they had seen the book in the company's office. Business Insider viewed images of a hardcover book with the same title — "The Mission at Corgi" — and the same cover image. It opens with a quote attributed to Laqua: "This is a short booklet of our mission at Corgi. If you principally disagree with any of the sentiments found therein, you are not a fit." Among those who may not be seen as a fit, according to the book: employees of retirement age. "All the best athletes, warriors, and chess grandmasters are 19-30 years old," the book says. "We need young energy! Boomers are slow and bad, we need energy, creativity, and cannot have layers of redundant management." It describes which workers should be fired: those who "don't care" and underperformers. "Fire anyone who doesn't work weekends," it says. Employees sleep in the office, and each employee will receive a mattress for the workplace with their offer letter, "preferably from Costco," the book says. At another point, the book says that Corgi will do what it needs, "even if we need to sleep in the office or sell our blood on the side of the road to get there." Corgi is one of many tech startups to embrace hardcore work schedules. Terms like "996" — working 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week — are common in Silicon Valley, though it doesn't appear in the book. Founders also flex their long hours online. Laqua has publicly spoken about the company's work schedule. "If your days off happen to be Saturday and Sunday every week, then you will not have a place at Corgi," he said on a podcast in May. The little red book details a grand vision for the insurance business. It says that insurance dates back to the Bronze Age and that without it, "the entire economy would nearly instantly collapse." The company's work will "indirectly but meaningfully" contribute to human progress, the book says. "We will help humanity reach the stars, cure diseases (and live forever ultimately), create new forms of entertainment and recreation, and create new businesses that advance us in ways we don't even presently begin to appreciate," it says. The book describes Corgi's insurance competitors — including Chubb, a decades-old insurance giant it mentions by name — in violent terms. "We are coming for their throat," it reads. Chubb declined to comment. It later says that the "only 'strategy' is the blade of the knife." The book also points to a broader startup market. The problem with these companies, it says, is that they are too nice. "This is WAR!" it reads. "We make our legacies here," the book reads. "With success, we get what our forefathers would have killed for. We are brothers and sisters in arms, though there are some mercenaries as well." The book ends with an image of a Corgi in a space helmet and a spacesuit with an American flag. Do you have a tip about Corgi? Contact reporter Henry Chandonnet via email at henrychandonnet@proton.me or on Signal at henrychand.30. Use a non-work email address and device; here's our guide to sharing information securely.

item.title: As a dietitian, here's how I turn Costco's $5 rotisserie chicken into a week of easy, well-balanced meals for my family
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.13
I'm always on the hunt for quick and easy weeknight meals. As a dietitian, I know the importance of healthy eating, but as a mom of three, I also know the chaos that comes with dinner time. It can be a huge struggle to get a healthy meal on the table while juggling weeknight schedules and routines. One of my mealtime heroes is Costco's Kirkland Signature rotisserie chicken when I want to keep dinners homemade, nutritious, and high in protein. And at $5, it's an incredible value. Here are five ways I use rotisserie chicken to build balanced, protein-rich meals for my family without shortchanging us on fiber and other nutrients. When paired with a few sides, Costco's rotisserie chicken is ready for tonight's dinner. If you're feeding a family of four or more for the week, then plan on grabbing two rotisserie chickens on your way home from work. They're typically still warm by the time I get home, so I pull off the drumsticks and plate them alongside a batch of air-fried little potatoes and broccoli. This makes for a simple, balanced hot meal on day one. Before I put the rest of the chicken away, I tear it into small pieces. It's easier when it's still warm versus waiting until the next day. It takes less than five minutes to pull all the juicy meat off the bones — I timed myself just to be sure. I also keep the carcass and use it to make a batch of broth by throwing the bones into the Instant Pot with water, a dash of vinegar, onion, and any other veggies I have on hand. If I'm extra busy or low on energy that night, I'll put the carcass into a ziplock plastic bag and into the freezer. That way, I can make broth at a later, more convenient time. Shredded chicken and bean tostadas are a great way to get everyone involved in dinner. I've been loving tostadas lately, since you can buy the crisp corn-tortilla bases precooked and ready to go. For this meal, I slather each tortilla with a thick layer of refried beans — a solid source of fiber that's as important as ever when so many people aren't getting enough of it. Then I put a handful of the leftover shredded chicken on top, followed by some grated cheese. After a quick zap in the microwave, everyone can choose their remaining toppings. This could include things like salsa, sour cream, guacamole, cilantro, and pickled onions. We definitely need some more produce with this meal, so I might slice up some cucumbers or radishes for an easy side dish. This chicken-salad snack plate should be your next no-cook dinner. This is the perfect no-cook meal, great for the hot days we've had in Seattle this summer. Plus, leftover chicken salad can be an easy lunch the next day. Mix the shredded chicken up with some diced celery, mayo, a little Dijon mustard, salt, pepper, and dill. I prefer using the chicken salad as a dip served alongside my favorite almond crackers (whole-grain toast would be a good option, too). Again, the more veggies the better, so I keep pre-cut options like snap peas, baby carrots, or sliced bell pepper on hand. This ensures we'll fill up on a variety of nutrients and much-needed fiber. Pesto pasta is always a hit in my house. This is basically a flavorful combination of shredded chicken, spaghetti, tomatoes, and sauteed zucchini, tossed with pesto and sprinkled with goat cheese. I typically choose chickpea or lentil spaghetti noodles since they're naturally gluten-free and high in protein and fiber. You can make your own pesto if you'd like, but a jarred variety will do just fine. Tossing in fresh tomatoes or sun-dried tomatoes adds a great burst of color and flavor. This quick meal is a perfect end-of-summer dish when zucchini and tomatoes are in season. Make this satisfying chicken tortilla soup now and save some for later. I like making this soup using my homemade broth when I can, but if I'm out, I use a carton of bone broth as my base. To make, add the shredded chicken, a can of crushed tomatoes with green chiles, a can of black beans, a small bag of frozen corn, and taco seasoning (or other spices) to the broth. Simmer the flavors together for 15 minutes or so, and add some spinach toward the end of cooking so it can cook down. I like to put all the leftovers from this one into the freezer so I have something easy to pull out at a later date when I'm not feeling like cooking. It's a win all around as I'm then able to avoid takeout, save some money, and eat healthy. My future self is always thankful.

item.title: 9 Hotels on Working Farms Where You Can Berry Pick, Hang Out With Animals, and Eat Fresh From the Field
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.91
Farm-to-table seems to be the restaurant style of choice for many hotels around the world, but not every hotel sources ingredients (or toiletries and floral arrangements, for that matter) directly from the property. Even fewer go a step beyond, getting guests involved in the agricultural process. The nine farm stay hotels on this list are each a world of their own, surrounded by acres of land and with a range of programming that reflects the region’s distinct terroir. There are Tennessee farms where you can pick your own berries and roam on-site apiaries, sprawling reserves in New Mexico teeming with bison, and rustic estates in Portugal’s Alentejo region that teach you how to transform wool into yarn. Some are smaller, like Puerto Rico’s El Pretexto, which invites guests to explore its chicken coops and coffee agroforestry, while others resemble private Italianate villas surrounded by olive groves. Whether you fancy getting down in the dirt or simply enjoy a countryside view, below are nine hotels on working farms around the world for every kind of traveler. - Read Full ReviewWhy we love it: Harvest suppers, cider tastings, composting workshops There’s so much to love about The Newt, it’s difficult to know where to start. Made up of Hadspen House, a Georgian mansion of Somerset sandstone with 13 rooms, and former outbuildings providing another 10 rooms, each accommodation is quirky, individual, and always the height of luxury. Room One in the main house overlooks the ancient tree avenue and has a glorious marble-lined shower, while the stables rooms offer four-poster beds in the stalls and serene white-shuttered rooms in the loft. There’s a spa with an indoor-to-outdoor pool, too, and the surrounding woods, orchards, gardens, and deer park are free for guests to roam around. A lovely bar overlooks the croquet lawn, and tastings are offered in the “cyder” cellar. Then there’s the food. The open kitchen offers a tasting menu and à la carte options in the Botanical Rooms restaurant, which combines the brightness of a Victorian greenhouse with the elegance of a gentleman’s club. Look out for the sugar snaps with smoked roe and mint and the delicious roasted eggplant. In the morning, gorge on enormous croissants from the Newt baker. You just can’t go wrong with a stay at this West Country idyll. —Jane Knight - Read Full ReviewLocation: Franklin, Tennessee Why we love it: Special farm suppers, Sunday farmers market, apiary toursSouthall Farm & Inn feels all of the 25 miles away it is from the hubbub of Nashville’s neon-lit honky-tonk scene. In fact, its 325 acres are a different world entirely. This bucolic setting is a sustainable oasis designed for a resort-style immersion experience. You’ll abandon your car on arrival and instead get around on foot, bike, ATV, or by staff-driven golf cart, allowing you to explore the property at a leisurely pace. Soak in the plunge pool, get centered in a sound bath, take the kids for a zip line, eat s’mores on the deck of your cottage, and never once leave the property. (Although if you choose to, historic downtown Franklin is less than four miles away.) Amenities are designed to make the most of the land and preserve its natural beauty. Take time to notice the details, such as custom wallpaper, glazed clay plates, and freshly cut flowers. —Margaret Littman - Read Full ReviewLocation: Franschhoek, South Africa Why we love it: Daily garden tours, wine tastings, Soetmelksvlei experienceIs it a farm? A garden? A spa hotel? It’s all of the above. Since 2010, Babylonstoren has drawn day-trippers and luxury farm stay seekers to its sun-kissed swathe of land in the Cape Winelands, with whitewashed Cape Dutch architecture, monumental gardens with incredible biodiversity, and delectable farm-to-table dining. Across its 2,600-acre spread—holding everything from edible gardens to cheese rooms and wine cellars—the options to spend your time are near-endless. There are 33 sets of accommodations at Babylonstoren, and each cluster offers something a little different, but they all retain historic details like farm doors, fireplaces, thick stone walls—and a whole pile of romance. One of the latest additions to the property is Soetmelksvlei, a refurbished 1890s Cape-style farmstead that functions like an interactive museum exhibit where guests are encouraged to interact with craftspeople going about their daily chores. It’s a short drive away from the main farmhouse and offers a range of experiences that include milking cows and churning butter, but also has a restaurant where you can stop for a hearty farm lunch and a shop for old-world keepsakes. —Arati Menon - Read Full ReviewLocation: Raton, New Mexico Why we love it: Conservation efforts, bison expeditions, greenhouse toursVermejo is the closest thing to a private national park. Part of Ted Turner's conservation-driven reserve portfolio, the property spans a staggering 558,000 acres—roughly twice the size of Grand Teton National Park—across the Sangre de Cristo Mountains in northern New Mexico. The terrain rolls from shortgrass prairie to 13,000-foot alpine peaks, its valleys populated by herds of bison, elk, and horses. Unsurprisingly, there's much to do here, and it's all included in your stay: On-site ambassadors shape itineraries for guests, drawing from more than 45 guided activities. Mornings might mean a horseback ride across open grassland or casting for Rio Grande cutthroat trout in a mountain stream; afternoons, mountain biking on forest trails or shooting skeet at the range; and evenings, a wildlife drive that rivals an African safari. Lodging spans historic cottages, mountain cabins, and grand private residences with dedicated chefs. Evenings end around the fire, under skies unspoiled by light pollution—there's perhaps no better place to disconnect and relax. —S.W. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Gardiner, New York Why we love it: Take-home harvests, animal feedings, apiary toursStep onto this picturesque Auberge Collection campus, in a meadow in the shadow of New York’s iconic Shawangunk Mountains, and you feel almost as if you’ve entered the world of a Hudson River School painting. It’s that pretty. And for all its comforts, which are considerable—the instant it opened its doors in 2022, it became the premier luxury escape in the Catskills—the hotel rightly recognizes that nature is its greatest amenity. Located on a 140-acre site that was once a tree nursery and a dairy farm, Wildflower leans into the region’s agricultural heritage with a working farm that supplies ingredients for cooking classes, the hotel’s progressive New American restaurant, Clay, and many of the treatments at the excellent spa, Thistle. Guests can swing by to tour the crops, feed the animals, and collect eggs from the chicken coop (to take home or pass along to the kitchen staff at Clay to prepare for breakfast). Just 4% of the property has been developed, leaving an extensive network of forest trails for visitors to explore on their own or to visit with a guide for ramp planting or forest-bathing experiences. And it’s easy to continue drinking in the beauty of the place from the 65 rooms, all freestanding cabins, cottages, and suites. In addition to offering fireplaces, well-curated minibars, and a stylishly warm, natural design aesthetic, they have extensive private terraces and floor-to-ceiling windows framing a view of woods, meadows, or mountains. —Jesse Ashlock - Read Full ReviewLocation: Te Awanga, New Zealand Why we love it: Bird watching, shepherding experience, garden workshopsFly into the little regional airport at Napier, drive through the city's Art Deco downtown, and continue along the coast and up into the hills until you reach Rosewood Cape Kidnappers, a 6,000-acre coastal country retreat and working farm perfect for unwinding in luxury. Many guests come here to golf—the Tom Doak–designed course is legendary. But this is also an ideal spot for wildlife lovers. Rosewood Cape Kidnappers is home to Cape Sanctuary, which brands itself as “New Zealand's largest privately owned and funded 'mainland island' conservation project.” Thanks to a predator fence, pest control, habitat restoration, and species reintroduction, this is one of the best places on mainland New Zealand for native wildlife, notably birds, including kiwis.—Stefanie Waldek - Read Full ReviewLocation: Alentejo, Portugal Why we love it: Ethnobotanical walks, wool-to-yarn workshops, olive harvestsA morning saunter through this 2,000-acre estate in Portugal’s Alentejo is a sensory journey back in time. Paths carve through the montado landscape, where wildflower meadows are punctuated by cork, oak, and olive trees. Lusitano wild horses mingle with cattle; the medieval hilltop town of Monsaraz looms in the distance, and granite dolmens give a glimpse of the region’s pagan past. Although it’s just 90 minutes from Lisbon, it’s conceivable that these views haven’t changed in centuries. The same cannot be said for São Lourenço’s luxurious lodgings. Balancing the rustic and the refined, the agricultural and the artful, this elegant 40-room hotel and organic working farm excels. Humble, whitewashed farm buildings have been sensitively transformed into sophisticated suites centered on a geranium-lined courtyard. The guest activities—beekeeping lessons, foraging, and stargazing (the region is a Dark Sky Reserve)—are almost as old as the surrounding hills. Two centuries of winemaking heritage make São Lourenço a key stop-off on Alentejo’s rota dos vinhos, which winds through the region’s best wineries. Here, robust native varietals have been skilfully tempered down and pair beautifully with polished takes on traditional dishes—gazpacho, migas, and cozido stews—that are as nourishing as late nights by the firepit. Effortlessly stylish yet wholly unpretentious, this rural retreat provides a compelling case for swapping Portugal’s coast for its countryside. —Ben Olsen - Read Full ReviewLocation: Menorca, Spain Why we love it: Farm-to-table dining, organic gardens, horse ridesIn any setting or landscape, Son Vell would stand out—it’s an imposing 18th-century Italianate villa surrounded by olive and fig trees, holm oaks, chestnuts, palms, and luxuriant formal gardens. In its actual setting and landscape, amid the gently undulating agricultural fields at the western edge of Menorca, it stands out all the more. Charming as they often are, it’s probably safe to say none of the island’s other farmhouses possess this kind of dreamy, exotic elegance. The pale lusciousness of the exterior provides the basis of the design scheme throughout the 34 bedrooms—6 in the main house, 28 in 5 bungalows—and is complemented by neutral-toned textiles, limewashed timber beams, and well-judged metallic accents. The views from the villa’s upper stories are wonderful, across treetops and gardens to the ruggedly dramatic coastline, which—if the temptation to relax by the pool or feast in one or other of the superb restaurants can be overcome—cries out to be explored on foot or on horseback. Son Vell was the first hotel to open under the family-owned Vestige brand, and since then, it’s opened five more properties across Spain. If Son Vell is anything to go by, the arrival of Vestige is nothing but good news and marks the beginning of an extremely interesting period for the Spanish hotel scene. —Steve King - Read Full ReviewLocation: Cayey, Puerto Rico Why we love it: Long table dinners, cooking classes, garden toursOpened in 2018 after the devastating hurricanes, El Pretexto, a celebration of Puerto Rico’s agriculture and natural beauty, was a labor of love by the young entrepreneur Crystal Diaz. Winding mountain passes edged with greenery lead the way to a mini farm, where the second thing you notice—after the breathtaking view, of course—is the beds of lettuce, tomato, and corn plants, and banana and avocado trees. Enjoy the scenery and the fresh mountain air, laze around in a hammock, or read a book. Four villas feature wood and stone elements; all have kitchenettes. Some have terraces that offer front-row seats to a chorus of coquisl; all embrace the surrounding mountain views. This is a one-of-a-kind experience in Puerto Rico. Even the most die-hard city slickers don’t mind a few days of being a country bumpkin here. —Kathleen Squires

item.title: How I Travel: Jannik Sinner Can Fall Asleep Anywhere—Especially on a Great Hotel Couch
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.94
Jannik Sinner is with me on a cruise. Not words I ever thought I’d say. But there he was, sitting across from me as our ship, the spanking-new Explora III, proceeded to dock in Marseille. Later, we would ride the elevator together, chatting about Formula One, and even play paddle on the same court (not at the same time; I could never). We weren’t traveling together, exactly, but we weren’t exactly not traveling together, either. Sinner, who is the luxury cruise company’s global brand ambassador and helps shape its athletic and wellness routines for guests, was fresh off his Wimbledon win—and not too far removed from what would be his quest for a second US Open title. His life as the men’s world No. 1 singles tennis player, he says, is spent on the road, so a different vantage point from the sea is both welcome—and calming. “It’s so nice to be far away from everything—hidden in a way,” he says. Sinner chatted with Condé Nast Traveler about traveling by sea, his go-to comfort food on the road, and how much he longs for time at his parents’ home in South Tyrol in the Dolomites. He also explains why, if you see him dashing through an airport terminal, you should probably resist the urge to stop him for a selfie. The one region in Italy he hasn't traveled enough in—and wants to go to: In Italy, it’s hard to go wrong, because we have everything: the sea, we have mountains, we have hills. But I think Tuscany, specifically the Tuscan Hills is a little bit underrated. It's very beautiful, with a lot of sunshine, a lot of nature, and a lot of peace. I've been there once, but I would love to go back some more. The trip he could never tire of: Has to be to my parents’ home [in the German-speaking province of South Tyrol] in northern Italy, to be honest, because I left home when I was around 13 years of age. So every time I come back to see my parents or family, it's something really, really special. It's what always helps me rest and recover as well. I don’t go a lot. Maybe two or three times a year and, yeah, it's never enough. A comfort meal he orders after a long day of playing tennis: We need a lot of carbohydrates, so I would say pasta… Probably a rigatoni, which is my favorite pasta shape, with some tomato sauce, and some salad as well. When I’m on a break from playing, and I go home to my parents, it’s a wiener schnitzel, this Austrian dish which is a crispy fried veal cutlet. That’s my comfort food. The items that always make it to his carry-on: An iPad for downloading movies or a television series, AirPods because I like to listen to music, and that's it really. I'm actually a good sleeper, so during flights I sleep a lot and the time goes way faster. The one thing I wish I could carry on my travels is my mattress! For us tennis players it's very difficult because we are constantly changing beds, as well as mattresses; every tournament we sleep somewhere new. So I would say having the same bed or mattress would be so good. What he thinks of journeying by sea: I mean [the Explora III is] very, very elegant. And the quality of the food… I've eaten here now for a couple of days, and it's really, really good. I think this basically is like an amazing hotel. A hotel that moves around the world. Yesterday we were in Genova, and today we are in Marseille. You know—as tennis players—we get so much attention all the time, and are always under pressure to perform. And of course everyone handles it differently, but I always like to step away from the limelight. Back when I was young I would've never thought about escaping to the middle of the sea, but it's somewhere where I feel like you're kind of untouchable, and you can switch off your phone. And that to me is priceless. Where we'd find him hiding on a ship: Well, there’s the amazing paddle court upstairs on deck 14. But being on a ship like this, I might get away to one of the swimming pools or perhaps a jacuzzi. Favorite feature of a hotel: Quiet and calm. I don’t like a hotel that’s too busy and full of people. And I’m kind of strict about that. We play so much tennis a year and recovery periods are so important, even if it’s a short one. To perform well, you need to be more rested. Any travel rituals we should know about?: It’s more a wellness ritual. After a tennis match it’s always an ice bath for me, which I know is not that relaxing but it's important. And then of course the jacuzzi, which releases tension and relaxes the muscles. Longevity is always top of mind as a player, and it's something you know you can work towards. There’s so many new tools, and you see new routines on social media all the time that you think you might try out. A sport (other than tennis) he enjoys traveling for?: It has to be Formula One. I'm a big F1 fan, so I like to, if I have the time, go to races. Because my schedule is very busy, it's tough to do, but I do enjoy watching a race. The qualifying race in Monaco would be really cool, especially since I live there—it's a bucket-list race and qualifying is always the most exciting part. I haven't been there in person yet, but it's on my list. His favorite hotel (or cruise) amenity: I'm someone who needs a great couch in my room. I'm a big couch lover, and sometimes I fall asleep at the couch and don't move to my bed even though it's three or four meters away. So that's definitely something that makes me very happy to have. It makes me feel “at home” in a certain way. Rapid-fire time: Arriving at the airport early or just in time? Just in time. Late enough that I nearly miss my flight. Aisle seat or window seat? Window always, so I can rest my head. Restaurant or room service? It depends on scenarios, to be honest, but I like restaurants a little bit more. Gets you out of the room. Carry-on or checked luggage? I need to go with checked because we carry so much stuff, but I would love to travel only with with carry-on—my backpack, and that's it. That's a dream.

item.title: How We Pulled It Off: A Monastery Wedding With Drag Queens in Sintra, Portugal
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.84
As a couple, Taylor Rains and Carter Joyce have a shared sense of romance, particularly as it relates to travel. “Exploring the world has just helped to deepen our relationship,” says Carter. Since meeting online in 2016, they’ve spent their holiday seasons in Belgium hopping around Christmas markets. It was during their 2022 trip that they became engaged. “We got our mulled wine and got on the Ferris wheel in the main market in Brussels, and Carter proposed,” says Taylor. “It took two full rotations of the Ferris wheel for me to pick my jaw up off the ground.” It makes sense, then, that they’d want to have their wedding in a storied venue or a gorgeous destination—or both. Their early research found the Charleston-based duo looking into opulent venues, such as the Biltmore Estate in North Carolina, chateaux in France, and villas in Italy. They realized that plotting a destination wedding would allow them to curate a gorgeous experience for their loved ones. “One of our favorite things to do is share recommendations—these are the restaurants, this is the little cafe, this is the person to ask for—and we saw this as an opportunity to do that on a grander scale,” says Taylor. “We could curate all these vignettes and experiences that you, as our guests, could then enjoy and experience.” Once they viewed their wedding that way, going international was an easy decision. Ahead, the grooms explain how and why they pulled off their unique 100-guest Portugal destination wedding—which featured a fado performer, drag queens, flamenco dancers, and a ceremony set within the crumbling stone walls of a 16th-century garden—in the magical town of Sintra. Find a planner who feels like a friend When they began their planning process, Carter and Taylor weren’t sure about which country they wanted to marry in—yet they knew who they wanted to oversee the wedding. In Taylor’s research of wedding planners who specialized in European destination celebrations, he found the London-based firm Matthew Oliver Weddings, and adored their Instagram feed. “One of our criteria when we were examining portfolios was that every event and every wedding had a unique identity and felt like an extension of the couple,” says Carter. Living in Charleston, the couple are accustomed to seeing cookie-cutter weddings with an established echoing the city, and they wanted theirs to be more reflective of who they are. Matthew Oliver’s events fit that bill. “That alone made them top contenders,” he says. In their first conversation with staff planner Georgia Haldenby, about a year and a half out from their wedding, they knew she was the one. “We all clicked, and she understood us very well,” says Taylor. “We didn’t want it to be a strictly transactional relationship, like ‘Here’s the final invoice, it’s been lovely seeing you.’ We wanted it to feel a friendship.” A small snag came when the couple had to pause planning due to one of their parent’s health issues. When they came back to Georgia, they were heartbroken to learn she’d booked up the rest of the year. They reluctantly started chatting with her recommendations for another planner—and then they got a happy text “She said, ‘I don't know what voodoo you worked, but one of my couples has canceled and you guys are back on,’” Carter laughs. Check every single possible box Georgia’s first order of business was a big one: helping the grooms determine which destination they should choose in the first place. In the months they’d paused their planning, the pricing on venues in France and Italy for their desired time frame had shot up. “Prices had doubled or tripled since we’d started looking at chateaux and villas,” says Carter. “So Georgia sat us down and we had an honest conversation about budget, as well as where we’d been in the world and what places we really liked.” She then encouraged them to imagine, in a dream world, what qualities their perfect destination wedding could include. Their list was: a place they’d visited together, with historical significance, that was architecturally stimulating and beautiful, with a modern (and wheelchair-accessible) resort for guests within walking distance, and an international airport 30 minutes away that offered nonstop flights from New York, Atlanta, and DC. Better than any AI generator, their planner immediately suggested Sintra, a town in Portugal 20 miles from Lisbon known for its whimsical castles—but which also had a sprawling Ritz-Carlton property, the Penha Longa Resort, that included all contemporary conveniences as well as multiple event spaces on site. “We both lit up,” Taylor remembers. “We loved Sintra. The castles are beautiful. The Portuguese people are so nice. The food is great. It’s super accommodating. We were surprised it had not entered our minds prior, to be honest.” Choose venues for their flow During the planning process, Carter and Taylor made two trips to Portugal: one for a gut-check visit to the venues, on which they’d already put down deposits, and one for menu tastings and other final vendor conversations. They did book the Penha Longa Resort, the place that had made their planner think of Sintra in the first place, and held all of their events within the property. While the convenience and historical significance of the venues were paramount, the spaces offered additional benefits. “They were beautiful—that much is a given,” says Taylor. “But the layout of the spaces could not have worked better for the vision we had of ushering people throughout the afternoon and evening, keeping them surprised and entertained.” Their welcome dinner was held at the charming pink mansion, Casa Dos Penedos, while the wedding day was held around a monastery. The ceremony itself—which was officiated by a friend—was set within the crumbling, 16th-century, stone-walled Nuncio Gardens, built near the monastery and featuring ivy-covered stone walls, archways, and a shallow reservoir at the center. A cocktail hour following in the monastery courtyard and dinner in the Sala Dos Arcos, a dramatic space with a ceiling comprised entirely of archways. Dancing occurred in the Salão Nobre, a soaring salon with wall-to-wall carvings and a stunning carved-wood fireplace. Keep the aesthetic simple While their wedding venues were stunning in their ornate details, from the peacocks painted on the ceiling of the Casa Dos Penedos to the blue and white tiles along the courtyard, the couple wanted to go slightly cleaner and more masculine with the wedding decor they’d be bringing in. “The brief was Ralph Lauren, late ‘90s, equestrian,” says Carter. “We didn’t want to compete with the setting and the property itself,” says Taylor. “We wanted that to be more of a flourish in the last five to 10% of the design, and really let the spaces breathe.” For their welcome dinner, they brought the formality down a bit with light linens, bamboo chairs, potted herb plants on the tables, and no assigned seats. Their ceremony was spare, with only a few urns filled with dusty pink and peach roses, while dinner featured loads of thin white candles set in bronzed candelabra at staggered heights. Their florist was Atelier Decorelle, while tableware and furniture came from Rental Co. Purge your people-pleasing tendencies As Carter and Taylor put it, giving people recommendations is their love language, so they were eager to help their guests plot their trips to Portugal—whether they were coming for just the wedding weekend or expanding their vacations to visit major cities like Lisbon, Porto, and beyond. They created a wedding website that included the pertinent wedding info, like hotels and schedules, but also offered their favorite spots in all the aforementioned cities. The couple was interested in helping their guests even more—”I would have rented a bus and driven [guests] from the airport to Sintra if anybody had asked me,” cracks Taylor—but Georgia gently stopped them. “She recognized our innate people-pleasing and how it could really hurt us in the long run,” says Carter. So while they did help their immediate families book their flights and accommodations, they simply listed their planner’s own contact information so she could field all questions about transportation, timing, and other logistics. “She served as a travel agent as much as a wedding planner,” says Carter. Start the weekend with a bang. To properly welcome their loved ones to Portugal, the couple threw a Portuguese barbecue dinner on Friday night. “It was an indoor-outdoor experience, with a bar overlooking the cityscape, the mountains, and the sea,” Taylor says. “We had our guests dropped off and they walked through the forest up to the venue. When they entered, we had flamenco dancers and live musicians playing.” Flamenco dancers from Rueda Flamenca lined the garden path while guests walked in, as a nod to Taylor’s mother who is Spanish. During dinner, a musician named Manel Ferreira performed fado, the Portuguese folk music, playing guitar and serenading guests. Front load the cultural elements The fado performer wasn’t the only hit of Portuguese culture the guests received upon arrival. In their hotel rooms, guests found welcome bags offering a hand-drawn map of the area, as well as the beloved pastry pastel de nata (egg tarts) and a fan printed with the designs of azulejos, the instantly recognizable blue-and-white ceramic tiles the country is known for. Food was another major way of integrating the local culture into their wedding. Aside from the Portuguese barbecue foods at their welcome dinner, their wedding meal featured several traditional flavors, such as cod fritters and sausage, while the mains were more continental. “We tried to balance it and make the appetizers very Portuguese, and the principal plates were a fish and a meat—turbot, a very flaky white fish, and a version of beef Wellington—still with Portuguese flavors, but identifiable for all the guests,” says Carter. Consider some cultural complications The elephant in the room of their wedding planning, says Carter, was that they were a same-sex couple trying to marry in a majority-Catholic country. “Even though we know that [most of] Europe is exceptionally accommodating and supportive, there’s always that tinge of concern, like ‘How’s this going to work?’” he says. Happily, they found that their vendors went beyond accepting; they actually were “amplifying,” as he put it, noting that they actually felt more comfortable being “loud” in their affection in Portugal than they did at home in the southern United States. Don’t be too precious in the pretty spaces The couple were thrilled to work within the lavish rooms in their chosen venues, but worried aloud about the possibility of damaging the details. But the events team at the Penha Longa Resort were particularly befuddled, for example, when they fretted about high-heeled shoes damaging or scuffing the gorgeous mosaic tile on the floor of one courtyard. “‘No, the tile’s meant to be walked on. You’re meant to experience it that way,” Taylor remembers as the response. Similarly, they were concerned about the Salão Nobre, which they used for the dancing portion of the evening. What if someone spilled a drink on the wood floors, or bumped against the plaster molding? The event manager responded that “This place has been around for 600 years with people having parties and carrying on, and it will be around far longer,” Taylor recalls. “It’s meant to be lived in and enjoyed and experienced.” Find a glamorous way to stay awake The dancing portion of the evening was powered by a DJ from Your Jukebox. But the couple knew that weddings in Portugal (and much of Europe) typically last until sunrise; their own rental of the space gave them free rein until 6 a.m. “We talked to Georgia about how to keep the momentum up, other than just pumping people with espresso martinis, which we also did,” says Taylor. “But how do we usher in a new element for the last three hours without shifting locations again?” The solution was drag queens. The newlyweds surprised their guests with midnight performances from three drag performers, via Pride Talent: one who was shockingly tall (at 7’8”), one who was playing the saxophone, and one who could breathe fire (though wasn’t permitted to do so within the historic venue, which understandably did have some limits). Starchy late-night snacks came out, too, including Belgian waffles and Spanish croquettes. “The arrival of the drag performers will live forever in my mind as the most fun reaction shot of the night,” says Taylor. “Their bringing in all the guests as part of their show, to walk the catwalk or dance, really propelled the party forward for another three hours.” The glamorous event finally wound down around 3:00 a.m.

item.title: 39 Best Hotels in Tokyo for Ryokan Stays and High-Rise Views
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.34
The world's largest metropolis, Tokyo is renowned for its incredible restaurants, exceptional shopping, one-of-a-kind skyline, and plethora of gorgeous hotels. There are so many accommodation options in this glittering Japanese city—whether you're interested in a classic ryokan that lets you connect with the city's history, or a modern high-rise that feels straight out of a sci-fi movie. Whatever your budget, there are great finds to be scored, from over-the-top five-star properties for special occasions to affordable spots for solo travelers. Taking into account the vast scope of hotels and Airbnbs available—and the city’s soaring accommodation costs relative to its other offerings—choosing the best of the best is no easy feat. Some fan-favorite brands already have multiple Tokyo flagships in their portfolio, and new construction just keeps coming as the country continues to be a tourism darling. But fear not, we did the research for you. No matter what you're heading to the Japanese capital for—delicious food, a futuristic cityscape, pop-culture highlights, or historic landmarks—there's a wonderful property just waiting for you to check in. Read on for our editors' picks of the 39 best hotels in Tokyo right now. Top picks: - Best for families: Mimaru Tokyo Asakusa Station - Best for romance: The Peninsula Tokyo - Best value: Hamacho Hotel Tokyo - Best for views: Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Otemachi - Read Full ReviewYou notice the building before you notice the hotel: nine stories wrapped in corrugated, rust-colored balconies, each filled with greenery, giving the structure a scalloped silhouette. It's the work of architect Kiyoaki Takeda,who came up with the design by walking the neighborhood and cataloguing the potted plants that residents keep on sidewalks. In lieu of a lobby, there’s Pizza Tane, a 20-seat pizzeria, and you check in at a reception desk beside it. With just 14 rooms across nine floors—two per floor at most—there are few chances to cross paths with other guests. Every room gets floor-to-ceiling windows and plenty of natural light, custom-dyed paper lamps, and plants both on the balconies and inside—some of them donated by neighbors. Head up to the pocket-sized rooftop, where a few tables and chairs sit beside a surprisingly lush herb garden, where they’re even growing eggplants and olives. Guests can also use the mellow co-working space above Parklet for free. —Melinda Joe - Read Full ReviewTravelers come here for a boutique-scale Four Seasons in the most useful location in Tokyo, newly reimagined by André Fu. When the hotel opened in 2002 on the lower floors of the Pacific Century Place office tower, its 57 rooms made it an outlier in a city that equates luxury with height. Yabu Pushelberg's original interiors worked around the architectural constraints—the massive columns among them. Two decades and a year-long renovation later, Fu treated the building's quirks as inspiration rather than a problem, turning structural necessity into a set piece. The effect is faintly Alice in Wonderland. Round the lobby, and a miniature rock garden appears through the window before the space opens onto a bright lounge under triple-height ceilings, where natural oak and grey marble meet washi panelling. It’s Art Deco filtered through a contemporary Japanese lens. The crowd is a mix of business travelers, families, and canoodling couples. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewThe Royal Park Hotel Ginza 6-chome is a playful newcomer to Tokyo's most polished shopping district. Bold, graphic interiors take cues from the Kabukiza Theater around the corner—muted greens and persimmon oranges drawn from the theater's iconic curtain carry through the 273 rooms—while the yellow-and-green entrance nods to the ginkgo trees lining the surrounding streets. Rooms deliver serious comfort at a price point well below Ginza's luxury competition, with exceptionally comfortable beds across all categories, including the cheerfully appointed suites.
