The real differentiator, though, is Kobikicho Club: an authentic "snack" bar hidden behind a mirrored door in the lobby, where the karaoke continues until 1 a.m. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewSet across the 38th to 43rd floors of the Akasaka Trust Tower, 1 Hotel Tokyo is a sanctuary above the city’s neon-lit chaos. This 211-key property combines the brand’s signature nature-inspired, calming interiors with subtle local touches, from revived Japanese crafts to upcycled moss artwork. Wellness is central, with in-room meditation beds, spa-like bathrooms featuring Bamford toiletries, and a plant-ringed indoor pool. The service style at 1 Hotel Tokyo is easygoing and never stuffy. It seems like team members, dressed in hip, minimalist Uniqlo-esque gear, have been briefed to keep their manner friendly, helpful, yet laid-back. Sustainability runs through every detail: no single-use plastics, recycled glassware, water-saving showers, and the 1 Less Thing initiative, which encourages guests to leave behind one item for charity. —Adam Turner - Read Full ReviewIn the early aughts the Park Hyatt Tokyo and its indelible Kenzo Tange–inspired tiered tower so inspired Sofia Coppola that she wrote an Oscar-winning screenplay around it. And that air of enchantment is as effervescent as ever after the hotel’s 19-month closure and thorough renovation. The graceful reinvention of this cinematic legend in Tokyo’s Shinjuku should please the most loyal of patrons, including Coppola, with its simultaneously reverent and refreshing take on masterful designer John Morford’s initial vision—a noticeable ramp up of contemporary residential-esque luxury that retains its subtly moody, slightly traditional, forest-imbued je ne sais quoi, not to mention many of the original artworks that now hang with new commissions from those same Japanese talents. —Kathryn Romeyn - Read Full ReviewThe lobby is a vast, bubble-era set piece—soaring double-height ceilings gridded with geometric lights, warm wood paneling, and a glowing staircase. At 3 p.m., pilots and cabin crew roll carry-ons past families at the check-in counter, business travelers make a beeline for the Club Lounge upstairs, and women linger over afternoon tea in the Atrium Lounge. Renovated rooms lean into subdued Japanese modernism: origami-inspired geometric patterns, custom carpets with a cherry blossom motif in grey with soft pink and indigo, and touches like a wine-colored cast-iron teapot or tea. The address is technically Akasaka, but you're on the Roppongi side of it, a short walk to that neighborhood's restaurants and bars, and around the corner from the US Embassy (should diplomatic business arise). Suntory Hall is two minutes away, which makes this the obvious choice on a concert night. Toranomon Hills and Azabudai Hills are both walkable for shopping and dining. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewAn event venue and planning service first and foremost, Trunk’s incredible popularity as a hotel venue has encouraged its founder to expand throughout Japan’s capital, first with Trunk(Hotel) Cat Street, set within the street- and outdoor-wear mecca just beyond the epicenter of roaring Shibuya, then Trunk(House)—an incredible, single-room hotel located along the cobblestone alleys of Kagurazaka. “Copenhagen-chic” is the prevailing style throughout the hotel. If you’re opting for an entry-level room, pay the extra coins for a view of the park instead of the backstreets—the square footage is limited; the views of the sky and trees lend a feeling of spaciousness. Take special note of the more colorful pieces of art on the various walls—all created by artists with special needs through a not-for-profit initiative and available for purchase. —Brandon Presser - Read Full ReviewAt the fresh-faced Hotel Groove, rooms come with colorful carpets and wooden paneling to elevate the offering beyond paint-by-numbers accommodations. It's a great pick for those who aim to spend minimal time in their rooms, but want comfortable—if predictable—digs for a good sleep at the end of a busy day. A boon to older travelers or those with special needs who need extra space to move around, Hotel Groove’s sleeping quarters—beyond the entry-level superior rooms—are reasonably large compared to other properties in this price range. Floor-to-ceiling windows create an even greater sense of grandeur, and decor is functional but with a few pops of texture and color to distance the vibe from cookie-cutter hotel blocks. At the higher end are suites designed by noted Japanese artists, not to mention some traditional-style accommodations (tatami and futons), too. Coin laundry is a surprise perk for long-staying travelers. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewThe Kitano is a family-run operation that takes service seriously, but lets personality shine through in the delivery. A minute's walk from Nagatacho station, the hotel sits in the heart of Chiyoda—Tokyo’s political nerve center and home to the National Diet Building and the Prime Minister's residence, with the leafy grounds of the Imperial Palace just beyond. The lobby is airy but warm, with sand-colored stone, natural wood, and modern Japanese details like latticed screens and gold-leaf artwork behind the reception desk. Upstairs, corridors wrap around a striking double-height bamboo atrium—real moso bamboo is planted at the building's core. The crowd skews well-traveled and unhurried, mostly European and Japanese guests, many with families in tow. The 70 rooms take their design cue from Japan's four seasons, each floor dressed in a different palette: cherry blossoms for spring, cool blue waves for summer, warm coppers with maple-leaf motifs for autumn, and snow rabbits for winter. But the property really distinguishes itself through its service. The meticulousness feels personal rather than corporate. Early arrivals are greeted with tea, and the head concierge, himself a former tea master, sets the tone for a team that takes hospitality seriously. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewThe world of Muji is headquartered at its Ginza shop, a venue of department store proportions cluttered in equal measures with objects and people. The lobby of the hotel doubles as the store's highest floor, where there's a charming café and communal reading room. From there, an elevator shuttles you up to your refreshingly spare room, perched in a distinctly quieter area of the building. The entry-level rooms at Muji Hotel come with only a whisper of design; everything's as simple as can be within the confines of minimal square footage. It's like Barbie's dream Tokyo apartment, where everything's teeny-tiny and low-slung—but the toilet still has all the expected bells and whistles. Come to live in the wonderful world of Muji for a few days. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewThis winner for small wallets outpaces its competitors in both the decor and wellness categories. Guests here are international travelers on the hunt for exceptional value sans credit card point deals. Most are first-time travelers to Japan who want to be in the center of the action and fully immerse themselves in the country's visual culture. This tower of tiny rooms is a smart place to start since the decor is inspired by traditional ryokans found mostly in rural Japan. The friendly staff will gladly guide you to the hundreds of restaurants littered throughout Shinjuku, Tokyo’s most electric, all-night neighborhood. Truly tight budgets shouldn’t wince at the hotel’s entry-level product—although the rooms are closet-sized, clever attention has been paid to maximizing the efficiency of the layout and giving the rooms a distinct Japanese touch: a low-slung bed, modern blond-wood furniture, and a small tatami area. Larger rooms allowed the designers more space to really go all-in on the ryokan sensibilities within the bones of a city-center business hotel. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewWhen it opened in 2005 in the Shiodome area, Conrad Tokyo neatly fit in among the pantheon of international luxury brands. More than two decades later, it remains as eye-catching as ever. Smack in the middle of the ground floor, a glossy red sculpture marks the moodily lit entrance and hasn’t lost its dramatic effect. Up on the 28th floor, a tall lobby soars with bold, black lines, which are warmed with light boxes dangling from the ceiling. It's a business hotel, but it's dressed to impress. The King Room Bay View hides nothing: windows do, in fact, frame Tokyo Bay. But even better, the panoramic view also includes the lush Hamariku Gardens, which flourish at the foot of the hotel. Modern furnishings borrow local motifs, whether they're the bedside lamps that vibe with Japanese lanterns or the Sumi-e cherry blossoms painted above the bed and woven across the floor’s lightly patterned carpet. —Keith Flanagan - Read Full ReviewFufu Tokyo Ginza is an urban oasis in every sense, with 34 suites boasting private gardens and natural hot spring baths sourced from Atami, all perched above the Ginza 1-chome intersection with direct metro access below. It's a rare property that makes the center of Tokyo feel genuinely still. The design is contemporary Japanese minimalism—shoji sliding doors, washi paper lamps, seasonal ikebana, a green tea–inspired scent threading through the common spaces—but with enough warmth to keep things from feeling austere. The first urban property from Fufu Japan, a brand known for intimate onsen retreats in quieter corners of the country, the Tokyo outpost, which opened in November 2025 inside the Hulic Ginza Building, takes the brand's signature stillness and drops it into one of the most electric neighborhoods in the country. Step onto your leafy private balcony and you're gazing out over Chuo-dori, the glittering boulevard that transforms into a car-free pedestrian paradise on weekends. Located in Ginza—Tokyo's answer to Fifth Avenue, and then some—the area surrounding the hotel is lined with flagship fashion houses, jewelers, and upscale dining options. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewAccor's first luxury hotel in Tokyo, the Fairmont is a serene perch above Tokyo Bay where warm tones, plush textiles, and wide, softly lit corridors create a soothing, sophisticated atmosphere. Thoughtful Japanese art and design details surface throughout, right down to the delicate botanical paper-cut installations in the elevators. Fairmont's first foray into Japan takes up floors 35 to 43 of the Maki & Associates–designed Blue Front Shibaura South Tower. With 217 rooms, the shining stars of the property are the Fairmont Gold Suites, which occupy the southwest corners of each guest room floor. From the living room, views sweep across Tokyo Bay to the east and out over the city's sprawl to the south and west, with Tokyo Tower front and center and, on a clear day, Mount Fuji in the distance. The bedrooms face the tower directly, and waking up to raise the blackout shades on that view is a delight. —M.J. - Read Full ReviewHoshinoya Tokyo is a serious, serene vertical ryokan hidden within the city’s corporate heart. Behind a massive cypress door, tatami floors, hushed rituals, and a deep sense of reverence replace Tokyo’s neon dazzle. Rooms are minimalist sanctuaries dressed in washi screens and ikebana florals and come with custom kimonos by designer Jotaro Saito, while communal lounges on every floor encourage slow tea sipping and quiet reflection. Dining is traditional and guest-exclusive, from restorative Japanese bento breakfasts to multi-course dinners that resurrect fading regional recipes. The highlight is the rooftop onsen (Tokyo’s rare true hot spring) fed by mineral-rich waters from nearly 5,000 feet underground. Service is exemplary omotenashi: graceful, intuitive, and—if you follow all the rules—warm. It’s not about views but instead, stillness, ritual, and retreat. An immersion into old Japan, improbably stacked 17 stories high. —Nicole Trilivas - Read Full ReviewIn Tokyo's Takanawa Gateway City—a well-connected development in Minato City—this new JW Marriott outpost is a surprisingly tranquil sanctuary for busy travelers. For JW Marriott fans, and particularly those who care about their Marriott Bonvoy points, the brand's entry into Japan is an exciting one. In keeping with the brand's global ethos, they focus on pure comfort, slinky settings, and at-your-service attendance, with the privacy and serenity that most Tokyo visitors will crave after soaking up the city's energy. Moody, low-lit hallways guide visitors to the rooms, the defining feature of which is a huge window looking out upon the sprawl of the city. Wood paneling from the doors to the armoire to the ceiling lends a warmth to the space, punctuated by glossy acrylic and velvet in tones of gray. The room has a global feel—nothing too distinctly Tokyo—though the chance to see Mount Fuji peeking through the clouds from some rooms will certainly ground you in the destination. The breakfast buffet, lavish in volume but also variety, should be your first sign that you will eat well here. Come dinner, Kakō offers seasonal ingredients in a tasting menu format, while Saki is an eight-seat experience led by Michelin-starred chefs. —Megan Spurrell - Read Full ReviewFor a serene walk through history, Hotel Gajoen Tokyo is an artful sanctuary that embodies local culture at every turn with over 2,500 pieces of Japanese art. You’ll embark on a sensorial journey from the moment you enter—think murals for your eyes, waterfalls for your ears, and culinary wonders for your taste buds. The peaceful serenity of the rest of the hotel extends into its guest rooms, which offer an oasis from city life. The rooms are more muted in color, allowing for a calming transition into me time. A pleasant surprise is the in-room steam sauna, which is offered in all accommodations, regardless of room type. Coupled with the whirlpool bath, city views, and spacious square footage, you’ll be whisked away into private luxury. With seven restaurants and a pastry shop, there is no shortage of choice for food here—traditional Japanese, Chinese, New American, and Italian included. It's located in Meguro City, a bit less touristy of an area that allows for a more local experience. And as long as you’re up for about a 10-minute walk uphill to the subway, it’s a quick train ride to most other parts of the city. —Taylor Mead - Read Full ReviewRising to the upper floors of the Nihonbashi Mitsui Tower, the 38th-floor lobby of the Mandarin Oriental is like a gallery to the capital’s best angles. It’s the same in the rooms: No matter the category, the view is paramount from your tranquil retreat in the sky, as the frenetic financial district eases down below and, on cloudless days, Mount Fuji glistens in the distance. Comfort is prime here, too. Beds are as supple as the sheets are slippery. And if you can’t find a perfect pillow on the extensive “pillow menu,” it’s not the feathers—it’s you. Room service can get expensive, but the menu itself is so long and varied (from macaroni and cheese to okayo don) that it’s worth a look. And yet, there are so many dining options on the property—from an actual pizza bar to haute Cantonese to a silver-lined French restaurant—that every in-house venue deserves a gander. For example, Sushi Shin by Miyakawa is perhaps the city’s most atmospheric sushi restaurant: A nine-seat L-shaped counter, made from a 350-year-old cypress tree, sits next to a floor-to-ceiling window that perfectly frames Tokyo Skytree. Dip sushi as the sun dips, too, and the city lights up by nightfall. If you care to step outside, the location is convenient. It’s just around the corner from famous kimono shops and department stores, and Ginza is a short stroll away. —K.F. - Read Full ReviewA ryokan-style hotel complete with mineral-rich onsen water set in the heart of Tokyo’s coolest neighborhood—need we say more? We will. Like the quaint Japanese inns found deep in the countryside, Yuen Bettei Daita leans hard into traditional wellness, and has become a favorite among international visitors and staycationing Tokyoites alike. The multi-course menus in the restaurant Tsukikage pay tribute to a panoply of seasonal ingredients. Plus, you're smack dab in the middle of Shimokitazawa, largely considered to be Tokyo’s most fun cluster of city blocks and a global hub of streetwear fashion. Expect a scatter of traditional and modern construction replete with chic espresso shops, vintage clothing stores, and plenty of curry parlors and ramen joints. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewOnly a few blocks away from Omotesando-dori, the city’s most coveted thoroughfare of luxury retail, the Aoyama Grand attracts a mod mix of young professionals in its various international dining venues. Upstairs, hotel guests are an assortment of domestic and international travelers who prefer more intimate digs in a trendy ‘hood to taking up residence in one of the more corporate quarters of the city. The loft-style rooms don’t shy away from bold furniture, light fixtures, and wall art. And out the floor-to-ceiling windows are views of one of the coolest neighborhoods in the world. Inside tip: Skip the six interior rooms, which face a light well rather than having windows looking out over the urban sprawl. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewExpect nothing but ultra-polished old-school Japanese hospitality. Retro luxury is alive and well at the Okura, and for a fraction of the cost of some of the city’s other high-end players. The mid-mod lobby is practically a museum dedicated to Japan’s post-war flourish in the 1960s, when the whole world witnessed the country’s ascent to the modern global stage. Now the Okura’s at it again with a phalanx of next-gen businessmen lounging on the lobby’s Eames- and Juhl-inspired furniture. Even if you’re not staying on-property, it’s worth checking out the hotel's diverse eating options from hallowed kaiseki multi-course meals to more playful teppanyaki options. Fun fact: the property lays claim to inventing teppanyaki—hot plate cooking with a pinch of chef acrobatics designed to delight visiting dignitaries during the 1964 Olympics. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewSmack dab in the middle of Shibuya’s Dogenzaka area, IHG’s Hotel Indigo Tokyo Shibuya is changing the face of the neighborhood from seedy hotels to trendier digs. Design details are a bit prescriptive, but no one seems to mind as the location is unbeatable and the cleanliness of the brand-new build earns an A+ from us. You can’t go wrong with any of the rooms here—they’re all lofted high enough in their tower to offer views of Shibuya and beyond below. Take your pick of your favorite angle: direct eyeshot over the Scramble Crossing, the busiest pedestrian crossing in the world; Mount Fuji in the distance, visible on a clear day; or simply the endless sprawl of the metropolis. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewA budget-friendly hotel disguised as a luxury stay, the Gate Hotel’s glass tower rises up over a bustling intersection in Ginza, offering those quintessential Lost in Translation views. The first thing you’ll notice when you step off the elevator is a lively Champagne bar inhabiting the lounge-style lobby on the building’s fourth floor, filled with a mix of hotel guests and local business folk enjoying an after-work coupe. The front desk around the corner may seem like an afterthought, but au contraire—service is as polished and capable as any of the city’s five-star offerings. Spic and span rooms come with a brightly colored accent pillow to enliven otherwise dim, nightlife-inspired decor. Light sleepers may want to request to avoid rooms facing the train tracks—though the double-glazed windows do an effective job of blocking out noise. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewA Tetris tower with lush greenery sprouting off the balconies, Hamacho is a plot twist for those who think cheap hotels in Tokyo are relegated to capsules and by-the-hour hotels. This new multi-use concept, proffering teensy hotel rooms and long-term living spaces, is breathing new life into an old-town neighborhood with more wooden roofs than steel-and-glass buildings. If you're opting for the smallest rooms, make sure you don't bring a large suitcase—there won't be space—but no one does chic efficiency better than Tokyoites. Spend a little more for a larger room and you'll get a shrub-lined terrace, city views, and plenty of sunlight. Clean design and perfect housekeeping keep the rooms feeling spare but luxe. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewLike the bulk of luxury brand hotels in Tokyo, the 164-room Andaz Tokyo commands a series of floors at the top of a shared skyscraper—except, unlike most skyscrapers, Toranomon Hills happens to be among the tallest. Check-in reflects this higher perspective as guests arrive on the 51st-floor Andaz Lounge. Instead of starting the process behind a counter, check-in happens in the lounge, offering a relaxed introduction that's more like a casual conversation than a stiff transaction. Blessed with edgy architecture, the rooms take shape along the skyscraper's rounded corner. The result? A panorama of floor-to-ceiling windows curving like an IMAX screen around the room’s focal point. Midcentury-inspired interiors boast moss-green carpeting, maroon leather chairs, white walls, and handsome walnut or color-blocked surfaces. —K.F. - Read Full ReviewPocketed between Shibuya and Harajuku, just off of the ultra-trendy Cat Street, Trunk(Hotel) is marked by a façade of glass, black steel, and stone, softened by the timber decks and ferns that line the wraparound terraces on each of the four floors. It’s a showstopper, for sure, but one that feels part of the neighborhood. Inside, a subdued vibe takes over common areas—all of which feel like a lounge, equally suited for a MacBook, a latte, or a cocktail. The Living Suite includes a lofted space for additional guests (up to four), while the interiors are all crafted by Japanese designers. There are only 15 rooms spread across two buildings here—meaning there’s more to this place than beds: The lobby café and bar slings just as many lattes as cocktails, and the main restaurant, Trunk(Kitchen), brings local flavor to international staples (burrata, for example, from a shop in Shibuya). —K.F. - Read Full ReviewThere’s an unspoken playbook for most luxury hotels in Tokyo: loft your rooms at the top of an office tower so guests can have unobstructed views of the sprawling city. The OMO5 Tokyo Gotanda has done exactly that, only its entry-level pricing is about one-sixth of the cost of a stay at one of Tokyo’s international luxury brands. Of course, the rooms are smaller and have fewer of the fancy bells and whistles, but you’ll still find eager service here, not to mention bold, big swings with the expressive decor. Also, while many of the city’s luxury hotels are relegated to more corporate neighborhoods, this property has sprouted up on the cooler west side of the city, only a stone’s throw from trending hubs like Meguro. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewPart of Hyatt’s Unbound Collection, the Hotel Toranomon Hills has the business traveler in mind, but that shouldn’t deter leisure tourists either. One of the biggest selling points is a dedicated hangout area modeled after an airport lounge. There’s plenty of complimentary coffee and snacks, but the best part is the resting room and shower facilities. If you arrive before check-in (or have a late departing flight), you can wash off the jet lag upon landing and start your day. Like flipping through a Danish design magazine, the hotel’s decor is pared back without being overly spartan. We do, however, recommend upgrading to a premium room—it’s worth the extra spend to indulge in a little more space, better views, and a few extra Scandi-style flourishes that’ll go great with the view of Tokyo Tower outside. —B.P. and T.M. - Read Full ReviewReady for some numbers? This five-star hotel commands the top nine floors of one of Tokyo's tallest buildings—and windows place you at eye-level with Tokyo’s second-tallest structure, Tokyo Tower. Inside is no less humble, and the restaurants and bars feel rich and handsome with dark finishes, plush chairs, and slick sights. There are two main views on offer—the Tokyo Tower view and the Mount Fuji view. Generally, Japanese guests want Fuji (really only visible on clear days with low humidity—it’s far), while visitors are keen to glimpse the city’s orange version of the Eiffel Tower (a few feet taller than the real thing, for those who are keeping track). Suites are double the size of the rooms and feel like a proper apartment in the sky; a great choice if you’re planning on sticking around for a while. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewThe collection of Mitsui Garden Hotels has a strong reputation in Japan for providing quality accommodations at prices that don’t break the bank—the Ginza-Gochome property earns bonus points for its great location and Edo-style baths inside. Most Tokyo hotels cater to a mix of business and leisure travelers—there are mostly tourists here; savvy visitors who like their lodging to have a distinct sense of place. Although most of the furniture is agnostic in style, the old-school nods to Japan feel welcome and never gaudy. Mitsui Gardens is a budget-friendly concept from Mitsui Fudosan, a well-established Japanese hospitality brand that has a keen eye for serving luxury travelers as well. Standard rooms have limited views from the windows, but the trade-off is the quietness in an otherwise busy neighborhood. Go for the Deluxe Twin room, which fuses East and West design—think a quaint tatami sitting area, low-slung beds, but a souped-up entertainment center and ultra-modern bathrooms. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewWith the opening of the Otemachi sister hotel to the longstanding Marunouchi property, the Four Seasons has reestablished itself as a major force to be reckoned with when choosing among the finest places to stay around town. Otemachi sits more in a financial hub than a proper neighborhood, but it’s a stone’s throw from bustling Ginza and temple-ridden Asakusa—and the gridded streets make it abundantly easy to navigate on foot. In the same space, find guests and ladies who lunch, sipping high tea, dining on Instagrammable snacks, and enjoying the unobstructed views of Mount Fuji across the lush gardens down below. Head farther into the property to find a passageway to some of the best dining in the city, and upstairs for rooms so plush—yet also somehow embracing Japanese austerity—that you’ll never want to leave. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewPaper walls, tatami floors, and oversized bathing suites are par for the course in this ryokan in the heart of the city; a fun way to combine the tenets of Japanese hospitality with the spirit of a city hotel—one that doesn’t hold you captive, but lets you explore your surrounds guilt-free, then retreat to your throwback digs. The clever idea: to take a few low-floor rooms in an aging hotel and completely reimagine them as a traditional Japanese inn similar to one that you’d usually find on the hillside of a quaint rural village. The secret perk of staying in one of the 16 Hanakohro rooms is unfettered access to the campus’s collection of executive lounges—one in all three of the towers—each filled with coffee bars, a snack carousel, and plenty of private seating nooks. Within the confines of the ryokan is a fourth lounge where guests can enjoy their oversized Japanese breakfasts and sample complimentary spirits—sake and umeshu—in the early evenings. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewThe decadent Bulgari Hotel Tokyo crowns the cloud-brushing apex of the 45-story Tokyo Midtown Yaesu tower, just opposite Tokyo Station. Against a backdrop of sultry black granite with pops of jewel tones, the deluxe hotel smoothly blends contemporary Italian design with Japanese craftsmanship and a glamorous sprinkling of Bulgari heritage. Picture hand-blown Murano lights suspended from temple-like wood ceilings; traditional Japanese textile motifs recreated in Venetian mosaic tiling; and, adorning the walls, photographs of celebrities visiting the Roman flagship in the 1950s, plus vintage advertising and jewelry sketches. The 98 guest rooms balance Japanese touches (woven bamboo wall vases, modern sliding screens, gold-flecked bed throws by Kyoto kimono textile masters Hosoo) with warm saffron fabric headboards, natural elm wood, and sexy black-granite bathrooms. —Danielle Demetriou - Read Full ReviewMimaru has established itself as the indispensable apartment-hotel brand that’s perfect for vacationing families or for those with dietary restrictions who need to prepare some of their own meals. Consider this entry on our list as an endorsement of all of the Mimaru locations across Japan’s capital—pick the location that most suits your travel tastes, be it this location among Tokyo’s old temples, Ginza’s fashionable department stores, or bustling Shinjuku. Tasteful Tokyo apartment decor prioritizes streamlined design, but this hotel is located on the doorstep of Tokyo’s most popular temple, Senso-ji, and its delightful shopping street, Nakamise-dori, which features snack and souvenir stalls that date back over a century. And with multiple bedrooms and bunk beds, there are plenty of configurations for visiting families or large groups of friends. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewOne of Tokyo’s most iconic pieces of art is not in fact in one of its museums—it’s in the lobby of the Peninsula Tokyo. The Lying Dragon Gate (which looks like a giant wooden eye) attracts legions of curious outsiders who sneak in for a glance. And when they walk through the lobby, they are immediately ensconced in the coziness of the entry’s dark wood and heavy fabrics. Rather than splurging on a suite upgrade at a middle-tier hotel, it’s worth eking into the entry-level rooms here, which never skimp on the Peninsula’s signature luxuries: plush interiors, lavish toiletries, and, most importantly, plenty of space. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewJapan’s capital is many things—sprawling, neon-lit, nocturnal—but one word not often used to describe it is relaxing. Something guests will forget about while floating 34 floors above ground, inhaling and exhaling with a meditation teacher in a white space, distracted only by vivid sunset views. Aman has, of course, long been a byword for a certain kind of crisp, zen wellness. The lobby still turns heads, with its towering ceiling, abstract blooms, and kimono-clad musician plucking the strings of a koto. The bedrooms always seem more akin to mindfulness spaces, with their aromatic hinoki wood, sliding screens, and staggered levels. The food and the service are impeccable—of course they are—but the spa is the real scene-stealer, a place of complete sensory purity that hovers unperturbed over the fizzing city. —B.P. - Read Full ReviewIt’s not easy being the Aman's new little sister, whose minimalist temples set the benchmark for escapist luxury. Yet when Janu Tokyo, the inaugural flagship, launched in Japan last year, it quickly made its mark with a playful, sociable spirit and—something of an anomaly in the Aman cosmos—splashes of color in the interior. The hotel, whose name means “soul” in Sanskrit, rises up to the 13th floor of a tower in the heart of Azabudai Hills, a major new urban development in Tokyo. It’s home to a culinary constellation of food and drink venues, including relaxed Janu Mercato, an Italian restaurant, and intimate sushi spot Iigura. A vast, four-level spa spans over 43,000 square feet, and 122 guest rooms with serenely minimalist decor hint at Aman's DNA. —D.D. - Read Full ReviewThe legendary property, so named as it’s the closest hotel to the Imperial Palace, lures wealthy Japanese guests with its demure luxury gloss; now, international travelers have gotten wise and are starting to book in as well. Back in the early 2010s, the Palace Hotel doubled down on its commitment to quality and completely demolished its historical property that was erected in the early 1960s, in time for the first Tokyo Olympics. A glimmering new luxury stay was born anew, with all the contemporary touches but maintaining its sedate charm born 50 years prior. When you think of modern Japanese design, it’s not these rooms—the decor at the Palace, while less than two decades old, feels like a retro nod to an earlier vocabulary of modernity. Muted beige and a palette of floral colors are a subtle nod to the ample views of the Imperial Gardens below. —B.P. FAQ: What is the best area of Tokyo to stay in? Pairing a luxury hotel with the right neighborhood can be a conundrum in Tokyo, where many modern high-end properties occupy the upper floors of skyscrapers in business districts—a model the Park Hyatt Tokyo popularized in Nishi-Shinjuku in the 1990s, since replicated across the city's corporate precincts. Consider Central Tokyo like a clock face along the JR Yamanote loop. For a fashion-forward base, look to the lower-left quadrant—around seven to nine o'clock—near Shibuya, including Jingumae, Daikanyama, Nakameguro, and Shimokitazawa. If history is more your speed, aim for two o'clock: Asakusa and the surrounding Shitamachi ("lower town") districts, which retain an older Edo-era street sensibility. Around three o'clock, Ginza and Marunouchi combine polished shopping with a strong cluster of luxury hotels, while nearby Toranomon has emerged as an enclave of design-driven high-rises. For serious food lovers, geography matters. The Ginza area places you within walking distance of many of the city's most acclaimed restaurants and cocktail bars. Shibuya and Shinjuku offer broader hotel options with easy access to lively dining districts, from yokocho alleys to natural wine spots in Ebisu, Daikanyama, and Nakameguro. For a more atmospheric base, Asakusa puts you close to emerging scenes in Kuramae and Kiyosumi-Shirakawa, known for specialty coffee and small independent eateries. How long should you stay in Tokyo? Four nights is the minimum needed to move beyond Tokyo's headline sights and begin to grasp its scale and texture. The city is made for unhurried wandering—lingering over dinner, ducking into a tiny specialty shop, spending an afternoon in a single neighborhood. Up close, it feels less like a sprawling metropolis than a patchwork of distinct enclaves. If Tokyo is part of your broader Japan itinerary, consider adding another day or two at the end of your trip. By then, you'll be more attuned to the country's rhythms and better equipped to go deeper, whether that means drinking at an eight-seater bar, finding time for proper omiyage (souvenir) shopping, or revisiting an area that deserves a second look. How do you get around Tokyo? A map of Tokyo’s metro system may seem intimidating with its dozens of interconnected subway lines—some managed by the government, others privately operated—but traveling aboard is now a breeze with the tap-to-use Suica and Pasmo cards available on your smartphone. English signage is abundant and trains are virtually always on time. For taxis between inconvenient points, or for when your luggage becomes too cumbersome (shopping is an inevitability in Japan!), there are ranks at all of the city’s major train stations, and your hotel can easily hail you a car—plus, they all accept credit cards. App users should prioritize GO for a ride-share vehicle. Note that passengers should never touch a taxi’s door; your driver will push a trigger that both releases and closes the hinges as you enter and exit. When is the best time to visit Tokyo? Tokyo’s busiest season is late March to early April, when cherry blossoms draw visitors from around the world and hotel rates can double. Book hotels at least four to six months in advance—earlier for top properties. Golden Week (late April–early May) and Obon (mid-August) also see heavy domestic travel, while Lunar New Year (late January–February) brings increased international traffic. Autumn foliage in November is another high-demand period. For better value, consider February or early December, when rates soften and the city feels calmer. Note that many independent restaurants close from around December 28 to January 5, though hotels often host festive New Year programming. How do you travel with luggage in Tokyo? Traveling with luggage in Japan is remarkably easy. Most hotels can arrange door-to-door luggage delivery (takkyubin), sending suitcases to your next hotel or the airport, often overnight. Forms are available at the front desk, and the service is efficient, reliable, and reasonably priced—allowing you to navigate trains comfortably and considerately. If you plan on taking the Shinkansen with very large bags (over 63 inches total dimensions), you must reserve a seat with access to the rear luggage space when booking. The reservation is free, but space is limited; boarding without one may result in a 1,000 yen (around $6) fee. How we choose the best hotels in Tokyo Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. More Tokyo recommendations Read our complete Tokyo travel guide here, which includes: This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 20 Fall Getaways From NYC for Apple-Picking, Wine-Tasting, and Leaf-Peeping
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.32
All the leaves are brown, and the sky is turning gray…well, not quite yet, but you can't stop us from dreamin'. Though instead of California, our seasonal hopes and wishes turn to the hues of fall foliage season just within reach. And if you live in and around the Big Apple, there's no better way to take your sweet time soaking in the vistas without carving into precious OOO hours than checking into one of the best weekend fall getaways around NYC. The most idyllic towns on the East Coast, charming enough to make any Transcendentalist swoon, are but a hop (in your car) and a skip (on a train) away—think the Hudson Valley, the Catskills, the Berkshires, the Adirondacks, and even some tucked-away corners of Pennsylvania and New England. And there are plenty of adorable hotels in these areas ready to welcome you with a warm flannel blanket and a generous mug of hot chocolate to kick off a cozy stay. The properties you see below are some of our editors' favorites because they go above and beyond being a place to rest your head. They're the secluded cabins snuggled into the woods with modern suites and crackling fireplaces. They're the lovingly restored inns that embody the souls of their small towns, and the multihyphenates that also function as cider mills, apple orchards, and pumpkin patches. Most of all, they're the best excuse to take that romantic getaway or family road trip you've been putting off. Without further ado, find our 20 favorite properties for weekend fall getaways around NYC—we promise taking an extra day or two off won't hurt. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Skaneateles, NY With a can’t-miss farm-to-table restaurant, an impeccable wellness area, live music, and a welcoming upstate atmosphere, Skaneateles Fields Resort & Spa is a mini-retreat that will satisfy all your off-the-grid cravings as an urbanite or Skaneateles resident. With 89 total rooms, options range from deluxe kings to double queens, as well as a family-style room with multiple semi-private sleeping areas for those traveling in a group. This is the kind of resort where I would have made core memories as a kid, with pools, trails, nine-hole putting, a pond (essential for childhood shenanigans), and nightly s’mores by the firepit. There’s also a game room with two racing games, a duck claw machine, and an old-school Pac-Man that was born out of the vision of the owner’s own young daughter. The caring staff has truly built something special here, and walking through the lobby every morning feels akin to being the suave, popular quarterback walking down a high school hallway, getting fist-bumps from everyone who passes. —Bridget Knowles Fall festivities: Welcome to the Finger Lakes, New York’s biggest wine region, where a Riesling is the glass to order, but there's much to discover beyond the area's famous bottles. Find all the fall foliage your heart desires and then some as you hike the 1.7-mile loop around Bahar Preserve and Carpenter Falls, where you'll get a chance to spot the trail's 90-foot waterfall misting the changing leaves. Bring home one of the season's best souvenirs by apple-picking at Beak & Skiff Apple Orchards to round off your trip. How to get there: Take the Amtrak Empire Service from Penn Station to Syracuse, and from there rent a car or take the regional bus to Skaneateles. If you're driving from the city, the route will take just over four hours. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Stockton, NJ For a woodsy escape to the Delaware River Valley, the Stockton Inn puts you in close reach of New Hope, Lambertville, and Frenchtown—each worth exploring for picturesque main streets, surprisingly good restaurants, and robust vintage shopping scenes. Brimming with history (once a place of retreat for F. Scott Fitzgerald and Jackie Kennedy Onassis), the 300-year-old inn was reinvigorated in 2024. While the interior design feels delightfully contemporary, every now and again you’ll get a glimpse of the past—for example, in the museum-worthy hand-signed registry of former guests splayed open in the guest lounge. The hotel houses nine rooms, split between the original inn and neighboring carriage houses, and each features king-sized beds, white marble bathrooms, and Sangra de Fruta bath products. Fresh pastries are walked in daily from nearby Stockton Market and made available in the guest lounge, while the Stockton Inn Restaurant, helmed by chef Bob Truitt, is a seasonal eatery that’s a destination in its own right. Perhaps one of the best ways to explore the area is with the hotel’s complimentary bikes, which you can take along the D&R Canal Towpath for a scenic ride along the Delaware River. —Jessica Sulima Fall festivities: The placid region of Bucks County has a certain celebrity allure, with stars like Leonardo DiCaprio and Justin Bieber spotted popping into town. But there’s far more to this bucolic stretch of land than its A-listers. Get to know its architectural spirit on a guided tour of Japanese woodworker George Nakashima’s home in New Hope, which is ensconced by the gorgeous golden treeline. And don’t leave the area without grabbing a PSL at Lambertville Trading Company (which also pioneered the coffee ice cube) just across the New Jersey border and hitting up the Golden Nugget, an expansive flea market where your next favorite comfy sweater is just waiting for you to pick it out. How to get there: Ride the Amtrak Keystone Service from Penn Station to Trenton, New Jersey. From there, book a local taxi service to Stockton. If you're driving, the route will take just shy of 90 minutes. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Big Indian, NY Big Indian isn’t Woodstock. It’s not even Phoenicia. It’s small and tucked away. That’s one of the best things about the location: the sense that you’re further away from things than you really are, and that makes it the perfect place to settle in and hunker down. But if being sedentary isn’t your thing, the McKenley Hollow Trailhead starts at the property line, and there are several other great hikes (the Hunter Mountain Trailhead, for instance) and attractions (West Kill Brewery) within driving distance. This cozy getaway is designed for vintage lovers and hygge seekers—and is almost guaranteed to make it onto your Instagram feed. Tucked deeper into nature than its older sibling in Windham, Eastwind Oliverea Valley derives its special sauce from its harmony with its surroundings, complementing rather than taking away from the landscape. Its wood-fire-warmed lounge, sauna, and proximity to ski slopes make for ideal companions as the mercury drops. A small but excellent seasonal food menu and cocktail list round out its offerings. —Arati Menon Fall festivities: Eastwind Oliverea Valley is a property made for fall. Case in point: its firepits for s'mores roasting, saunas for warming up from the crisp fall chill, and on-site Dandelion Restaurant & Bar, where hearty root veggies, crisp apples, and sumptuous squashes are the high notes on the menu. Should that not be enough to satisfy your wanderlust, stretch your legs on the McKenley Hollow Trail, which starts just steps from the hotel. How to get there: The easiest way to reach Big Indian is by renting a car and making the 2.5-hour drive, but it is possible to make the trek from Port Authority on the Trailways ADT P704 bus that will drop you off right in town. The drive should take just under 3.5 hours. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Manchester, VT The Weston is the latest endeavor of the Sharp family, whose impressive hospitality lineage includes The Carlyle and Gramercy Park Hotel in New York City and the Beverly Wilshire in Los Angeles. Formerly the Inn at Weston, the two-building property with nine uniquely designed rooms underwent a sweeping two-and-a-half-year renovation that left no detail unattended. Visiting the exquisitely restored property feels like being hosted in your well-traveled aunt’s country home. Turns out, there's a good reason for the hotel’s worldly, yet distinctly personal, atmosphere: Much of The Weston’s decor is sourced from the Sharps’ personal art and antique collection. The small-but-mighty spa offers massages and facial treatments featuring the Natura Bisse skincare line. Overall, The Weston shines during winter, but remains a lovely getaway in nature regardless of the season, with plenty of year-round activities available both on- and off-site. —Hannah Towey Fall festivities: Ditch the Central Park horse carriages and opt for a tractor ride through the corn maze at Equinox Valley Nursery. Make sure you go jack-o'-lantern shopping through the giant pumpkin patch before you leave. Afterwards, take a deep breath and let the alpine cure of the mountain air work its magic. While you could also break into a sweat hiking up nearby Prospect Rock or Equinox Mountain, save your energy and leaf-peep in style by riding the sky gondola up Stratton Mountain. Manchester itself is just as worth perusing as its scenic landscapes, with the Hallmark-movie-worthy Northshire Bookstore and the art lover's haven that is the Southern Vermont Arts Center. How to get there: The best way to get to Manchester from NYC is by renting a car and taking the four-hour drive. While there's not much in the way of public transit that makes this New England more accessible, this is a road trip that is well worth the gas money. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Hudson, NY This is all of the upstate charm of Hudson in a nutshell, far and away from the hokey and kitsch. Hudson is oft-cited as the “downtown of upstate,” and if we're expanding on the analogy, then consider this inn the subtly cool address in town in-the-know regulars keep in their back pockets. With one of the best restaurants in Hudson just downstairs, plus the fact that it's within walking distance of the Amtrak station and offers easy access to the city's innumerable and impossibly cute shops, the inn truly moves to the heartbeat of the city. No two rooms across the inn's three buildings—The Merchant House, Wm. Farmer, and the Annex Suites—are the same. Whether you're traveling on a weekend getaway for two, a retreat for a large crew, something in between or beyond, the inn's combined portfolio of 15 rooms and suites has your needs covered. —Kat Chen Fall festivities: Step into “upstate’s downtown,” where Hudson Valley’s eponymous crown jewel is always keeping things fresh. Restock your home decor to better fit the fall with antiques on and around Warren Street. Or, take a short drive up to the High Falls Conservation Area, where there's a moderately challenging 1.5-mile loop. If you like your art with a little side of the outdoors, find Art Omi in nearby Ghent, a 15-minute drive from Hudson, which boasts an impressive 120-acre sculpture park made for frolicking. How to get there: Ride the Amtrak Empire Service up to Hudson for an easy hop up that lasts shy of two hours, or take the equivalent amount of time driving. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Kingston, NY It's clear from the outset that Kinsley is a beautiful hotel, fit for guests who expect more than unblemished greige carpeting from their stays. You can expect sophisticated, if slightly bubbly, spaces; think solid-wood midcentury credenzas, ivory-and-maroon checkered hallway carpeting, deep red oriental rugs, white-as-the-driven-snow Frette linens, a bar that just looks like it makes a delicious cocktail (and boy, does it), and a top-tier selection of art, dispersed all around the space. In short, good looks are a cornerstone of the project. The 42-room hotel, restaurant, and cocktail bar are all part of a collection of four architecturally distinct buildings, tastefully restored from the 17th through 19th centuries. That said, don't miss the on-site dining at the Kinsley, where the seasonal New American cuisine with Southern and French influences comes courtesy of Spencer Coplan, or the bar, where you’ll find unfussy, albeit complex cocktails in an intimate, well-lit space. Kingston, in many ways, feels like Brooklyn—if Brooklyn wanted a hit of fresh air. You’ll find the same kooky, slightly off-beat vintage shops and artfully spare apothecaries lined with overpriced tinctures, along with the same bushy beards and blunt bangs plastered on the folks that frequent them. —Betsy Blumenthal Fall festivities: The on-site restaurant offers autumn dishes like squash doughnuts, pumpkin mole tacos, and chicken pot pie; you can also enjoy craft cocktails made with apple cider and local spirits in the chic, historic setting. Off-property, visit Kingston’s farmers market, where you can pick up seasonal produce and handmade fall goods; take a quick drive to Olana State Historic Site, the home of late artist Frederic Edwin Church, for a hike and sweeping views of the Hudson Valley's fall foliage. Hudson River Maritime Museum will give you a peek into the region’s history, then enjoy a scenic riverfront walk for even more fall colors. How to get there: Around a two-hour drive or a two-hour Metro-North train ride to Kingston from Grand Central. The town is walkable, so the train is a convenient option for this urban-meets-rural getaway in the heart of the Hudson Valley. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Washington, CT The Mayflower Inn and Spa is in Litchfield County, Connecticut—a stunning area of New England that still feels like somewhat of a secret, though urbanites have been moving here for some time in search of a place close to New York City and Boston with both outdoor space and city comforts. The resort itself attracts a similar crowd of New Yorkers and New Englanders looking for a weekend getaway where there’s something for everyone—including fantastic food, outdoor activities, and an unforgettable spa. The stately hotel looks grand and impressive from the exterior, with its manicured gardens and white lounge chairs. But inside is a property updated for what we’re looking for when we travel now: fun. The common spaces are places to linger, from the yellow parlor room to the quiet library. The aesthetic doesn’t sound like it would work on paper—mustard yellow walls, striped couches, tasseled chairs, a gallery wall of floral prints, and antique furniture. But thanks to designer Celerie Kemble's careful vision, it gets pulled together into a relaxing space where there's always a new detail to catch your eye. —Stephanie Wu Fall festivities: You can spend hours cozying up and indulging in s’mores by the fire, but the hotel also hosts seasonal cooking classes focusing on fall harvest ingredients. You can also enjoy a luxury spa day with autumn-inspired treatments, like pumpkin facials and apple cider massages. Nearby, explore Steep Rock Preserve, a stunning area for hiking with vibrant fall foliage, waterfalls, and scenic views. Take a short drive around Litchfield County for the best farm-to-table restaurants, cider tastings, and local weekend festivals, and visit the White Memorial Conservation Center for a hike through forested areas with fall colors in full bloom. How to get there: The property is about a two-hour drive from NYC, or you can take the Metro-North to New Haven, Connecticut (about two hours), then drive 30 minutes. Driving offers the greatest flexibility for exploring the retreat’s semi-rural surroundings. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Tannersville, NY In Greene County’s town of Tannersville, you’ll find the 18-room restored oasis that is Hotel Lilien, formerly the Washington Irving Inn. The Victorian gem dates back to the 1890s and was recently (and impeccably) restored with modern touches, most noticeable in the guest bathrooms, which now include brass fixtures and marble floors. Luxury lies in the velvety feel of the property, where natural light pours in from the stained-glass windows and bounces off dark wood paneling. Since opening, the cocktail bar and dining spaces have become a hub for a trendy local crowd, who have the option to join guests enjoying the wood-burning stove. The hotel is just five minutes away from the region’s buzzy Hunter Mountain, too. —Jessica Chapel Fall festivities: Other than leaf-peeping from your hotel window, you can relax near the fire in the common lounge area with a craft cocktail, around the pool table or jukebox, or while enjoying a s’mores dessert skillet. Off-property, visit Tannersville’s local shops and farm stands—be sure to pick up some pumpkins, apples, and cider. Nearby is also the small, artsy town of Hunter, where you can take part in pumpkin-carving contests or browse through fall farmers markets. Park at Kaaterskill Falls for waterfalls surrounded by vibrant autumn foliage—take the Escarpment Trail for extra-special panoramic views. How to get there: Hotel Lilien is just over a two-hour drive from NYC or a two-hour Metro-North ride to Hudson, followed by a 30-minute drive. It’s best to drive directly from NYC if you can, as it’s easier to access the Catskills region and navigate hot spots surrounding the semi-remote hotel. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Chatham, MA The Chatham Bars Inn, considered a benchmark of luxury on the Cape, manages to reinvent itself over and over again to keep up with the times. If you’re looking for a full-service resort with all the bells and whistles and then some, this is it, including one of the better spas on the Cape; an expansive pool deck with food and beverage service; a private quarter-mile beachfront; tennis courts with lessons available; and a 24-hour gym. Check out its popular farm-to-table dinner series, held a few miles away at the resort’s very own eight-acre farm. —Todd Plummer Fall festivities: The hotel's farm-to-table menu highlights fall ingredients like squash, apples, and root vegetables. You can take in the breathtaking view of Cape Cod's fall coastline from the on-site spa, which offers seasonal treatments like pumpkin facials. Off-site, explore Chatham’s pumpkin patch tours or visit local farms like Cape Cod Organic Farm for seasonal produce and apple picking. For a day of adventuring, take a scenic drive along Cape Cod National Seashore, where the fall colors meet the coastline in harmony, and pay a visit to Monomoy National Wildlife Refuge for bird-watching, strolling, and discovering the area's wildlife. How to get there: This iconic Cape Cod inn is around a 4-hour drive from NYC, or you can take Amtrak to Boston (about 3.5 hours), followed by a bus or a 1.5-hour drive to Chatham. The direct drive is the most convenient and scenic option for exploring the Cape. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Bedford, PA 11 US presidents have stayed at this 2,200-acre old-fashioned resort in the Allegheny Mountains; it takes you back in time in style. For more than 200 years, the property’s eight springs have served as a gathering place and still feature in the treatments at the 30,000-square-foot spa. With the utmost respect for its heritage, the resort has restored some guest rooms; most include balconies with rocking chairs overlooking the creek or mountains. The 1796 Room is the signature steak and chophouse; at Frontier Tavern, linger over artisanal brews or toast marshmallows over a firepit. The Crystal Room is one of the oldest restaurants in America and serves breakfast, lunch, brunch, and dinner, all created by a fantastic chef. —Stefanie Waldek Fall festivities: Indulge in the resort’s Autumn Harvest Afternoon Tea, with seasonal teas, pumpkin bread, and cinnamon scones. For those interested (and even for those not), the resort’s on-site golf course offers breathtaking views of the surrounding fall landscape. Nearby, visit the Bedford County Fall Foliage Festival, one of the top autumn festivals in the region, which features craft vendors, local produce, and live music. Or, explore the Allegany National Forest for hiking, biking, and scenic drives. How to get there: Omni Bedford Springs Resort is nearly a 5-hour drive from NYC, or you can take Amtrak from Penn Station to Harrisburg (3.5 hours), and then it's a 1-hour drive from there. That said, driving directly from NYC is the most straightforward option for this remote destination. - CNT Triple CrownGold List 2024Readers' Choice Awards 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025Read Full ReviewLocation: Nantucket, MA Nantucket's hotel scene has grown up quite a bit over the past few years, with exciting new boutique offerings (Faraway, Life House) making waves and drawing younger, more trend-setting travelers to the island than ever before. But the most tried-and-true hotel here is one of the oldest: the harborside White Elephant, a historic inn-and-cottages resort that masters classic New England chic whilst keeping up with the times. Case in point, the resort is a 54-key hotel with 11 on-site cottages, including an artist-in-residence program and airy interiors paying homage to the island's basket-weaving and seafaring heritage. Cerulean textiles, brass elephant-head door knockers, wood-and-leather armchairs, and marble accents complement the ocean and white caps just beyond your window (or spacious seating area and balcony, if you spring for a suite). The serene great lawn and Brant Point Grill make up perhaps the most spacious stretch of waterfront dining on the island—perfect for a hearty lobster-leaning breakfast, or a perfectly balanced cocktail and raw-bar spread if you're just visiting to take in the bobbing sail boats and passing ferries. And it's all mere steps (or a complimentary bike pedal, all of about three minutes) from all the cobblestones, climbing roses, and crowds in town—something that, on this historic and well-loved island, you really can't beat. —Shannon McMahon Fall festivities: Sip a warm cider cocktail on the inn’s terrace while enjoying the cool autumn breeze and views of the harbor. Outside, the charm of Nantucket in fall, with its mild weather and peaceful atmosphere, provides an idyllic escape. Take a fall ferry ride through Nantucket Sound to witness the coastline’s autumn transformation; Explore Nantucket’s Cranberry Bog, where you can watch as the berries are harvested; and walk or bike along the island’s Sconset Bluff Walk for sweeping views of changing leaves. How to get there: From NYC, it’s around a four-hour drive to Hyannis, followed by a one-hour ferry to Nantucket; alternatively, you can take Amtrak to Hyannis (about five hours) and then the ferry. Of course, driving gives you more flexibility—but the island itself is walkable and easy to navigate without a car. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Aurora, NY The Inns of Aurora is a five-inn lakeside property of meticulously restored buildings from the 1800s and early 1900s. Guest rooms are decorated with furniture and art from founder Pleasant Rowland’s personal collection, and each inn has a distinct feel. Initially constructed in 1833, The Aurora was the first of the inns to be restored in 2003, and was the property of Edwin Barber Morgan, co-founder of the New York Times and American Express. Four more properties were restored to their former glory over the years, the last of which was the 1909 home of Morgan’s grandson, Robert Zabriskie. Renovations were finished in 2019. —Alexandra Sanidad Fall festivities: A quintessential Finger Lakes experience, this property offers seasonal wellness packages, including autumn-inspired spa treatments using apple cider and pumpkin for skin rejuvenation. Off-property, enjoy apple picking at The Apple Farm in nearby Ithaca, one of the best spots in the region for fresh apples, cider, and fall produce. Head to Cornell University's Botanical Gardens for vibrant fall walks and to experience nature in full autumn glory. Or, spend an afternoon at Long Point State Park, where you can hike (or lightly stroll) through trails with views of Cayuga Lake’s fall foliage. How to get there: This property is a four-hour drive from NYC, or you can take Amtrak from Penn Station to Syracuse (about three hours), followed by a one-hour drive to Aurora. Driving offers a more direct and scenic route through the Finger Lakes. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Eldred, NY Rustic and upscale design meet here to create a dreamy forest getaway. There are plenty of great stays in the Catskills, but as Goldilocks might say after a breath of relief, this one feels just right. Off a winding road bordered by tall, full trees, the property structures wrap around the parking lot where guests first enter. The lobby boasts a simple yet classy design adorned with heaps of glass, wood, and stone. Floor-to-ceiling windows can be found throughout the majority of the resort's 11 on-site structures, and the openness allows for the sweeping forest backdrop to take center stage. From stand-alone cabins to the sweetest suites, the rooms are spacious and nature-forward, with delicate oak and a light palette on the painted walls. As the resort is located on the gigantic, lush, and historic Eldred Preserve, there’s serenity to be found amidst the trails and three ponds on the grounds. The vastness of the 600-acre preserve, though, remains unassuming—until a meander through the property’s trail network, where guests will approach the serene 65-acre Sunset Lake and perhaps soak in the outdoor ambiance of a dinner at The Homestead. Set adjacent to a pond, restaurant diners enjoy a clear view of the stars with their farm-to-table meals. From day to night, the property feels like a welcoming, warm, decadent paradise in the middle of the woods. —J.C. Fall festivities: Staying on-site means dreamy fall amenities, like rustic country dining, floor-to-ceiling windows, and in-room fireplaces, all surrounded by a colorful mountain backdrop. Don’t skip out on local farm stands and apple orchards in Bethel for a taste of fresh seasonal produce, or a visit to Bethel Woods Center for the Arts for an autumn festival. How to get there: Expect slightly longer than a 2.5-hour drive from NYC or a 2-hour Metro-North ride to Port Jervis, followed by a 30-minute taxi or Uber ride (you can also call the hotel’s concierge for their ride suggestions). Driving is most convenient, as the hotel is tucked in a more remote area. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Beacon, NY The Roundhouse brings a touch of modern flair to the idyllic town of Beacon. With a chic, industrial aesthetic and stunning waterfall views, it finds a balance between the edgy and the bucolic in a very Hudson Valley way. With a popular on-site restaurant and an even more popular wedding venue, the Roundhouse has become an institution in East Beacon, where it sits surrounded by cute coffee shops and swanky boutiques. The nearby contemporary art museum Dia: Beacon and the many fantastic hikes within walking distance of the hotel make it a great home base to explore the lower Hudson Valley. After a long day, guests in one of the penthouse suites can enjoy a bath in a freestanding tub surrounded by large, curved windows showing off the incredible natural surroundings. —Oscar Moss Dorr Fall festivities: Enjoy seasonal cocktails crafted with local apple cider and pumpkins from nearby farms, or cozy up by the riverside fireplace with a glass of mulled wine. Nearby, find fall hiking trails at Mount Beacon (with some of the best leaf-peeping views in the Hudson Valley), or visit wineries like Millbrook Vineyards (in our opinion, one of the best wineries near NYC) for fall tastings. Every Sunday, head to Beacon Farmer’s Market to pick up some seasonal produce, pumpkins, and fresh apple cider. And don’t miss out on Dia:Beacon, an expansive tree-lined art museum housed in a former factory, offering year-round exhibitions with a tranquil atmosphere in the fall. How to get there: Nearly 1.5 hours by car from NYC, or just over a 1.5-hour train ride on Metro-North from Grand Central to Beacon. The Roundhouse is a short walk from the train station. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Bridgehampton, NY Topping Rose House is the Hamptons’ ultimate refined hideaway and feels like a cultivated sanctuary—where splendid white wooden beams meet open-air vistas, spa rituals follow sunset poolside prosecco, and spacious, colorful rooms cradle you. Tucked in the quiet, ritzy town of Bridgehampton, this historic and iconic stay balances grandeur with warmth, and feels like a quiet and classy celebration of old and new. Rooted in a 1842 Greek Revival mansion, the property now offers 22 historic rooms (16 spacious guest rooms and 6 one-bedroom suites). Inside, each of these spaces feels intimate yet expansive, elevated by on-site Jean‑Georges dining, holistic wellness at Naturopathica, and polished personalized service (from wellness programming to private transportation). Topping Rose is home to lawns trimmed to perfection and alcoves of blooming hydrangeas tracing pathways from the main house to a heated pool, where aqua sparkles under beige umbrellas and Adirondack chairs clutch rosé-chilled glasses. —J.C. How to get there: By car, Bridgehampton is around 2.5 hours from NYC, and you’ll have a far better chance of evading the dreadful Hamptons traffic once the summer fades and fall comes around. You can also take the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) from Penn Station to Bridgehampton, which takes around 2 hours; however, driving offers more flexibility once you’ve arrived. Fall festivities: On the property, surrounded by colored leaves, guests can indulge in autumn-inspired dishes when dining on dishes made using local seasonal produce. Nearby, explore local farms like The Apple Farm for apple picking and pumpkin patches. - Read Full ReviewLocation: North Adams, MA Inspired by the American roadside motor lodge of yore, Tourists is built for contemporary design lovers, with lots of light wood on the banks of the Hoosic River. Many of the large windows in the guest rooms look straight into nature, helping blur the line between the outdoors and indoors. Opened in 2018, Tourists still feels like the cool new kid on the block, with the clientele to match. Ideally situated for those exploring Williamstown and North Adams, it’s approximately three miles from the Clark Art Institute, Mass MoCA, and Bright Ideas Brewing. If you’re visiting this corner of the Berkshires, there’s nowhere more stylish to stay. —Devra Ferst Fall festivities: Guests can enjoy s’mores by the firepit in the evenings, a perfect way to unwind after a day of exploring. Just a short drive from Tourists, Mass MoCA is one of the largest contemporary art museums in the US, featuring rotating exhibits and installations, including seasonal and fall-themed exhibits. How to get there: Tourists is a little over a 3.5-hour drive up the Taconic Expressway. If you need to make a pit stop, the charmingly old-school Millbrook Diner is almost exactly at the halfway point. - Read Full ReviewLocation: New Paltz, NY Experience living history at Mohonk Mountain House, where you will be immersed in the wholesome pastimes and stunning natural beauty of an American icon. Mohonk offers a seemingly limitless array of activities to try while visiting; choose your own adventure or simply embrace doing nothing at all. The spa is a must-visit for time in the tranquil setting that frames the nearby Shawangunk Mountains alone. Whether enjoying the Belgian waffles with caramelized bananas at the divine breakfast buffet or grabbing cookies and tea as an afternoon snack, service is warm and personal. The rooms achieve a cozy elegance by leaning into what makes Mohonk so special: incredible views, simple luxuries like wood-burning fireplaces and claw-foot bathtubs, and an eye for aesthetic details inspired by the Arts and Crafts movement. An ideal place for a solo trip or a family gathering, Mohonk offers a respite from our overstimulated, overscreened culture. Visit and get back to the most important things in life: nature, connection, beauty, and the best breakfast buffet this side of the Atlantic. —Katie Mathews Fall festivities: The on-site spa offers autumn-inspired treatments like pumpkin facials and apple cider massages. Join other guests for the hotel’s bonfire nights: a cozy, fall tradition where guests gather around a firepit in the evenings to enjoy hot cider, warm blankets, and marshmallow roasting. Off-property, head to Minnewaska State Park—located about 10 minutes from Mohonk, the park is famous for its fall hiking, with panoramic views of the Shawangunk Ridge. And with over 85 miles of trails, Mohonk offers one of the best fall foliage experiences in the region. (Hike up to the Sky Top Tower for panoramic views of the colorful landscape.) Dressel Farms in New Paltz offers apple picking and cider tasting throughout the fall; visit nearby wineries such as Whitecliff Vineyards for tastings, located just 20 minutes from the resort. How to get there: It’s around a two-hour drive from NYC to Mohonk Mountain House. You can also take a bus via the Adirondack Trailways from Port Authority to New Paltz, or take an Amtrak or Metro-North train from Grand Central to Poughkeepsie. Book the Mohonk Mountain House Shuttle service in advance—they will organize a seamless transfer from either of these stations. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Newport, RI In the Agassiz mansion, no two rooms are alike. And while this is a historic property, everything is beautifully maintained, and far from dusty. We stayed in the duplex Turret Suite, which occupies, as the name suggests, the property’s iconic highest point. The king-sized bed was cozy, the antique millwork felt reminiscent of another time, and–the pièce de résistance–a spiral staircase leads into the highest section of the mansion’s turret, where a freestanding soaking tub sits surrounded by windows, offering panoramic views of Newport. It is, by any measure, sublime. Fine dining aside, Castle Hill also gets it right with its more casual outposts, too. The Terrace Bar offers elevated takes on grilled New England fare, with an infallible burger, and a housemade peach barbecue sauce I’m still dreaming about days later. A full gourmet breakfast is included for (and exclusive to) overnight guests. Castle Hill is also a great spot for drinks—there are few more quintessentially Newport experiences than posting up in one of the Adirondack chairs on The Lawn, ordering a Dark and Stormy, and waving to the sailboats that go cruising on by. —T.P. Fall festivities: The hotel provides warm fireplaces in the lounge and dining areas, making it the perfect place for a cozy evening. You can also find one of the best spots to view fall foliage in Newport nearby: the Cliff Walk is a scenic 3.5-mile walk along the coast, offering ocean views and picture-perfect colorful leaves. Find apple picking and wine tastings at Sakonnet Vineyards, a short drive away from the property, as well as a handful of local fall festivals, like the Newport Harvest Festival (typically in early October) or the Newport Food and Wine festival. How to get there: It’s about a four-hour drive from NYC to Castle Hill Inn. You can also take the Amtrak to Kingston Station, then meander through a 40-minute drive to Newport with coastal views (the Inn offers free transport from the rail station). - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lake Placid, NY Built in 1883 as a private home, this Adirondack Mountain resort is on the shores of Mirror Lake, one block from Main Street and close to the Olympic Center. Mirror Lake Inn wrote the book on customer service—staff welcome you back with open arms and treat you like family. Rooms have mahogany walls, vaulted ceilings, polished walnut floors, and private balconies with beautiful water vistas. Although there are plenty of things to do on-site throughout the year, the inn’s proximity to the center of town and nearby Whiteface Mountain makes it easy to try many outdoor activities. An absolute must is a massage in the spa. The lakefront Cottage Café serves pub-style dishes. —Charu Suri Fall festivities: Other than views of Mirror Lake’s dreamy fall foliage, guests can enjoy autumn-inspired dishes with locally sourced ingredients, as well as s’mores by the lakeside fireplaces. Off-site, head up Whiteface Mountain on the aptly named Cloudsplitter gondola and take in views from atop a mountain where Olympians have trained. Or you can head downtown and see the Olympic Museum, with exhibits spanning the history of the Games (in case you missed it, Lake Placid is the only US town to host the Winter Olympics twice). How to get there: Around a 5-hour drive from Manhattan up I-87, or a 6-hour trip from Penn Station on the Amtrak Adirondack line to Westport Station, which is about a 40-minute cab or Uber ride from the inn. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Finger Lakes, NY Upstate New York’s Finger Lakes region, a nine-county sweep of state parks and small towns, forests and farmland, has pulled vacationing families and nature lovers to its 11 slender, digit-like lakes for more than a century. But it's really only over the past decade that the area has come into its own as one of the country’s top wine regions, pulling a new crew of savvy visitors who come as much for the local vintages as for the Walden-esque natural setting. The newly reimagined Lake House resort on the north end of Lake Canandaigua, one of the loveliest (and toniest) corners of upstate, sits at the intersection of old guard and new. The expansive compound of recently built white gabled structures on the site of a former roadside motel retains some of the old local flavor but is casually upscale enough for well-heeled weekenders from Toronto and New York City. Rooms have a New England resort feel—plenty of white painted wood and four-poster beds—and the food is excellent: Sand Bar turns out the perfect lobster roll alongside potent classic cocktails, while the more upscale Rose Tavern taps into the area’s local bounty. But, truth be told, you’re there for the lake: To watch it go from blue to pink-gold from the Adirondack chair on your balcony, to head out for the afternoon in a canoe with a picnic lunch, and to listen to it settle for the night from a shorefront firepit as you toast marshmallows or sip a local off-dry Riesling—or, better yet, do both.—Jesse Ashlock Fall festivities: Guests can photograph the foliage around the lakes and indulge in seasonal dishes featuring locally grown squash, apples, and pumpkins. (Menus change with the harvest.) Drive down to Naples (stop and grab a picture at the County Road 12 scenic overlook), or hit a U-pick farm and gather apples. If you want more of an adrenaline rush, take the chairlifts to the top of Bristol Mountain during the fall months for the Fall Sky Ride weekends. How to get there: A leisurely five-hour drive from New York City on I-80 toward Rochester gives you ample time to marvel at the foliage along the way. There is also Amtrak service from the city to Rochester, which is 45 minutes away from Canandaigua Lake. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Where to Shop in Nagaland, Northern India's Creative Enclave
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.23
Though Nagaland falls among India's least populated states, it punches above its cultural and creative weight. The misty highlands and dense forests of the region, which borders Myanmar in the east, are home to some 17 Indigenous tribes and long-held textile-weaving traditions. Nagaland's capital, Kohima, or its largest city, Dimapur—accessible by flights from New Delhi or Kolkata—are good gateways to the region and offer plentiful homestays and vibrant workshops that reimagine local materials into the likes of upcycled suiting and understated home furnishings. In December, Nagaland's annual Hornbill Festival may draw global travelers to celebrate its Indigenous histories, but the state's centuries-old craft heritage—found everywhere from stylish boutiques to artist studios—gives plenty of reasons to linger longer. Designed and decorative For textile arts, Heirloom Naga, founded in Dimapur, is a must-visit. The mainstay's range has expanded over 30 years from a line of color-blocked linens and cushions to bags, display bowls, fans, and wall tapestries. Visit its Heirloom Naga Centre to shop, stay at the property's eight-room guesthouse—done up with signature throw blankets and pillows—or take a traditional loin-loom weaving or basketry workshop hosted by Heirloom. Grab a bite at the center's restaurant, Heirloom Eatery. Modern mekhalas For a clothing label whose name directly translates to “communities” in the Indigenous Ao Naga language, Dimapur-based Kintem's focus is exactly that. Founder Moala Longchar employs a network of intergenerational weavers from local communities to create reinterpreted mekhalas, or draped dresses, and shawls using loin-loomed panels; many pieces are embellished with geometric motifs, tassels, and cowrie shells. Find casual sarong-style wrap skirts in shades of olive and sandy orange, or explore its bridal edit, which features züngijang, or “cucumber seed” embroidery, in gold as well as elevated mekhalas adorned with tiny bells. Woven once, woven twice If you've ever wondered if a Dior men's button-down pairs well with a cinched handwoven corset, Otsü Clothing Co.'s answer is yes. Whether you've got your eyes on shirting lined with colorful hems, dresses of distressed patchwork, or pencil skirts that have loomed cotton pockets, there is no shortage of vibrantly upcycled and vintage creations reborn with Naga materials and techniques. The Dimapur brand also hosts the pop-up series Otsüverse, a makers market spotlighting Northeast Indian cuisine, sound, and style. A bit of everything Wild-grass tapestries and handbags made from banana fiber, bamboo vessels, and twill-woven basketry are a few of the many goods you may find at Runway Nagaland, a welcoming menagerie of colorful accessories and earth-toned home decor off Full Nagarjan Road in Dimapur's Thilixu village. Runway began as a jewelry label in 2011 after its founder, Nengneithem Hengna, left her corporate career. It's only grown since, now offering workshops and fiber art training to students, locals, and curious travelers alike. Beaded beauties Shells and semiprecious stones find life as statement necklaces and bangles at Hues of Hills, available at lifestyle boutique Vayu - Design for Living in New Delhi.
