Especially memorable designs include its Naga choker, wherein each gem represents ornaments worn by a different native tribe, and its Naga orchid necklace, inspired by the nearly 400 species of the flowering plant found in the region. An earth-to-bead approach continues in the town of Wokha, roughly 46 miles north of the capital, with Zaben Murry Design, where Naga heritage reverberates via Lotha-tribe colorways and brass pendants in the shape of abstract Naga heads, a popular motif across the state. New traditions At Kohima-based design studio Woven Threads, organic cotton and natural dyes are threaded into items for the body and home. From indigo-dyed structural outerwear to patterned bed runners, blankets, and pillows, each loin-loom collection is made by Indigenous artisans across Nagaland who create from their home while continuing to practice essential seasonal farming, such as paddy cultivation, and are encouraged to mentor younger creatives to keep the state's weaving process alive. This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: Can This Stylish Anti-Theft Tote Outsmart Pickpockets? I Tried It to Find Out
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.86
I’ve been lucky, so far, to have traveled widely and frequently without ever being robbed—something all the more fortunate given how often I travel solo. It’s not something I’ve thought too deeply about, but then a colleague told me a story that jolted me into paying attention. She had just landed in Paris after a grueling long haul from Australia and, within minutes of leaving the airport, was stepping onto the train when a group of men surrounded her, boxing her in so tightly she couldn’t move. Before she could realize what was happening, her wallet was gone. And by the time she reached her hotel, $2,000 had been spent on her credit card. Most unsettlingly, it was almost impossible to prevent in the moment. What would I do in that situation, traveling alone? I’d be in real trouble. Fortunately, there are travel bags designed to help prevent this sort of thing—but many feel more functional than fashionable. Rachel Bloom is one of the few brands striking a convincing balance, offering chic leather handbags you can carry from the airport to dinner, all while concealing a number of clever security features. I put the brand's Smart Anti-Theft tote to the test on a couple of weekend trips to Paris and Milan over the past few months. Here’s how it fared. Aesthetics At first glance, this is a clean, fairly structured everyday tote in a classic black or tan colorway. It’s made from real leather that feels soft and supple (and smells as good as you’d hope). It’s roomy enough for daily essentials, with a main compartment, two card slots, a generous section for bulkier items like a sunglasses case, plus smaller pockets for your phone and bits and bobs. The Smart tote comfortably holds everything you’d need for a day out or a flight—though it’s worth noting there’s no dedicated laptop sleeve. The straps are wide enough to feel genuinely supportive, sitting just as comfortably on my shoulder at the end of a long day of walking as they did at the beginning. Safety features The standout detail is the fingerprint locking system, which ensures the bag only opens when you want it to. A built-in sensor on the side unlocks it instantly with a light—no keys or codes needed. It’s easy to set up in the Rachel Bloom app and works well—just as quickly as your phone’s fingerprint sensor does. It’s easily the bag’s most compelling feature: When locked, it becomes completely impossible for pickpockets to dip into it, no matter how dexterous or well-organized they are. You can add up to 25 fingerprints to each bag, so the whole family (and some of your friends) can share. While researching this piece, I also sadly learned of “slash-and-run” theft—where a thief cuts into the bottom of a bag so valuables fall out, or slice through the straps so the whole thing can be snatched in seconds. I was blissfully unaware of this before, but I can now see the validity of the bag’s next important feature: a cut-resistant inner layer. This is hidden beneath the leather, adding extra protection without any visible bulk. For an additional $75, you can opt for GPS tracking, allowing you to locate your bag in real time via the app. It’s a reassuring extra, particularly for frequent travelers. However, if the price feels steep, a separate luggage tracker tucked inside does the same job nicely. There’s also an RFID-blocking card included, designed to protect against electronic pickpocketing by preventing unauthorized scans of your bank cards and passport data. The app The app is easy to use and adds a few extra functionality points. One of my favorite features is less about theft and more about everyday forgetfulness: an alarm that shows your bag’s last known location—ideal if, like me, you’re prone to leaving things behind or forgetting where you’ve left them. It’s pretty loud, so you’ll be able to hear it across the room. This therefore means that you’ll know that if you can’t hear it, you’ve left it elsewhere. You can also unlock the bag remotely and, if you’ve opted for GPS, it’s through the app that you’ll be able to track it directly. All the features on the app work seamlessly with no learning curve required. The verdict This is a smart, well-designed tote that conceals some seriously useful tech. It’s at the pricier end of the spectrum, but for the added peace of mind—especially when traveling solo or in unfamiliar cities—it feels like a worthwhile investment. You’re also not sacrificing style for security, which makes it a win-win. For solo travelers especially, this feels like an important upgrade to your luggage lineup. Wherever I’m headed next, this will be coming with me.

item.title: Long Live the Hard Rock—Inside the Kitsch, Memorabilia, and Excess That Lives On
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.52
I was about nine years old when my dad first took me to the Hard Rock Cafe in New York, and I still remember being completely taken with the walls. My dad and I gushed over everything together: That's Eddie Van Halen's suit—look, Jeff Ament's bass! There's no way that's Jimi Hendrix's actual handwriting. Of course, it's his signature, messy, cursive—a write-up of the classic track, Midnight Lightning. How about those massive, towering stage boots and custom bass guitars? Yep, they were used and worn by none other than Gene Simmons himself. My dad was a rock ‘n’ roll traveler then, in the way some are food travelers today. Concerts determined where he went, and he had stories about bands the way others have stories about family vacations. We bonded deeply through music—so when we walked into a Hard Rock in any city, it wasn't simply a chain to me. Instead, it was a portal—filled with scents of hairspray, greasy burgers, and a touch of booze—that cosmically actualized the music so intrinsic to our relationship. If you've ever walked into a Hard Rock Cafe, you already know the lore: memorabilia displayed behind glass with plaques like artifacts, cult-favorite souvenir T-shirts stacked in the Rock shop, and music playing live or streaming on every television. Some might mistake these spaces as tourist traps—and sure enough, you'll find your out-of-towners here. But I’ve always associated Hard Rock's hubs with a different kind of traveler: the nostalgia-forward, music-obsessed folk who collect the pins, know the songs, and are willing to embrace a little kitsch in pursuit of something travel can sometimes take itself too seriously to deliver: fun. That simple pleasure is the throughline of Hard Rock's evolution. For more than five decades, the brand has grown without sanding down the personality that made its original spaces memorable. What began as one London restaurant is now a global hospitality and entertainment empire, spanning cafes, hotels, casinos, resorts, and live venues in cities across the globe. And it's still building outward: Within the next two years, Hard Rock is expected to bring its most recognizable piece of architecture yet to the Las Vegas Strip, with a brand new guitar-shaped hotel rising where The Mirage once stood. Hard Rock Cafe's journey began in London in 1971, when two homesick Americans, Isaac Tigrett and Peter Morton, brought the comforts of a classic American diner to the British capital. What later became its most enduring calling card—the memorabilia—arrived almost by accident. In 1979, Eric Clapton reportedly sent the cafe a guitar in exchange for the right to reserve his favorite barstool; Pete Townshend swiftly followed with a guitar of his own, scrawling, “Mine’s as good as his! Love, Pete.” That friendly bit of rockstar one-upmanship became the first note in what would grow into a vast global archive of more than 88,000 historic pieces. As crowds gathered and the idea caught fire, Hard Rock began taking its particular mix of burgers, band tees, and music history around the world, eventually opening its first Asian cafe in Tokyo in 1983. Its next major chapter came in 2007, when the Seminole Tribe of Florida acquired Hard Rock International following a competitive bidding process led by Jim Allen, the CEO of Seminole Gaming for 30 years and now chairman of Hard Rock International, a role he has held for nearly two decades. The deal marked a historic first: according to Allen, it was the first time a Native American tribe had acquired an international company of Hard Rock’s scale. More importantly, it set Hard Rock on an entirely new trajectory. Under Seminole ownership, the company expanded beyond its restaurant roots, evolving into a full-fledged entertainment brand spanning hotels, integrated resorts, casinos, retail, and live-music venues. In the years since, its reach has nearly doubled from 46 countries to more than 80 today. One of Hard Rock's greatest goals over the past two decades, according to Allen, has been to be more intentional about its curation—to create a museum-like experience. From building location-specific collections around local music history to adding QR codes that allow guests to learn more about a piece, turning the company’s vast inventory into something more than decor. “When you can look at artifacts—in this case memorabilia—that represent individual celebrities or individual songs, or certain periods in life that reflect very favorably on positive times, that’s something that’s very valuable in the perception of brand,” Allen says. That evolution is important because it gives the brand’s history a physical, almost theatrical presence. And if you can appreciate a little glitz and historical lore in all its buzz and excess, the effect can be surprisingly transportive. My own Hard Rock infatuation came full circle on a 2022 mother-daughter trip. We were seeing Incubus's (epic) live performance at the Hard Rock's Atlantic City hotel, and while waiting in line, my mother—another rockstar-at-heart—turned to me and said: “This is probably the only ‘museum’ you could ever get me to." There, we realized it had been almost exactly a decade since we first traveled together to Hollywood, Florida, to see Bon Jovi play live at the iconic Seminole Hard Rock Hotel and Casino—long before its Guitar Hotel changed the skyline. My dad, who first introduced me to the Hard Rock world via its Cafes—had passed away in 2010, and in the years after, the Florida property had become part of a different family tradition—my mom’s side of the family loves to gamble, so beginning around 2012, we started traveling there together, often twice a year. And while the hotel was certainly a different kind of spectacle—tamer and more refined than its Cafe counterparts—there was always another corner left to discover, or a new extension to look forward to on the next visit. At a time when I was too young to gamble, I spent nights wandering around, reading up on all the iconic artifacts, from Madonna’s Like a Virgin dress or Elvis Presley’s signature blue pajamas and motorcycle from the ’70s. It was my very own bizarre rendition of Night(s) at the Museum. It's no secret that Hard Rock creates these sorts of long-lasting memories for travelers all over the globe. If you spend enough time at a Hard Rock location, you'll often find a superfan or few that check off these spaces on their travels. “It's absolutely worth popping into a Hard Rock wherever you go, if they have one,” a solo traveler once told me over drinks at the Hard Rock Cafe bar in Amsterdam. “Part of the fun is just how different they all are.” It's true, when it comes to consistency—Hard Rock has it down pat: You know the logo, you know there will be music, and you have a pretty good idea that there will be a guitar or two on the wall. But what you can't know is what the place will mean in that particular city—or what you'll happen to remember from being there. One of the Hard Rock's staying powers comes from making that familiarity feel rooted in the destination. “There is only one universal language—and that is music,” Allen says. So when the company enters a new destination, the team begins with digging local: “We look at the culture of the specific country, location, and city that we’re in, as well as the music history of that particular region.” he says. That research shapes the memorabilia, local performers and, at the cafes, even parts of the menus. A property in Davos will look different from one in Punta Cana or New York; in Las Vegas, Allen says the collection will include artists associated with Nevada and the city, alongside big celebrity names, like Beyoncé, Bruce Springsteen, and Taylor Swift. On a recent visit to both the Hard Rock Cafe and hotel locations in New York, I found it oddly comforting that the Cafe remains the maximalist portal I remember: The wall of stacked guitars—against which my late father and I posed for countless over-priced photos—still remains as if it was built yesterday. I hadn't been here in years, but it all was all too familiar; a sight of one table even pulled me right back to a memory of us two sharing chicken wings while a Pink Floyd track played real loud. (It's one of my earliest memories of knowing the band, now one of my favorites.) Today, neon-blue lights still frame the bar; TVs stream an old Creed music video; tourists stop mid-meal to photograph whatever they recognize; and local musicians continue to perform live. Five blocks away on 48th street, Hard Rock Hotel New York, which opened in 2022, feels like the next generation—brighter, more airy, and refined, with Beyoncé and Jay-Z’s custom outfits by the elevator bank, sweeping views from its rooftop bar, RT60, home to tasty cocktails worth lingering over. “When I first started [working here], I assumed it was mostly about music and memorabilia,” says David Salcfas, the hotel's general manager. “Those things are certainly important, but over time I've realized Hard Rock, as an entity, creates something far more personal, more wholesome." I know the feeling, although I first encountered it over a cafe booth rather than a hotel bar. The hotels may have made the experience bigger, and in many cases more refined, but it’s the Cafes that still give me that old jolt. I can walk in for a comfort burger, look up at the walls, and suddenly I’m nine years old again, standing beside my dad and reading the stories behind the artifacts. That collision of food, kitsch, and memorabilia is the portal I grew up with—and, even now, my favorite kind of time travel. Our team's favorite Hard Rock memories “I grew up in South Florida, so for years the Seminole Hard Rock in Hollywood was something I’d see while driving around the area. But when the 450-foot Guitar Hotel went up in 2019, it became impossible to miss—especially because, well, South Florida is nothing if not flat. Now that I live in New York, seeing those guitar strings of light from the plane when I fly back into Fort Lauderdale feels strangely heartwarming. It’s so very Florida, in the best way. And when I run into a Hard Rock somewhere else, like I recently did in Niagara Falls, it still feels like a little piece of home.” —Madison Flager, commerce director “When Hard Rock Cafe arrived in Bombay in 2006, it landed in a converted textile mill and quickly became a key part of the city’s social life. I remember its tall blue cocktails turning up in blurry photos, Nirvana tribute nights by bands from Ohio that we’d never heard of but lined up to see, and local bands getting a stage, too. Most of all, it was a place that let a motley crew of college kids, models, and happy-hour work crowds be their wilder selves under the watchful gaze of Alice Cooper’s leather. It gave us permission to grow up, with all the messiness that came with it. I recently learned that Hard Rock’s Indian franchises have all closed, and it really does feel like the end of an era.” —Arati Menon, global digital director “My Hard Rock memory goes back to a family vacation in Gatlinburg around 2002. During lunch, a familiar song came on and every server stopped, put down their trays, climbed onto the tables, and started dancing. I remember being completely amazed: you were allowed to do that? Years later, I started collecting the little guitar pins from Hard Rock locations around the world, even when I wasn’t actually eating there. I eventually stopped, but the pins are still sitting in a bin at my parents’ house in Florida—and somehow that feels exactly right.” —Taylor Eisenhauer, editorial operations manager

item.title: In Uzbekistan, a Prized Religious Artifact Sits at the Heart of a New Museum
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.31
At Tashkent's new Islamic Civilization Center in Uzbekistan, the star attraction is built around a single object. The Uthman Quran, a seventh-century manuscript written in Kufic lettering on gazelle parchment, sits beneath a 213-foot dome in a space designed for maximum impact. Lapis-lazuli-inlaid steps lead toward the holy text. Portuguese pink marble wraps the walls. Eight handwoven silk carpets, each inscribed with Quranic verses, hang like royal tapestries. Guards are posted throughout to protect one of the oldest surviving Qurans in the world, and a full sound-and-light show—incorporating over 1 million Swarovski crystals—fills the hall from floor to ceiling. The effect of the Quran Hall, which anchors one of the most ambitious cultural projects in Central Asia, is almost psychedelic, like a Pink Floyd concert reimagined as an act of religious devotion. Opened in March on the grounds of the Hazrati Imam ensemble, a 25-acre architectural site that includes a historic mosque and madrassa, the center is a research library, a digital learning hub, and the world's largest museum of Islamic civilization. Beyond the Quran Hall, its exhibitions trace Uzbekistan's history from pre-Islamic cultures and Silk Road exchanges to the Timurid period and the country's modern era. Interactive displays, rare manuscripts, and newly repatriated artifacts show how this part of the world became an intellectual crossroads; objects in the collection range from a 10th-century Samanid silver tray and copper inkwell to Baburid armor, a silk covering once used at the Prophet's tomb in Medina, and Bactrian-period gold pieces related to the Amu Darya Treasure. The center arrives as Uzbekistan's design profile is rising, fueled by growing interest in ikat, suzani, and ceramics, plus a new wave of arts investment that includes the Bukhara Biennial, the forthcoming Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent, and Tadao Ando's planned National Museum of Uzbekistan in Tashkent. But for all that momentum, the Quran Hall may be the clearest expression of the country's cultural ambition: a lavishly staged encounter with a sacred text bound up in centuries of faith, scholarship, craft, and Uzbek identity. This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: Asanas at Sea? The Best Places for Yoga Around the World Are Also the Most Unconventional
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.21
The best places for yoga are at once picturesque and contemplative, whether it be pranayama in Ladakh’s austere landscape, dhanurasana in the thick of Thailand’s jungles, or shavasana beside an Alpine lake in New Zealand. These experiences offer as much external peace as they do internal, and even long after the session and trip have ended, it's those stirring, outdoor moments that endure. They feel like they’ve stopped time and are worth going out of the way for—planned or spontaneous. And what's better than practicing your asanas in a phenomenal natural setting? With these 10 best places for yoga, grab your go-to mat and embrace your inner yogini. Lux* South Ari Atoll, Maldives The middle of the Indian Ocean is possibly the most unique spot one can find to do yoga. Practice asanas while sailing on a traditional wooden dhow at this Maldivian resort. Lux* South Ari Atoll organizes this cruise at golden hour with an instructor guiding you on Tibetan Sound Bowl therapy, breathwork, and yoga. Sip on a refreshing drink, inhale a mood-enhancing oil blend, and float on the waves as you meditate and feel your mind reset. The Kyagar, Nubra Valley, India This boutique hotel is located on the ancient Silk Route in Ladakh’s stunning but stark landscape. Sitting on the sandy banks of the Siachen River and surrounded by the icy Karakoram peaks, it has a very special location that owner Rinchen Kalon believes furthers your yoga practice. To that end, she hosts a retreat at the property every season, and when the weather permits, outdoor classes are held on a river trail surrounded by wildflowers and sea buckthorn bushes. The Kyagar's regular yoga classes are free of charge for guests and last 30 to 90 minutes. Haritha Villas and Spa, Sri Lanka This luxury villa property in Hikkaduwa has an open-air jungle yoga pavilion nestled amidst lush tropical greenery, overlooking the serene canopy of the surrounding forest. Haritha offers hour-long, private lessons in Hatha Yoga, which are apt for beginners. Guests love the serene jungle setting with sweet birdsong in the background and a gentle wind rustling through the trees. Many cite the yoga lesson as one of the most memorable parts of their stay here. Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar Resort, Oman This rocky mountain resort is one of the highest hotels in the world and has a spectacular deck which can be booked for a yoga session (based on weather and availability). Diana’s Point is a platform where Diana, Princess of Wales, once stood back in 1986 and has a breathtaking canyon view of the fabled Green Mountain. Anantara offers hatha, sarvanga, meditation, and monthly full-moon yoga classes, but this spot is not for the fainthearted, as it juts out into a valley with a steep drop-off. March to May is rose season in this region, and the entire valley below erupts into unbelievably fragrant Damask roses. The Kumaon, India The exquisitely-designed Kumaon is located in a remote part of the Himalayas, and its most magical setting for yoga is the rooftop terrace located at the highest point of the property. Views extend to the valley of the Kosi River on one side and the Binsar Forest on the other, all under the watchful gaze of the upper Himalayas, including the divine Nanda Devi peak. With reclaimed Himalayan slate as the cooling floor of the terrace, a wispy breeze scented with pine and carrying birdsong, Kumaon's yoga space feels magical. It offers traditional hatha yoga along with basic pranayama, and guests describe them as rejuvenating and peaceful. Qasr Al Sarab, Desert Resort by Anantara, Abu Dhabi Doing yoga surrounded by vast sand dunes is certainly an unusual proposition. The wellness and meditation center at Qasr Al Sarab by Anantara is nestled on the edge of the resort, a sanctuary that opens to an uninterrupted panorama of the golden Liwa Desert. Guests can practice in the midst of raw nature as the sun rises or sets; in the early morning, the desert sky turns pink and gold, while at twilight, it twinkles with stars. Yoga instruction is available year-round, and the resort also collaborates with yoga gurus specializing in yin yoga, immersive sound healing, and yoga nidra from October to April. Those looking for silence and stillness to escape a chaotic lifestyle will truly appreciate this setting. Keemala Resort and Spa, Thailand This luxury jungle resort in Phuket has a special focus on wellness with a tropical spa, healthy cuisine, and eco-friendly operations. Keemala has two outdoor yoga spaces, one intimate wedding venue nestled within the forest, and the other on a rooftop, offering scenic views. The forest yoga takes place amid lush foliage under a 300-year-old Takian tree; guests are encouraged to practice barefoot so that they can ground themselves directly to the earth for a soulful experience. The resort also has a meditation cave with a waterfall designed to help guests heighten their focus and fully immerse in the present moment. Group classes are complimentary, and private instruction is available at an additional charge. Aro Hā Wellness Retreat, New Zealand A world-famous retreat in the Southern Alps, Aro Hā is located on serene Lake Wakatipu, just 40 minutes from Queenstown. Its yoga classes take place in the Aro Hā Room, which is well known for its striking views of the alpine lake. It offers a range of hatha styles that cater to a wide range of skill level, and all classes are complimentary. Yoga is a key element of their larger program, which also includes subalpine hikes, daily massages and spa time, and a variety of wellness workshops. Jumeirah Olhahali Island, Maldives You may have done yoga on a beach, but have you ever done yoga on a private sandbank? Jumeirah Olhahali Island takes guests on a five-minute speedboat ride to reach a private sandbank at sunrise or sunset. Its Oceanic Balance Retreat is an all-encompassing yoga experience tailored to its surroundings, whether energizing at dawn or grounding at sunset. Pleasant ocean breezes, uninterrupted horizons, and the sense of pure seclusion create space for profound clarity and calm. Acro Suites, Greece Located on the cliffs of Crete, Acro Suites describes itself as a restorative retreat. Its asana wellness studios are sleekly designed with bamboo and local stone, overlooking the Aegean Sea and dramatic cliffs of Mononaftis Bay. The studios offer a variety of yoga styles, including hatha, vinyasa, yin, and yoga nidra, all guided by certified instructors. In addition to complimentary daily practices, guests can also partake in intimate couples sessions, healing circles, and sound healing journeys, each designed to deepen connection. A version of this article originally appeared on Condé Nast Traveller India.

item.title: Dive Into These European Airbnbs With Pools, From Italy to Greece
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.04
Jumping into one on a hot day, a nighttime dip under a blanket of stars, or a few leisurely laps to get you started in the morning; whatever your preference, access to a swimming pool on holiday is a welcome treat. The best hotels will have their own, yes, but Airbnb offers the chance for unfettered access to your own private lagoon, for blissful secluded swims whenever you please. I’ve picked out the most fabulous homestays with pools to book into on your next European trip, ready to dive into and lounge beside throughout your visit. We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. Our top picks: - Best for couples: The Hoam House, Styria, Austria - Best for families: Finca Las Brisas, Jávea, Spain - Best for big groups: Villa des Rêves, Normandy, France - Best for a room with a view: Dalmatia Vibe, Čelina, Croatia - Number of guests: 7 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Views, terrace, proximity to SplitFloor-to-ceiling glass wall-to-wall views blend seamlessly into the shimmering Adriatic at this ultra-sleek coastal haven in Čelina. With a prime location above a picturesque pebble beach, the three-bedroom villa has a crisp, contemporary design and a secluded location with bags of Mediterranean charm. The open-plan living space opens onto a sun-soaked terrace where a heated infinity pool overlooks idyllic views of the sea. Plus, you’re just a 10-minute hop from the historic town of Omiš and an easy drive from Split, so you’re spoilt for choice whether you’re after island-hopping adventures or long days relaxing on the beach. Location: Čelina, Croatia What to do nearby: Split, Omiš, island hopping - Number of guests: 12 Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Air-conditioned suites, cinema room, two kitchens, padel courtGlorious 1930s architecture meets five-star luxury at this grand estate in Villers-sur-Mer, which is just moments from the pretty seaside resort town of Deauville. It’s a sprawling fever dream, with 37,674 square feet of landscaped gardens and room for 12 guests. If you want a weekend where you rarely stray too far, this is a great choice—it has five air-conditioned suites, its own cinema room, and two fully equipped kitchens. Head outside and there’s more delights: a year-round heated pool, bubbling hot tub, and Normandy’s only private lit padel court for evening challenges with friends. With options to book private chefs, yoga instructors, and the arrival of daily continental breakfasts, it’s a lavish bolthole in a prime position for exploring Normandy’s glorious coast. Location: Normandy, France What to do nearby: Deauville, Normandy's coast - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Alpine views, fitness studio, alpacasPretty alpine views, a great gulp of fresh air, and cool loft-style design come together at this unique mountain sanctuary, perched up and away in the clouds near the vibrant city of Graz. Inside is achingly minimalist, like an art studio—the perfect place to unwind after workout sessions in the shared fitness studio. The showstopper, however, is the heated outdoor pool, which transforms into a steamy panoramic hot tub during the snowy winter months. Then there’s the resident herd of friendly alpacas roaming nearby—put it together and you have a delightfully whimsical, offbeat Austrian getaway for four. Location: Styria, Austria What to do nearby: Graz, Alps - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Terrace, office space, barbecue, gardenSweeping mountain vistas make a theatrical backdrop for this tranquil Spanish retreat in Jávea. This is real indoor-outdoor living, with three bedrooms and plenty of creature comforts coupled with lush, sun-baked outdoor spaces and ritzy seagrass umbrellas. Should you be able to muster up the strength, there’s an office space for any important emails, while evenings mean big group barbecues on the shady terrace and a few lazy laps in the glittering pool. When it’s time to settle in with a book, take your pick from two open terraces and a quiet, secluded garden with wondrous views. All that and you’re just a few minutes’ drive from the vibrant Costa Blanca coastline. Location: Jávea, Spain What to do nearby: Costa Blanca coastline - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Rustic interiors, view of the Alps and Côte d’AzurVisit in January or February, and the mimosa forests that surround Tanneron will be in bloom, blanketing the quintessential French village in burnished gold. This Airbnb is surely the best bolthole from which to explore the many walking paths in the area. Once a stone shepherd’s home, it’s now one of the most serene, thoughtfully decorated retreats around. Inside, beautiful rustic interiors amp up the coziness, with rich, warm caramel tones befitting its mimosa-dusted surroundings—and beyond the windows, expansive views over the Côte d’Azur and the snow-capped Alps. Location: Tanneron, France What to do nearby: Walking paths, Côte d’Azur - Number of guests: 3 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 2 baths Why we love it: Terrace, sea views, glass infinity poolThere are infinity pools, and then there are glass-walled infinity pools cut right into a cliff face overlooking Lefkada’s most gorgeous golden beaches. That’s what you get with a stay here. This villa is huge, with a spacious terrace from which to enjoy Greece’s famous sunsets (and sunrises, for morning people). It’s modern-as-you-like, built only in 2021 and outfitted in cool minimal tones and no-frills furniture—the focus is kept squarely on those sparkly sea views. It’s just a five-minute stroll to bouncy Kathisma Beach, with its variety of restaurants, bars and shops to explore. Location: Kathisma Beach, Greece What to do nearby: Lefkada, Kathisma Beach - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Panoramic views, olive trees, waterfallBe warned—to get to this Airbnb, you’ll have to take a walk while the hosts escort your cases via tractor. But when you set off, you’ll see just why you’d book here. Panoramic views over the Mediterranean Sea and wave upon wave of olive trees hug the landscapes surrounding this peaceful Tuscan farmhouse, with pretty vistas on offer from every room in the house. Cool off when you arrive in the plunge pool, or just sit up beside a lounger and enjoy the ambience courtesy of the trickling waterfall. The village of Metato is sleepy and quaint, but you’re well-placed for buzzier adventures—Pisa, Florence, Lucca, plus the imposing marble quarries of Cararra, Pietrasanta, Viareggio are all under an hour away. Location: Metato, Italy What to do nearby: Pisa, Florence, Lucca, Cararra, Pietrasanta, Viareggio - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Nearby trails, breakfast, gardenPull on your hiking boots and get ready for an outdoorsy weekend; your suite here is surrounded by some of Portugal's loveliest wild nature, with a wealth of pretty trails right at your doorstep. This one-time Algarvian farm is now home to three charming guest suites, and this is the largest of the lot, with 452 square feet decked out in breezy neutrals warmed up with smidges of caramel. Wake up every morning to breakfast cooked for you, then peter out to the natural pool, which is set among a fragrant Mediterranean garden. When it’s time to head out, the historic center of Loulé is just five minutes away in the car, and you’ll be walking along windswept coastlines in under half an hour. Peckish? The hosts live on site, providing a changing menu of snacks, salads, sharing plates, and refreshments each day. Location: Loulé, Portugal What to do nearby: Walking trails, historic center of Loulé, coastline - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Antiques, garden, on-site hostsAfter years spent renovating their spectacular 16th-century French château, owners Alison and Costas decided to open up a string of cozy cottages in the grounds to guests. This one—the smallest—sleeps just two; there’s a big en suite bedroom packed with carefully curated antiques and a shared kitchen and sitting room a few footsteps away. The swimming pool is the focal point of the fairytale gardens: It’s a blissfully peaceful spot to unfurl between days exploring the nearby Provençal towns of Uzès and Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Alison is often found pottering around the grounds—so she’s always on hand to dish out local restaurant recommendations and day-trip tips. Location: Saint-Victor-la-Coste, France What to do nearby: Provençal towns of Uzès and Châteauneuf-du-Pape - Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Cave home, hot tub, airport transferAll of the other boltholes on this list have a pool, but only this traditional Grecian cave home possesses one inside the property itself—and a heated one with a hot tub to boot. Enter this cozy space, once the village’s bakery, and you’ll be snugly wrapped in a spot renovated sensitively to honor the unique local architecture. The palette throughout mimics that of the sea (and the pool), and there’s a generous outdoor space with a barbecue. A daily breakfast is provided—to eat at the table while perched on a swinging seat—and the hosts can offer airport transfers, car and bike rentals, catamaran excursions, horseback riding, and massages upon request. Location: Vothonas, Greece What to do nearby: Catamaran excursions, horseback riding - Number of guests: 7 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Private garden, excellent location, daily housekeepingDown a quiet cobbled street in the heart of Porto’s Old Town, this two-bedroom villa comes with all the finger-clicking perks of a hotel (daily housekeeping, breakfast deliveries, and a private chef to summon), but the total freedom to do your own thing. Colorful art and jaunty cushions brighten up crisp white linens in the bedrooms, and there’s a huge sofa and TV loaded with Netflix in the sitting room. However, this property’s real coup is the private garden and swimming pool—a little urban oasis, hidden in plain sight—and a perfect spot to while away a post-sightseeing afternoon. Location: Porto, Portugal What to do nearby: Porto's Old Town - Number of guests: 16+ Bed and bath: 12 bedrooms, 12 baths Why we love it: Art, balconies, terraceWith their faded frescoes, colorful antique tiles, beautiful furniture, and walls lined with Renaissance paintings, most of the rooms at this splendid Amalfi Coast villa feel more like museum pieces. Some of the bedrooms open onto balconies with dizzying views of the rocky shoreline, and there’s plenty of space to enjoy sundowner spritzes and suppers on the vine-covered terrace. The pool is the real scene-stealer here—teetering on the cliff edge, it looks straight out over the tumble of pastel-colored houses spilling down Positano’s lemon-scented hillside (it’ll certainly help if you have a head for heights). Location: Positano, Italy What to do nearby: Amalfi Coast - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 baths Why we love it: Terrace, hidden thermal pool in an underground caveIt took owner Giovanni seven years to restore this two-story, loft-like space in San Miniato, an extraordinarily pretty hilltop Tuscan town. The result is a rental for serious aesthetes—and a beguiling mash-up of medieval and modern. Vintage brushed lamps hang from Renaissance brick arches, midcentury furniture in the industrial-style kitchen, and a 16th-century cobblestone terrace accessed via steel-edged sliding doors. Even more remarkable is the property’s most unexpected detail. In the master bedroom, there’s a trap door; pry it open, and you’ll stumble across a hidden thermal pool, squirreled away in a secret underground cave. Location: Tuscany, Italy What to do nearby: White truffle festival, Tuscan hills - Number of guests: 7 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 baths Why we love it: Solarium, garden, shaded lounge in the backyardIt's hard to believe you can stay in this historic villa in southern Italy's countryside. Float among the trees in this expansive pool, then take a leisurely afternoon nap inside the cool, stone-walled bedrooms (there are three, two with doubles and one with a queen, and three bathrooms). There's a solarium, a garden to check out, and a cheery yellow lounge in a shaded part of the backyard. Location: Ceglie Messapica, Italy What to do nearby: Southern Italy - Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 baths Why we love it: Hot tub, coastline, deep bathtubJust a short drive from Crikvenica’s azure coastline and long, sandy beaches, this spacious cottage offers charm and style in ample measure. The master bedroom has a deep tub—always a welcome treat—and the home itself couldn’t be prettier, with pastel blue shutters and wobbly sandstone brickwork finished with ruby trailing leaves. The pool area benefits from a shady spot most of the day, allowing for maximum time soaking up the views, with the odd dip into the pool to cool off in between. Inside, a large hot tub invites you to recline with a glass of fizz. Location: Crikvenica, Croatia What to do nearby: Coastline, beaches - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 baths Why we love it: Heated pool, smart TV, vineyard views, outdoor showerWarm, earthy Travertine stone features throughout this picturesque French villa, creating a comfy countryside feel that perfectly complements the secluded rural location. But that’s not to say you’ll be without modern comforts—the brand-new space is decked out with all mod cons, including a smart TV, strong Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth speakers. Take a dip in the pool—it’s heated, so great for night swims—and enjoy the views over vineyards and towards the sea; the Testa di Ventilegne, Caldarello Tower and, on good days, the Sardinian coast are all within sight. When you’re done, refresh yourself in the outdoor shower and set up on the covered terrace (no sunburns here) for a lazy afternoon. Location: Figari, France What to do nearby: French countryside - Number of guests: 6 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 baths Why we love it: Mountain views, fireplace, infrared shower, beer tapLuxury is the order of the day here in Austria, where this sweeping 1,772-square-foot chalet pays homage to the beauty of natural materials with impressive effect. Wood, the dominant element, features heavily throughout, while slate and concrete ebb and flow, adding welcome contrast. Inside, a statement freestanding fireplace will warm you up as you return from a ski session—and, of course, there are infrared seats and an infrared shower to ease aching muscles. A beer tap, liquor fountain, and teppanyaki grill ensure evenings go without a hitch in the kitchen. Head outdoors, and you’ll find a covered outdoor kitchen with a barbecue, luxurious heated seats, and a huge swimming pool for lazy laps surrounded by those picture-perfect mountain views. Location: Brand bei Bludenz, Austria What to do nearby: Alps - Number of guests: 4 Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bath Why we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows, spiral staircase, heat and ACSmall but perfectly formed, this pointed chalet is the ideal spot for a romantic spell exploring Turkey’s lush Sapanca region. Floor-to-ceiling glass windows look out over the heated pool, which glows atmospherically after dark, inviting you in for a midnight swim among the trees. A spiral staircase leads you up to bed, and you can order breakfast from the nearby market, bringing your goodies right to your door. A heating system and an air conditioner keep conditions just right year-round. Location: Sapanca, Turkey What to do nearby: Sapanca region, nearby market

item.title: The UK’s oldest recorded town has more than 2,000 years of history – and where it is may surprise you
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.97
When I found out where the UK’s oldest town was, I wasn't expecting it to be a place I've passed through quite so frequently, or one still thriving today. I’ve been lucky enough to travel the breadth of Britain over my 31 years, from tiny hamlets in the Scottish Highlands to artsy towns in Cornwall. I’ve spent half my life calling London home and the other half in East Anglia; holidayed in Wales, visiting beaches accessible only by wooden swing; slept in cabins in the Cotswolds; road-tripped through Northern Ireland; and spent years studying in Newcastle. All of which is to say, if you’d asked me to guess where it was, I’d have imagined a barely-there archaeological site somewhere in rural Northumberland, rather than a thriving modern city in Essex, close to the Suffolk border and just 60 miles northeast of London. I’m talking, of course, about Colchester. Today, the city is popular for its fast commuter trains into the capital, relatively affordable housing, open green spaces and, of course, its rich history. But in around AD 43, it was known as Camulodunum: the first major Roman city and the initial capital of Roman Britain, before it was destroyed during Boudica’s rebellion in AD 61. The story of the Roman settlement didn’t end there, however, and Colchester was rebuilt in the years that followed. During the Anglo-Saxon era, the city was largely neglected before later falling under Viking control. In AD 917, Edward the Elder drove the Vikings out, and Colchester began to regain its former stature. Following the Norman Conquest, Colchester Castle was built in 1066 over the ruins of an earlier Roman temple. Dating to the 1070s, it became the first and largest of the Normans’ great keeps, cementing Colchester’s importance as one of England’s key centres. But the city’s history stretches back even further than the Roman conquest. Colchester began as an Iron Age settlement, ruled by Cunobelin, known as the ‘King of the Britons’. Evidence of this early history can still be found in the city today, including a collection of Iron Age and Roman artefacts at Colchester & Ipswich Museums. There’s something slightly confusing about calling Colchester the oldest town in the UK, given that it is also one of the country’s newest cities. It gained city status in November 2022 as part of the late Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours, one of eight towns to receive the upgrade. It joined Doncaster, Milton Keynes, Dunfermline, Bangor, Wrexham, Douglas and Stanley. Of course, when compared with some of the world’s oldest cities, Colchester is relatively young in the grand scheme of human history. Jericho, on the West Bank near the Jordan River, is thought to have been inhabited as early as 9000 BCE, and is often described as the world’s oldest known walled city. Across Britain, several places lay claim to the title of oldest town, from Thetford in Norfolk and Ipswich in Suffolk to Amesbury, near Stonehenge, where evidence of settlement dates back as far as 8820 BC. Colchester’s claim rests on a specific point of difference: it is officially recognised as the UK's oldest town on record, based on a reference to the settlement by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder.

item.title: St Michael's Mount is the historic UK island only reachable at low tide
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.92
Cornwall is bursting with stunning sandy beaches, historic castles and lush gardens, so it’s no wonder that it’s a popular holiday spot for both Brits and visitors coming from abroad. But this region of the UK also has a secret of its own. Some 500 metres from mainland Cornwall, there is a small island that can only be reached at certain points in the day. Looked after by the National Trust alongside the St Aubyn family, St Michael’s Mount is only reachable at low tide and is the English twin of the French monastery Mont-Saint-Michel, which sits on a tidal island off the coast of Normandy. Cut off by the tide for much of the day, St Michael’s Mount is only accessible on foot via a cobbled causeway during low water – a small and fleeting window that makes the journey feel all the more unique and special. The island is linked to the beach town of Marazion by a giant causeway you can wander across to reach the fairytale-like castle and gardens. Once you’ve made it across, you’re greeted with swathes of history and nature in the form of the castle’s medieval stonework and floral terraced gardens that have a history of their own. But there’s also a harbourside village worth exploring, before setting your sights on the castle and its grounds. In its heyday, the harbour was a busy port, but today, it’s smaller and more of a transient location for visitors. However, it’s still home to the St Aubyn family and around 30 islanders. Inside the castle, you’ll be able to step back in time to the 12th century with historic rooms, artwork – such as a series of portraits of Sir John St Aubyn – and artefacts collected over hundreds of years. Surrounding the castle, there’s an unusual but beautiful subtropical terraced garden with flowers nestled amongst cliff faces, initially designed in 1878 for the St Aubyn family. Due to Cornwall’s milder climate, these gardens are filled with plants you’d normally associate with or find in warmer places. And now onto the main event: the spectacular sea air views of Mount’s Bay, the Lizard Peninsula and Penzance from the castle, and as you wander around this small but mighty island. This viewpoint is regarded as one of Cornwall’s best panoramic spots and for good reason. On a clear sunny day, these views are magnificent and filled with awe and beauty. If timings don’t quite work out on your holiday or you want to try a different way back to the mainland, you can also access St Michael’s Mount via boat. From 1 April-31 October when the tide is high, you can access the island via a regular boat service, which takes passengers to and from the mainland from one of three landing points: Chapel Rock, Gwelva and Top Tieb. Back on the mainland, Marazion is one of Cornwall’s oldest towns and is well worth exploring, too. This ancient market town pairs safe sandy beaches with a relaxed food scene, alongside art galleries and independent gift shops that make it an easy place to spend the rest of the afternoon.

item.title: Can American Southern cuisine finally take hold in London?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.99
“A decade ago, I had customers who didn't know what brisket was!” Mursal Saiq, co-owner of Afghan-Texan barbecue outfit Cue Point tells me. Now, Austin barbecue restaurants InterStellar BBQ and la Barbecue are about to kick off a residency at The Ned. Texan barbecue is one area of Southern cuisine gaining meaningful traction across the city. Following an initial wave of Texan barbecue-inspired outfits like Texas Joes and Smokestak, a newer generation is emerging. “We meet diners from across Wales, London, Ireland, on any given day. We’ve seen that the UK market is interested in us, so it makes sense to bring our style of Texas barbecue over,” InterStellar BBQ owner and pitmaster John Bates tells me. “Folks in London are mad for barbecue right now!” “We’re rooted in classical Austin barbecue,” he adds. “So we’ll be serving the trinity tray of brisket, ribs, sausage, but we’re also nudging barbecue into the future with new ideas." “We also play around, adding ingredients like kimchi, for instance,” says Ali Clem, owner and pitmaster at la Barbecue. “Barbecue has been around for centuries, so it’s always been evolving.” The Big Smoke That spirit of experimentation is increasingly evident in London. At Cue Point, Mursal and co-founder Josh Moroney combine low-and-slow Texan barbecue with Afghan recipes. Traditional Texan brisket, delightfully but not overly sweet, comes with crisp Afghan naan and toasty cowboy butter, whilst a rainbow of lively toshi pickles brings crunch and acidity that cuts through the richness of the meat. The combinations don't feel cacophonous – a risk with fusion. “Many Texan barbecue rubs and sauces actually use spices found in our cooking,” Mursal explains. “Like cumin – that’s basically our national spice!” By drawing on Afghan recipes through Texan methodology, Mursal is preserving her identity on her own terms, whilst also catering for wider cultural and religious dietary requirements. “It's a barbecue for the many, not the few.” Hon’s BBQ moved into a slick canalside space in Hackney Wick this summer and also amalgamates culinary cultures. The pièce de résistance is the Sichuan peppercorn short rib – a gustatory firework display, bringing different notes of pepperiness and spice to beautifully cooked slices of meat that gently tumble from the bone like a stack of dominoes. “No one writes the rules of fusion,” says Hon, who built up his Texas barbecue expertise at InterStellar. But here the principles of Texas barbecue remain sacrosanct. “It’s the triangle of happiness,” he explains. “The correct balance between infusing a great flavour profile, the right level of smokiness and the right level of tenderness – not mushiness.” Over at Black Cactus, I taste layered spices in the Caribbean brisket croquettes (influenced by curry goat), whilst their pastrami croissant cleverly leverages the textural pleasure of flaky pastry whilst allowing the rosy meat to shine. On Saturdays, Texan roots are honoured with a generous platter including beef sausage tinged with fennel and paprika, and glistening melt-in-the-mouth slices of Wagyu ox cheek that resemble the cross-section of a crystal. Owners Josh Alcock and Matt Kears practised their craft alongside Texan barbecue experts like Schulze’s Pit Room and Burnt Bean. Beyond barbecue At All Roads, opened in Brixton earlier this year, Southern inflections come through in plates like expertly charred Creole shrimp with a heartening, resoundingly flavourful sauce (we don’t leave a single streak behind!) and succulent lamb ribs harnessing the sweetness and tartness of pomegranate. It feels distinctly London, rooted in its surrounding community while bringing a less narrow vision of Southern cuisine to the fore. “We wanted to create something brasserie-style, to showcase more of Southern cooking outside of barbecue,” says co-founder Malika Greene. Appalachia, which opened in June in the former Counter 71 space in Shoreditch, draws from this region (which covers some of the American South but stretches beyond it). I’m pleasantly surprised by the bold aromas of the Old Bay omelette for example, initially dubious as to whether it would offer sufficient wow factor for a main course. “We’re nodding to how Old Bay seasonings are paired with seafood in places like Maryland and beyond,” says co-owner Ryan Sheenan. Appalachia allows its London context into the cooking. “It’s nice to have a chef who’s cooked here bring that into what they do,” says Ryan, referring to head chef Ali Borer, formerly of Smoking Goat. “To bring in their skill and flair to put their own stamp on dishes whilst still referencing the region.” I sense this approach in dishes like the soulful butter-brined chicken and miso-infused grits, full of warmth and umami, or the uplifting cheddar and Jalapeño cornbread madeleines. The drivers and challenges Both John and Mursal credit institutional recognition as part of the growing interest in Southern food, with both InterStellar and La Barbecue awarded Michelin stars in 2024. Further, television, music and social media have opened up Southern culture to global audiences – from the high kicks of the pristinely manicured Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders, to Beyoncé’s modern country anthems, to food-focused explorations like Deb Freeman’s recent documentary about Edna Lewis, a grand dame of Southern cooking. “People love drooling over these gigantic pieces of meat sliding off the bones on socials,” says Josh. But don’t always understand what it takes to achieve it.” “Time is a huge ingredient in our cooking,” says Ali. “The recipes take days.” “We’re not batch smoking, which is labour intensive, and tough in London,” says Josh. “An industrial area allows more freedom, but further out you lose more of the central London customer base.” The enormous smokers are expensive and difficult to accommodate within health, safety and fire regulations. As Black Cactus is currently housed within a brandy distillery, I see parallels with the technical apparatus required for distilling. Both processes require large-scale equipment, time, experience and obsessive attention to detail for an excellent result. There is also the cultural learning curve. “You’ll have customers demanding something that’s run out,” says Mursal. “We have to explain that you cannot make another brisket in an hour! That wouldn’t happen in the US because there’s an understanding of the nature of barbecue – that when it sells out, it sells out.” The skill involved can be similarly misunderstood. “When I started, some chefs would look down on this as a lower art form,” Mursal tells me. “But you have to learn how to form and adapt very particular chemical equations, the sound of fire at different stages. You’re working with nitrates, haemoglobin, figuring out whether to go slower or not.” Another challenge is how Southern food is perceived. “There are still biases about Southern cooking,” says Tom Zahir Browne, founder of Louisiana-focused hospitality project Decatur. Having lived in the US and travelled extensively, particularly around New Orleans, he felt that much of the representation when he returned here in 2013 was “a poor facsimile” of the food he had come to revere. For Safiya Robinson, who champions Southern Black foodways under the moniker Sisterwoman, the problem is acute around soul food. Of Jamaican, British and Black American heritage, she felt that “a lot of people didn’t extend their appreciation of gastronomy to Southern Black American food.” She adds, “there’s this belief that it’s just fried chicken, unhealthy, scraps, full of salt. My work around the philosophy of ‘intentional nourishment’ deconstructs this.” Her plant-based cooking foregrounds the breadth of this culinary tradition, with dishes like butter beans and hot pepper vinegar, grilled okra with ackee spicy mayo, and peach and hemp barbecue sauce alongside smoked jackfruit brisket. These misconceptions affect perceptions of price. Southern food can be perceived as low-value because its most recognisable dishes are associated with affordability, despite the skilled labour and quality, often farm-to-table produce involved.“We’re cooking fresh and from scratch,” Malika tells me. “That has to be accounted for!” Then there is the nebulous question of ‘authenticity’. What does it mean to attempt to reproduce a cuisine thousands of miles away from the culture and agriculture that birthed it? “This food is closely connected to its land, for example we don’t get collard greens en masse here, so we have to use spring greens instead,” Safiya highlights. “We also don’t have the community numbers to form an initial customer base, so you’re marketing to unfamiliar audiences from the start.” Ryan says Appalachia has been praised by diners from the region as more evocative of the Southern cooking they know than the stereotypical ‘all you can eat’ excess. He shares how one guest from Kentucky described dishes as reminiscent of acclaimed Southern chef and restaurateur Sean Brock. However, others have said it isn’t what they consider Appalachian. “When you develop from a regional cuisine, you’ll face interrogation,” he says. “Local pride is understandable, and we’re constantly and willingly learning. But we can’t cook like everybody’s grandma. We’re paying a tribute whilst creating something of our own.” “Cooking from a London perspective, multiculturalism translates into the output,” says Safiya, who, for instance, serves a sweet potato tart infusing Japanese fermentation techniques. “But the ambition is to think creatively about what I can offer, that stays true to the essence of the cuisine.” Cultural significance Despite the challenges, exploring these cuisines reveals important histories and customs. “This food has such a long line of history, with relationships to many different cultures,” says Malika. For example, the ‘house pot’ at All Roads reflects similarities between Southern and Caribbean slow-cooked dishes, whilst Mursal observes how “Southern barbecue wouldn’t have become what it is without the enslaved Africans who developed pits, or the contributions of Indigenous Americans.” Safiya tells me about her gumbo z’herbes, a custom of abstaining from meat throughout Lent, made with seven or nine greens to represent good luck and the number of friends one will make that year. Similarly, Malika learned Hoppin’ John is a New Year’s tradition for prosperity. Young Nola, which took up a permanent location in Shoreditch this summer, fuses New Orleans and West African dishes, two historically connected cuisines. By contrast, Safiya has a bread pudding that illustrates the connection between Britain and former Southern colonies. The European connection is also explored at Appalachia. Ryan notes the parallel (observed by Ali, who is from Wales) between Southern country ham and Carmarthen cured hams. European settlers adapted their recipes and techniques to the ingredients around them – learning how to use corn from Indigenous communities, whilst uncertain winters encouraged preservation, smoking, curing and pickling. “We want to capture some of that history in a way that makes sense for this city today.” What comes next? Safiya shares how “it’ll be great to see more places where we can experience these foods with a degree of ceremony – after all these cuisines developed through ceremonies and entertaining!” For Tom, aside from spots like Plaquemine Locke, there are still few restaurants that replicate classic Creole or Cajun cuisine, but we’re seeing modern iterations of this cooking. However, he points to Cardinal Rule in Manchester as an example of the Southern food niches he expects we’ll see more of in London. “A business focused on Southern biscuits would have been unthinkable to me a decade ago!” But Tom thinks London still has room for an elevated Southern dining room with plenty of covers. “And we might eventually see a big-name chef from the South deciding to take London on.” Mursal predicts models like more US-style barbecue drive-thrus. For now, noteworthy developments are happening away from the canonically Southern, like Afghan and East Asian recipes meeting the pit and Southern family recipes revisited with creative licence. Perhaps that is what makes this moment feel different. London has had its share of Southern kitsch – cloyingly sweet sauces, pools of melted cheese, theme park aesthetics and quantity prioritised over nuanced flavours. What is emerging now feels more considered. Rather than imitating what’s come before, newer ventures are cognisant of the depth of these cuisines, whilst engaging with them in the vernacular of London’s own culturally layered dining scene.

item.title: Is your vagus nerve the real reason travel wrecks you?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.89
Scroll far enough on social media and you'll hit a quick fix promising to calm your nervous system in seconds. The vagus nerve in particular has become wellness shorthand for ‘calm on demand’ but there's actual science behind how you do it properly – and it goes far beyond a 15-second clip. So, what is the vagus nerve? Essentially, the longest cranial nerve in the body, travelling from the brainstem down through the neck and chest into the abdomen, brushing past the heart, lungs and gut. It's the main line of the parasympathetic nervous system – rest, digest, repair – as opposed to the sympathetic system that gears you up to handle a threat. “If you think of your body as a car, the autonomic nervous system is the drivetrain and brakes,” says Lou Atkinson, clinical wellbeing lead of Yōjō, a health and wellness platform specialising in vagus nerve stimulation or VNS. “The sympathetic nervous system is the accelerator, while the vagus nerve is your essential braking system, slowing your heart rate, initiating digestion and lowering inflammation.” Activating the vagus nerve can help us feel calmer, but the issue with quick fixes is that we are treating the symptoms of nervous system dysregulation – like anxiety, insomnia, a need to control everything – rather than the dysregulation itself. “If we treat the symptom without ever getting to the root cause, it becomes a tireless battle managing something that cannot dissipate unless we leave the state we're in,” explains Sarah Baldwin, a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner. What happens to our nervous system when we travel? Travel obliterates almost all our comforting routines and habits. “It’s essentially a stress-test for your autonomic nervous system, and vagal tone takes the hit," says Human Potential Coach and Breathwork Practitioner, Rob Rea. “Crossing time zones desynchronises the body's rest-and-digest rhythm from local day and night – a large part of why jet lag brings poor sleep, a racing heart and low mood, not just tiredness.” Short nights, dry cabin air, dehydration, alcohol and caffeine all tip the body further towards fight-or-flight, leaving less room for recovery. For some, it goes way deeper than jet lag. Leaving a familiar environment removes our daily safety anchors, and unresolved stress can resurface as anxiety or hypervigilance amid the unpredictability of new places. “Long after we’ve arrived, and the danger has passed, the body can keep replaying that same protective response – that’s why so many of us feel anxious or shut down for reasons we can't quite explain, especially when travelling,” trauma psychotherapist Emmy Brunner says. “Release isn't about forcing it – it happens through small, repeated doses of safety, not pushing through.” In practice, this looks like having a vagus nerve toolkit you can turn to when you need it most. "Splash cold water on the face – cold exposure activates the vagus nerve and can pull you out of a spiral almost instantly,” Brunner advises. Another tip she says is to: “Slowly look around the room and name a few things you can see – it reminds the nervous system it's present and safe." Another surprising method that works is quiet humming. “It stimulates the vagus nerve directly through the vocal cords,” says Atkinson. If you feel too conscious doing this in a public place, longer exhales also help engage it: "Breathe gently through your nose, inhale for four seconds and exhale for six," says Rea. "Let the breath become quieter rather than bigger, and continue for two to five minutes." Making travel easier on our nervous systems Perhaps the best advice is to think of nervous system work as part of your pre-travel prep, along with your packing and booking. “People often wait until they're deeply dysregulated to start regulating, but the earlier you start, the better,” Baldwin advises. She recommends getting outdoor light at both ends of the day to recalibrate your circadian rhythm, before, during and after your trip. As is having a piece of home with you. “Bringing something familiar, a candle, a journal, a photo and orienting to a new room by consciously noticing its colours and sounds both help signal safety, too,” she adds. For frequent flyers wanting something more hands-off, wearable vagus nerve stimulators like yōjō deliver gentle electrical pulses to the ear's auricular branch, nudging the body into rest-digest mode without requiring meditation mid-flight – wearable while working, watching a film or trying to sleep. But ultimately it’s about incorporating vagal nerve work into your daily life. “The goal is not a quick fix; it’s to discharge small amounts of activation to lessen our dysregulation by even 5 per cent,” Baldwin says. Our nervous systems need something called disconfirming experiences. “These are moments where we show, not tell, our nervous systems that the thing it thinks is dangerous is actually safe,” she says. After doing that, our nervous system has enough data points to see that the perceived danger is actually safe, and we no longer experience the anxiety we once did. None of this promises to make flying enjoyable – particularly if you struggle with it. But understood and practised properly, vagal tone could be the deciding factor in whether a trip leaves you restored or wrung out. That’s worth knowing, next time you're stuck in seat 34C convincing yourself it's turbulence, when it’s actually your nervous system on overdrive. - Emmy Brunner’s residential retreats combine hypnosis and somatic practice. The Compass, a four-week online course, fuses evidence-based clinical tools with belief and identity repatterning. - Sarah Baldwin’s online programs Navigating Your Nervous System and Nervous System Essentials can be found here. Listen to her podcast, You Make Sense Podcast, on Apple or Spotify. - Rob Rea’s Autumn Equinox Day Retreat will be at 1 Hotel Mayfair, London. Follow him online.

item.title: Nepal floods: the latest updates, government advisories, and how to help
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.69
This is an evolving news story – the information below is up-to-date as of 10am BST on Tuesday 1 September 2026. For the latest updates in the UK, visit BBC News and Gov.uk. On 26 August, a devastating flash flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the Tibet border, killing more than 1,000, while more than 3,900 remain missing, according to the latest figures from Nepali authorities. At least five more people have died on the Chinese side of the border in Tibet. The number of missing includes hundreds of tourists, trekkers and pilgrims, with nationals from more than 39 countries reported unaccounted for. The disaster began after a major glacier and rock collapse near the Nepal-China border sent a surge of water, mud and debris through the Bhote Koshi river system. Earlier reports attributed the flooding to an avalanche, but subsequent assessments have pointed to a glacial collapse and the resulting debris flow as the trigger, rather than an earthquake. Search and rescue operations remain underway, with the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force deployed across affected areas. Helicopters are being used to reach isolated communities and evacuate survivors, while teams continue searching riverbanks and downstream settlements. China is conducting a parallel operation in Tibet’s Gyirong County, where hundreds remain missing. Fresh flood threat Nepal also issued a fresh flood warning on 28 August after water levels rose at the site of the original disaster. "Information has been received that the flow of water mixed with debris and mud has increased again on Friday in the same area of the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa, where a major flood occurred on August 26," the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said in a notice, reports IANS. The new danger is linked to a barrier lake formed near the Nepal-China border after debris blocked a river. Chinese authorities had warned Nepal that around 2 million cubic metres of water had accumulated in the lake, with another 3 million cubic metres potentially flowing into it over the following days. Nepal Police also said they had received information that a water dam on the Tibetan side had burst again. The lake subsequently began overflowing, temporarily forcing rescue operations to be suspended in some areas. The risk is particularly serious because a sudden breach could send another large volume of water and debris downstream into areas already devastated by the first flood. Authorities are therefore monitoring the lake closely and have asked residents, rescuers and others in the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridors to remain on high alert. Areas in and around Nepal impacted by the floods In Nepal, Syapru Besi and Timure in Rasuwa district remain the worst affected areas, while damage has also been reported along the Trishuli River in Nuwakot. On the other side of the border, the Gyirong area of Tibet also recorded fatalities. “At approximately 10:30 am, due to a mudslide occurring on the Nepalese side, major casualties and missing persons were caused at the Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Shigatse City, Tibet,” Xinhua reported. Regions lying around and below the Bhote Koshi river, which flows from Tibet to Nepal, remain on high alert with local authorities confirming the main road to Kathmandu – which is an important commercial and passenger corridor connecting the capital city to western Nepal, the southern plains (Terai), and the border with India – is closed. The effects are also being monitored downstream in India, where authorities in Bihar have put six districts along the Kosi, Gandak and Ganga systems on alert over the possibility of rising river levels as floodwaters move south. Travel disruptions Travellers flying to Nepal should distinguish between Kathmandu airport operations and access to the flood-hit north. Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu is continuing to list domestic and international arrivals and departures, so passengers with flights to or from Kathmandu should check their individual flight status with the airline before leaving for the airport. The main disruption is on the ground, with roads and bridges leading towards Rasuwa, Syabrubesi and the Tibet border damaged by the floods. Authorities have advised against travelling into affected areas while rescue operations continue. Travellers with onward road transfers, trekking itineraries or Kailash Mansarovar plans should contact their operator before setting out and should not assume that a previously arranged vehicle or route remains operational. Those already stranded in affected areas should follow instructions from local authorities rather than attempting to cross damaged roads or river corridors. Is it safe to travel to Nepal? The UK government's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) handle on X is advising travellers in the region to follow local guidance and stay alert. UK citizens requiring assistance can call (+977) (0)14237100 from Nepal or +44 (0) 207 008 5000 from the UK. At the time of writing, there is no further specific advice warning against travel to Nepal, but travellers heading to the country, especially on tour itineraries, are advised to sign up for the latest alerts. Is it safe to travel to Tibet? Travel to Tibet is permitted only after obtaining a permit through specialist travel agents based in China. Authorities are known to stop issuing permits at short notice, while travel can be restricted even for those in possession of one. There is also a more generalised risk of violent protests. The UK FCDO has not issued specific travel advice for Tibet following the natural disaster, but travellers with planned tours through the region in the coming months are advised to keep up to date here. What is the latest government travel advice? For the latest UK-specific travel advice, see ‘Is it safe to travel to Nepal?’ The Nepal Tourism Board has issued an urgent advisory asking tourists to avoid flood-affected areas and postpone non-essential travel. It has specifically flagged Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan, as well as the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors, and urged travellers to check road conditions before setting out. The Board has also shared emergency contact numbers on X. Visitors can call the board’s helpline at 1234 (toll-free), 1144 (emergency hotline) or contact the Tourist Police on (+977) 9851289445. People can also reach out to Nepal's Ministry of Foreign Affairs Emergency Control Room, which is set up specifically for foreign nationals affected by or missing after the flood. Reachable by phone or WhatsApp at +977 9744441227 or +977 9744441228, or by email at emergency@mofa.gov.np, this is the consular-style channel is the best way to get in touch with the government directly about someone who isn't Nepali. The US Embassy in Kathmandu has triggered a security alert, urging American citizens in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan and Tanahun to avoid riverbanks and low-lying areas, seek higher ground and stay away from flood-affected areas. For urgent assistance, US citizens can call (+977) 1-423-4000 or email KathmanduACS@state.gov. Malaysia’s Foreign Ministry, through its embassy in Kathmandu, issued a note saying they are actively monitoring the situation after losing contact with 11 Malaysian nationals believed to be in Rasuwa. Malaysians in Nepal have been urged to remain vigilant, follow instructions from local authorities and contact the embassy if they need assistance. Alongside its existing Level One advisory for Nepal, South Korea’s Foreign Ministry issued a special travel advisory for Bagmati, Gandaki, Koshi, and Lumbini provinces, urging visitors to relocate to safe areas and advising non-residents to cancel or postpone travel. “We will continue to closely monitor the flood situation in Nepal and review whether further adjustments to the travel advisories are necessary,” the ministry said in a release, reported by The Korea Times. The New Zealand government has updated its advice level to ‘do not travel’ for the China-Nepal border area and asked any citizens in the country to follow local guidance and check in with their families. Those who need consular assistance can get in touch with the authorities by calling the 24/7 Consular Emergency line at +64 99202020. The Embassy of India in Kathmandu has issued emergency contact numbers for Indian nationals affected by the floods: (+977 985 131 6807), (+977) 970 910 7500, ( +977) 981 032 6117 How to track and support relief ops The Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers (OPMCM) has launched the Rescue Request Portal. Here travellers and their families can submit rescue requests, register missing persons’ reports, and check on records of relief supply distributions. The Ministry of Home Affairs, National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and the Department of Roads have also come together and set up a ‘Setu Rapid’ portal. It is a platform designed to serve as a go-to resource for rescuers in the field, command centres and field fleet operators – all trackable on a live map. If you are looking for a missing person, Hemkunt Foundation's Nepal missing person tracing portal hosts a public, searchable database of people reported missing in the floods, which is filterable by status (missing, found safe, found injured, deceased, closed) and built from reports submitted by family members and travel operators. This portal was built by the Hemkunt Foundation, a Delhi-based nonprofit that works on relief aid, healthcare and education. If you're trying to locate someone, search the list first; if they're not on it, you can file a report directly through the linked form. Anyone with updates on an existing case can also submit one through the ‘update a case’ link. How to help Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund The Government of Nepal's official disaster fund, processed through Nepal Clearing House Ltd., is the official channel authorities have asked all donors to use under its "one door policy". Private individuals and groups aren't permitted to independently collect relief funds for this disaster, so this is the most direct route to the official response. It takes international debit/credit cards, mobile banking, UPI, and QR codes, in both USD and NPR. Nepal Red Cross Society Nepal's largest humanitarian organisation, present in all 77 districts and backed by emergency funding from the IFRC, has been on the ground since the first hours, conducting evacuations, search and rescue, and distributing tarpaulins, blankets, first aid, and drinking water. Donations go straight to the society and fund this frontline response. The Himalayan Trust A New Zealand-registered charity founded in 1965 by Sir Edmund Hillary, The Himalayan Trust has worked on development and poverty reduction in Nepal's Everest region for six decades. It has opened a dedicated flood emergency appeal, with funds going toward the official relief effort in the affected districts. Rotary Club of Kathmandu Mid-Town's Disaster Fund As a district-specific relief channel (District 3292, Club No. 26776), the club is accepting direct bank transfers to Nabil Bank Ltd. Rotary Club of Kathmandu is working in three phases: supporting government-led search and rescue, then relief (food, water, medicine, shelter), and lastly rebuilding infrastructure and livelihoods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli catchment areas.
