Donors can mark their transfers as ‘one-time donation for Rasuwa Flood'. Per Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) regulations, single transfers are capped at roughly £4,762 per transaction. This article was first published by Condé Nast Traveller India.

item.title: The UK will have a three-day working week in 2027, thanks to ‘substitute’ bank holidays
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.45
Bank holidays are often just what we need to feel back on track. Whether it's a long weekend spent with loved ones, the chance to enjoy a full weekend with a bonus round of life admin or the chance to escape on a longer break without using up all the annual leave, we often find ourselves counting down to the three- and four-day weekends. With the spring and summer bank holidays behind us for another year following the long August weekend, and many of us already set on our Christmas plans and whereabouts, we're looking ahead to what 2027 and 2028 have in store. And, luckily for those of us on a routine Monday to Friday pattern, things are looking promising when it comes to maximising annual leave. Next year, many of us will enjoy a three-day working week around Christmas, thanks to the way the bank holidays fall on the calendar. In 2027, Christmas Day and Boxing Day fall on a weekend, meaning ‘substitute bank holidays’ come into effect, so that the holidays are officially observed on Monday 27 December and Tuesday 28 December instead. What's more, 1 January 2028 falls on a Saturday, so the ‘substitute’ holiday for New Year's Day will be Monday 3 January 2028. This means that if you book just three days of annual leave on 29, 30 and 31 December 2027, you'll get 10 days off from 25 December to 3 January. According to the government website: “If a bank holiday is on a weekend, a ‘substitute’ weekday becomes a bank holiday, normally the following Monday. Your employer does not have to give you paid leave on bank or public holidays. Bank holidays might affect how and when your benefits are paid.” Here's how the UK bank holidays fall in 2027 and 2028… 2027 bank holidays in England and Wales 1 January – New Year’s Day 26 March – Good Friday 29 March – Easter Monday 3 May – Early May bank holiday 31 May – Spring bank holiday 30 August – Summer bank holiday 27 December – Christmas Day (substitute day) 28 December – Boxing Day (substitute day) 2028 bank holidays in England and Wales 3 January – New Year’s Day (substitute day) 14 April – Good Friday 17 April – Easter Monday 1 May – Early May bank holiday 29 May – Spring bank holiday 28 August – Summer bank holiday 25 December – Christmas Day 26 December – Boxing Day

item.title: Tate Britain is bringing the 90s back to life with the biggest art and fashion exhibition of its kind
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.29
In the latest of an exciting series of autumn/winter exhibitions coming up in the capital, Tate Britain is set to stage the first exhibition exploring the art, photography and fashion of the 1990s from 8 October 2026. The 90s: Art and Fashion is a deep dive into a decade synonymous with optimism and an audacious spirit, exploring the decade’s surge of creative energy through the world of almost 70 artists. Former British Vogue editor-in-chief Edward Enninful OBE is the lead curator, lending his decades of industry experience and knowledge to the season’s hottest showcase. As the economic uncertainty of the 1980s faded somewhat, the turn of the decade welcomed a resourceful new generation of young talent in Britain. The crowd’s taste for imperfection and ‘realness’ opens the exhibition space with photography by the likes of Corinne Day, Nigel Shafran and Juergen Teller, the talent behind the lens for magazines such as i-D, Dazed and Confused. Further on, Roshini Kempadoo and Eileen Perrier examine the influence of print media and how it expanded mainstream notions of beauty during what’s now seen as one of the most iconic fashion eras of recent times. Film and photography present the youthful attitude of the ’90s, with exhibits including Mark Leckey’s 1999 film Fiorucci Made Me Hardcore to images documenting young people at iconic club nights across the UK, including the Haçienda in Manchester and Bagley’s in London. In a similar vein, Dave Swindells, Peter J. Walsh and Tony Davis document the birth of acid house and its influence on the decade's culture. Other key highlights of the exhibition include an exploration of the ‘Cool Britannia’ movement, Chris Ofili’s Turner Prize-winning 1998 painting No Woman, No Cry – a poignant tribute to Doreen and Stephen Lawrence – and work from artists such as Hamad Butt that responded to the ongoing impact of the AIDS crisis. The exhibition ends with artists and designers who, at the close of the 20th century, reckoned with Britain’s past and addressed questions of its future, from Yinka Shonibare to Maud Sulter, via icons including Vivienne Westwood. The 90s: Art and Fashion runs at Tate Britain from 8 October 2026 – 14 February 2027.

item.title: The Indonesian island that time forgot is one of travel’s most exciting new destinations
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.07
There are not many places left in the world like the tip of Rote. It’s a fragment of coastline on an island off West Timor, which itself is a far-flung extremity of the eastern Indonesian archipelago, closer to Darwin than Jakarta. Aussie surfers started coming here 40-odd years ago, arriving for Rote’s long, clean waves, magicked up by a rare blend of wind, swell and bathymetry. There are other elements that give Rote its dream-come-true energy: tropical weather, white sand beaches, dense fringes of coconut palms, lingering sunsets, a steady trade wind in the dry season that keeps the mosquitoes down. Rote is, alluringly, always on island time. Crucially, it’s not easy to reach – good for surfers who don’t much like sharing a wave. The long journey to get here is why Rote has stayed Rote, one of the most wonderfully inconvenient places out there. Amid all this remoteness, the first top-end resort has just opened, Nihi Rote & Hospitality Academy, sister property to Nihi Sumba, west of here. Both these hotels – a few hundred miles apart – front one of the most coveted waves in the world. When I visit, the hotel is still taking shape. At the eastern end of the bay is a clutch of thoughtfully designed, thatched, low-rise villas, each with a swimming pool; the interiors in mine use local materials such as lontar palm and ikat textiles. The gathering place is beach club Nammo, with its poolside restaurant and watersports instructors, smack in front of Bo’a break. Here I wait for the tide to turn before paddling out. When Nihi Rote launches fully in October, there will be 21 villas, three pools, a spa, a pump track and a golf simulator. It is also planning to build and sell multimillion-dollar residences alongside the property. One night I’m invited to Rote Hospitality Academy, where Timorese trainees have prepared an endearing evening of traditional song and dance, storytelling and a feast of coconut rice with lemongrass, rendang beef stew and grilled fish with sambal. Sitting around the firepit, toes in the sand, the students share stories with me about the cuisine; traditional string instrument the sasando, made of bamboo; and their struggles with learning to swim. For many, it is their first job, or their first job in hospitality, and it’s been a fast-track whirlwind. Before the hotel opened, they had already hosted a big-splash 50th birthday party for its owner, Michael Schwab, son of investment firm founder Charles Schwab. “We’ve never seen anything like this on Rote,” says one student. Change is not always easy, especially in a place that, until recently, relied on seaweed farming and fishing. I feel a pang as I drive past Rote’s cinder-block and tin-roof huts, women on the porch pausing to wave as they plait each other’s hair, sepia-tinged frangipani blossoms strewn on the ground. Rote has long been open to outsiders – and that is increasingly rare in this world of ours. “Do you live here?” This is a regular refrain from locals as I freewheel around town. It is always uttered with a smile – on the harbour, at a café, down on the beach. When I reply that I am passing through, they say: come and live here, you are welcome, bring your family. Many have taken up such invitations, seduced by the island’s stress-free go-slow rhythm. “We were also passing through,” a South African surfer tells me, echoing my line. “But that was two years ago.” He and his partner have had a baby, bought some land and are now building a cottage. I borrow a bike to explore the main coastal road, sealed but potholed and set back from the seafront, with sandy lanes trailing down to the beaches. Village merges into village, and the only demarcations are bollards painted “Selamat Datang” – welcome – or a trio of life-sized crucifixes, prettily decorated despite being a symbol of execution: one is painted lavender, another strewn with flowers. The churches here are enormous and numerous, towering vaulted monuments, one resembling a gigantic Noah’s Ark. Catholic, a man tells me, then to be contradicted by his wife: no, Presbyterian. Another says Methodist. The pastor tells me Calvinist. Tropical Christianity, let’s agree on, and fervent. At Easter, I’m told, crowds enact the Stations of the Cross, parading through the streets in the garb of Roman soldiers. The rest of the year there’s not much more than a scrap of traffic. One day I drive 40 minutes and count two motorbikes and one water bowser. I reach the end of a road that peters out into scrub, nothing beyond and nowhere for me to go. Although there are few vehicles, there are scads of roadside vendors selling petrol in fancy glass bottles that look more like love potions. Lines of laundry flap. Animals are everywhere: languorous cows, silky-haired goats atop bathroom-tiled gravestones and broods of chickens crossing the road, I could only assume, to get to the other side. This easy-going scene belies the region’s bloody colonial history. Timor was fought over by the Dutch and Portuguese – a battle rooted in the sandalwood and spice trade – resulting in its split into East and West. The British muscled in, but only for a few years, and the Japanese occupied the area during the Second World War. Remnants of history and cultural heritage are not obvious at first glance; some can be seen in the weaving of tessellated tenun ikat textiles, and the Ti’i Langga, resembling a ten-gallon cowboy hat made of lontar palm, worn by men, with a phallic spike on the brim. The best way to explore Rote, with its offshore islands, reefs and consistent breaks, is by boat. At one rocky outcrop I find a vast cave of screeching fruit bats; I drop into the water with a mask and snorkel, and fast-float in the choppy current to spy triggerfish and parrotfish. I was told oceanic manta ray and whale sharks congregate here, so I focus my eyes towards the deep, which falls away fast; the next strike of land is Australia. I check out surf sites, ending up on the far side of Ndana Island, Indonesia’s most southerly point. Nobody is around. I spend most of my time crashing and splashing, but nothing can beat the occasional moment standing aloft, feeling the push of a wave, the water so clear I can see fish dashing about the coral. A couple of haggard, sun-smashed Aussie surfers arrive close to the end of the day, so I bow out of the wave, instead bobbing about straddling my board to watch the colours of the sky shift. Back on land I meet locals and newcomers with surf shacks, market stalls and motorbike hire shops. Hotelier Mick Fogarty is just opening on Rote, after more than 30 years in Bali running the fabled Mick’s Place on Bingin Beach. When I ask him if he feels an ache about leaving Bali, he says “no” before I’ve finished the question. He and his Danish wife, Sascha Hansen, have three pretty self-catering bungalows, and, sensibly, used the best land to build a house for themselves. “We were going to build a restaurant but then thought, why don’t we build a home,” says Fogarty. That sums up the spirit of those who come to Rote. “Everyone moves here for the lifestyle,” he continues, “not to turn a profit, just to sustain a life.” After sunset, when everyone lopes back from the beach, there are a few couples hitching their gear onto motor scooters and a few families carrying babies, bags and boards, toddlers in tow. Everyone’s sandy with wet, tangled hair. It’s a strong, fit, healthy scene: “no drugs, no nightclubs”, as I keep hearing on repeat. One hotel owner points out, “Many of the people here already had their 20 crazy years, so now we can all chill.” Another labels Rote a “retirement village for surfers, who come for peace and quiet”. Carla Lázaro Ferro from the Canary Islands calls it differently. She lived here, then moved to Berlin, where she found herself “crying for Rote”. “Here you feel you can give back; life is more meaningful, more chaotic, more free,” she tells me. On my last night, I sleep out on the deck of my villa at Ferro’s dreamy resort, Bo’a Vida, overlooking the Bo’a wave and the Timor Sea. Here on the southern edge of Indonesia, the stars glow like light bulbs, even on the horizon. Only the dazzle of the rising moon dims them. I feel as far away as I could be. Shacks, bungalows, resorts and more NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy Following the success of its sister resort in Sumba (to the west of Rote), this 21-villa property on Bo’a Beach opens the renowned surf sites to top-end travellers. Villas are a mix of one-bedroom, duplex and family-style set-ups, and larger residences are planned. The westerly rooms have the best views of the Bo’a break. An on-site training academy allows guests to give back to the community. Bo’a Vida Owner Carla Lázaro Ferro opened a thatched shack 15 years ago atop a rocky outcrop at the end of Bo’a Beach, overlooking the legendary wave of the same name and the sunset beyond. Now she has six climate-conscious villas, five of which were designed by her husband, award-winning architect Álvaro Carrillo Eguilaz, with stone paths meandering down to slips of sand and the yoga sala. Ferro also runs Indika café in town, which serves fruit bowls until 5.30pm, when everyone heads out to catch a wave. Rote Island Huts Nat and Matt Thistlewaite came here from Australia in 2011 after finding the island of Rote on Google Earth. They arrived with the aim of creating a nonprofit holiday retreat that channelled income into local education and the community. There are five simple huts: three are family-style with bunks, all have beachfront access. It’s a heartening enterprise and they are now preparing to hand over management to local Rotenese, as they always intended. Sardine Beach Rote Pika and Pascal Chevillot, a Slovenian and a Frenchman, used to own Sardine, one of Bali’s top restaurants. Here on Rote they’ve created a spectacular three-villa property in five acres of gardens on one of the island’s best beaches. The rooms use lontar palm and coconut leaf to create traditional roofing, panelled walls and sconces. Pascal’s breakfast is a real event, with Parmesan omelettes and smoked Spanish mackerel. I notice a copy of Tao Te Ching on a side table, which just about sums up the place. Mick’s Place Rote Aussie Mick Fogarty and Sascha Hansen from Denmark are the creators of these three delightful beachfront bungalows with private courtyards in a glade of coconut trees. The couple are strong on sustainability, harnessing solar power, reusing grey water for the gardens and lending bicycles for guests to get around on. The lap pool is set to be the gathering place. Minimum one-week stay. 81 Palms Close to the T-Land break at Nemberala Beach, Spaniards Julia Davila Solana and Jose Miguel Murgui have built six A-frame cabins on the soft sand, plus they’ve recently opened four smaller bungalows at their new Next Door property. The Spanish restaurant is the best place for dinner in Rote, with former Michelin-starred Murgui in the kitchen cooking up gazpacho, tapas and seafood paella. Natural World Safaris (01273 691642) can arrange an 11-day trip combining a B&B stay at COMO Uma Ubud on Bali and a seven-night full-board stay at NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy on Rote, from £5,800 per person. The price is based on two people sharing and includes all transfers and domestic flights. International airfare is excluded.

item.title: 10 best hotels in Bath for a romantic weekend getaway 2026, complete with Roman thermal spas and feasting menus
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.75
Bath has long been a popular choice for city-breakers, and some of the best hotels in Bath are also some of our editors' favourite places to book for a last-minute staycation. Like us, many are attracted by the city's combination of healing waters and Regency history. After all, where else can you start the day in Ancient Rome and end it with a Jane Austen-themed afternoon tea? Perhaps unsurprisingly, it’s got a thriving hotel scene, with a mix of accommodation to suit every taste. There are heritage properties, like the Gainsborough Bath Spa and Royal Crescent, where five-star luxury is a given; the hipster boutiques, like No 15 Great Pulteney, and gallery-come-hotel 8 Holland Street, which cater to discerning eyes; and the country piles located just outside the city centre, where you can cosplay as an extra from Bridgerton as you roam the grounds. Without further ado, here’s our guide to the best hotels in Bath. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Bath - For couples: The Francis Hotel - For families: Lucknam Park, Emblems Collection - For the spa: The Gainsborough - For an affordable stay: The Yard in Bath How we choose the best hotels in Bath Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page. This is our edit of the best hotels in Bath.

item.title: "If the industry won't give it to us, we’ll give it to ourselves”: how a Caribbean food festival in East London is changing our perception of jerk
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.35
“No Caribbean restaurant has ever been given a top culinary award in the UK,” Jackson Mclarty, founder of Black Eats LDN, mused recently. In the run-up to Jerk Fest, the UK's first food festival dedicated to the Jamaican art of jerk, this dilution, underrepresentation and misunderstanding of one of the Caribbean's most iconic dishes was front of mind. On a balmy summer weekend in Hackney Bridge, Black Eats LDN – the UK's first and only black-owned restaurant directory – brought together 6,000 hungry Londoners to crown the best jerk in the UK. After all, as Mclarty notes: “If the industry won't give it to us, we’ll give it to ourselves.” London's Caribbean diaspora is thriving. According to the 2021 UK Census, there are 345,405 people who identify as Black Caribbean in the capital. The biggest celebration of Caribbean culture, Notting Hill Carnival, is now famous world-over. But jerk, Jamaica's most famous dish, hasn't been given the reverence it deserves. Until now. Mclarty spent his formative teenage years in Jamaica, and revisited earlier this year following Hurricane Melissa. “This festival is personal for me," he commented. “I know what authentic jerk is and how it should be represented, and coming back to the UK without seeing that, I want to revive it and uphold the standard.” So Hackney Wick became, for the weekend, a little Jamaica – with street food vendors hawking their takes on the best jerk recipes to a live soundtrack of reggae and dancehall. At the heart of the festival, 11 vendors went toe-to-toe for three awards that celebrate the community's excellence: Best Jerk in the UK and Jerk Innovation, chosen by the attendees, and the Judge's Choice, chosen by a panel from Caribbean food culture. As for who won the top prizes? Best Jerk in the UK The thousands of Jerk Fest attendees crowned Yard 2 Yard the best in the country. The award-winning team are based out of Romford. Find them cooking until 9pm daily at Sandys 111. Jerk Innovation The guys at Quick Tingz say they're “inspired by soul food, rooted in Caribbean flavours”, and their recipes won them the title of best Jerk Innovation. The team currently caters from their base in North West London – keep an eye on their Instagram to see where they're popping at festivals and street food events throughout the year. Judge's Choice Whats On The Menu Ish was awarded by the expert Jerk Fest judging panel: find the Caribbean seafood specialists near Hackney Wick six days a week to judge for yourself.

item.title: How London became the day party capital of the world
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.82
Like many people born in the early ’90s, I spent a large portion of my youth camping out in muddy fields, surviving on a few Nutri-Grain bars between long weekends of music with friends. I wouldn’t change a minute of it. I’ve always believed that nowhere does music festivals quite like the UK. The weather might be unpredictable, but there’s a particular camaraderie in trudging through ankle-deep mud to make it to the main stage, come rain or shine, that you simply can’t find elsewhere. These days, I’m a little longer in the tooth and expect a touch more finesse from my festival experiences. I’m no longer able to survive on fumes alone, and I’m certainly less inclined to partake in the infamous “roll throughs”. When I moved to London from Cornwall almost a decade ago, I quickly discovered a new favourite way to enjoy music with friends: the city’s seemingly endless roster of day festivals and raves. Spending an entire day dancing to my favourite artists, then being tucked up in bed by midnight with the next day still vaguely intact, felt like a win-win. As the years passed, I noticed more and more day parties cropping up across the city. It left me wondering: is this the result of our growing focus on health and wellbeing, or a response to London’s increasingly fragile nightlife scene, as bars and clubs continue to close across the capital? I spoke to some of the people at the heart of the city’s music scene to find out. If the night is disappearing, party by day This explosion of daytime partying might seem at odds with the increasingly common narrative around the “death of club culture” in London. The statistics certainly make for grim reading, with Mixmag reporting that a predicted 57 per cent of London’s pubs and clubs could close by 2030. So what’s behind the downturn in late-night venues? “It’s less about law and more an accumulation of challenges that have made operating late at night in London increasingly difficult,” says Luke Huxham, managing director of Broadwick Live. “Since Covid, the industry has faced rising operating costs, inconsistent licensing frameworks and planning decisions that allow residential development next to venues that were there first.” In some ways, the rise of day parties feels like a direct response. If it’s becoming harder to party all night, why not dance all day? “Partly it’s the industry adapting to how hard it’s become to operate late at night in London,” Luke agrees. “But partly it’s a shift in how people want to socialise, drinking less, craving new experiences and still wanting to dance even if late nights don’t fit their lives anymore.” It’s a shift I’ve noticed in myself and my peers, too. While Millennials might occasionally roll their eyes at Gen Z’s obsession with health and wellbeing, there’s something increasingly appealing about a party that doesn’t require sacrificing an entire weekend to recover from. DJ Moxie has been at the forefront of both London’s late-night and day party culture and recognises this wellbeing shift: “Nightlife and club culture bring so much to our city, but it’s not for everyone”, she says, “I think having the option to dance and still have a relatively early night is attractive for a lot of people.” It represents a significant departure from the all-nighters and unapologetic hedonism so deeply entwined with the history of clubbing and festival culture. But perhaps that’s exactly the point – London’s party culture isn’t disappearing, it’s just changing shape. How do you curate the environment to keep the energy of a nighttime rave? “You have to really think about how the spaces look and feel, from daytime into dusk and sunset into night, and storyboard that journey,” Simon Denby co-founder of Body Movements explains. “The space has to be lit very thoughtfully, as, for example, beams of light don’t work in the same way in daylight as they do in a dark club, without the haze over the dance floor.” For Luke Huxham, who has worked on events at some of London’s best-known venues, including Printworks and Drumsheds, it’s about creating an experience that evolves throughout the day. “Sound, lighting, stage design and the physical journey through the space all contribute to how the energy builds,” he explains. “Magazine Open-Air is a great example. We’ve got this incredible location on the Thames, surrounded by London’s skyline. Rather than shutting those things out, we’ve designed the experience to make them part of the event.” The future of London’s party scene Two forces seem to be driving the boom in London’s day-rave scene: the increasing difficulty and cost of operating late-night venues, and a broader shift in how people want to socialise. It’s a complicated dichotomy, but the conversations I’ve had with people at the heart of the scene leave me feeling optimistic. They aren’t suggesting that the rise of daytime partying has to come at the expense of nightlife. Instead, they see it as another way for communities to create the spaces they need and keep London’s music culture moving forward. “True ravers know day parties have always been around,” says London-born DJ and producer Maya Jane Coles, “I don’t think it takes away from nightlife at all – it just means there’s something for everyone at different times.” When I asked what they thought the future of London’s nightlife looked like, the responses were surprisingly hopeful: “My hopes are that we continue seeking joy in all corners of the world, especially in London, and nightlife thrives under a new wave of people who are dedicated to encouraging silliness, fun, and chaos,” says Glyn Fussell, co-founder of Mighty Hoopla. Luke agrees that the future doesn’t have to be either-or. “What’s exciting is that the definition of going out is becoming broader. Day parties are a part of that, but so are grassroots venues, community events, festivals and cultural spaces that make London what it is.” “London needs all of it,” he says, “and I hope we keep moving towards an ecosystem where all of that can coexist.” Perhaps that’s the real secret to London’s day-party boom. It isn’t that we’ve stopped wanting to party at night. We’ve simply found more ways to do it. And in a city that has always reinvented its relationship with music, maybe the future of nightlife looks less like an ending and more like the start of a new, very long, day. The best day parties to go to Body Movements, Southwark Park Body Movements Festival is described as a space for “queer [and] trans art to be discovered [and] applauded, queer exploration to be encouraged, and queer expression to flourish” and toted as the city's first outdoor queer arts and music celebration. Field Day, Brockwell Park Field Day has been a popular London day festival mainstay since it started out in 2007 with a lineup consistently comprised of rising stars alongside big-name headliners. Previously hosted in East London’s Victoria Park, the festival is now setting down new roots in the South. Rally, Southwark Park Held in leafy Southwark Park every August, Rally is a relative newcomer on London’s festival scene but has been heavily praised for its programming and production value. Mighty Hoopla, Brockwell Park One of the UK’s most inclusive pop festivals, Mighty Hoopla is a glitter-strewn celebration of alternative culture where new and established pop acts perform alongside cabaret shows and drag performers. Pxssy Palace, across London Pxssy Palace is a collective that celebrates Black, black, indigenous and people of colour who are women, queer, intersex, trans or non-binary. They regularly host club nights in diverse venues across the capital, as well as programming their own stage at Maiden Voyage festival. Maiden Voyage, Burgess Park Electronic music festival Maiden Voyage has been going from strength to strength over the years, from the team behind the famous Camden Jazz Cafe. Unfold, Canning Town A weekly Sunday rave held at Canning Town’s, Fold, Unfold is a celebration of electronic music and the queer community. The Cause, East London Docklands The Cause is up there as one of the best venues in London, and hosts not only late-night events but plenty of daytime raves too. It’s great for summer day parties with its recently developed outdoor staging. GALA, Peckham More than a decade since its debut in South London, Gala has grown into one of the mainstays of London’s festival scene. Usually at the beginning of the season, it’s a great way to kick off the summer and let loose a little.

item.title: 7 cheapest nicest hotels in Barcelona for under £200 per night
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.81
As a city, Barcelona exudes a knowing, effortless quality that makes it undeniably – there’s just no better word for it – cool, and some of the cheapest, nicest hotels in Barcelona are a reflection of that. If the Spanish city were a person, you might find they combine a certain beachy, salt-sprayed insouciance with impressive cultural nous and urban grit. You’d definitely want to be part of their inner circle, and the good news is that you can be – even when on a budget. Despite frictions stemming from overtourism, the Catalan capital still extends a welcoming hand to travellers, and there is a crop of affordable boutique hotels that mean it remains one of the most appealing city breaks in Europe. At any given moment, you might be taking in Antoni Gaudí’s Modernisme masterpieces, retreating from the city’s swelter on a lively golden beach, catching a soul-stirring notes of Catalan guitar on a panoramic rooftop, or imbibing the kind of languid tapas lunch that inevitably ends in a siesta. For the very best budget-friendly places to enjoy the latter, read on for our edit of the cheapest, nicest hotels in Barcelona right now. item.title: My favourite Airbnb: an earthy-toned lodge on the hilltops in Milos with steps into the sea
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.62
The landscape on Milos is endlessly surprising; there’s more to this volcanic island in the Cyclades than its cerulean waters – though those are reason enough to visit. But it’s also home to gorgeous fauna and flora and raw, natural terrain. Wildflowers scatter the island in spring, and sage, thyme, oregano and lavender grow along its winding wild paths. That’s the scent I smell as we arrive at our Airbnb, which is based just outside the beautiful town of Trypiti. The scent permeates around me; it's almost distracting – so good I want to bottle it. We are welcomed by Nausicka, the owner of the homes that perch on this private nine-acre property. She shows us to our sea-view villa and tells us that each room is named after Greek herbs, trees and plants that grow on the land. I am wowed by the view beyond our glass doors where oat plants and red grass dance in front of the sea. Beyond our outdoor kitchen and terrace, two small deck chairs sit at the end of a curving path. They look more like sculptural pieces of art than actual seats, surrounded by a calming palette of brown and green. Immediately, I know I’ll feel at peace here. And there was that smell again, carried through the room with the breeze. The interiors are minimal, and the walls are made of local stone. It feels fitting here: why compete with such a perfect setting? I never want to be far from a swim, so I was pleased to know there was access to a private cove just a short walk beyond the winding path in front of our room. Stairs built into a cliff led right to the rocks; no beach beds in sight, just a sun-warmed stone platform to lay your towel next to a ladder directly into the sea. We were told the space was shared with guests from the neighbouring lodges, but no one came. We felt lucky to have it all to ourselves, so I devoured a book and listened to the ambient sounds of the waves knocking the rocks for hours on end. I nodded off watching sailboats meander by. Later, we climbed the stairs back to the room, sticky from the sea salt, and I headed straight for the outdoor shower, leaning my head up to the open blue sky, as I washed off the salt in my hair. Wrapped up in a towel, hair dripping wet, I do as everyone does on their holidays: make a beeline for a chair to dry in fresh air, swapping the classic balcony-and-bag-of-Lays for a chair on a cliff, a sea view and a crisp glass of local Greek wine. The southern side of the island is known for its sunsets, and it's easy to see why. At first, I don’t focus on the sky; instead, I focus on the changing colours of the plants and herbs, which light up and glow like little orbs. Browns turn to gold as they catch the light, and the sky turns pink as we walk back to our room with empty glasses. We don’t want to leave the room, and thankfully we don’t have to. Nausika tells us that a nearby taverna can deliver dinner. We lit candles and settled into our outdoor kitchen. In the morning, a breakfast basket arrived at our door – an additional cost but one worth every penny. I dig through my haul of fresh, local goods: the Greek yoghurt I had hoped for, fat juicy strawberries, peaches, homemade jam, boiled eggs and freshly squeezed juice. Checking out was bittersweet, but as we followed the island’s rocky roads, we felt sure we’d be back soon.

item.title: The Farm at Avebury: A stylish farm stay that has a play barn, tractor rides, ponies to groom and lambs to bottle feed
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.38
My city-born children still gasp when they see a cow, so a farm stay where they get to see animals up close is the ultimate weekend away in their eyes. We’ve been to lots around the country but The Farm at Avebury, in Wiltshire, is the one my five and nine-year-olds keep asking to return to. The reason? The owner Alice has designed a stay that she knows will delight children. The farm, known as Galtee More since the 1890s, is a working farm that has been in the Hues family since 1922. Rob Hues, the current farmer, and his wife Alice are the fourth generation to work it, growing crops and rearing livestock. But, with the increasing challenges of running a family farm, they spied an opportunity for diversifying and decided to convert six dilapidated stables into stylish holiday “hideaways”, which were completed in 2021. Driving along the single-track farm road, my nine- and five-year-olds were excited to see Aberdeen Angus, Highland cattle and goats grazing in the fields, and, we discovered later, pigs snuffling around in the woods. The farmhouse is a beautiful building dating back to 1737, and the holiday accommodation is two parallel, long red-brick buildings arranged along two sides of a central courtyard, planted with waving verbena and decorated to encourage groups to gather outside with a festoon-lit pergola, clusters of seating and a shared BBQ. Rooms range from one to three bedroom self-catering units and are named after spots nearby: Silbury Hill, Long Barrow, Windmill Hill, Longstones, Swallowhead and Greyweathers. Each one has been given a distinct character rather than a house style. We loved the plaster-pink bathroom in Long Barrow, which we stayed in, and the king-sized bed, which we found up steep steps on a separate floor to the girls' twin room downstairs. Friends we were travelling with (and this is where the farm really comes into its own – it is perfect for groups who want separate lodgings) were in Greyweathers. My kids envied the climbing wall that lead up to a bunk bed in a mezzanine above the lounge. But climbing walls aside, children rarely get excited about interior design. Instead, hidden extras that Alice, a mother of three daughters works into every aspect of the farm. There’s a wooden playground in the orchard, guarded by Samuel the sheep (“just push him out the way if he’s a nuisance,” were the instructions). Then there’s a barn filled with toys ranging from a bouncy castle to ride-on diggers and bikes of all sizes, a table football machine and ping pong table. There's also a supply of craft materials sourced from the Wiltshire Scrap Store, a reuse project that takes offcuts and end-of-line stock that would otherwise be waste. The Granary is the on-site cinema room filled with beanbags where Alice and Rob’s own children can often be found, eager to host and meet new friends during the holidays. That would have been enough, but Alice is full of surprises that are beautifully linked to the rhythm of a working farm. When we visited, there was a lamb in the farmhouse kitchen that she let visiting children bottle feed; there were piglets in the barn who “needed” morning attention from eager little helpers, and on Saturday afternoon, as we were sitting out in the courtyard, Alice came past with a couple of ponies, asking my girls if they wanted to help groom (they did). She also arranged a tractor ride to the top of West Kennet Long Barrow, a 5,000-year-old chambered tomb you can walk into, before taking us down to a nearby pumpkin farm to pick our own. If you need even more entertainment, Mud and Guts, a Wiltshire outfit running den-building and outdoor sessions, can be booked to come to the farm to run sessions for the children from £25h/pp (min group size 6). It’s hard to tear yourself away from the farm – or at least persuade children that they should go out – but along with the scenic walks (the farm’s website has downloadable maps for “big walks” and “little legs”) there are the ancient stones to go and see. A visit to Avebury makes you wonder why so many people bother with Stonehenge: Avebury henge is similarly magical, but it’s not fenced off, meaning you can touch the stones. It’s also a great spot for people watching as it attracts the mystically-minded; we saw two wizards in full regalia. There are lots of dining out options nearby, including The Waggon & Horses pub at the end of the drive, or Red Lion pub in the middle of the stone circle in in Avebury, but as we were staying with another family, both with youngest children who go to bed at 7pm, cooking at home was the best option for us. The farm makes that easy: it sells its own farm produce; beef, lamb, pork and rapeseed oil. You can order ahead of time and have items like pre-made lasagnes and sausages waiting in your fridge, along with essentials like bread, milk, coffee and tea, or purchase on site. If you’re hiring the whole place out – say for a birthday party or wedding – there are two event barns that can seat big parties: The Granary seats ten and The Barn 42, and private caterers brought in. When you travel with children you become accustomed to eyeing up the next thing to entertain them, which can be mentally exhausting. Here, all that was taken care of – by someone who knows exactly what will delight them next. Instead, our children had the privilege of roaming free – running back and forth to the play barn, all within earshot – while we, and our friends, couldn’t believe our luck that we were able to sit for a few hours just as grown ups, and enjoy a glass of wine in peace.

item.title: 9 best hotels in Albania for an affordable escape in 2026: from luxurious Riviera stays to buzzy boutique favourites in Sarande
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.37
Ask any visitor to Albania, and they'll tell you the same thing – it's the warmth of the people that makes this country so memorable, and some of the best hotels in Albania present a stellar example. Yes, it has crystal clear rivers, snow-dusted peaks, a glittering Ionian shoreline, and ancient UNESCO heritage sites galore, but it’s the Albanians and their innate kindness and hospitality that make a visit here truly special. For decades, Albania was cut off completely from the outside world due to a brutal communist regime. Under dictator Enver Hoxha’s iron grip, the country was in a state of self-imposed isolation. Religion was outlawed, private property seized, and travel beyond its borders was unthinkable. Even today, echoes of its past linger in the thousands of stark concrete bunkers that pepper the landscape. Recently, however, the small Balkan nation has been making its way onto the world stage. And thanks to a series of new flight routes, it is now firmly on the tourist map. Visitor numbers are increasing year on year, and, with EU membership pending, and development occurring at every corner, this is a place to discover now. Larger brands and resorts are moving in fast, and there’s a distinct sense that Albania is repositioning itself as an upmarket destination, much like neighbouring Montenegro and Croatia. However, for the time being, there are still plenty of lovely hotels in Albania – from traditional guesthouses to boutique boltholes and heritage properties – these stays bridge the old and new, which could be the country's best USP. item.title: The best neighbourhood restaurants in the UK to plan a staycation around
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.08
Whenever I think about going out for a really nice meal, buzzy city centres and downtown areas typically come to mind. Often, the best restaurants are clustered in these areas to attract locals and tourists alike, and invite those just passing by to walk in. But nowadays, I find myself more drawn to the humble neighbourhood restaurant. No longer just for the local community – diners are becoming increasingly willing to travel far and wide for a table at these establishments. Neighbourhood eateries are usually smaller and more intimate, offering lunch or supper that feels closer to eating like a local than being thrust into a thronging crowd of tourists in the middle of the city. And while this feeling is particularly evident in London, a number of neighbourhood restaurants serving incredible food can be found all across the country. These are the best ones to visit on your next staycation. Chakana, Birmingham The neighbourhood: Moseley This modern Peruvian restaurant is located in the small-but-artsy suburb of Moseley in southern Birmingham. It's owned and run by Peruvian-born chef Robert Ortiz, who brought London’s Lima its first Michelin star in 2014, and co-owner Steve Dickinson. The space is lively and welcoming, the food vibrant and the menu largely gluten-free. Here, diners will find classics like zesty ceviches and creamy causa, as well as Peru’s lesser-known culinary delights including Andean potato stew, made with spuds grown at an altitude of 3,500 metres in the Peruvian Andes; steamed cod with yuca stew and kiwicha, a superfood grain native to the country; suckling pig with a chocolate sauce and charapita chilli; and more. Address: 140 Alcester Road, Moseley, Birmingham B13 8HT Website: chakana-restaurant.co.uk Palmito, Brighton and Hove The neighbourhood: Brunswick Town Smack bang between Brighton and Hove lies Palmito, a tiny, slightly chaotic restaurant that everyone wants to literally squeeze into. There are only 20 seats in here, so expect to be rubbing shoulders with your table neighbours. It’s difficult to really advise anyone on what to order in Palmito as chefs and founders Kanthi Thamma, from South India, and Diego Ricaurte from Ecuador, tend to play things fast and loose, drawing culinary inspiration from whatever tickles their fancy from week to week and depending on what is available on the market. As Grace Dent put it in her 2023 review, diners “go on a journey” when they visit the restaurant, and it would seem to be a journey to all of Ricaurte’s favourite culinary destinations. The menu may not be predictable, but many dishes are vegan, and the menu is split between vegetarian and vegan dishes, fish plates and meat-forward dishes, so there’s something for everyone. Address: 16 Western Road, Brighton and Hove, Hove BN3 1AE Website: palmito.co.uk Wilson's, Bristol The neighbourhood: Redland Located on what is said to be perhaps the best culinary street in Bristol, Wilson’s on Chandos Road is small yet mighty. The farm-to-table restaurant, which was awarded a Michelin star in 2025, has been feeding people and championing zero-waste kitchen practices since 2016. It was founded by Chef Jan Ostle and his partner Mary Wilson, and you may recognise Wilson’s from Apple TV+’s culinary documentary series Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars. The intimate space houses big ambitions in both food and sustainability. The couple have their own “market garden” just 20 minutes away from the restaurant, where they grow their own produce. In the kitchen, anything we would normally consider destined for the compost bin is brought back into the menu through preserving, fermenting, and other ways to minimise waste. Oste and Wilson approach their restaurant as an extension of their home and will happily chat with customers and passers-by about their food, which changes with the seasons. Address: 24 Chandos Road, Redland, Bristol BS6 6PF Website: wilsonsbristol.co.uk Pompette, Oxford The neighbourhood: Summertown Husband and wife duo Pascal and Laura Wiedemann opened their charming French restaurant and wine bar Pompette – meaning tipsy in the language of love – in late 2018 as a way of spending more time together after the birth of their son two years prior. But despite the romantic notion behind the restaurant’s story, Pompette doesn’t do dimmed lights, candlesticks and white tablecloths. Instead, the restaurant feels relaxed and bustling, with quirky and interesting art covering the exposed brick walls and mismatched tables giving it a casual, unbothered atmosphere, a place where everyone is free to be themselves. The Wiedermanns focus on seasonality and cooking everything from scratch, and their menu draws inspiration not only from France but from across Europe, so expect dishes like English summer salad with fresh produce like radishes, beetroot, cucumber, peas, broad beans, and more; Turkish-style stuffed aubergines; classic steak frites; and French cheeses or English strawberries for dessert. Address: 7 S Parade, Summertown, Oxford OX2 7JL Website: pompetterestaurant.co.uk Queen of Cups, Glastonbury The neighbourhood: Near St John's Square Queen of Cups is not strictly a neighbourhood restaurant, but it is located off Glastonbury’s main street of organic herb shops, crystal and sage sellers, and witchcraft supplies, so we’re counting it as one. Set within a 17th-century coaching inn, the Queen of Cups – named after the tarot card that symbolises feminine energy and empathy – serves Middle Eastern fare inspired by executive chef and founder Ayesha Kalaji’s Jordanian roots. Kalaji uses local produce and ingredients to create dishes such as horaa osbao, a vegan Syrian lentil dish from Damascus; brik au truite, her own take on a Tunisian dish of trout wrapped in crispy, delicate brik pastry with a gloriously runny egg and olives waiting inside; and grilled Nabulsi cheese with Persian black lime honey, crunchy preserved lemon skins and wild za’atar. Go for the incense boutiques – stay for the Queen of Cups. Address: 10-12 Northload St, Glastonbury BA6 9JJ Website: queenofcups.co.uk Belzan, Liverpool The neighbourhood: Wavertree If a Liverpudlian friend says “I know a place”, they are most likely talking about Belzan (and if they’re not, then this is your time to shine). In the student enclave of Wavertree, this “friendly neighbourhood bistro” is exactly that – cosy, welcoming and the kind of place you want to spend a few hours in with good company and even better food and wine. Founded in December 2017 by owners Chris Edwards and Owain Williams and chef Sam Grainger, Belzan is creative, ambitious and unpretentious in its menu, a balance rarely struck that works really well here. Must-orders include their signature Guinness rarebit potato, a multi-layered cheesy wonder smothered in a tangy tomato and herb dressing; deviled ox cheeks with parmesan polenta and bitter leaves, if in season; or any whole fish dish that is on the menu depending on the time of year you visit; it changes often but is always delicious. Address: 371 Smithdown Rd, Liverpool L15 3JJ Website: belzan.co.uk Lucky Lychee at The Green Man, Winchester The neighbourhood: St Michael Winchester does not immediately come to mind when thinking of culinary hotspots in England, but Lucky Lychee has certainly put it on the foodie’s map. This Malaysian restaurant is located in The Green Man pub on Southgate Street, immediately south of Winchester’s city centre. It was named Britain’s best restaurant by The Good Food Guide in 2025 and continues to gain praise from restaurant critics and discerning diners. Lucky Lychee was founded by Nicole Yeoh and James Harris in 2020. Together, they bring flavours from Yeoh’s hometown of Penang, Malaysia, which is famed as one of the world's best food capitals. The menu changes each month, but you can rely on their roti-focused brunch menu for flaky, buttery rotis paired with all manner of dahls and curries. For dinner, you can’t miss the crispy, herby sesame prawn toast bao and charcoal-grilled satays (choose from chicken, beef or paneer). If you are lucky enough to nab one of just eight daily portions of char siu wonton noodles, you must have that. If not, the Nyonya king prawn curry and honey Marmite fried chicken are no consolation prizes – they’re also winners. Address: The Green Man, 53 Southgate St, Winchester SO23 9EH Website: luckylychee.uk Bavette Bistro, Leeds The neighbourhood: Horsforth Helmed by chef Sandy Jarvis and his husband Clément Cousin, both formerly of The Culpeper in east London, Bavette Bistro is a true neighbourhood gem. The restaurant takes its cues from the couple’s London bistro roots, serving hearty yet elegant dishes made with seasonal ingredients, so the menu tends to shift with the seasons. But some dishes are staples on the menu, such as the must-order Cantabrian anchovies and saffron aioli on panisse, the twice-baked crab soufflé with bisque sauce and fennel salad, and the namesake bavette, which comes with classic fries and a salad. Reservations are hard to come by – but so worth it once you get your foot in the door. Address: 4-6 Town Street, Horsforth, Leeds LS18 4RJ Website: bavettebistro.com Nora's, Plymouth The neighbourhood: North Hill Meat is firmly on the menu at Nora’s, a modern British bistro in the neighbourhood of North Hill, just outside Plymouth city centre. Led by chef Lewis Craig, the laid-back spot is heavily focused on big hunks of steak and cooking over charcoal, but they also have plenty of other protein options including chicken, pork and fish. But really, you’re heading here to fulfil a craving for steak, which you’ll be pleased to know are responsibly sourced from a variety of local butchers. They also source their fish from a local fishmonger, who supplies Nora’s with plenty of fresh catches of the day, oysters and scallops. It’s the place to be for a relaxed dinner with plenty of friends, with a notable wine list of natural and low-intervention wines that are easy to drink and not eye-wateringly expensive – so the good times can flow. Address: 40 Drake Circus, North Hill, Plymouth PL4 8AB Website: norasplymouth.co.uk Melton's, York The neighbourhood: South Bank South Bank and Scarcroft Road, where Melton’s is located in York, have previously been described as a “Goldilocks neighbourhood” where everything is just right. For the past three decades, Melton’s has fit right in, winning over locals and visitors alike with exceptional food and a warm ambience. Run by husband-and-wife team Michael and Lucy Hjort, this fine dining restaurant manages to create a relaxed, friendly and inviting atmosphere – no intimidating white tablecloths, stuffy waiters or scary wine lists here. It’s a real community gem, where locals are greeted by name and first-time visitors feel instantly at home. The three-course menu is limited, with just three options per course (one meat, one fish, one vegetarian) to choose from, but this is a sign of a restaurant that is really confident in what it does, and you won’t walk away disappointed. Address: 7 Scarcroft Road, York YO23 1ND Website: meltonsrestaurant.co.uk Beckford Canteen, Bath The neighbourhood: Walcot Set against the backdrop of the prettiest neighbourhood in the already impossibly pretty Bath, Beckford Canteen is a breath of fresh air. From the shades of verdant green that characterise the restaurant’s interiors to the window countertops that invite you to watch the world go by or the relaxed, holiday feel of the outdoor seating area, Beckford Canteen is a breath of fresh air. Offering a polished modern British menu that draws from European and Mediterranean influences, it’s easy to see why Beckford Canteen is That Girl when it comes to dining out in Bath. Seasonal ingredients, local produce and creative cooking result in simple yet stunning dishes like meaty and moreish hogget shoulder with imam biyaldi (Turkish stuffed aubergines) and labneh; refreshing tomato and red pepper gazpacho; hyper-local fish from day boats that could be anything from seabass to lemon sole, accompanied by violet artichoke and salsa rossa. Address: 11-12 Bartlett Street, Bath BA1 2QZ Website: beckfordcanteen.com Argile, Edinburgh The neighbourhood: Marchmont The vibe: There’s something so thrilling about sitting right up in front of a kitchen, watching the chef prepare your dinner right in front of you – it’s why open kitchens and omakase restaurants are thriving right now. But the idea of having one such restaurant in your neighbourhood may seem outlandish, unless you’re in Edinburgh and you get a reservation at chef Jack Montgomery’s small 10-seater chef’s table restaurant in the Marchmont suburb. Montgomery serves up seven perfectly formed courses, cooking and plating them all within arm’s reach of the diner and speaking in detail about each dish so customers learn where the ingredients come from and the story behind how the dish came to be. It’s a special, intimate place that is well worth the 20-ish-minute walk or very short cab journey from Edinburgh Old Town. Address: 21 Argyle Place, Edinburgh EH9 1JJ Website: argilerestaurant.co.uk Big Counter, Glasgow The neighbourhood: Southside In 2024, Condé Nast Traveller named Southside Glasgow’s coolest foodie neighbourhood, and this reputation is thanks, in part, to Big Counter. Big Counter has big personality, big plates and big flavours – a 2026 review by restaurant critic Chitra Ramaswamy in The Times raved about how they serve already-buttered bread, without a hint of stinginess, and wrote luxuriously of the steak tartare, battered monkfish cheeks and asparagus with clams and ham she had at the time. The pan-European menu is ever evolving though, so you never quite know what you’re going to get. Favourites include fish bathed in rich chistorra butter sauce; steak with decadent blue cheese, fried potatoes and sun chokes; fresh cherry pie, likely a summer special. Unusually for such a hyped restaurant, Big Counter doesn’t have a website and barely has a social media presence, so you can only book a table via ResDiary and you better be quick about it. Address: 76 Victoria Road, Govanhill, Glasgow G42 7AA Website: instagram.com/bigcounter Ember, Cardiff The neighbourhood: Pontcanna There’s an element of “expect the unexpected” when it comes to Ember, which is located in the trendy suburb of Pontcanna in Cardiff. At first glance, you’d be forgiven for thinking it must be a Scandinavian restaurant, with all its light wood furnishings, white tabletops and open shelving. But it is run by a Welsh chef, Dave Killick, who is known for bringing a refined touch to otherwise rustic Welsh fare – there’s also a notable Italian influence in his cooking at Ember. But never mind the slight confusion, this Michelin Guide-recommended restaurant is a real neighbourhood gem and serves up some truly impressive dishes. From the Pembrokeshire lobster, accompanied by fennel, bisque and a giant chip – a nod to Wales’s apparent reputation for impressively long chips; to the braised rabbit and smoked bacon lasagne with peas and asparagus; or the linguine with Pembrokeshire cockles, mussels and anchovies, Ember is absolutely top-notch. Address: 5 Romilly Crescent, Pontcanna, Cardiff CF11 9NP Website: embercardiff.co.uk Harry's Restaurant, Exeter The neighbourhood: Longbrook Street Barely outside of the city centre, but far away enough to get away from the madding crowds of Exeter is Harry’s Restaurant on Longbrook Street. Housed in a striking Victorian Gothic building that was once the workshop of renowned Victorian sculptor Harry Hems – hence the name – this family-run establishment is a part of the fabric of local life. Chef-owner Samantha Pounds leads the kitchen alongside her daughters to ensure a warm and lively atmosphere, and the menu is unpretentious, with seasonal ingredients sourced from Devon’s farms and producers. Harry’s offers quite an extensive menu, including a rather large steak section; don’t miss out on the Bloody Mary soup or Brixham crab on toast, nor the classic burger full to the brim with bacon, cheddar and a signature burger sauce – finish your meal with any of their delightful sweet treats for pudding. Address: 86 Longbrook Street, Exeter EX4 6AP Website: harrysrestaurants.co.uk

item.title: Will Bangladesh join the Mecca defense alliance?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 6.59
There has been widespread speculation about Bangladesh becoming part of a mutual defense deal struck last month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. But the South Asian country says it has yet to receive an invitation. The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed into force in early August, is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression. It stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries would be regarded as an attack on all. Some analysts believe the pact has already changed the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East and South Asia. "Although it is a collective defense understanding, from a strategic perspective it is primarily an initiative to maintain the regional balance of power and advance the respective interests of the participating states," Navine Murshid, a political science and sociology professor at North South University in Dhaka, told DW. Bangladesh govt. in favor of Mecca pact Any move by Bangladesh to join, however, could complicate its foreign relations, particularly with neighboring India. The two countries share a 4,096-kilometer (2,545-mile) land border, and have strong cultural and economic ties. India, a fierce rival of Pakistan, sheltered many Bangladeshi refugees and provided military support to Bangladesh during its independence war against Islamabad in 1971. However, ties between New Delhi and Dhaka have become increasingly contentious since a deadly student-led uprising in 2024 toppled then Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was considered a close ally of the Indian government. Now living in exile in India, Hasina has since been convicted in absentia for crimes against humanity during the uprising. She has denied the charges. Bangladesh's current government, headed by the center-right Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), is in favor of the Mecca agreement. "We view this pact positively," Bangladeshi Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman said in response to a question in parliament last week. But he insisted that the question of Bangladesh joining the pact, or even considering membership, had not yet arisen, as that would depend on the intentions of its current members. "If they express an intention to include Bangladesh in the pact, we will certainly consider it positively," he said. When asked about the remarks made by Bangladeshi officials, India said the pact had implications for its national security and that it was closely monitoring the situation. "We continue to follow all developments that have a bearing on India's security and take all necessary steps to safeguard it," Randhir Jaiswal, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs, told reporters in New Delhi last week. Competing geopolitical interests Analysts said Dhaka needs to consider its interests carefully before making any move to join the joint defense pact. "The scope for direct conventional interstate war or military conflict in South Asia is limited. Therefore, the primary role of such an agreement is not confined to conducting border wars," said Murshid. "In international relations, its significance lies mainly in strengthening bargaining power and maintaining one's position against the influence of other regional countries." Murshid added that Pakistan's interest in bringing Bangladesh closer through this agreement "is driven by geographical and political considerations." "For India, the security of the Siliguri Corridor and its eastern frontier are important considerations," she said, referring to India's narrow land link to its northeastern states, which wraps around Bangladesh to the north. "If Pakistan's defense-related influence in Bangladesh were to increase, New Delhi could view this as a development capable of affecting the regional balance of relationships." In such circumstances, Bangladesh would have to clearly define what it would and would not do by joining this alliance, she explained. "In particular, a clear position would be necessary regarding Bangladesh's role if a military conflict were to arise between India and Pakistan. Taking Pakistan's side during such a conflict could create political and diplomatic pressures for Dhaka that may exceed Bangladesh's capacity to manage," she stressed. Dhaka-based former diplomat M Humayun Kabir sees no reason for Bangladesh to join the pact. "Bangladesh has not joined any military alliance over the past 50 to 55 years. As far as I am concerned, I believe that position remains unchanged to this day," he told DW. "They are talking about a regional security arrangement, but the region in question concerns Pakistan and the Middle East. We are not part of that region or geographical area. Bangladesh is located in the eastern part of South Asia. Therefore, there is no direct geographical rationale for Bangladesh to participate in such a military alliance," he added. Would Bangladesh benefit from joining the pact? Murshid stressed that Bangladesh needed to develop its own defense infrastructure and security systems sustainably. She believes that becoming part of an international security agreement could help modernize Dhaka's defense capabilities and facilitate access to military technology. "The text of the agreement does not directly mention trade, labor markets or economic relations. However, it is natural for economic elements to become linked with a security framework, a phenomenon known in international relations as issue linkage," she said. However, Kabir fears joining the pact could limit Bangladesh's geopolitical options and recommended a balanced approach. "We contribute to peacekeeping missions around the world under the auspices of the United Nations, and that is important to us. Our economy is interconnected with many different countries in various ways, which is also important. Our workforce is present in countries across the world, and that, too, is an important consideration," he said. "Therefore, before making any decision on this issue, we must take into account the many different dimensions and forms of our national interests." Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

item.title: Iran says it will return to ceasefire if US does
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.57
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Tuesday said Tehran would reciprocate any US move that signals a return to the collapsed interim ceasefire deal. "I state explicitly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the ... memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action," Pezeshkian said on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Pezeshkian accused the US of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms. At the time, the US carried out strikes on Iranian targets after what it called "continued aggression" against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, with an Iranian drone striking a Panama-flagged tanker. Tehran has repeatedly said it will allow free navigation through the Strait, but on its terms. A diplomatic solution to the conflict remains elusive. Pezeshkian's comments come shortly after the US and Iran traded fire for the first time in over a month. The US said it struck Iranian minelaying forces on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday and Iran targeted US forces in the Middle East in response. US President Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday that there will be a "response" to the Iranian attacks, but said the latest strikes did not mean a return to full-scale war. Putin and Xi meet at SCO summit Pezeshkian met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday. Russia's President Putin told his Iran's Pezeshkian that the Russian people stand in solidarity with Iran, and that the two countries maintain their economic and trade relationship despite the current political environment. Pezeshkian thanked Putin for Russia's stance on the sanctions against Iran, also criticizing the US for having "no right" to impose sanctions on other countries. The meeting takes place as Russia's full-scale invasion into Ukraine continues to rumble on for more than four years. Earlier, Putin met Chinese President Xi Jinping, who has provided Russia with implicit economic backing during the Ukraine war. According to Xi, the China-Russia pact has become "more solid" and that its "prospects will be even brighter." On his side, Putin said the two countries' cooperation was "successfully developing on all fronts." The SCO is a bloc promoted by Russia and China as an alternative to Western power, which has in the past mostly served for economic discussions, with Moscow and Beijing pushing its significance in recent years. Its 10 members also include India and Pakistan, while its 15 "dialogue partners" being Turkey and Qatar, amongst others. Edited by: Wesley Rahn

item.title: As glaciers melt, can communities be protected?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.84
High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall. The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released. Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is known as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Blatten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods. How much is climate change to blame? The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists. Levan Tielidze, research fellow in glacial geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, said the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact." "As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he told DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream." Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucasus Mountains of North Ossetia in Russia. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24 kilometers (15 miles) and killed around 125 people. "The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," said Tielidze. Meanwhile, the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability. Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century. For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches." "These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he added. Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s. The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event. However, the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," said Chapagain. The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometers, noted Tielidze. "These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he said, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change. Is it possible to adapt to more extreme glacier collapse impacts? The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blatten resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse. But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, said Tielidze. "In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he said. "We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings." For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning," he added. Chapagain said the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems. However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal." "What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," said Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group cocoordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement. A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures. "We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," said Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt." Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: The great lake divide: Collapse vs. comeback
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.48
Some of the world's largest lakes could shrink substantially within this century, with far-reaching consequences for ecosystems and roughly a quarter of the global population that lives in affected regions. Although restoration efforts have proved successful in some cases, many inland bodies of water face extreme challenges. Caspian Sea: A shrinking giant Despite its name, the Caspian Sea is actually a lake. Bordered by Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, it is the largest inland water body on Earth. But its surface area has been rapidly receding since the 1990s. This shift is partly due to the use of dams and water-management practices in the Volga River basin. But hotter conditions driven by burning fossil fuels to power homes and businesses is also a contributing factor, with rising temperatures increasing evaporation rates. Scientific models project that water levels could fall up to 21 meters (68 feet) by 2100. Even a decline of 10 meters could leave large parts of the shallow northern basin dry, eliminating nearly one-third of the lake's current surface area. The consequences are already becoming apparent. Ports require increasingly extensive dredging, fish stocks and wetlands are coming under growing pressure and habitats used by the endangered Caspian seal are drying out. Scientists have also warned that the exposed lake bed could release dust and pollutants. Joint conservation efforts among the five coastal states remain politically challenging. Lake Constance: A pollution turnaround Like much of Europe, Lake Constance has been impacted by high temperatures this summer. Bordered by Germany, Austria and Switzerland, the 63-kilometer-long (39-mile-long) lake has experienced high evaporation rates that have caused water levels to fall significantly in some places. In the late 1970s, however, low water levels were not the main concern. At the time, the lake was suffering from severe nutrient pollution and was at risk of ecological collapse. Massive algal blooms and oxygen depletion in deeper waters threatened fish populations and led to swimming bans. The expansion of wastewater treatment facilities and removal of phosphorus from sewage significantly reduced nutrient concentrations. That led to the stabilization of lake trout, which had been at risk of disappearing. Local communities also benefited. Around 4 million people in the southern German state of Baden-Württemberg now rely on Lake Constance for their drinking water. Yet the ecosystem is far from fully restored. Shoreline development, invasive species and climate change continue to pose major challenges. Restoring more of the lake's natural shoreline could help strengthen its resilience. Aral Sea: A disaster with glimmers of hope The Aral Sea in Central Asia has become one of the defining examples of how water extraction can devastate even the world's largest lakes. Only a few decades ago, it was the fourth-largest lake on Earth. During the Soviet era, vast amounts of water were diverted to irrigate cotton and rice fields, creating an environmental catastrophe whose effects continue today. By 2010, the surface area had shrunk by more than 50,000 square kilometers (19,300 square miles). Thirty fish species that once supported commercial operations have disappeared, and entire communities along the former shoreline have vanished with them. The Aralkum Desert has emerged where the water once shimmered, covering roughly 62,000 square kilometers. Today, dust and sandstorms carry salt and toxic residues from the former lake bed across surrounding regions, posing serious risks to human health. But the North Aral Sea has benefited from the Kok-Aral Dam, which raised water levels. In areas where a return of the lake is considered unrealistic, saxaul shrubs are being planted to stabilize the sand and contaminated dust. According to the Kazakh government, more than 1.8 million hectares have been planted since 2018. Muskegon Lake: The big clean-up For decades, Muskegon Lake in the northern US state of Michigan was polluted by industrial waste and contaminated sediment. Extensive clean-up efforts by local environmental authorities removed contaminated soil and more than 110,000 tons of historic sawmill waste. As a result, 54 hectares about 130 acres) of habitat along the shoreline and in surrounding areas were restored. In 2025, authorities finally removed Muskegon from the list of severely degraded lakes. According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, restoration efforts now generate an estimated $28 million (€23 million) in additional recreational value annually and attract roughly 500,000 extra visitors each year. However, the lake is not entirely free of pollution. Authorities continue to warn against eating certain fish species because contaminant levels remain too high. Lake Chad: A region fighting for survival The vast Sahel forms the transition zone between the Sahara Desert to the north and the African savannas to the south. Stretching across the continent from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, it is home to one of Africa's most distinctive ecosystems: Lake Chad. Shaped by sand, wind and harsh environmental conditions, the wetland ecosystem is a critical source of water for people and wildlife and supports livelihoods across the region. In the 1960s, during periods of high water, Lake Chad covered up to around 25,000 square kilometers, slightly more than the area of New Jersey. During severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s, it temporarily lost more than 90% of that area. Since then, the lake has partially recovered. Its size now fluctuates considerably depending on rainfall and the season — ranging from roughly 12,000 to 20,000 square kilometers. Climate change, irrigation and deforestation continue to put pressure on the lake. According to aid organizations, its decline has contributed to a wider ecological crisis across the region and threatens the food security of millions of people. Some 30 million people depend on the resources of the Lake Chad basin. Hundreds of bird species migrate from Europe and Asia to Africa each winter, and many use Lake Chad as an important stopover site. Some waterways previously blocked by dams have been reopened.
