In May, the African Development Bank, the Lake Chad Basin Commission and five neighboring countries launched investment projects worth $10 million. The funding is intended to help preserve the lake both as a habitat and an economic lifeline for the region. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Influential humanists: These are the winners of the Goethe Medal 2026
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.31
Estonian classical music composer Arvo Pärt, Italian literary translator Anita Raja and Greek theater director and actor Prodromos Tsinikoris are the three recipients of the 2026 Goethe Medal, an annual award that honors international public figures who contribute to creating cultural bridges between Germany and partner countries. The annual award, presented this year on August 28 in Weimar, is one of the most prestigious awards in Germany for international cultural work. So what connects these three personalities to Germany's culture? A prolific German exile: Estonian composer Arvo Pärt Considered one of the most influential figures in contemporary classical music since the 1960s, the Estonian composer is renowned for his minimalist, contemplative compositional technique called "tintinnabula." With his iconic works including "Für Alina" (1976), "Fratres" (1977), "Tabula rasa" (1977) and "Spiegel im Spiegel" (1978), Pärt is one of the most performed living composers in the world. In 1980, the composer was forced to leave his home country, and his works were banned in the Soviet Union. After leaving then Soviet Estonia, Pärt settled in West Berlin with his family. He lived in Germany for nearly three decades. "Germany plays such an important part in my father's work," Michael Pärt told DW. The composer's son added that his renowned father found creative freedom through his collaborations with different German conductors and musicians. He was also inspired to compose works to German texts. Pärt's minimalist and spiritual works found a broad audience in the West thanks to the recordings of Manfred Eicher, founder of the Munich-based record label ECM. After Estonia gained independence in 1991, Pärt reestablished contacts with his home country and returned there permanently in 2010. The composer, who turned 90 in September 2025, now lives in the Estonian village of Laulasmaa, where the Arvo Pärt Centre opened in 2018. It is directed by his son, Michael Pärt, who will be traveling to Weimar to pick up the award on behalf of his father. One of the most significant translators from German into Italian: Anita Raja Born in Naples in 1953 to an Italian father and a German mother, Anita Raja studied literature in Rome, where she still lives. Specialized in the translation of modern German-language authors, Raja introduced East German author Christa Wolf to Italian readers with her translation of "Cassandra" in the early 1980s. "Anita Raja's translation is a translation from woman to woman. It's very empathetic, very powerful. It shows that there really was a surprisingly magical connection between the author and the translator," noted renowned Italian actor Sonia Bergamasco at a recent event marking the release of a new edition of the novel. Wolf became a widely celebrated author in Italy thanks to this first translation, and Raja then went on to translate many more of Wolf's novels. She has also translated the works of other major German-language writers, including Georg Büchner, Franz Kafka and Ingeborg Bachmann. All while translating literature, Raja also worked full-time as a librarian in Rome. She became the founding director of the Biblioteca Europea in Rome in 2005, heading it for more than 10 years. She turned the library into a model project focusing on the promotion of European cultures, languages and international cooperation. Prodromos Tsinikoris: Documentary theater as a bridge between cultures Born in the West German city of Wuppertal in 1981 as the son of Greek labor migrants, Prodromos Tsinikoris is one of the leading voices in contemporary Greek and European theater. As a theater director, actor and dramaturg, he creates documentary productions exploring the themes of migration, social inequality and historical perspectives. His audio walk "In the middle of the street" centers on homeless people during Greece's financial crisis. The documentary theater production "Clean City," co-created with Anestis Azas, focuses on the lives of migrant cleaners, juxtaposing their personal testimonies with the rhetoric of neo-fascist movements who want to "clean" Greece of its foreigners and refugees. In the play "96%" Tsinikoris deals with the Holocaust of the Jews of Thessaloniki and the looting of their property during the Nazi occupation. From 2015 to 2020, Tsinikoris directed the Experimental Stage at the National Theater in Athens. Today, he is co-curator of the International Forest Festival in Thessaloniki and teaches at the National Theater's directing school in Athens. Many of Tsinikoris' plays have been developed and presented in Germany. His work has also circulated broadly across Europe, particularly through documentary theater festivals and major public theaters. Edited by: Brenda Haas

item.title: Can new Apple CEO John Ternus fix the tech giant's AI woes?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.27
On September 1, a new era begins at Apple as John Ternus becomes just the third man to hold the CEO role at the tech giant since 1997. Ternus was announced as Tim Cook's successor back in April, bringing Cook's 15 years at the helm of one of the world's biggest companies to an end. Since then, Ternus, a leading hardware engineer at the company, has been working closely alongside Cook in preparation for the big job. Just as Cook had when he took over from the iconic Steve Jobs, Ternus has big shoes to fill. Apple's share price has increased by more than 2,000% since Cook took over in 2011 and the company has sold more than 3.1 billion iPhones in that time. Ternus faces a range of challenges at Apple, but his ability to keep the company at the top will hinge on how he reshapes its AI strategy. Apple has struggled to successfully embrace the technology so far, with critics saying it has fallen far behind its rivals. September 9: John Ternus makes public debut Ternus will make his public debut as CEO at Apple's autumn product launch event on September 9. Dubbed "Surprise and Shine," Ternus is expected to announce the company's first foldable iPhone as well as a new version of an AI-powered Siri, Apple's virtual assistant. Francisco Jeronimo, VP for Data and Analytics at tech research group IDC, said Apple's forthcoming announcements were planned during Cook's time in charge and that it will be 2027 before the direction Ternus wants to take the company in becomes apparent. "Of course, September 9 will be quite an important milestone for the company around foldables and around innovation," he told DW. "But I don't think we have seen anything that could indicate that Apple is behaving in a different way or is showing a different kind of strategy because Tim Cook is not in the job anymore — yet." Apple's huge AI challenge What observers will be looking out for from Ternus on September 9 is the extent to which he focuses his remarks on AI. While it was already undeniable when he was announced in April that the artificial intelligence boom would be pivotal to his time at the helm, it has become even clearer in the five months since the unveiling that the AI revolution is here to stay. "It's becoming clear that AI is not a fad, is not something that will go away in the next two or three years," said Jeronimo. "It's something that will dictate the future of most tech companies and indeed all companies." He reckons AI could be "the most consequential technology" for Apple because it could either help it maintain its lofty position or create a set of daunting challenges. The biggest challenge he sees is that Apple doesn't "control" AI infrastructure the way it could previously in terms of designing and controlling both the hardware and software for its key products. "Maybe that will be what John Ternus will be doing differently from Tim Cook, because at the moment, even if Apple built their own AI technology, the reality is that they still depend on someone else," he added. Apple's reliance on other companies in the AI realm has led it into unfamiliar territory. It struck a deal with OpenAI in 2024 to integrate ChatGPT into the iPhone, but that has led to a bitter dispute between the companies. Apple sued OpenAI earlier this year, alleging that the AI company stole its trade secrets. Earlier this year, it announced a deal with Google, whereby the search giant's Gemini models would be used for Apple's own AI models and its new AI-powered version of Siri. "The risk for Apple is to become less relevant in a world where companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are leading in terms of technology, in terms of awareness, in terms of services and potentially in terms of hardware," said Jeronimo. For decades, Apple's success has been built on its physical products, from the iPad to the iPhone. "If devices from OpenAI become available, that could be very, very risky for Apple. They could completely disrupt the experience and the way we interact with technology. And if Apple is not on the front of that innovation, that is a big risk," he said. A combination of Jobs and Cook? Ternus' background as an engineer who worked on Apple's core products, as well as innovations such as the Apple Watch and AirPods, means he will be expected to lead the way on new AI-driven products for the company. He also played a central role championing Apple's shift to designing its own chips instead of relying on external suppliers like Intel — precisely the kind of independence Apple would like to achieve when it comes to AI. Jeronimo thinks Apple still has big advantages, given its massive volume of users as well as the company culture of having dominated innovation in tech for decades. He thinks if Apple can get to grips with AI under Ternus, it could lead to huge success. "What we will see in the next years will dictate whether Apple is on the right track or if they are really struggling," he said. For Ternus, the first task will be to simply fit smoothly and convincingly into a role that both Jobs and Cook undeniably made their own. "Steve Jobs was the guru of innovation and disruption and Tim Cook was the guru of execution," said Jeronimo. "I think John Ternus can be a combination of both." Edited by: Rob Mudge

item.title: Norway's new King Haakon VIII takes oath in parliament
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.20
New King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance to Norway's consititution in the parliament in Oslo on Tuesday, following him succeeding his father Harald V, who died last week. This follows a day after Harald's coffin was taken to the chapel of the royal palace, where it will remain for the public to pay their last respects until a funeral on September 9. What happened in the parliamentary ceremony? Haakon was driven the short distance from the royal palace to the Storting, or parliament in Oslo. House speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the official announcement of Harald's death and Haakon's succession before the new constitutional monarch took the oath. "I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in according with its constitution and laws, so help me god, the almighty and omniscient," the 53-year-old said. Queen Mette-Marit skips event amid complications following lung transplant Ahead of he ceremony, the palace said that Haakon's wife Queen Mette-Marit would not be attending. She had made her first public appearance since assuming the title on Monday in the coffin procession but is recovering after a lung transplant in June. In a statement, the palace quoted Are Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo's University Hospital, as saying that complications following a transplant are not uncommon and that Mette-Marit had experienced them on several occasions, including Tuesday. "As a result, the Queen must remain under observation throughout the day. Unfortunately, the Queen will therefore be unable to attend the swearing-in ceremony at the Storting today," he said. What's the role of Norway's largely symbolic monarchy? Norway's royal family can trace its roots bak to the ninth century. When the country regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters supported the idea of reinstating a largely symbolic constitutional monarchy in a plebiscite. Most political power lies with the elected government and parliament, but Norway's royals retain a predominantly soft power role in diplomacy and promoting the country around the world. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first. Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

item.title: Germany terminates lease for Berlin's Russian House
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.14
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has announced that the contract under which the Russian House is operated will be rescinded. This is one of several measures in retaliation for Russian involvement in the attempted airport drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4. The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin. The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state, its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore. French authorities have previously linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services. "In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations, the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin at the beginning of August. Back then, in response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that the fate of the Russian House is linked to that of the Goethe Institut in Moscow, and that any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other. German tax money for Russian propaganda? The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation. Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany. Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian." Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website. The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda. Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, films were shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis. Germany fears closure of Goethe-Institut in Moscow The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes. Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term. Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine. It is an open secret that the German government has been shying away from conflict over the Russian House because it fears the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. The institute was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia. A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts. So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year. Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible In recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations." This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties. Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contact provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible. This article was originally written in German and first published in August 2025. It was updated and republished in September 2026 to reflect news developments.

item.title: Iran: US launches fresh strikes as hostilities flare again
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.87
Hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz flared up again on Tuesday evening as the United States launched fresh strikes on Iranian targets in and around the strategic waterway. "Explosions were heard again in Bandar Abbas city and Qeshm island," Iranian state television reported, adding that blasts were also heard on Lavan island, home to one of Iran's Gulf oil export terminals. Oil prices rose in the wake of the latest attacks with US crude up by as much as 5%. The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region." US President Donald Trump said the strikes, which he described as "large and powerful," were retaliation for "failed" Iranian attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz and the firing of "eight missiles" towards a US military base in Jordan, all of which he claimed were shot down. "If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump wrote in his latest social media threat. "But it will not be the biggest attack of them all. That is waiting in the wings." Iran: IRGC vows to respond to US strikes An IRGC spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, about 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's joint military command said its armed forces would deliver what they described as "crushing and devastating blows" against the US, while state media said the army had launched operations against unspecified US targets in the region. The Tasnim news agency said a "decisive operation by Iran's armed forces in response to the US enemy has begun. The US bases and interests in the region are being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones." G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran Meanwhile, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran. "We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina. "We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support." He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with the IRGC. "We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime." Iran's Pezeshkian meets Putin The latest flare-up comes just hours after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said earlier on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate any US move that signals a return to the collapsed interim ceasefire deal. Pezeshkian, speaking after the US and Iran had already resumed exchanges of fire for the first time in over a month, accused Washington of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms. Pezeshkian was speaking on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he also met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday. Putin reportedly told Pezeshkian that Russia stood in solidarity with Iran, and that the two countries would maintain their economic relationships despite the current turbulence. Pezeshkian thanked Putin and criticized the US for having "no right" to impose sanctions on other countries. Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.86
The death of Ratko Mladic should have closed one of the darkest chapters in European history. Instead, it has reopened old wounds, proving that both the Dayton Accords that ended the 1992-95 Bosnian war and the three decades of international engagement that followed never came close to addressing the causes that led to the conflict. When Mladic, the former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, died on August 27, 2026 in a prison hospital in The Hague, his conviction for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes — including the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo — had been final for nearly a decade. What was never settled, however — and what, it seems, was never even seriously attempted — is the question of how a society lives with a man who remains a convicted criminal in the eyes of an international court but is viewed by some as a hero and symbol of the Serbian people. For this reason, the reactions that followed Mladic's death came as no surprise. Mladic openly mourned in Republika Srpska In Serbia and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska, one of the two semi-autonomous entities created within Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, Mladic's death was mourned as the loss of a national hero, not the end of an era of crimes — a narrative that stands in direct contradiction to the facts established by international courts. Senior officials in Republika Srpska, which covers around 49% of the territory of the former Yugoslav republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, called on citizens to gather in squares and light candles "for the salvation of the general's soul." Milorad Dodik, still the most powerful political figure in Republika Srpska despite stepping down as its president last year after a six-year ban on holding public office imposed by Bosnia's constitutional court, called Mladic's death a "murder," suggesting it was "an organized approach that was meant to lead to a fatal outcome." In Banja Luka, the de facto capital of Republika Srpska, Mayor Drasko Stanivukovic expressed his condolences to Mladic's family and confirmed that Mladic is not perceived as a man convicted of genocide but as a symbol of "a time and a struggle." Institutional support in Belgrade In the Serbian capital, Belgrade, this stance received institutional backing. Serbia's justice minister announced a funeral with the highest state and military honors. President Aleksandar Vucic accused the tribunal in The Hague of "uncivilized behavior" for not allowing Mladic to spend his final days outside his prison cell. Former Interior Minister Aleksandar Vulin spoke of Mladic in the same breath as other Serbian national heroes, invoking a narrative linking World War I to the 1990s, saying, "From Gavrilo Princip to Ratko Mladic, the best Serbs are killed tied up." A very different response elsewhere in Bosnia In the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the other main entity in Bosnia, where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, news of Mladic's death was met with unanimous condemnation of the deceased, given that Mladic was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, a town in eastern Bosnia where around 8,000 men and boys were killed in July 1995. Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin Konakovic, framed the official Serbian response as Serbia's conscious choice. "No one is forcing Serbia to treat Mladic as a hero, nor to attribute his crimes to it. Serbia is choosing this itself," he said. Representatives of victims and survivors pointed out that any public glorification is a direct insult to the families of those killed. The European Commission, responding to questions about the announced state funeral, said that "glorifying convicted war criminals is contrary to the most basic European values" and that such practices have no place in either member states or candidate countries. The European Movement in Serbia warned that a state funeral would amount to "institutional glorification" and a "serious moral, legal and political attack on Serbia." It urged the Serbian government to abandon the plan. How can this happen? But how is it possible that a man who has been finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica is still honored as a military commander? The answer is not simply that he is viewed by some as a national hero. It is structural, and it begins with the Dayton peace agreement itself. The 1995 Dayton Accords ended the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina by turning existing front lines and territorial control into the constitutional architecture of a new state. One of the fundamental elements of the agreement was Republika Srpska, which is recognized by all signatories and embedded in the constitutional structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That division was not an administrative technicality; it reflected the political reality on the ground at the time negotiations were held, including territories under the control of forces commanded by Mladic. The compromise was necessary to stop the bloodshed. The problem is that since 1995, it has never been accompanied by a mechanism for dealing with the past that would match the political compromise. Dayton created a complex constitutional architecture — a state divided into two entities and the Brcko District with a total 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — for a country of just 3 million people. It is a system built to prevent war, not a system built to produce common citizenship, and was described by the Council of Europe's Venice Commission as long ago as 2005 as "neither rational nor efficient." In such a system, where ethnic identity is built into the very logic of power, denial or relativization of crimes is not a marginal phenomenon, it is a political resource. In other words, each side sees itself as a victim, which makes joint recognition of committed evil as a precondition for reconciliation impossible. Price of missed responsibility Bosnia-Herzegovina has state-level legislation that criminalizes the public denial, gross minimization or justification of genocide and the glorification of persons convicted of such acts. In reality, however, enforcement of this legislation remains uneven. Serbia has no such law, and its public authorities, instead of distancing themselves from Mladic's legacy, openly embrace it. This is not just a symbolic difference, it is the difference between treating the wartime legacy as something shameful to be overcome or as a resource to be politically exploited. Dayton Accords helped maintain status quo The international community, which stopped the war in 1995 through force and diplomacy, has subsequently retreated into the role of administrator of the status quo. The Office of the High Representative, the international envoy empowered to impose laws and remove obstructive politicians under the Dayton Accords, did indeed impose laws and remove obstructive politicians for decades. But in doing so it only stabilized the system without dismantling its causes. The result is twofold: a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 30 years since the end of the war, and the fact that an ideology that gave rise to that war is still very much alive. Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

item.title: Norway's King Harald dies at 89
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.58
Norway's King Harald, Europe's oldest living monarch, has died at 89, the royal court said on Friday. The monarch had been receiving treatment for a rare blood condition, hemolytic anemia, at Oslo University Hospital since mid-August. His son, Prince Haakon automatically becomes King Haakon VIII, with the Norwegian Royal Court also confirming on Thursday that his wife, Mette-Marit, will become queen. The Norwegian monarch is head of state, but has a largely ceremonial and representative role. What the palace said about King Harald's death "It is with deep sadness that we announce that His Majesty King Harald passed away today. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, August 28 at 6:35 a.m.," the palace said in a statement. Harald's condition worsened over the last few days, and his wife, Queen Sonja, and son, Haakon, canceled all their engagements to be at his bedside. Harald, who had been king since 1991, suffered a series of health problems in recent years and had increasingly scaled back his official duties. However, he repeatedly ruled out abdicating, saying the oath he had taken on becoming king "lasts for life." Hundreds of well-wishers gathered outside the royal palace in Oslo overnight, holding a vigil as the king's condition deteriorated. King's body moves from hospital to palace A motor procession carrying King Harald's casket left Oslo University Hospital for the royal palace, as per television images. Thousands of people have gathered outside the palace to pay their respects to the late king and bid him farewell. They laid down flowers, cards, cuddly toys and Norwegian flags. "He was the king of the people," mourner Kristoffer Hamre told AFP. The government has announced a period of national mourning, and flags were flown at half mast on Friday. "I think he has been such a down-to-earth king who has cared about all of us, and the words he always uses when he gives a speech are so wise and so valuable," Vigdis Haug, 65, told AFP. Will King Haakon VIII be crowned? Haakon VIII will take his oath of allegiance to the constitution in a ceremony scheduled for next Tuesday. He is due to deliver a short address that will be broadcast on TV, with parliament saying the address will focus on the monarch's limited power. Norway no longer stages a traditional coronation. "King Haakon will promise and swear to govern Norway in accordance with the Constitution and law of the land," President of the Storting [Norway's Parliament], Masud Gharahkhani, said in a statement. World leaders, royals pay tribute Britain's King Charles expressed his condolences for Harald's death, paying tribute to a "towering figure" who guided his country with "warmth and humility." Norway's prime minister, Jonas Gahr Stoere, said Harald demonstrated an "unwavering faith in the Norwegian people" and "helped us to see the best in ourselves – and in one another." Swedish King Carl XVI Gustaf said the late king had "been a good friend" and would be "mourned by many in our country." "I wish my dear Godson Haakon, who now succeeds his father as head of state, success and good fortune in the important role that lies ahead of him," he added. King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark praised Harald's "warm personality and rock-solid calm," saying he "combined duty and responsibility with presence and humanity. He was loved like few others and will be missed by many." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described him as "a true European and a lifelong servant of his people." "In moments of joy and sorrow, he brought Norwegians together," she said. NATO chief Mark Rutte said Harald "showed himself to be a dedicated leader. His own military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO." How will King Harald be remembered? Born in 1937, Harald became Norway's first prince to be born in the country in more than 500 years. As a child, he fled Norway with his mother and sisters following the Nazi invasion in 1940, spending much of World War II in the United States. Harald succeeded his father, King Olav V, in January 1991 and went on to modernize the Norwegian monarchy during more than 35 years on the throne. He was widely praised for his response to the 2011 far-right terrorist attacks that killed 77 people and later drew attention for speeches stressing tolerance, diversity and LGBTQ+ equality. The king's death comes after a turbulent period for Norway's royal family. Crown Princess [nonw Queen] Mette-Marit has faced scrutiny over her past correspondence with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced in June to four years in prison after being convicted of two rapes and dozens of other offenses, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed the verdict. Edited by: Natalie Muller

item.title: What 'The Odyssey' can teach us about climate chaos
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.30
Christopher Nolan's latest blockbuster has drawn tens of millions of viewers into a world of stormy seas and cities on fire. Minus the monsters, that world is based in reality. "The Odyssey" — a post-Trojan War survival story — is set during the Bronze Age collapse of civilization. A new study links that collapse to a severe climate shift. And the authors warn of "implications for the future." Scientists have long known about a mysterious and severe drought that struck more than 3,000 years ago, overlapping with the disintegration of kingdoms and states across the Mediterranean. Research published in July has shed light on the potential cause of that drought: a slow drying trend and a quicker natural cycle of dry weather stacked on top of each other. By the late Bronze Age, the West African monsoon system had been shrinking for thousands of years, turning a green Sahara into desert. Less rain over Africa meant less over the Mediterranean. That trend amplified when the region hit a dry spell caused by natural climate cycles from the Atlantic, which saw the region swing between decades-long wet and dry periods. Katherine Power, the Stockholm University scientist who led the study, said the environment at the time could explain the mass migration and conflicts of the Odyssey era. For decades, scholars have speculated on the reason for the large-scale movement during this time — which is also referred to as the period of the so-called Sea Peoples. Archaeologists have argued that climate shifts could help explain the migration and political collapse at the end of the Bronze Age. The new findings add puzzle pieces. "We don't know necessarily why those people moved," Power said. "But if we can say, 'Hey, the climate was getting worse and worse to survive,' that could be a potential reason." 'A perfect storm of calamities' And that, she said, is relevant to today. Europe's major rivers are at record lows, and drought is creating conditions for devastating wildfires as well as fueling historic crop loss. That includes France's lowest maize harvest in 50 years. The same cycles of wetting and drying from the Atlantic are still at play, but they're now happening in the context of a world that's heating as a result of humans burning oil, gas and coal. "I think it is even more alarming and even more of a threat," Power said. But does what happened then give insights into what might happen now? Eric H. Cline, an archaeologist at George Washington University who wrote a book on the roots of the Bronze Age crisis, said drought and disease were part of the "perfect storm of calamities" that led to societal downfall. He sees parallels to today. In an email to DW, he said "we should be very concerned" about climate change as a stressor for the collapse of civilization. "That fear is not too dramatic at all," he said. Cline added that on his most optimistic days, he believes "we will come to our senses and sidestep that possibility at some point." Was there a trigger moment for the collapse? Power's research sought to explore what patterns might lie behind isolated Bronze Age drought events. They started by examining plant spores, ice cores, cave stones and other natural records that pointed to drought. Then, she and co-author Stockholm paleoclimate scientist Qiong Zhang turned to modeling to get a broader picture. Their model looked at the whole planet, overlaid with a grid, each cell covering an area with an atmospheric resolution of roughly 125 kilometers (78 miles). A supercomputer then calculated the conditions in each of these cells, for every month, across thousands of years. That let the scientists look at the entire Mediterranean. "We're not now stuck with just one core or one cave," Power said. "We can see farther afield and build a whole picture." What they found was not a single event that dramatically and suddenly changed the climate. Instead, shorter cycles of wetting and drying lined up with a longer warming trend. "When we are looking for connections between climate changes and civilization changes, we often are looking for that big, huge, abrupt, catastrophic event," Power said. She added that it is "slow, gradual changes that push a society over a threshold." She said it could have been a steady fall in water supply that led to a slow decline in crops, which prompted people to migrate, triggering conflict. "It doesn't take very much to push a society over the threshold that they're comfortable with," Power said. "What if you add something more to the mix? Maybe then that pushes you a bit farther, and you can't quite recover from that." Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Ratko Mladic, the man behind Srebrenica massacre, dies at 84
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.12
More than 30 years after the end of the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic, the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army. Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later. At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II. The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children. Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the three-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country half of its total population at the time. 'Butcher of the Balkans' In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague. International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans." He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian war. Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy. "Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying. Career in the Yugoslav army At the beginning of the Croatian war in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentally changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence. Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic. Flight, arrest and final verdict At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just 2 years old when his father, a Partisan follower of Yugoslavia's longtime communist leader Josip Broz Titos, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview. As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class and quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state. Serbian nationalist Before the end of the Bosnian war in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years. Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure. The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined. Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian war. War criminal who saw himself as a hero Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. UN officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long overdue, but an important acknowledgment of their suffering. Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic." Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls. While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding, and later survived several strokes while in prison. Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.46
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it. "Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance," DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo. "Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control," he added. Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities. "This outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it, but it can be stopped," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told journalists last week. The United Nations has appealed for more funding as humanitarian agencies struggle to keep pace with the increasing number of cases. "International attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground," Guterres said, warning that the world "must also overcome another virus — the virus of indifference." Vaccination campaign gathers momentum As researchers continue trials aimed at developing a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain, Congolese authorities have rolled out a vaccination campaign focused on front-line health workers. The vaccine was originally developed for a different Ebola variant, but officials hope it will provide some protection against the current outbreak. Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses had already arrived in the country. "We will cover all the provinces that are around Ituri, moving in a ring towards the center of the outbreak, that is to say towards Ituri. But we have enough doses for all healthcare providers," he said on August 28. Some health workers remain confident despite uncertainty over how effective the vaccine will be against the Bundibugyo strain. "It is a vaccine that has already proven itself. We are talking about Ebola Bundibugyo, of Ugandan origin. But the vaccine that they want to administer to us was the vaccine that had succeeded for the Zaire type," said health worker Arnaud Batumbu. "Since both cases involve a viral disease, I hope the vaccine will work for us now as well," he added. Communities seek protection Residents in hard-hit areas say they are ready to take the vaccine if it is properly explained to them. "I will be ready to get vaccinated if only someone explains to me the importance of this vaccination," Clemency, a student in Tshopo province, told DW. Others are calling for wider access. "Children need to be vaccinated too. They go back to school; there are many of them in class," said local resident Carine Lobwadji Some community members also fear vaccine supplies may not be enough. "I have learned that this is an insufficient quantity. I ask the authorities to add other doses for Tshopo and that we vaccinate everyone, especially those who will voluntarily agree, since some are afraid," said Onyeka Treasure, a photographer. Violence hampers response The latest outbreak is unfolding against a backdrop of violence and mass displacement in eastern DRC, complicating efforts to stop transmission. Ebola response teams have reported attacks while carrying out their work, including during operations to safely handle Ebola-related deaths. "We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives," Floribert Magene, a member of an Ebola response team, told The Associated Press on Monday after an attack in Ituri province. Magene said his team was assaulted near Mambasa while responding to a call to secure a body. Economic toll grows Beyond the health emergency, the outbreak is worsening economic hardship for many families. Schools have reopened in towns such as Bukavu and Bunia, but many parents are struggling to afford basic school supplies. Stationery shop owner Furaha Mpangu Esperance told DW that demand has collapsed as families prioritize food and other essentials. "In any case, it doesn't work. The situation is serious because there are no customers. We have even lowered the prices but there is no one to buy. Before, we even sold 10 boxes, 20 boxes a day. Today not even three boxes, not even two! The situation is critical," he said. To reduce disruption to education, the government has proposed radio-based learning for children unable to attend school. "For us, it's a double objective: to ensure that children continue to go to school, despite the epidemic, and to ensure that distance learning is the device that will help them," Education Minister Raissa Malu told DW. Teachers, however, say many areas lack the infrastructure needed for effective distance learning. "We, the teachers, are ready, but we don't have the tools. In sensitive areas, even picking up frequencies is quite a problem," said Patrick Girinegi, president of the Ituri teachers' inter-union alliance. "The first-grade children can't read, nor do the parents. Several schools don't have printers or computers. How will it go?" Many students and parents would rather see classrooms remain open with stronger health measures in place. "It's easy for me to understand when it's my teacher himself who explains it to me. Saying that the child stays at home to listen to the radio, I don't think it's going to work. We [must] find ways to go to school without contaminating ourselves," said Viviane Tshipamba, vice-president of the Ituri children's committee. Despite the challenges, health authorities point to a positive sign: more than 1,360 people have recovered from Ebola so far. For many Congolese, those recoveries offer hope that with stronger support, increased vaccination rates and improved security, the outbreak can still be brought under control. Marcus Loika, Gaston Mukendi and Mitima Delachance contributed to this article.

item.title: US irks Germany, Europe with Russian G20 invite, press bans
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.19
G20 finance ministers and central bank heads gathered in Asheville, North Carolina for two days of talks. The session is being overshadowed by dissatisfaction over the White House welcoming Russia to the meeting but not some critical reporters, the war with Iran and its economic fallout, and Donald Trump's latest trade dispute with Canada. Who is representing Russia at the meeting? Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov made an unexpected appearance as talks opened late on Monday. He held a bilateral meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. "We like getting along with everybody," Trump told reporters when asked about the first in-person Russian invite since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The US currently holds the rotating G20 presidency and so is hosting the session. The US government told several news agencies on condition of anonymity that Bessent used the meeting to tell Siluanov that the US would not give Russia economic relief until it brings its four-and-a-half-year invasion to a close. How did European delegates respond? "Receiving the Russian finance minister here sends a troubling signal," German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said. He said he and his European colleagues made clear that they would not appear in the traditional "family photo" alongside the Russian media, saying this was a common EU position. The photo was ultimately taken without Siluanov and away from the media. Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski told the Reuters news agency that he recognized the right of the G20 hosts to invite guests, but that he was unhappy to see Moscow represented. "We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them," he said. "So for me it would be very difficult to have any kind of conversation with Russia." Which reporters and outlets were excluded? As leaders gathered in Asheville, three giants of the US media landscape complained of either no or limited access to the meeting. The business-focused Bloomberg News said that its team was not allowed access, while the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times both complained that certain journalists who would typically cover such events were refused media credentials. Following a challenge from the DJV German journalists' union on Monday, Klingbeil was critical on the matter. "I believe the press has a completely legitimate interest in reporting openly and freely on this G20 summit," he said. "I consider it unacceptable for journalists or entire editorial teams to be excluded." Intractable Iran war weighing down global economy Klingbeil had also said in a German political podcast last week that he would bring a simple message to the US regarding what he called Donald Trump's "irresponsible" war in Iran — that it needed to come to an end. Host Bessent, however, was trying to drum up support among allies for the US plans for what it calls "Operation Economic Outcast," an intensified sanction regime against Iran reliant in no small part on third parties outside the US who still do business with Tehran. Iran has withstood decades of extensive US and western sanctions, but Bessent tried to argue when asked by reporters that it could swiftly be made to collapse if its remaining trading partners joined in. "I think it could be within weeks or months — and the economy doesn't have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses," he said. Trump's latest Canada meltdown unsettles allies The other major source of strain at the meeting was last week's sudden deterioration in trade talks between the US and Canada. This quickly descended into the tit-for-tat imposition of tariffs, and President Trump launching various social media jabs before unilaterally redesignating Lake Ontario as Lake America, at least on the books in the US. Canada's Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne sought to stress that even the recent friction did not impact his participation. "Canada has always been at the table and constructive, ready to discuss," he told reporters, stressing the need to ensure continued economic growth and "bring back some stability in trade." If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first. Edited by: Wesley Rahn

item.title: War and sanctions deepen Iran's fuel crisis
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.09
Only days after Washington announced a new round of economic sanctions on Iran, the country's gasoline shortage has become increasingly visible on the streets. In cities across Iran, drivers are reporting hours-long waits at filling stations. Videos circulating on social media show some people arriving before midnight or sleeping in their cars to secure fuel the following morning. Some stations are closing before serving everyone in line. The situation is even more difficult for diesel. Truck drivers say lines at filling stations near major cities can stretch for kilometers, forcing them to wait overnight simply to obtain enough fuel to return to work. Iran already faces a gasoline deficit of roughly 15 million liters (ca. 4 million gallons) a day. War damage, difficulties importing refined products and a tightening US blockade have made an old structural problem much harder to manage. Hours in line for a few liters of fuel A resident of Karaj, a city west of the capital, Tehran, told DW that some filling stations were limiting individual purchases to around 5 liters (about 1.3 gallons). "I'm in the gasoline line right now. It took about 45 minutes just to get this far," he said. "Yesterday I went to several stations. Some were closed, some had no gasoline and others had very long queues." He said he returned at 6 a.m. the next morning hoping to avoid the crowds, but again found a long line. He suspects the shortages are partly being used to prepare public opinion for higher gasoline prices, a claim that could not be independently verified. For truck drivers, waiting means losing income. "Our whole life is either spent in the diesel line or on the road," one driver said. He described sleeping at a station while waiting for a tanker that might arrive around midday and supply only a few dozen trucks. Another driver said he had been waiting since 8 a.m. after failing to obtain diesel the previous day. For drivers whose earnings depend directly on keeping their vehicles moving, every lost day adds to rising insurance, tire, oil, repair and maintenance costs. Is Iran adulterating its gasoline? The shortage has coincided with the use of methanol in domestically produced gasoline. Vahid Ghaneifard, chief executive of Persian Gulf Star Oil Company, recently confirmed that the refinery had begun testing methanol as an oxygenate in its gasoline. The company says methanol makes up around 0.5% of the mixture. Iran's refining authorities say the national fuel standard permits methanol concentrations of up to 3%. Officials insist the trial complies with technical requirements. But the timing has fueled public suspicion. Videos shared online show motorists holding bottles of unusually clear fuel and claiming that gasoline quality has deteriorated. Some have alleged that water or excessive alcohol is being mixed into supplies. The allegations have not been independently corroborated. There has, however, been at least one confirmed incident involving water contamination. In the city of Rafsanjan, local authorities acknowledged that water had been mixed with gasoline at a filling station after videos showed cars and motorcycles experiencing problems. Officials said the incident resulted from a technical fault and was being investigated. Distrust over fuel quality grows For motorists already facing shortages, isolated incidents can reinforce wider fears. A Tehran resident told DW he had spent about 1 billion tomans — roughly $5,250 (€4,529) at current exchange rates — repairing his car after its crankshaft failed. He believed poor-quality gasoline had caused the damage, though such a connection has not been independently established. He said he was reluctant to publicly protest. Another resident in Rey, south of Tehran, told DW that motorists had gathered outside a filling station after several cars were allegedly damaged following refueling. The concern is not simply technical, as it reflects a deeper collapse of trust between consumers and authorities at a time when the government is also discussing higher gasoline and diesel prices. Tehran has argued that the current subsidy system encourages excessive consumption and smuggling and imposes an unsustainable burden on state finances. But consumers point to other issues such as inefficient cars, inadequate public transport and incomes that have failed to keep pace with inflation. Is a price increase in the works? Economist Hassan Mansour believes the government is preparing the political ground for higher energy prices. Officials have repeatedly argued that Iranian gasoline prices are artificially low, that large volumes are smuggled abroad and that the economy consumes far more energy per unit of output than comparable countries. The proposed solution is to bring domestic fuel prices closer to international levels. "Once again, the government finds itself preparing the ground for raising the price of energy carriers," Mansour told DW. But the problem runs deeper than subsidized gasoline. Mansour pointed to the financial condition of Iran's oil industry. Budget documents indicate that the National Iranian Oil Company has tens of billions of euros in debt to the central bank and commercial banks, while the company also owes substantial sums to the National Development Fund and faces major tax liabilities. When these debts cannot realistically be repaid, Mansour argued, they weaken state finances and contribute indirectly to currency instability and inflation. Raising gasoline prices could, therefore, serve both as a demand management measure and a source of additional revenue. A politically dangerous choice The government has few easy options. While imports are harder to finance and transport, domestic production is struggling to keep pace with consumption. Increasing output quickly requires investment and technology, while reducing consumption means either rationing fuel more aggressively or raising prices. Yet both carry political risks. Iranian authorities remember what happened in November 2019, when a sudden gasoline price increase triggered nationwide protests followed by a deadly crackdown and an internet shutdown. Today, the economic environment is considerably more fragile. The war has damaged infrastructure, international sanctions are tightening and household purchasing power has fallen sharply. Long fuel lines are just another source of frustration. For Tehran, raising prices might help reduce the gasoline deficit. But doing so while people are already waiting overnight for fuel could turn an energy shortage into another crisis of public anger, which is something far more difficult to control. Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

item.title: Meta's new AI transcription model can distinguish between multiple speakers and languages in real-time
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 6.41
Meta's new AI transcription model can distinguish between multiple speakers and languages in real-time It's the latest release from Meta Superintelligence Lab (MSI). Meta has introduced its first real-time audio model, Muse Voice Transcribe. The model can handle dictation and transcription for more than 20 speakers and can seamlessly handle multiple languages at once, Meta says. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who recently returned to X after three years of not posting on the platform, shared an example of the model's ability to handle multiple speakers and languages at once. In the video, the transcription is able to automatically distinguish between multiple speakers and switch between languages. It's even able to pick up on "code-switching" and transcribe sentences that use words from multiple languages. Muse Voice Transcribe is MSL's first real-time audio perception model — rolling out today. SOTA in streaming speech-to-text, it handles speaker diarization, and endpointing natively in a single model. pic.twitter.com/LViMDSkbim — Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) September 1, 2026 "The model decides when to listen. It waits a little longer on hard words and commits faster on easy ones, using adaptive delay to predict each token and increase accuracy," he explained. "It holds up on messy, real audio too — trained across 70+ languages (with 25 validated at launch), handles mid-sentence code-switching, and manages hour-long sessions with 20+ speakers. Meta's release comes less than a week after Google Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, its own audio model that boasts similar capabilities. But while Google is baking its audio model into Android and (eventually) Chrome, it's not clear if Meta has plans to integrate Muse Voice Transcribe into its flagship services. For now though, people can experience the new mode's capabilities in Meta's recently released Meta AI Mac app. Because the Mac app is able to power voice-enabled features on other apps, Muse Voice Transcribe will now power dictation features on other services. The model is also available to developers within Muse Code and Meta's Model API. It's priced at $3 for 1,000 audio minutes. Additionally, theres a demo version of the Muse Transcribe on Meta's research blog. 3/ already powering dictation in the meta desktop app and muse code. live now via meta model apihttps://t.co/MFosERCV0E pic.twitter.com/UESTQhKJrH — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) September 1, 2026 Muse Voice Transcribe is the latest release from Meta Superintelligence Lab (MSI), which has been churning out new AI models and tools. In the last few weeks, the company has also introduced its first dedicated coding agent, an open-weight model and the aforementioned Meta AI Mac app.

item.title: Are all TVs at risk from burn-in? Here's how to avoid the problem altogether
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.91
Are all TVs at risk from burn-in? Here's how to avoid the problem altogether OLED screens run the biggest risk, but with a little common sense you can mitigate the issue. If you're shopping for a new TV or monitor, you may have heard that OLED offers some of the best picture quality available today. While OLED TVs often cost a premium compared to budget and even mid-range LCDs, you get excellent contrast, vivid colors and deep blacks in return. However, there can be one major caveat to the display technology: the possibility of permanent image retention or burn-in. While the term burn-in may sound alarming, especially if you're on the verge of spending hundreds or thousands of dollars, it's not something you need to worry about immediately. And even though it's inevitable, burn-in remains unnoticeable in many cases and takes years to appear even if it does. Better yet, you can take some simple precautions to significantly reduce the risk and extend the lifespan of an OLED display to keep burn-in at bay until it's time to upgrade. So, what exactly is burn-in, what causes it on modern TVs and how can you minimize the risk? Here's a quick rundown. What is burn-in and what causes it? An OLED display is made up of millions of tiny organic light-emitting diodes — hence the name OLED. This is unlike an LCD, which relies on a backlight to illuminate its pixels. This means that each pixel in an OLED generates its own light and can be dimmed or turned off independently. But while this granular control provides excellent contrast and deep blacks, it also means that individual pixels can wear out independently of each other. Each time you use an OLED display, these individual pixels undergo some infinitesimal amount of degradation. In the real-world, this wear translates to a dimmer light output. To further complicate matters, each pixel is actually made up of several smaller sub-pixels that produce different colors, typically red, green and blue. These sub-pixels don't necessarily age at the same rate, either. Practically speaking, the OLED display is continuously varying the brightness of each pixel and sub-pixel to reproduce the colors you see on the screen. Over time, though, this can cause some pixels can experience more wear than others and become dimmer. Eventually, the difference in brightness can become noticeable enough to our eyes. Put simply, burn-in occurs when some pixels appear brighter than those that have experienced greater wear, creating a persistent outline or ghosting of previously displayed content. Static elements like channel logos have a higher potential to cause OLED burn-in, since the sub-pixels in that region wear out unevenly. This is why OLED displays aren't the best choice if you exclusively watch news or sports channels for several hours each day. Playing the same game for hundreds of hours can also have the same effect, as on-screen text and other fixed elements can accelerate burn-in in certain localized spots. Is burn-in still a risk for modern OLED TVs? If you end up buying an OLED TV, you can still take several steps to prevent rapid burn-in. Besides turning off the display when you're not actively watching content, one of the most consequential accelerators for burn-in is brightness. High brightness levels place greater strain on the LEDs that make up the display, which can cause premature wear. The organic material used in an OLED panel also degrades faster when exposed to heat, with higher brightness levels exacerbating this effect. This is one reason OLED manufacturers have historically been more conservative with sustained brightness, although newer generations have pushed the envelope in this area. Still, running an OLED display at maximum brightness for extended periods of time can result in noticeable burn-in. The solution is simple: head into the TV or monitor's settings menu and lower the brightness setting. This will lengthen the lifespan of each pixel, which should keep burn-in at bay for a long time. Having said that, I wouldn't worry about image retention if you only use your OLED display for a few hours each day, especially if it's mostly to watch varied content with no static elements like channel logos. Modern OLED displays have plenty of burn-in mitigation features, ranging from pixel shifting and refreshing to automatic dimming in bright scenes. I've owned the same OLED TV for five years and haven't noticed any burn-in even though I frequently watch HDR or high-brightness content. Do LCD TVs suffer from burn-in? If you'd like to avoid the risk of permanent burn-in altogether, a modern LCD TV can be a great alternative to OLED. Since LCD panels don't use self-emissive pixels, they don't suffer from OLED-style burn-in caused by uneven pixel degradation. While LCD backlights can and do sometimes fail with age, you can watch content with static elements like news channels without worrying about wearing out specific areas of the display. Having said that, LCD panels can also exhibit temporary image retention after displaying static content for long periods of time. This is less of a concern for LCD than OLED, as the image retention typically recedes on its own as you switch over to more varied content. Modern LCD TVs with Mini LED backlighting technology can offer excellent black levels and contrast, although they cannot match OLED's perfect pixel-level control. High-end models can also get significantly brighter than OLED since they don't rely on organic light-emitting material. This makes high-end LCD TVs a perfect choice for bright, sun-filled rooms or if you don't want to think about the risk of image retention at all.

item.title: QHD, WQHD, 4K, and 5K resolution: What do they mean and which is best for you?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.74
QHD, WQHD, 4K, and 5K resolution: What do they mean and which is best for you? Display resolutions quickly become an alphabet soup that are hard to distinguish, but you can cut through the confusion. If you set out to become a display nerd, you'll quickly realize you're headed into a bottomless rabbit hole. You'll start by trying to pick apart the difference between various resolutions, only to find yourself in a labyrinth of panel and backlight technology types, subpixel arrays, gamma and gamut and goblins and... wait, one of those seems wrong. The point is, it's complicated. Even something as simple as distinguishing between various resolutions quickly gets messy. At its core, resolution simply means how many pixels comprise a display or piece of media. If you've shopped for a TV, computer monitor or even a smartphone, you may have seen manufacturers refer to their products' display resolutions using various terms. By now, we're familiar with 720p HD and 1080p full HD (FHD), but moving up in resolution, you'll find 2K, QHD, and WQHD, as well as 4K and even 5K. Each of these is an umbrella term for a cluster of slightly different pixel counts, and can have different meanings depending on whether we're talking about cameras, displays or media. For our purpose, we'll focus on displays and how they interact with the content you view on them. QHD and WQHD are both 2K, which is silly When looking at PC monitors or smartphones, you may have encountered products claiming their displays are QHD, while others boast WQHD. If the difference between the two seems hard to parse, that's because there isn't one. QHD stands for Quad High Definition, while WQHD stands for Wide Quad High Definition, but both refer to a resolution of 2,560 x 1,440 pixels. This is also known as 1440p or 2K. WQHD is often used as a marketing term for monitors and phones with a widescreen 16:9 aspect ratio. Some devices, like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 (our review), do implement 2K resolutions at other aspect ratios (in the Fold's case, 4:3). However, 16:9 is the industry standard ratio for widescreen 2K displays. Graduating to ultrawide 21:9 will put you into UWQHD (ultrawide quad HD) territory, which is 3,440 x 1,440. 2K resolutions are a sweet spot for many devices. Even though a smartphone could have a 4K display, most people would stress about the strain on its battery life before they noticed any visual improvement. And while PC gaming at 4K is rarified air for those privileged enough to afford a high-end graphics card, the best monitors for lower budgets are far more likely to pair with a system that can consistently render games at 2K. Many productivity- and gaming-focused laptops still come with 1080p displays, with 2K being the step up. 4K laptops are still relatively rare (despite having been on the market for more than a decade) due to their prohibitive costs and limited use cases. 4K is perfect for cinema and high-end gaming While 2K resolutions often opt for acronyms in their marketing, you'll see fewer of these when moving up in resolution. 4K is most often sold as 4K, if for no other reason than because the public is broadly aware that the label means "very high resolution." But many display resolutions that are accepted as 4K don't actually hit 4,000 pixels along either axis. Televisions are usually classified as UHD 4K, which is actually 3,840 x 2,160. This is also the resolution for 4K Blu-Ray discs. The "4K" comes from it being four times the resolution of 1080p. Meanwhile, actual 4K movies resolve at DCI (Digital Cinema Initiatives) 4K, a film industry standard of 4,096 x 2,160 pixels. That's the resolution likely used for movies at your local theater. This means that the 4K you're seeing at home is a slightly lower resolution than what's used in professional or cinematic settings. High-end gaming PCs also tend to pair well with 4K displays, as the latest and greatest GPUs (like the Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 and 5090) can render games at high frame rates in UHD. When is 5K the best choice? 5K brings us back to monitors, as it's a resolution often used for creative applications. There are two standard 5K resolutions: 5K UHD measures 5,120 x 2,880 pixels, while 5K Ultrawide measures 5,120 x 2,160. Others exist, but as with the variety of odd duckling resolutions included under the umbrellas of 2K and 4K, there's no need to get bogged down in them all. While editing photo or video, 5K monitors allow full-resolution editing of 4K content while leaving enough room onscreen for toolbars and other interfaces. The most prominent examples of 5K displays include the Apple Studio Display XDR (our review), as well as some Dell UltraSharp and LG FineGear models. These are marketed toward creative professionals rather than gamers, as gaming tends to top out at 4K for most high-end home builds. While some 5K gaming monitors do exist, such as the LG 5K2K UltraGear evo OLED, they are far less common. These can only run games at full 5K when paired with extreme top-end consumer graphics cards, making it a prohibitively expensive setup for most.

item.title: What more can you delete from your iPhone to free up space?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.71
What more can you delete from your iPhone to free up space? There are more storage-wasters hiding on your iPhone than you might think. You're probably familiar with the basic steps to take when your iPhone storage is cluttered. Uninstalling apps you never use and deleting old photos and videos will make the biggest difference, especially if you don't have an iPhone with much room to begin with. But once you've done these, what else can you try to free up space on your phone? While they might not have as big of an impact, there are other, less obvious methods to clear some space on your device. Some won't affect any personal data, while others clear items you probably forgot about anyway. To begin, visit Settings > General > iPhone Storage. This shows a breakdown of the data that's taking up space, along with apps that hog the most. Take action on any obvious entries that stand out first, like a streaming app you aren't subscribed to anymore and forgot about. This page can also highlight some lesser-known storage users, though. Clean up message attachments While you might have removed giant videos and photos from your gallery, they can live in other places on your device. They'll continue taking up space in the app where you received them, whether that's Messages or a third-party tool like WhatsApp. If you see Messages using a lot of space under iPhone Storage, tap it and use the headings under Documents to review and clean up the largest items. You can check Photos, Videos and other types of media in turn. Other messengers will show their data usage here, but you need to open the respective app to manage attachments. In WhatsApp, for example, go to You > Storage and data > Manage storage to find big items you can clean up, including a per-chat option. Before deleting anything important from these, make sure you've saved that data elsewhere (like Apple Photos, Google Photos or a computer). If you have automatic media downloads on for WhatsApp, photos were likely downloaded and then uploaded to Google Photos or similar, but it's worth being sure. To optimize in the future, consider disabling auto-saving so memes from your friends don't waste room. Finalize recently deleted items In many iPhone apps, deleting items actually sends them to a Recently deleted folder. This gives you a chance to recover them if you change your mind, but it also continues to use storage. Check these folders if you're tight on space, especially if you've just erased a lot of items.
