item.title: The Real Risk of a Trade War With Canada
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.43
In late October 2025, the automaker Honda had to indefinitely shutter a Mexican plant that manufactures its SUVs, thanks to an unanticipated shortage of parts. More than 2,000 miles away, in Canada, it had to slash the production of its popular Civic model in half. The shortage panicked companies across North America. Stellantis created a war room to monitor the availability of critical components, and Ford began to track the run-out dates for its inventory. Hundreds of thousands of Mexican and Canadian jobs were at risk if the impact of the parts shortage spread across supply chains that were highly integrated with those in the United States. Honda would later report production-related losses of roughly $300 million from the incident. The cause was a simple but deliberate Chinese policy. Beijing had suddenly banned global exports of semiconductors made by Nexperia, a little-known Chinese company whose parts go into airbags, braking systems, and other automotive essentials. Chinese President Xi Jinping made the move as retaliation against actions taken by the Dutch government and by U.S. President Donald Trump. Xi reversed the throttling of Nexperia’s exports only when Trump agreed, later that month, to delay the implementation of a new U.S. export control regime. This episode bluntly revealed just how integrated North American supply chains have become—and how exposed they now are to Chinese economic coercion. An auto component can cross the U.S.-Canadian or U.S.-Mexican border seven or eight times before it ends up in a fully assembled vehicle. If Beijing targets even one country, the entire North American supply chain could shut down. Yet all three North American governments are looking the other way. Trump’s tariffs on Canada and Mexico in 2025 and his escalating trade war with Canada this year have turned the countries’ attentions inward, onto disputes among the three partners, at precisely the moment when the threat is coming from the outside. Washington’s refusal to renew the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) on July 1 has set up an implicit renegotiation of the pact. The debate must not focus on the terms the three countries impose on one another; rather, it should focus on the terms they set to help one another counter China. China’s monopoly power across a variety of sectors fundamental to the North American economy is growing fast—and the more it expands, the more Mexico City, Ottawa, and Washington each become vulnerable to the relationships the other two have with Beijing. On a continent that is already tightly integrated, Washington cannot fix its own exposure to Chinese coercion unless Mexico City and Ottawa fix theirs, too. Since 2018, Washington has begun experimenting aggressively with a mix of policies to fight back against China’s growing market dominance. Canada and Mexico will need to make a more coherent and concerted effort to join these campaigns—and the United States will need to work much harder to invite them along. The USMCA renegotiation is the place to start. MISSING THE FOREST In his 1992 presidential campaign, the American entrepreneur Ross Perot famously warned that the North American Free Trade Agreement would create a “giant sucking sound” as U.S. industries relocated south of the border to take advantage of Mexican workers’ lower wages. Although the pact did depress the earnings of U.S. blue-collar workers in areas with industries most exposed to new import competition from Mexico, the antipathy was mostly misplaced. One comprehensive 2015 study that added up NAFTA’s impact on consumers, workers, and industries found that it increased the United States’ economic well-being, albeit modestly, by 0.08 percent. (The impact on Mexico was slightly more positive, at 1.30 percent, and slightly negative for Canada, at negative 0.06 percent.) NAFTA nonetheless became a political vulnerability for Democrats. After Trump entered the White House in 2017, he made renegotiating it an immediate priority. When the USMCA officially replaced NAFTA in 2020, Trump declared that its improvements constituted a “colossal victory.” The reality, however, is that the two agreements differed very little. Both mainly reduced trade barriers and committed all three governments to avoid policies that inhibited commercial flows with one another. (The second Trump administration, with its tariffs on Canada and Mexico, has subsequently proved that commitment to be meaningless.) Both agreements, in other words, were designed to encourage trade among the three countries—not to deal with the risks posed by Chinese monopoly power. But that threat is now pressing. Xi’s 2025 semiconductor ban was his second attack on North American auto supply chains in less than six months. His first responded to Trump’s April 2025 imposition of a 145 percent tariff on imports from China; Beijing then halted global exports of rare-earth permanent magnets, another essential input for car seats, windshield wipers, motors, and cameras. Because China controls 90 percent of the world’s supply of rare-earth magnets, the shortage required Ford, among other companies, to temporarily shut down its Explorer SUV plant in Chicago—and forced Trump to reverse his tariff. Beijing’s effective use of export restrictions in 2025 was the culmination of its so-called dual circulation strategy, which aims to make China less dependent on North American and European supply chains and simultaneously make foreign economies more dependent on China. The restrictions proved that Beijing, as Xi put it in 2020, can implement “powerful countermeasures and deterrent capabilities based on artificially cutting off supply to foreigners.” Europe’s experience with Chinese investment reveals risks for North America. If left unchecked, China’s monopoly power—and its value as a weapon—is likely to grow in the years ahead. The country already possesses 85 percent of the world’s battery manufacturing capacity. It accounts for over 90 percent of global refining for rare earths and graphite and more than 60 percent for cobalt, lithium, and nickel. And China has an ever-increasing global presence in other foundational sectors, including steel, aluminum, chemicals, and telecommunications equipment. Chinese leaders have acknowledged that the country’s statist economy leads to involution, or excessive domestic competition and superfluous production—a situation that is unlikely to change any time soon. That means China’s monopoly power, and its ability to weaponize it, will expand as its surpluses force more and more foreign companies out of business. But China’s economic juggernaut goes beyond exports. In high-tech sectors, Chinese multinational companies such as BYD, CATL, and Ming Yang are now global leaders in electric vehicles, batteries, and wind turbines, investing abroad to acquire or build up manufacturing capacity in foreign countries. Consider the growth of Chinese companies in Europe, the target of nearly a quarter of all Chinese outbound investment in 2025. Hungary has received the largest of those investments to date, with the Chinese automotive industry establishing not only a new center of gravity for European supply chains but also additional competitiveness concern for legacy French, German, and Italian carmakers. The European experience with Chinese investment reveals multiple additional risks. Chinese subsidiaries manufacturing electric vehicles, security inspection equipment, and wind turbines in Europe have all been accused of competing unfairly with local firms by benefiting from Beijing’s subsidies. Hungary’s reliance on Chinese investment has increasingly put it at odds with the EU on other priorities, including efforts to sanction Chinese firms for their support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. ONE market, ONE RISK Washington knows it cannot unilaterally change Beijing’s economic approach. After China acceded, in 2001, to the World Trade Organization, the United States initially focused on containing the threat of unfair Chinese trade practices by imposing narrowly targeted import restrictions. When those had little effect, the first Trump administration launched a trade war; by the administration’s end, new tariffs covered roughly two-thirds of what the United States imported from China. The Biden administration maintained and made modest additions to those tariffs. But tariffs alone proved insufficient to tackle the security risks that come with Chinese monopoly power, and Washington has begun to experiment with many more tools of industrial policy. Like the Biden administration, the second Trump administration has used government support to incentivize U.S. and allied companies to build new sources of supply outside China, including for critical minerals, chips, and batteries. Washington has discouraged Chinese firms from investing in the United States and expanded the list of American products that cannot be exported to China. It has also renewed an American interest in stockpiling. Although the USMCA was negotiated relatively recently, it was not designed to counter the threat of Chinese market dominance. Beijing’s 2025 export restrictions showed how vulnerable each country now is to an attack on another—and revealed how much more resilient all three could be if their economies and policies were more in sync. Coordinating their efforts effectively requires some alignment of the three countries’ tariff regimes toward China, an issue on which the USMCA is mostly silent. The negotiators of the original pact did not need to contemplate how the three countries would implement complementary subsidies, investment restrictions, or export controls, as such policies were not then in vogue. Now they are. North America’s economic integration is worth trying to save. The more the United States undertakes comprehensive efforts to reduce its vulnerability to Chinese economic coercion, the more important it becomes for Canada and Mexico to align their own policies. Misaligned tariff rates across the three countries incentivize the transshipment of Chinese goods to U.S. consumers. They also create concerns that industries may unfairly locate in one country because it allows access to cheaper Chinese inputs not available to firms operating in the other two. Indeed, it may be impossible to retain an integrated North American market without policy alignment. And North American integration is worth trying to save: the greater scale offered by one large USMCA consumer market permits companies to spread their fixed costs over more units of production. Fundamental differences among the three countries allow for specialization based on what workers and companies in each do best. Diversifying sourcing across a wider geography mitigates threats from climate change and public health crises, not only geopolitical risk. Policy alignment to create alternative sources of supply outside China will entail costs. In addition to the fiscal burden of subsidies, North American consumers will have to give up some access to cheaper Chinese products today to curtail excessive dependence in the future. And all three countries will need to prepare for the unavoidable costs of Chinese retaliation. THREE-PART HARMONY Trump’s 2025 and 2026 tariffs pursued too many contradictory objectives. Beijing’s economic coercion clarified the most important task: to quickly create new sources of supply outside China. The ongoing USMCA negotiations present a political opportunity to pursue that objective by better aligning the countries’ tariff policies along three dimensions. First, Washington needs to reduce tariffs on imports from Canada and Mexico back to their January 2025 levels. If Ottawa and Mexico City are to bear some costs for jointly strengthening non-Chinese supply chains, they must be able to share in the jobs, profits, and other benefits that come from some North American production. Then, Canada and Mexico need to raise some of their tariffs on China. In 2024, Canada had already matched most of the tariff increases that the United States had imposed on Chinese steel, aluminum, and electric vehicles during the first Trump administration and the Biden administration. Mexico, too, has taken steps toward tariff alignment over the past few years, including a major hike in December 2025 that covered Chinese steel, autos, and auto parts. The United States, Canada, and Mexico may need to work together to raise tariffs strategically in the future to address other vulnerabilities. Future downward tariff adjustments with China will also need to be done in concert, lest they undermine collective North American interests. For example, Trump has proposed that the United States and China reduce their tariffs on each other on a limited set of “non-sensitive” products under a so-called U.S.-China Board of Trade. But unilaterally increasing U.S. clothing imports from China, for instance, would come at the expense of Mexico’s export opportunities. Expanding U.S. agricultural exports to China would be unhelpful if it displaces Canadian sales to China. If managed trade proves necessary to deal with China’s statist model, solidarity requires something more akin to a North America–China Board of Trade. Aligning subsidies is also critical, because maintaining fair competition among North American companies and scaling up entire cross-border supply chains will be difficult without harmonizing how each country’s government supports its industry. Lining up industrial policies across countries is an even harder task than coordinating tariffs. Canada has a smaller economy than the United States, and Mexico is poorer, affording each a smaller budget. And asking taxpayers to fund subsidies that could end up benefiting another country’s workers is not a winner on the campaign trail. Some progress has already been made on aligning subsidies in North America. In 2020, the first Trump administration established a Canada-U.S. Joint Action Plan on Critical Minerals Collaboration, which allowed Ottawa and Washington to co-fund some small-scale Canadian cobalt, graphite, tungsten, and rare-earth projects. Or consider the bipartisan U.S. CHIPS Act of 2022. Although it focused on creating more U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, the program also supported developing workforces in Mexico for the final supply chain step of finishing chips. Beijing’s 2025 export restrictions worked only because chip factories outside China had to ship wafers back to Nexperia’s plants in China for finishing. Some subsidies built into the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 reinforced a North American agenda. For example, its consumer tax credits for electric vehicles required those vehicles to be assembled in North America, not simply in the United States. (Canada subsequently offered Volkswagen support to manufacture batteries in Ontario to better align with the IRA’s generous tax credits.) The IRA’s subsidies for critical minerals were also not limited to mining and processing within the United States. The act effectively sought to create a North American and allied supply chain preference, rather than a purely “Buy American” rule, by offering subsidies to companies that mined or refined critical minerals in Canada, Mexico, and other free-trade-agreement partners or recovered critical minerals through recycling within North America. Trump has forced Canada to divert resources away from the China challenge. So far, however, the second Trump administration’s approach to subsidies has been mostly national. In response to the 2025 rare-earth magnet crisis that its own China tariffs triggered, the administration moved quickly to fund alternative supply chains for numerous critical minerals—deploying money from the Department of Energy and the Department of Defense, including the latter’s Office of Strategic Capital, to grant loans, set up offtake agreements, and guarantee price floors. It has even taken equity stakes in entities such as MP Materials and Lithium Americas’ Nevada mine. But these interventions are aimed at production on U.S. soil and none were coordinated with Ottawa or Mexico City. Canada holds substantial deposits of many of the same minerals and has its own critical minerals strategy; Mexico nationalized its lithium reserves in 2022. Nothing in the USMCA obliges the three governments to work together, let alone keep their subsidy programs from bidding against one another. More recent announcements suggest that the Trump administration may have recognized the speed and cost benefits that come from supporting mining and refining in allied countries. In August, it provided a $400 million loan to an Australian firm to develop a scandium mining project in New South Wales. The administration also announced a U.S.-Mexico Action Plan on Critical Minerals in February, although it has not yet led to any projects. Nevertheless, Trump is simultaneously undermining any such alignment with his trade policy. Ottawa, in particular, has been forced to divert attention and fiscal resources away from the China challenge to address the challenge to its economy from Trump’s tariffs. Instead of escalating a trade war with a longtime ally, Washington should be encouraging Canada to put its considerable critical mineral resources to better collective use. ALIGN OR DIE Canada and Mexico have already shouldered costs from Chinese retaliation because of their policy alignment with the United States. In 2018, after the U.S. Department of Justice asked Canadian authorities to arrest a Huawei executive, China detained two Canadians for nearly two years. In 2024, when Ottawa aligned its import restrictions on electric vehicles, steel, and aluminum with those imposed by Washington, Beijing imposed retaliatory tariffs on Canadian exports of canola, pork, and seafood. And in 2025, when Mexico raised duties on Chinese autos and steel, China put tariffs on Mexican pecans. China’s retaliatory playbook often entails targeting exports from politically powerful industries with few alternative markets—especially farm products with a short shelf life. But North American leaders can better protect their countries against such retaliation. One way is by keeping their import markets open to one another. Another is by directing government funds to further diversify exports away from China to alternative markets. Trump’s deployment of tens of billions of dollars to U.S. farmers hurt by Chinese retaliation during both his first and second terms was politically expedient. Knowing a bailout is coming, however, may inadvertently encourage farmers to sustain their dependence on the risky Chinese export market. Stockpiling critical inputs should also be a tool of alignment. An input that is essential at one stage of a North American supply chain is essential at every stage. Because each country would benefit from more stockpiling, each needs to share in the costs. And if stockpiles grow large enough and their size is adequately advertised, they could even deter China from restricting exports in the first place. In early 2026, the Trump administration launched Project Vault, a multibillion-dollar public-private initiative to stockpile critical minerals for commercial use in the United States. Canada recently announced its own critical minerals stockpiling regime for defense purposes. Each of these efforts needs to go much further and be more North American in scope to contribute to the fight against Chinese market dominance. Canada, Mexico, and the United States cannot afford to become a “Fortress North America.” When it comes to Chinese investment, Washington has thus far mostly worried that Chinese firms could use Mexico as a back door to circumvent U.S. tariffs and regulations. The concerns were driven, in part, by reports in 2024 that BYD and Tesla were scouting Mexican locations for massive new plants and encouraging their Chinese suppliers to follow suit; pushback from Washington undoubtedly contributed to the fact that relatively few such projects have been completed. But the United States, Canada, and Mexico may someday want to attract more Chinese investment that does not pose security risks, especially in high-tech sectors that might benefit North American competitiveness. And at that point, the three countries will need to align their policies to avoid the confusion that has accompanied Chinese investment in Europe and to protect North American economic integration. Each must strengthen its investment screening regulations. Even Washington, for example, will have to expand the scope of the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, which scrutinizes only the acquisition of existing American companies, not factories foreign investors build from scratch. All three countries will also need to create new regulatory regimes to make sure that Chinese firms operate fairly and do not continue to benefit from Beijing’s subsidies or from its discriminatory allocation of exports of essential inputs. As daunting as it might seem to get all these policies aligned, renegotiating the USMCA is just a first step to tackle China’s market dominance. Even an integrated North America does not have enough scale to compete with China and its 1.4 billion domestic consumers. And so Canada, Mexico, and the United States also cannot afford to become a “Fortress North America,” completely shielded from trade with other like-minded, market-oriented democracies that share their concerns about Chinese monopoly power. Any efforts to align North American policy under a new USMCA must retain an openness to trade with these other countries to facilitate a broader alignment in the future. China’s market dominance demands that all three North American countries work together to take on more activist policies. The most immediate need is for the Trump administration to stop implementing policies and circulating rhetoric that undermine North American unity. If Canada, Mexico, and the United States turn on one another, each will be weakened in the one economic fight that really matters. item.title: Why Are Yields on U.S. Treasury Bonds Rising?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.78
Why Are Yields on U.S. Treasury Bonds Rising? The fluctuations could have huge impacts on the U.S. and global economy. The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond—effectively, the rate of interest on U.S. government debt—peaked last week at 5.33 percent, its highest level in 19 years. This may be the product of the normal laws of supply and demand. But the fluctuations in the vast market for U.S. debt have effects that are profound for both the U.S. and global economies—and, in this case, for U.S. politics, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has now assumed responsibility for trying to bring that interest rate down. Why exactly are yields rising? How is Bessent’s background as a bond trader informing his actions as treasury secretary? And is the Treasury Department’s intervention in bond markets encroaching on the Federal Reserve’s turf? The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond—effectively, the rate of interest on U.S. government debt—peaked last week at 5.33 percent, its highest level in 19 years. This may be the product of the normal laws of supply and demand. But the fluctuations in the vast market for U.S. debt have effects that are profound for both the U.S. and global economies—and, in this case, for U.S. politics, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has now assumed responsibility for trying to bring that interest rate down. Why exactly are yields rising? How is Bessent’s background as a bond trader informing his actions as treasury secretary? And is the Treasury Department’s intervention in bond markets encroaching on the Federal Reserve’s turf? Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter. Cameron Abadi: Why exactly are yields rising? As the prices of bonds go down, their yields go up and there are broad supply-and-demand mechanisms that affect the prices and yields of bonds. But is this right now a matter of too much bond supply—too much U.S. debt—that is reducing the prices, or is there a softening of demand that is driving the reduction of prices? Adam Tooze: This is a truly important news story that’s really developed with real urgency over the summer this year, which is this global move in yields. It’s happening across the board with the vast majority of advanced economies, where a big issue is government debt. And as you say, it’s counterintuitive. So it’s worth repeating the logic: As the relative attractiveness of bonds falls and so therefore their price falls—the effective interest rate, the yield on that bond goes up. Because you end up paying $98, $97, $95 for a hundred dollars’ worth of bond, which then pays you a coupon of $4 a year in interest. And then all of a sudden, you’re looking at a much more attractive interest because you bought it for less than the $100 face value. And so what’s happening in global markets—there’s two figures out there for government debt in the U.S. right now. One is $40 trillion. That’s the total of debt that’s been issued, of which about $8 trillion is held by other government agencies. So this is debt owed by the American government to itself. About $32 trillion is in the hands of the market. And that is almost exactly the same as U.S. GDP. So we’ve crossed two critical thresholds, $40 trillion for overall debt and $32 trillion, 100 percent of GDP, in the hands of the market. And even those numbers by themselves, I mean, they are oceanic, that is huge. A trillion is a thousand thousand million. So it’s a million million Those markets are being moved by just the awesome flow of new debt into the markets and, on the other hand, the growing anxiety around the persistence of inflation, and the availability of other types of assets that are attractive by comparison with debt treasuries. Equities and private debt. And all three of those forces are acting at the same time. So there is a huge issuance of private-sector debt, notably AI-related debt, by very, very highly rated, very high-quality business names, which attracts a bid. There is persistent anxiety about inflation, unsurprisingly, because we’ve had a series of shocks starting with COVID, then Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, then most recently Israel and America’s war against Iran, which have triggered surges in price. The inflation rate is now 3.7 percent. And if you’re holding a bond with a nominal face value, every inch, every percent of inflation eats away at the value of your bonds. So that makes bonds less attractive, reducing the bid. And then there is absolutely gigantic issuance. So $40 trillion is the amount outstanding. But America actually has to replace outstanding debt about somewhere between $8 trillion and $10 trillion a year. Because a lot of the debt is rather short term. It’s running a deficit of 6 percent of GDP, which amounts to $2 trillion in new issuance. And so there is a huge volume of new paper coming onto the market all the time. The daily churn in this market is over $1 trillion. And the whole thing adds up to this shift, which is affecting not just the U.S., but everyone really. French government debt, British government debt, we’ve spoken about that a couple of times on the show. Even German, even Japanese. The only country whose bonds have not seen a substantial increase in yield is basically China, I think, where they operate in a relatively closed financial system and there’s no inflationary pressure. So that gives you an idea really of how capacious this is. CA: Bessent was someone who, as a bond trader in the 1990s, was on the other side of these kinds of mechanisms, identifying situations where a government didn’t have the ability to hold a bond market at a certain price and betting that they couldn’t and then profiting from that. Does that inform how he’s approaching this situation now that he’s a government official? AT: I mean, I think a lot of the Trump people are kind of caught in a dilemma. On the one hand, they have some degree of technical competence, otherwise they wouldn’t be in the jobs they’re in. And on the other hand, you can’t be a Trump underling without being basically a sycophant. So you’ve got to sort of follow the boss’s story. And then they, in various contorted ways, try and twist narratives around that. And foreign-policy people do that in various ways. And what we’re seeing with Bessent is a guy who was not a terribly successful hedge fund guy, he’s no macroeconomic super brain, but he’s somebody who does have a deep understanding of how Treasury markets work, at least at the kind of superficial technical level. And so he oscillates between technical justifications for his various interventions—which have included swap lines for Argentina and, you know, supporting the Japanese currency by selling euro without telling the Europeans first—and now this intervention. Now, modern monetary theory people will say this is all terribly artificial, the Treasury could print dollars, too. It could just create its own purchasing power. Which is true, but it would overturn all existing institutional structures, and it would massively destabilize the financial status quo in the U.S. So that’s not on the cards. So then you ask yourself, “What is Bessent’s endgame here? When people call his bluff, where’s this going to go?” And the answer seems to be, “The boss said we should do something, I did something, that’s all that really matters here.” And the bond market isn’t like that. I mean, it’s not a historically wise thing. But this is going to come at a price, this intervention, I think. Especially because it also puts the Federal Reserve in a really, really tight spot. CA: Normally, if there was going to be an intervention to correct the vast global market for U.S. debt, it would be the Fed, and the new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, that would have responsibility for intervening. Is Bessent encroaching on Warsh’s territory here? AT: Yeah, this is really one of the dramatic aspects of what’s been going on. And so in this moment, where Kevin Warsh is having to establish himself as Fed chair, it’s not been going terribly well so far. His second press conference in particular was widely rated to have been a disaster, because Warsh is trying to move the Fed to a regime of much more tight-lipped, much less garrulous, much more explicit navigation of the relationship with the bond market. And here comes Bessent making these cack-handed interventions which are widely being interpreted as a sign of panic and mounting insecurity on the part of the Treasury. Which is the last thing the Fed needs. And so the question now is what is Warsh going to say? And in some ways, he could, if he was ultimately going to play the political card, he could align or he could avoid making any comments on Bessent’s intervention. Or on the other hand, if he actually wants to establish his bona fides with the market, he is now in a position where he almost needs to say something about Bessent’s intervention, which will put him explicitly at odds with the executive branch. Which is not where the Fed is going to want to be. People have long forecast that it would come like this. I think most people imagined it would be in the manner of [U.S. President Donald] Trump bullying, that we’ve seen plenty of, after all and the legal war on the Fed is still continuing. But I don’t think we anticipated the Treasury stepping in as an activist player in its own right and so egregiously and openly seeking to manipulate the price of the U.S. Treasury. And doing so with such patently inadequate tools. So it’s either doomed to fail or begging for somebody else to come and sort it out. CA: What is at stake in terms of which government body has this authority to intervene in bond markets? AT: This is a really fundamental question that goes to the heart, I think, of the democratic legitimacy of these procedures. And it’s at first sort of rub a puzzling question. Isn’t this so technical? Does this really belong within the purview of democratic oversight? Would we want Congress to be having a voice in this? Would we want the executive branch to be doing this? I think the general feeling was exactly as you were suggesting, that this is so technical, it’s such a fast-moving operation when you want to do it effectively, and you need really unlimited financial power that the only actor that really sensibly could exercise that role is the Fed. Because that’s its designated place in the modern Constitution. It may not have been spelled out as such, but the Supreme Court with its recent judgments has come pretty close to conferring on the Fed—though this has no standing in American constitutional jurisprudence—a special position. In other words, the key figures in the Fed are protected from presidential intervention in the way that other federal agencies are not, according to the Supreme Court. Which reflects, I think, the Supreme Court’s understanding that the Fed sits in a fundamentally different relationship to major social forces, notably the financial markets and any other body of the American government. So I think that’s where this conventional sense comes from, that Bessent has overstepped a line that it is the Fed that properly deals with this stuff. But the problem, of course, is that that judgment itself is highly conventional, not to say contentious. Because ultimately what we’re talking about here are nothing more nor less than huge distributional questions, right? The whole debt issue is fundamentally a distributional question. The vast majority of American debt is held domestically. So it’s owed by Americans to Americans in the name of the American government to be paid by American taxpayers. So this is an internal American-on-American issue. And there isn’t a real limit to how much debt you compile up, other than the fact that as you raise the volume of debt as interest rates go up, you have to churn larger and larger amounts of money through the tax system, through the fiscal apparatus, and pay that out again as interest payments. And almost by definition, the people who hold large quantities of financial assets, including Treasuries, tend to be wealthier. So what you’re doing is taking from a relatively broad tax base and distributing to people who receive interest on government debt. And this is obviously politically delicate. And right now, we’re already churning more through on interest payments than we are on the Pentagon’s budget, which is already hugely inflated. So this is a very delicate balancing act. So if you view it that way, manipulating the interest rate at which those bondholders are compensated is a huge political intervention. It’s a form of tax. So in the most contentious interventions we’ve seen in the last week, Citadel Securities, [Stanley] Druckenmiller, people like that have essentially openly accused Bessent of what they call financial repression. Which is really a technical term for a way of managing the financial system—managing the relationship between interest rates and inflation—but, not improbably in this context, is actually taking on a highly political connotation. In other words, what you’re doing is shifting the balance of interest here through artificial interventions to the benefit of taxpayers and to the detriment of those who are investing in financial assets. That’s what you are doing. You’re artificially squeezing the price up and squeezing the yield down. So existing holders benefit, future lenders will get lower yields. It’s a huge operation on the American distribution of income and wealth that you’re engaged in. And what they’re saying is you shouldn’t be doing this, it should just be the market that does this. Which of course is its own kind of value judgment, right? So I personally think financial repression, we’ve spoken about it on the show, is probably the best way out of America’s fiscal dilemmas. But if you’re going to do it, you’re going to have to do it with more purpose and more coherence and with bigger instruments than the ones that Bessent is mobilizing. Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Is BRICS Losing Its Mojo?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.01
Is BRICS Losing Its Mojo? Security matters have rocked the boat, but here’s how to steady it. When the low-key grouping of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa announced a major expansion at a 2023 summit in Johannesburg, the wealthy West finally sat up and took notice. By the time the dust had settled two years later, and 16 years on from its founding, BRICS counted 10 core members (up from five), with Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates as new entrants. A lower tier of 10 “partner countries” was also announced. When the low-key grouping of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa announced a major expansion at a 2023 summit in Johannesburg, the wealthy West finally sat up and took notice. By the time the dust had settled two years later, and 16 years on from its founding, BRICS counted 10 core members (up from five), with Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates as new entrants. A lower tier of 10 “partner countries” was also announced. But as leaders fly into New Delhi for its 18th annual summit on Sept. 12, an undercurrent of anxiety is in the air. What seemed like a triumphant coming-out of the global south—from which a vast majority of BRICS states are drawn—is starting to feel a little bit like a dysfunctional family getting together for Christmas (or Diwali). Host India has worked hard on its sumptuous agenda of “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.” But, given the indigestion of its rapid expansion and its modest impact on the ground, the overarching question of where BRICS goes next looms. BRICS’s troubles began almost immediately after the expansion was initiated. Most unexpectedly, they emerged from its African contingent. New members Egypt and Ethiopia refused to endorse South Africa as a member of a reformed U.N. Security Council (UNSC), despite the two states apparently having made a prior commitment to do so. In September 2024, a foreign ministers’ meeting failed to issue a joint statement, the first time this had ever happened for BRICS. The failure was repeated in the follow-on meeting in April 2025. (Since its 2011 summit, BRICS declarations have routinely included mention of South Africa, as well as Brazil and India, in connection with the group’s advocacy for U.N. reform.) Ultimately, the BRICS summit declaration later that year in Rio dropped any reference to South Africa, mentioning only Brazil and India in the paragraph on UNSC reform. The outbreak of serious warfare between the United States, Israel, and Iran in early 2026—a war that quickly embroiled the UAE—further complicated matters. The previous year, Brazil had succeeded in shepherding a joint statement when the conflict was still contained. But that fragile consensus didn’t last long as the war resumed and expanded. The BRICS foreign ministers meeting in May 2026 again failed to issue a joint statement. Acrimonious exchanges between Iran and the UAE roiled the meeting of national security advisors which followed. Iran insisted that BRICS’s condemnations of terrorism—a staple since the grouping’s early years—also include what it called “state terrorism,” a reference to Tehran’s perceptions of the United States and Israel. Most other members were reluctant to go that far. Ultimately, India issued a chair’s statement and a press release summarizing its perceptions of the main discussions in the two meetings. Major-power competition had rocked the BRICS boat right from the beginning of India’s current chairing. In January 2026, South Africa conducted a naval drill with China, Iran, and Russia. Pretoria showcased it as a BRICS exercise, and all BRICS member states were invited. The UAE sent a corvette but decided to keep it docked. Brazil, Egypt, Ethiopia, and Indonesia restricted their participation to being observers. And New Delhi pointedly stayed away, characterizing the exercise as “entirely a South African initiative” and “not a regular or institutionalized BRICS activity.” Iran’s presence drew sharp criticism from Washington. Pretoria ordered the Iranians excluded, but Tehran’s ships reportedly did not leave. Ultimately, South Africa ended up investigating its own navy for apparently violating the orders of its president. It was not BRICS’s finest hour. Recent flaps notwithstanding, it would be a mistake to call BRICS a failure. In less than two decades, BRICS has succeeded in creating the first truly transcontinental club outside the wealthy West. It now includes all regions of the global south and has overtaken the G-7 in terms of economic output. Development finance is among its clearest success stories. The New Development Bank has been functioning for a decade now with high credit ratings. Thickening interactions between BRICS states are also helping forge better policy alignment across a range of issues important to the global south. More recently, though, an expanding BRICS is meeting a more conflictual world. It was easier to build consensus on conflicts involving non-BRICS countries—for example, Syria and Afghanistan. Even tackling the thorny issue of Ukraine was manageable, as practically all global south countries backed diplomacy and saw the conflict as having more complex drivers than most Western states did. But as the fires of war are spreading, more BRICS states are finding themselves picking a side. Taking a common position becomes extremely challenging under such circumstances. So, could BRICS find a way to stay away from the security agenda altogether? After all, the club’s origins lie squarely in the economic and financial domain. Its four original members, taking their cues from a paper by Goldman Sachs’s head of global economics research, started meeting in 2006 at the foreign minister level as BRIC. But even during its first leaders’ summit in 2009, BRIC stressed security-oriented themes: a multipolar global order; collective security and UNSC reform; opposition to terrorism. These three themes have appeared consistently in the 16 summit declarations since. And the security agenda has only expanded. The 2011 summit declaration in China contained a paragraph on NATO’s Libya intervention; the Arab-Israeli conflict, Syria, and Afghanistan made it to the 2012 New Delhi summit; and stand-alone meetings of national security advisors were launched in 2013. New research aggregating data across all its summits indicates that, though economic development is the top area of focus for BRICS, geopolitical and security issues come a close second. It is simply too late to de-securitize the BRICS agenda. It is also impractical in our times when everything seems to be securitized. BRICS has experienced two positive inflection points since its coming out in 2009. The first was the 2012-14 period, when an innovative proposal from India and hard work by Brazil and others leading up to the 2014 summit led to the birth of the New Development Bank. The second wind was the membership expansion launched at the 2023 summit in South Africa, detailed previously. To avert paralysis and stay relevant in the contentious world of the foreseeable future, BRICS needs a third wind. Going forward, remaining true to its reformist roots and resisting the temptations of radicalism ought to be a key guiding principle for BRICS. Also crucial is not losing sight of delivery: real impact on the lives of real people in the global south. This means, first and foremost, a major scale-up of developmental goods. And the security agenda needs a scale-down, too. There is no need to take a position on every single raging war, especially if the position taken is unlikely to lead to much action. Focusing on issues with the deepest roots and maximum buy-in within BRICS can, however, be productive. For example, BRICS can have a concrete impact on working together to counter nonstate violence—specifically, terrorism, piracy, and organized crime. These challenges are serious and only multiplying. Reforming the UNSC, though an ambitious and long-haul task, must also be relentlessly pushed. BRICS also quietly serves as a forum in which bilateral tensions can be eased—for example, the 2024 Kazan summit served as an important site for India and China to calm tensions that had spiked with their 2020 border clash. In less than two decades, BRICS’s leaders have managed to build a transcontinental coalition that has only grown, with thickening interactions, and a few success stories. Its impact is still modest, but the survival and growth story is itself impressive in an international system still dominated by the West. Over time, and if it avoids security-related land mines, a reformist BRICS will have increased developmental impacts and helped plug the glaring deficits in the current international system. With some luck, BRICS could even help stabilize vulnerable regions and build greater resilience to systemic shocks. Sarang Shidore is the director of the Global South Program at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. He focuses on the geopolitics of the global south, Asia, and climate change. item.title: The U.N.’s Next Leader Will Be Either a Secretary or a General
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.59
The U.N.’s Next Leader Will Be Either a Secretary or a General The race to succeed António Guterres has started—and four very different candidates are in the running. For a world mired in conflict and desperate for an unbiased interlocutor, the election of the next United Nations secretary-general couldn’t have come at a better time. The U.N.’s top boss is expected to be the peacemaker-in-chief, at least in theory, and perhaps more importantly, the guardian of a collective moral compass, regardless of national affiliations. Are any of the eight candidates up to the task? As the race heats up, a former U.N. diplomat, who spoke with Foreign Policy on condition of anonymity, quipped that the key question is whether the P5—the permanent five Security Council members, which each hold a veto—want a secretary or a general. For a world mired in conflict and desperate for an unbiased interlocutor, the election of the next United Nations secretary-general couldn’t have come at a better time. The U.N.’s top boss is expected to be the peacemaker-in-chief, at least in theory, and perhaps more importantly, the guardian of a collective moral compass, regardless of national affiliations. Are any of the eight candidates up to the task? As the race heats up, a former U.N. diplomat, who spoke with Foreign Policy on condition of anonymity, quipped that the key question is whether the P5—the permanent five Security Council members, which each hold a veto—want a secretary or a general. A general might take a hands-on approach to the various conflicts engulfing the world and try to revive an institution struggling to remain relevant as regional actors offer mediation services while the U.N. itself is bogged down by its own bureaucracy and undermined by the United States, its biggest sponsor. But the powerful countries that have the most say in the ultimate decision seem to prefer a secretary—someone who can manage the clashing interests of global powers without grabbing attention. The sitting U.N. chief, António Guterres, has had a tough ride under U.S. President Donald Trump, who has made no secret of his contempt for everything that the United Nations stands for: respect for due process, human rights, international law, and equal status for all in the family of nations. Guterres’s successor can expect to navigate a minefield, as the United States openly links its funding to further national interests as Trump sees fit. However, Trump’s lack of faith and transactional approach won’t be the only problem. China is the second-biggest contributor, rising from contributing 1 percent of the costs in 2000 to 20 percent this year—comparable to the United States’ 22 percent. China is also assessed to contribute more than 23 percent of the budget that goes toward the organization’s peacekeeping forces, a little under the United States’ 26 percent. Insiders say that Beijing is clamoring for a bigger say. Meanwhile, Russia intends to continue exploiting its position on the U.N. Security Council (UNSC) to gain leverage in other theaters. The United Kingdom and France also hold a veto, but their geopolitical weight is less of a factor and isn’t expected to sway the election. The selection process has begun, with two rounds of straw or informal votes having already been held by the 15 members of the Security Council—a process undertaken to determine whether any of the five permanent members appears likely to block a candidate. Based on those straw-poll votes, and also the geographic turn-taking that the United Nations often adheres to, most believe the next leader will be from Latin America. Specifically, the race is largely believed to be between four Latin Americans, three of whom are women. Former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan is among the top candidates. She was the front-runner in the first straw poll conducted by the UNSC, which includes 10 temporary members in addition to the five permanent ones. The poll is split into three categories: encourage, discourage, and no opinion, and nine “encourage” votes—as well as no vetoes from the permanent members—are needed to win. Ten nations “encouraged” Grynspan’s nomination in the first round, while only one expressed apprehension. If she is the final choice, she would be the first woman and the first Jew to hold the top U.N. position at a time when Israel’s relationship with the organization has hit rock bottom. Trump shares Israel’s mistrust of some of the U.N.’s bodies that are active in the Middle East, such as the U.N. Relief and Works Agency which is mandated to look after Palestinian refugees displaced from their homes as a result of the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, and the U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), the peacekeepers in Lebanon. The United States’ refusal to renew UNIFIL’s mandate has killed the organization; its mandate expires at the end of the year. There is no established link between Grynspan and the Israeli establishment and no insinuation she would take a sympathetic view of Israeli policy. Instead, she has been critical both of Hamas and the “continued bombardment of the IDF hitting civilians, hospitals, shelters, schools and UN facilities in Gaza.” Israel’s view of Grynspan remains unclear, but she might have earned American ire when she warned against the negative impacts of U.S. tariffs on developing countries while serving as the head of the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD). Grynspan worked closely with China on development projects as UNCTAD chief . She is among four of the eight candidates who visited Beijing in recent months to discuss her plans for the U.N. and, according to the Chinese mission to the organization, expressed her commitment to “the one-China principle”—a veiled reference to support for China’s position on Taiwan. Russia may decide based on its experience working with her on the Black Sea grain deal, which temporarily allowed for continued export of grain following outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war. In the second round of polling, however, Grynspan fell down a few notches in the estimation of the Security Council—to seven “encourage” votes while four discouraged her candidacy. Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, the head of the U.N. nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, is a more well-known name in the contest. Grossi is perhaps the United States’ most-favored candidate owing to his experience with the Iran file, according to the former U.N. diplomat who spoke to Foreign Policy. Any resolution to the crisis with Iran and its nuclear program will almost certainly involve U.N. inspections, and Grossi could offer valuable expertise. “If there is anything that sets me apart from the other candidates, it is that I am addressing very sensitive and delicate issues with all of them today, right now. What is happening in Iran, in Syria, in Ukraine,” Grossi said, referencing collaboration with the P5. “So, I believe that this working methodology that I have managed to establish with all of them allows me to think that it can be replicated at the United Nations, but with great prudence.” However, Russia has already expressed its objection. In his current role, Grossi is also keeping an eye on the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine and has apparently irked Moscow. In August, the Russian government criticized him for canceling a trip to the plant over security concerns, implying a lapse in Russian security arrangements at the key installation, and blamed Ukraine instead for refusing to assure his security. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova also criticized Grossi’s handling of the Russia-Ukraine war and dismissed his description of the U.N. “dying slowly” as a bid to earn “extra points” ahead of the elections. China may not back Grossi either, either on behalf of Iran or to appease Russia, Beijing’s “no-limits” partner. Rumor has it that even the U.K. is ill-disposed toward Grossi owing to the ongoing sovereignty dispute with Argentina over the Falkland Islands, or Las Malvinas. Grossi has maintained seven votes in favor in both polls, but his “discourage” votes have risen from two to six. And he is not the only one who appears to be backed by the United States while still failing to make the cut. Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki threw her hat in the ring after the first round of voting, following a meeting with the U.S. president. If that meeting was meant to suggest that she had U.S. blessings, it didn’t work. Her performance in the second and the only poll that she contested was dismal—not a single UNSC member voted in favor. Some experts said that was a sign that ties with Trump alone can’t boost numbers. “Traditionally, candidates who come in at later stages do not do well in the voting. The Security Council needs some time to get familiar with the candidates,” said the former U.N. diplomat. Then there are candidates who are likely opposed by both the United States and China. Michelle Bachelet, Chile’s first woman president, fell sharply from the first to the second vote—from six votes in favor in July to two in August. Bachelet might get a Russian nod but may find it hard to secure U.S. approval; she is a socialist and a former U.N. human rights chief. The force blocking Bachelet might, however, be China. In 2022, under her charge, the U.N. human rights office released a damning report about alleged abuses of the Uyghur community in Xinjiang, alleging torture, sexual abuse, and possible crimes against humanity. “China will never forget that,” said the former U.N. diplomat. At the time, China reportedly even tried to bury the report. That leaves two African candidates and two more Latin Americans. Uganda’s Olara Otunnu and former Senegalese President Macky Sall, who is also a former chair of the African Union, are in the running but hold precarious middle positions in the polls. Sall maintained his tally in both votes, but with nearly half the UNSC—seven out of 15—discouraging him. “At this stage, discourages are more important. If you have seven discouraging votes, that means the chance[s] of a veto-holding power having an objection are high,” said Syed Akbaruddin, a former Indian U.N. ambassador. Former Guyanese Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and former Ecuadorian Foreign Minister María Fernanda Espinosa are both top contenders in addition to Grynspan. The Guyanese candidate led the second poll. Espinosa, despite securing fewer “encourage” votes, was also tied for the least-discouraged candidate in that round—on par with Rodrigues-Birkett. In the U.N.’s 80-year history, there has never been a woman in the top job, and only once has a Latin American held the role. A Latin American U.N. chief might prove to be useful for Trump, especially since the Washington’s latest National Security Strategy document emphasizes the Western Hemisphere. The competition appears to be between the Latin Americans. However, there is no consensus candidate so far, and more could enter the fray even in the final months. According to the New York Post, Trump himself has backed Gianni Infantino, the head of world soccer federation FIFA, while some reporting suggests that the United States was considering Nickolay Mladenov, the head of Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza. There is some concern that Trump may field a real estate agent or a family member, but fears of the United States walking out of the U.N. and threatening its survival are exaggerated, Akbaruddin said. “Even in the past, the U.S. has called for budgetary discipline; I remember the Reagan era,” he said. “And fears that any of the P5, who gain the most from the UNSC, will want to kill the organization are inflated.” The United States needs the U.N. to do the “dirty jobs,” said the former U.N. diplomat who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “If you don’t want to send American boots to resolve a problem but want to impose your solution, who do you ask? The U.N. put together a Haiti gang-suppression force; the U.N. sends peacekeepers; and the U.N. approved Trump’s Board for Peace for Gaza. The U.S. then pays 25 percent of the costs, not the total, because the rest is borne by others.” The United Nations needs the United States, but the United States also needs the legitimacy and heft of the only universal organization—or the “parliament of nations,” as it is often called. The next secretary-general, like all others before, will have to navigate the clashing interests of global powers, particularly the P5 countries. But the U.N. still has a role in dealmaking and peacemaking and doesn’t have to relegate that job to the G-20, G-7, or G-2; instead, it should build cooperative frameworks with regional mediators. Despite its many flaws, the United Nations is still perceived as the most impartial institution, and that is its biggest asset. A U.N. secretary-general still has credibility that few global leaders can boast of. The biggest challenge for the new boss will be to find a way to be both a secretary and a general. item.title: Moscow’s Moment of Global Summitry
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.40
Moscow’s Moment of Global Summitry The war in Ukraine may rage on, but Russia remains far from an international pariah. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Russia’s attendance at key international conferences, how renewed conflict in Iran sparked a global bond sell-off, and the fallout of Zambia’s disputed presidential election. The Kremlin Refuses to Be Sidelined Russian forces launched a sixth straight day of missile and drone strikes at the Ukrainian capital and its surrounding areas on Tuesday, killing at least 12 people in attacks that damaged residential homes. At the same time, several high-ranking Kremlin officials participated in a slew of global conferences focused on advancing Moscow’s economic and diplomatic agendas. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Russia’s attendance at key international conferences, how renewed conflict in Iran sparked a global bond sell-off, and the fallout of Zambia’s disputed presidential election. The Kremlin Refuses to Be Sidelined Russian forces launched a sixth straight day of missile and drone strikes at the Ukrainian capital and its surrounding areas on Tuesday, killing at least 12 people in attacks that damaged residential homes. At the same time, several high-ranking Kremlin officials participated in a slew of global conferences focused on advancing Moscow’s economic and diplomatic agendas. Russia’s ability to engage with the international community at the highest levels despite its continued war against Ukraine signals that Moscow has managed to avoid becoming the global pariah that many Western powers have advocated for. Nowhere was this more obvious than in Asheville, North Carolina, where U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov on Monday on the sidelines of the G-20 finance ministers’ meeting. This was the first time that Moscow’s top financial official attended the global gathering in person since the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022. Axios reported on Monday that the two officials discussed U.S. President Donald Trump’s Russia-Ukraine peace proposal, opportunities for economic growth, and G-20 engagement. Although Bessent reportedly ruled out economic relief for Russia while the war continues, many European countries were unhappy with Washington’s decision to invite the Kremlin. “We do not trust Russia,” Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski told Reuters. “They lie constantly, and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them.” European Union economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis stressed that “we do not think now is the time to normalize Russia” or its presence at the G-20. And German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said he’d assured his European colleagues that he would not pose for a photo with the Russian finance minister. But Moscow refuses to be sidelined. The Kremlin also had a prominent presence at this week’s Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit, further cementing its partnerships with key U.S. allies and adversaries, including China, India, Pakistan, and Iran, and bolstering Moscow’s efforts to challenge Western hegemony on the world stage. On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin jointly signed the summit’s “Bishkek Declaration,” which condemns U.S. and Israeli military action against Iran and its proxies as well as denounces Western sanctions on some of the SCO’s members, including Russia. After the SCO summit, Russia then turned its attention to the Eastern Economic Forum. Hosted in the Russian city of Vladivostok, the conference welcomed delegations on Tuesday from 80 countries to discuss ways to foster greater trade among Asia-Pacific nations, attract foreign investment, and improve quality of life. Of the VIP guests, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s attendance signaled Russia’s growing interest in Southeast Asia. Today’s Most Read - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal - Yes, We’re in an AI Bubble. Just Look to 1980s Japan. by Howard W. French - Jordan Sees Bigger Threat From Israel Than Iran by Sean Yom What We’re Following Global bond sell-off. Government bond yields hit record highs on Tuesday, as renewed fighting between U.S. and Iranian forces reignited worldwide inflation concerns. Notably, Japan’s 10-year and two-year benchmarks jumped to 3 percent and 1.81 percent, respectively, for the first time since 1996. And in the United Kingdom, 10-year bonds rose more than 9 basis points to their highest level since the 2008 global financial crisis. Germany and France also recorded significant government bond jumps. Economists point to ballooning government debts, high costs of living, and rising energy prices due to the Iran war as the main causes of the global bond sell-off. On Tuesday, Brent crude exceeded $92 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate reached more than $88 per barrel, and European natural gas prices reached their highest level since March. Speaking on the sidelines of the G-20 finance ministers’ meeting, Bessent tried to downplay the global bond sell-off and defend Washington’s decision to intervene in the market last month. “The U.S. bond market has been the best performing market since the president came in,” Bessent said. Yields on 30-year Treasuries are currently close to their highest level in 19 years. Inauguration amid arrests. Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema was sworn in on Tuesday for a second, five-year term, following a disputed Aug. 13 election marred by a government-led crackdown against the opposition. Yet several African leaders—including Kenyan President William Ruto, Botswanan President Duma Boko, and Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa—attended Hichilema’s inauguration, granting foreign support for the election’s results. While votes were still being counted on election night, security forces launched a raid on the home of Hichilema’s main challenger, Brian Mundubile, arresting 11 people that authorities claim were “in possession of high-grade military weapons, ammunition and other materials for use in armed insurrection.” Opposition party member and former Transportation Minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally shot during the operation. The raid forced Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, to go into hiding at a United Nations building. However, after Hichilema put pressure on the U.N. to turn them over, Mundubile and Zulu surrendered to police, upon which they were arrested on treason charges. On Aug. 18, Zambia’s electoral commission declared Hichilema the winner, with around 60 percent of the vote versus Mundubile’s roughly 38 percent. Mundubile rejected the results, citing alleged voting irregularities. But the courts would not accept Mundubile’s legal challenge, as they were sealed off from accepting petitions. Taipei’s seat at the table. China condemned Taiwan’s attendance on Tuesday at the Pacific Islands Forum, arguing that the island does not qualify for participation. “The Taiwan authorities sent [Taiwanese Foreign Minister] Lin Chia-lung and other Taiwan independence separatists to make sneaky visits around in a vain attempt to attract eyeballs and attention, and the result can only be inviting disgrace upon themselves,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said. Qian Bo, China’s special envoy for Pacific Island affairs, added that “there will always be consequences” for Taiwan’s involvement. “It’s not a threat.” Beijing does not recognize Taipei’s sovereignty, and in recent years, it has made substantial headway in pressuring other Asia-Pacific nations to abandon diplomatic relations with Taiwan. Only three Pacific Island countries maintain formal ties with Taiwan: the Marshall Islands, Tuvalu, and Palau, the last of which is hosting this week’s summit. It is unclear what China’s threatened consequences might entail. However, the forum’s 18 permanent members appear committed to Taiwan’s involvement, which will include attendance at meetings and side events as a development partner. “The Pacific Islands Forum determines what happens here, not any other country,” Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday in response to China’s remarks. Odds and Ends It’s the end of an era. After leading Argentina to the 2026 FIFA World Cup final this summer, 39-year-old soccer star Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international soccer on Monday. “It was a decision that hurt—and still hurts deeply—but I understand that the time has come,” Messi wrote in a letter posted on Instagram. The letter was originally dated July 21, two days after the World Cup concluded, but Messi said he chose to hold off publishing it while his father suffered from health issues; his father, Jorge, died on Aug. 8. Messi’s 21-year legacy includes 207 games and 125 goals at the international level, making him the world’s No. 2 scorer behind longtime rival Cristiano Ronaldo. Messi will continue to play at club level with Inter Miami. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. Subscribe Subscribe Already a subscriber? . item.title: What in the World?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.28
What in the World? Test yourself on the week of Aug. 22: A U.N. monitoring mission goes to Congo, the U.S. unveils an economic plan against Iran, and Putin issues a warning. U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” this week. Beyond that eye-popping story, what else happened? Find out with our international news quiz! Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” this week. Beyond that eye-popping story, what else happened? Find out with our international news quiz! 1. In a video released on Sunday, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella announced he would order the country’s immigration service to begin doing what? Recent government data suggests that there are hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans who have fled economic and political crises to Colombia—and now they have to worry about deportation, FP’s Catherine Osborn writes in Latin America Brief. 2. A United Nations-backed monitoring mission deployed to the Democratic Republic of the Congo on Monday. What is it meant to oversee? 3. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday unveiled a plan to cut Iran off from the global economy. What is that campaign called? If policymakers work on the assumption that the worst of the economic fallout from the Iran war is behind us, that could lead to true economic catastrophe, FP’s Emma Ashford and Matthew Rojansky argue. 4. What did Russian President Vladimir Putin say on Monday would happen to privately owned critical infrastructure facilities if their owners failed to protect them from Ukrainian attacks—or repair them after strikes? Concerns of nuclear escalation if Russia were on the verge of losing in Ukraine are misplaced. Other great powers have previously been humbled in conflict without resorting to nuclear warfare, Andreas Umland argues. 5. The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group. What will now happen to its remaining fighters? The practical and symbolic nature of daily governance in the Kurdish-led northeastern territory, formerly known as Rojava, remains fraught as it integrates into Syria, Hanna Davis reported earlier this month. 6. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that CIA director John Ratcliffe traveled to Russia earlier this week to do what? The trip came after new U.S. intelligence assessments suggested that Putin could seek to launch a limited attack on a member of the trans-Atlantic alliance, FP’s John Haltiwanger and Rishi Iyengar write in Situation Report. 7. Zambian police said on Thursday that opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate are in police custody after being questioned in connection with which alleged crime? The results of the presidential election earlier this month are still being contested amid allegations of interference by incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief. 8. Taiwan’s opposition-controlled parliament on Thursday rejected the government’s proposed special military budget that would have focused on funding what? 9. A humanoid robot set a new world record in the 100-meter dash at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. Which human set the previous record of 9.58 seconds? (Hint: It was in 2009.) 10. Fat Marmot Week kicked off in Colorado on Monday, aiming to raise money for what? You scored It’s a big world out there! Brush up on global goings-on by subscribing to World Brief, Foreign Policy’s flagship daily newsletter. Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. item.title: A Book as Big as the War
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.70
World War II books have a habit of being as enormous as the conflict itself. The average war buff owns at least a couple of hefty tomes that could, in a pinch, stop a bullet or two, whether it’s Gerhard Weinberg’s classic A World at Arms (1,208 pages), Richard Overy’s Blood and Ruins (1,040 pages), or Antony Beevor’s The Second World War (880 pages). Even a relatively svelte volume like John Ellis’ One Day In a Very Long War runs over 400 pages. The third world war could be fought by using World War II books as artillery shells. Jonathan Parshall’s 1942: Crux of War is a 17-year labor of love—as well as dogged perseverance and inveterate curiosity—that, at 1,280 pages, can easily hold its own among the big boys. The book is a sprawling, blow-by-blow account of a single year, but one that was the linchpin of everything to follow. As Parshall notes, 1942 encompassed the crux of the entire war—12 months in which everything started out catastrophically for the Allies and (nearly) ended up swimmingly. That was the year that featured the battles of Midway, Guadalcanal, El Alamein, and Stalingrad, all of them crushing victories for the anti-fascist coalition. World War II books have a habit of being as enormous as the conflict itself. The average war buff owns at least a couple of hefty tomes that could, in a pinch, stop a bullet or two, whether it’s Gerhard Weinberg’s classic A World at Arms (1,208 pages), Richard Overy’s Blood and Ruins (1,040 pages), or Antony Beevor’s The Second World War (880 pages). Even a relatively svelte volume like John Ellis’ One Day In a Very Long War runs over 400 pages. The third world war could be fought by using World War II books as artillery shells. Jonathan Parshall’s 1942: Crux of War is a 17-year labor of love—as well as dogged perseverance and inveterate curiosity—that, at 1,280 pages, can easily hold its own among the big boys. The book is a sprawling, blow-by-blow account of a single year, but one that was the linchpin of everything to follow. As Parshall notes, 1942 encompassed the crux of the entire war—12 months in which everything started out catastrophically for the Allies and (nearly) ended up swimmingly. That was the year that featured the battles of Midway, Guadalcanal, El Alamein, and Stalingrad, all of them crushing victories for the anti-fascist coalition. As Winston Churchill said after British church bells rang for the first time after victory at El Alamein in November 1942, “This is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.” Parshall tells the story of every action in every theater of war with careful detail and an eye to answering the question, how did we get here from there? The biggest virtue of Parshall’s book is that he can write empathically from the viewpoint of the time, not with the benefit of eight decades of hindsight. It’s easy, if discomfiting, to look back on the rebar remains of Hiroshima or on bombed-out Berlin and believe that Allied victory in World War II was a foregone conclusion. But as Parshall stresses throughout, “It sure wasn’t obvious at the time.” There are probably a million books on World War II, catering to every taste and fancy. There are books on single battles, or extended campaigns. There are one-volume histories, two-volume couplets, and some lovely trilogies. There are wonderful books on the naval war, the strategic bombing campaign, and the Battle of the Atlantic, from both sides. There are books focused on economics, war production, and even food. And memoirs galore, of course. What makes Parshall’s book special is his ability to tell the story of the whole war at a time when the conflict still seemed to hang in the balance. The first three years of the war were an unmitigated disaster for the Allies, from Poland to Norway, France, the Low Countries, the Balkans, Greece, and North Africa. Then came the invasion of Russia, the mass surrender of Soviet forces, and the Germans at the gates of Moscow—plus the U-boat offensive in the Atlantic. And then it got worse. The Japanese attack on U.S. Pacific possessions at Pearl Harbor and the Philippines, coupled with a lightning attack on British colonies in Hong Kong and Malaya, were hammer blows both to the troops on the ground and, above all, the leaders in London. When British forces in Singapore, Britain’s greatest fortress, fell to an invading Japanese army with one-third as many men in early 1942, Britain’s warlords were despairing. The head of the British Army, “General [Alan] Brooke confided to his diary that he ‘certainly never expected that we should fall to pieces as fast as we are, and to see Hong Kong and Singapore go in less than three months plus a failure in the Western Desert is far from reassuring.’ Noting Britain’s previous powers of recovery, he wondered ‘whether we shall again bring off a comeback?,’” Parshall writes. The comeback that they did pull off—the British as well as the Americans and the Soviets—make up the rest of the 1,200-odd pages of this very thorough and thoroughly enjoyable book. Parshall cracks his knuckles and sets to work with a month-by-month chronicle of the crucial year, with a detailed analysis of every theater of war. There is a lot of old-school military history (Parshall’s vocation by training) with corps, divisions, and brigades marching over maps or holding river lines. Woe betides the reader who confuses the 22nd Panzer with the 24th Panzer or the Australian 7th Division with the British 7th Armoured Brigade. To his credit, for a historian who was weaned to his craft by a fascination with the Pacific theater, and whose previous great work was on its pivotal battle, Parshall gives every theater its due—even if there are plenty of cruiser-on-cruiser battles and a good few pages on the Battle of Midway. But the beauty of Parshall’s book lies elsewhere. Parshall prefaces each monthly bulletin with a big-picture essay; taken together, these would make for a great book in their own right. They range from detailed analyses of the economics of tank or aircraft production, to the difficulties the United States faced in mobilizing slack industrial capacity for total war; from managing a cumbersome U.S.-U.K. command system, to the transformation of the Red Army from cannon fodder to deep battle specialists. Parshall ties all the theaters of war together in a way largely unparalleled in World War II history. He offers a vision that is certainly lost in narrow biographies of battles, but which also fails to cohere even in the best supposedly comprehensive histories. To pluck one example at random: When, on a lark in the spring of 1942, the Imperial Japanese Navy launched a nonsensical raid into the Indian Ocean and raised havoc with British naval forces and merchant shipping, the Royal Navy’s response was to leave a strong naval force in East Africa. That starved the already-beleaguered Mediterranean Fleet of ships precisely at a time when it was actually losing the naval war against Italy, which had nasty implications for the war in North Africa, as Gen. Erwin Rommel and Germany’s Afrika Korps nearly took Egypt. For a book about events 80-some years ago, there sure is a lot of suspense. That takes us back to Parshall’s original point: For the statesmen, generals, soldiers, sailors, and airmen of the time, there was a lot of suspense. Victory was a slogan, not a given. There was nothing deterministic about it. I think this might be my desert island book—and not just because, in a pinch, it could be a serviceable shelter.
