item.title: Nepal’s Deadly Floods Put China and India on Edge
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.11
Nepal’s Deadly Floods Put China and India on Edge Geopolitical conflict will only get worse with climate change. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief. The highlights this week: Deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border exacerbate China-India tensions, the United States and China prepare for their upcoming summit on AI security, and a Chinese-born crypto billionaire’s personal essay sparks backlash. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief. The highlights this week: Deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border exacerbate China-India tensions, the United States and China prepare for their upcoming summit on AI security, and a Chinese-born crypto billionaire’s personal essay sparks backlash. Deadly Floods on Nepal-Tibet Border The catastrophic floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have become the latest flash point in China and India’s Himalayan dispute. In the wake of the disaster, Indian commentators initially blamed China and its mega-dam project in Tibet, prompting an angry response from Beijing. The actual cause was a glacial collapse and landslide on the Nepali side of the border, which unleashed a tremendous surge of water that devastated villages and pilgrimage routes to Mount Kailash, a sacred site in Tibet. More than 1,000 people are dead, and thousands more are still missing. It is unclear how badly the floods hit Tibet, in part because China has censored coverage and independent media has almost no access to the region. But this should not be mistaken for a cover-up. Chinese authorities automatically resort to censorship, especially on the issue of Tibet or after major disasters, which can derail the careers of local officials. China and India have long-standing territorial disputes in the Himalayas, where China claims the Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh and India claims the Chinese-controlled territory of Aksai Chin. The countries fought a brief war over the territories in 1962, and today, the two sides are separated by the Line of Actual Control, where Indian and Chinese forces engage in sometimes-deadly clashes. Part of the trouble is that mountain borders are tricky to demarcate, and GPS works poorly in mountain terrain, creating opportunities for conflict when both sides believe that they are operating in their own territory. That appears to have been a factor in the deadly incident in the Galwan Valley in 2020. When China and India clash—in the Himalayas or elsewhere—the media on both sides often defaults to nationalism, becoming locked in a tit-for-tat exchange of accusations that is usually broken by the Chinese government stepping in and ordering its own media to stop. However, Nepal is not buying India’s anti-China narrative this time around. After a brief period of speculation, public anger in Nepal has instead focused on Kathmandu’s initial refusal to accept foreign assistance for search-and-rescue operations. Nepal, which borders the disputed territory, generally faces pressure from both China and India to legitimize their claims. Beijing and New Delhi have courted Kathmandu with foreign aid and investment since a reformist administration led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah took office in March. Both countries sent rescue teams to Nepal this week; they are likely to compete to demonstrate their generosity. Shah has tried to walk a careful path of nonalignment, reversing the generally pro-Chinese orientation of his communist predecessors while still accommodating Beijing on sensitive issues. Last month, for instance, the Nepali government intervened to block a conference on Tibet following Chinese pressure. The geopolitical conflict, however, will only get worse as the climate warms. Climate change is making it harder to tell where India ends and China begins, as retreating glaciers expose new terrain and landslides bury roads under rubble. China is by far the world’s largest carbon emitter, producing roughly three times as much as the United States, though less per capita. India is the third largest emitter. Nepal, meanwhile, sits in the 95th spot, yet, as Bibek Bhandari reports, it is consistently one of the countries most affected by climate change. As rising temperatures alter the landscape of the world’s highest mountains, disputed borders will become less clear, water will become scarcer, and clashes between the two Asian giants will become even more likely. And Nepal will remain caught in between. What We’re Following Xi, Trump gear up for summit. As Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump prepare for their summit on artificial intelligence security, set for Sept. 24, Chinese state media has launched a rhetorical attack on U.S. firm Anthropic. The barbs send a clear signal that the United States cannot expect to impose rules that target Chinese firms but neglect its own. China appears genuinely interested in finding some common ground with the United States on AI security, despite mutual distrust. Rapid advances in AI have exposed shared risks—for instance, the concern that offensive cyberattacks will become far easier than defensive measures and potentially accessible to ordinary users. Trump, meanwhile, is busy posting AI-generated memes and trying to portray Beijing as responsible for Americans’ overwhelming opposition to data centers—an industry in which Trump’s family is heavily invested. Taiwan included in regional forum. China is kicking up a fuss over the Taiwanese foreign minister’s attendance at the Pacific Island Forum, threatening vague “consequences.” This year’s meeting is hosted by Palau, one of just 12 countries that still recognizes Taipei over Beijing. Other attendees, including Australia, have also pushed back against China’s attempt to strong-arm the forum into excluding Taiwan. China’s diplomatic campaign against Taiwan is often counterproductive because it is so aggressive that it often triggers backlash. But Chinese officials have little room to maneuver: Any concession on the issue can easily be turned against them by political rivals at home. FP’s Most Read This Week - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal - Everything You Always Wanted to Know About IR Grad School by Stephen M. Walt - A Cabinet Full of Roy Cohns by Michael Hirsh Tech and Business Crypto billionaire melts down. Crypto billionaire Justin Sun, known for his publicity stunts, posted a bizarre essay claiming that he broke up with Chinese actress Jing Tian after she asked for $50 million as part of their plans to have a child together via surrogacy. He also said he was suing her to recover a 30-million-yuan ($4.5 million) dowry paid to her parents. Rumors about powerful Chinese men engaging in high-end financial relationships with actresses are common, reflecting both sexist fantasies and the realities of an often-exploitative industry. (I’ve heard the Beijing Academy of Drama described as a “girlfriend factory for the rich” by one former student.) The Chinese public has largely sided with Jing, who said that while her “judgment in men is still poor” she would never “sell” her “love for money.” Sun’s outburst—which spends pages dwelling on his extreme wealth—also seems to have further damaged cryptocurrency’s reputation in China. Car troubles. China is still grappling with a domestic auto market battered by price wars and weak demand. Car sales have plummeted this year, and new regulatory measures aimed at raising production standards and curbing the race to the bottom on prices are hitting automakers hard. There is one bright spot: Overseas, Chinese firms are rapidly expanding their market share and in some cases even surpassing their sales in China. U.S. protectionism could open up more markets, including in Canada, where Chinese automakers have shown interest in filling gaps left by U.S. companies amid the ongoing trade war. item.title: Japan’s Narrowing Path to Permanent Residency
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.02
Japan’s Narrowing Path to Permanent Residency Takaichi’s new policies are pushing away foreign workers. Rural areas and strained industries will pay the price. As Japan takes a harder line on immigration, its nearly 2.6 million foreign workers are caught in a puzzling bind—desperately in demand yet steadily pushed away. Take Japan’s strained care sector, which employs 90,000 foreign workers and still faces an estimated shortage of around 250,000 workers under the pressures of a rapidly aging population. So long as they worked as certified care workers in Japan for at least five years, foreign nursing students, predominately from Southeast Asian countries like Indonesia and Vietnam, have long been eligible to receive generous scholarships, full-time permanent contracts, and new, easier pathways to care worker certification. “Facilities are so happy to have them,” said Reiko Ogawa, a professor at Chiba University who is researching migrant care workers. “Without them, a number of facilities would have already gone under.” As Japan takes a harder line on immigration, its nearly 2.6 million foreign workers are caught in a puzzling bind—desperately in demand yet steadily pushed away. Take Japan’s strained care sector, which employs 90,000 foreign workers and still faces an estimated shortage of around 250,000 workers under the pressures of a rapidly aging population. So long as they worked as certified care workers in Japan for at least five years, foreign nursing students, predominately from Southeast Asian countries like Indonesia and Vietnam, have long been eligible to receive generous scholarships, full-time permanent contracts, and new, easier pathways to care worker certification. “Facilities are so happy to have them,” said Reiko Ogawa, a professor at Chiba University who is researching migrant care workers. “Without them, a number of facilities would have already gone under.” But under new proposed measures revealed in July, these foreign care workers would no longer be able to acquire permanent residency in Japan. Many who planned to live in Japan for the long term are now reconsidering their plans or have begun to send earnings back home, instead of investing in real estate and permanent homes, workers’ representatives told Foreign Policy. It’s not just in the care sector. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government will raise permanent residency visa fees by 20 times this October and has proposed requiring permanent residency applicants to make more than the average annual household income, which is currently 5.8 million yen (around $36,000). That figure effectively disqualifies foreign workers in a broad range of sectors, including the care sector, hospitality, agriculture, fishing, tourism, and manufacturing, all of which have average salaries well under 5 million yen. The proposed changes fit into a general conservative swing in immigration policy under Takaichi, whose Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) is adapting to increasing anti-immigrant sentiment amid electoral challenges from the ultra-nationalist right. The result is a contradiction that has become common in immigration debates among aging and rich nations in North America and Europe. But removing one of the key incentives for much-needed foreign labor—stable, permanent residency—could ring a death knell, especially in Japan’s critically underserved rural regions. Japan’s leaders are well aware of its labor crisis. Throughout the 2010s—especially under the conservative LDP-led governments of Shinzo Abe—Japan invested extensive resources and created immigration pathways to help fill its shortages in at-risk industries and regions. The Technical Intern Training Program and specified skilled worker status address areas like nursing, manufacturing, and hospitality. The highly skilled professional visa encouraged accomplished scientists, academics, and business managers to reside in Japan. In 2017, Japan started allowing foreign workers to qualify for permanent residency based on a point system that tabulates factors like income, education, Japanese language ability, and career accomplishments. These policies have been impactful. Japan’s foreign workforce almost doubled from 2012 to 2025 and is continuing to boom, despite a complete pause in foreign hiring during the COVID-19 pandemic. “We are seeing steady growth in our recruitment and placement of foreign staff, well above the Japanese staff,” said Kei Chiyoda, a manager at Staff Services, a major Japanese recruitment firm. According to Kenichi Shishido at JP Mirai, a nongovernmental organization working to improve conditions for foreign workers in Japan, the highest demand for and fastest growth in foreign employment comes from automobile manufacturing in Japan’s central Toyota hub; IT and logistics in Tokyo; and hospitality and tourism in popular tourism destinations like Hokkaido and Okinawa. The largest growth in foreign workers have come from Indonesia, Nepal, and Myanmar. (Vietnam has tapered off due to a weaker yen and growing Vietnamese economy.) Recent years, however, have seen developments that curb the potential for foreign workers as well as benefits for Japanese companies and communities. Japan already shut down accepting specified skilled workers in the restaurant industry in April. New changes to the business manager visa status, which raised the minimum capital requirement from 5 million yen to 30 million yen, has resulted in around a quarter of foreign-owned businesses considering either closure, sale, or merger. Culturally, tensions are on the rise. In a 2025 poll from the Yomiuri Shinbun and Waseda University, 59 percent of Japanese, including 71 percent of respondents aged 18-39, disagreed with the statement of “Japan should actively accept foreign workers as a part of its workforce,” flipping from majority support just one year earlier. Reflecting national discomfort about the growing number of both foreign residents and tourists in Japan, the ultra-nationalist Sanseito party grew in popularity and took votes from the ruling LDP in elections for the upper house of parliament in 2025. The LDP won big in this year’s lower house election, in part because of Takaichi’s willingness to capitalize on Sanseito’s momentum and speak to its constituencies’ concerns about immigration, public safety, and cultural integration. Labor gaps and shortages aren’t distributed equally across the nation. Between 2019 and 2024, Tokyo was the only prefecture in Japan with significant population growth, while rural prefectures like Akita in northern Japan have lost nearly 8 percent of their population. Rural companies and governments have been especially proactive over the last decade in devising ways to attract foreign workers and make them comfortable: building regional recruitment platforms, funding Japanese language education, and creating foreign student scholarships. Some areas, including Kochi prefecture, have established comprehensive demographic strategies that promote foreign families to build communities. These initiatives require plenty of time and effort to bear fruit. “There’s a much higher hurdle for recruiting foreign workers in rural areas,” Chiyoda said. “It’s faster and smoother to hire in areas where foreigners already live and are integrated, like Tokyo and Aichi.” In the countryside, meanwhile, schools are forced to merge, long-running businesses fold without successors, and communities struggle. “Concerns voiced in regional areas are suggesting the situation is becoming critical,” Shishido said. “It’s no longer a simple matter of a labor shortage but a challenge to maintain essential functions like medical care and transportation infrastructure.” The decline of rural areas isn’t just a problem for the people living there. Japan’s food self-sufficiency fell to 37 percent this year, one of the lowest among developed nations. Japanese villages are repositories for cultural treasures and natural resources. Just a few examples of crafts with economic and artistic value that have nearly zero apprentices or successors are: Iwate prefecture’s shrine carpentry; Ibaraki prefecture’s bark-gathering, which is required to make traditional Japanese paper; and Wakayama prefecture’s high-quality charcoal-making. The decline of the rural forestry industry threatens city-goers and suburbanites alike with landslides, flooding, and sediment runoff. “More and more companies in the Japanese countryside are realizing they need to think strategically about how to encourage young people from other countries to be a part of the local community,” said Adam Fulford, CEO of Fulford Enterprises, a Tokyo-based consultancy that works on regional revitalization projects in rural Japan. “If Japan is not perceived as welcoming to these workers, there is a severe risk that companies will find it more difficult to recruit.” Industry insiders highlight the need for two-way education: helping foreign workers learn local customs, and Japanese locals adjust to outsiders. “Japanese businesses need to have the mindset, resources, and manuals to create an environment that accepts foreign workers,” Chiyoda said. Takaichi’s proposed measures recast permanent residency as a prize for elite white-collar workers—those who will contribute tax money but not sustain the nation’s valuable traditions or fill its critical labor shortages. Keeping permanent residency as an attainable goal at lower salary bands is essential to attract and retain integration-minded migrants in threatened rural areas. The damage that will accompany stricter immigration policy may prove particularly severe in the care industry, which already hemorrhages around 14 percent of its workers annually due to harsh conditions. “There are now more risks for foreign workers around prejudice, especially care workers, who have to interact with patients in person,” Ogawa said, citing a recent incident in which a patient physically attacked a Chinese nurse out of anti-China sentiment. “Do [anti-foreigner] patients not understand that without foreigners, there is no care?” The proposed measures, and the deleterious effect they may have, reveal a widening gap between Japan’s national and local governments on immigration. Localities and prefectures will be the ones to suffer the material changes on the ground—plummeting food self-sufficiency, shuttering businesses, and an increasing struggle to maintain basic infrastructure like transportation and health care. They will likely continue to drum up all the incentives they can to attract and retain foreign labor. But there is only so much that local governments can do without national pathways to stable residency. “We’ve seen thousands of foreigners quit because of poor conditions,” Ogawa said. “Workers have their hopes pinned on permanent residency.” The hope may prove a fleeting one. Eric Margolis is a writer and Japanese-language translator. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. Subscribe Subscribe Already a subscriber? . item.title: Getting Confucius Wrong
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.57
Getting Confucius Wrong A new translation of a key Chinese text is dangerously lacking in expertise. Save for Mao Zedong, there may be no more famous Chinese figure than Confucius, who is believed to have lived from 551 to 479 B.C. Acclaim started early: Soon after Confucius’ death, all sorts of sayings were attributed to him, often collected in writing. Of these collections, the Analects became the most important, emerging between the 2nd and 1st century B.C. Confucius and the Analects became foundational aspects of Chinese culture, and one of the main lenses through which to understand China. Since the 1930s, Confucius has stood next to Moses on the east pediment of the U.S. Supreme Court Building. There are now so many translations of the Analects into English alone that it has been possible to compare them through natural language processing models. Chinese President Xi Jinping and other leaders often promote the Analects, and the People’s Republic of China promotes its own worldwide Confucius Institutes for studying Chinese culture –even though it viciously attacked Confucianism for three decades after its foundation. Save for Mao Zedong, there may be no more famous Chinese figure than Confucius, who is believed to have lived from 551 to 479 B.C. Acclaim started early: Soon after Confucius’ death, all sorts of sayings were attributed to him, often collected in writing. Of these collections, the Analects became the most important, emerging between the 2nd and 1st century B.C. Confucius and the Analects became foundational aspects of Chinese culture, and one of the main lenses through which to understand China. Since the 1930s, Confucius has stood next to Moses on the east pediment of the U.S. Supreme Court Building. There are now so many translations of the Analects into English alone that it has been possible to compare them through natural language processing models. Chinese President Xi Jinping and other leaders often promote the Analects, and the People’s Republic of China promotes its own worldwide Confucius Institutes for studying Chinese culture –even though it viciously attacked Confucianism for three decades after its foundation. The Analects: A Contemporary Translation by Erin Cline, a professor at Georgetown University, is a new translation that aims, in Cline’s account, to counter inaccuracies in how the text has traditionally been read in its depictions of women. This follows her 2022 book, The Analects: A Guide, in which she corrects what she considers another problem: the lack of discussions of the Analects as a “sacred” text. Unfortunately, both works fail to acknowledge centuries of studies that have already extensively covered these issues. Take Analects 8.20, a passage central to Cline’s argument that the Analects is not misogynistic. Analects 8.20 references King Wu, the founder of the Zhou dynasty who was celebrated as a model ruler. Wu played a crucial role in overthrowing the previous Shang dynasty, which was also known as the Yin dynasty. As it’s written, Analects 8.20 includes the sentence “There is a woman among [King Wu’s ministers], nine persons, and that is it.” A previous passage refers to Wu having ten advisors. It is just as confusing in Chinese as in English, and many interpretations supposed some text was missing. Cline takes it to show that, “[c]ontrary to what some commentators and contemporary translations have suggested, there is nothing in the original to suggest misogyny.” To Cline, the sentence suggests simple acknowledgement of a female advisor. While some translators have opted for more misogynistic interpretations, such as reading Confucius as suggesting that Wu had only 9 advisors, implying that the woman didn’t count, the issue is not as simple. Ancient texts are often messy. Analects 8.20 is a complex passage, much discussed in the literature. Shortly after the compilation of the Analects, commentators such as Ma Rong (who lived from 79 to 166 C.E.) and Zheng Xuan (127 to 200 C.E.) suggested that this passage contains an error. They say it should have read, “There was a Yin person among [King Wu’s ministers]”. At some point the character for “woman” was mistakenly used in place of the character for “Yin,” the type of error that was common in the world before print. The “Yin person” version was carved onto ancient steles in the 2nd century, which we can no longer see but that these commentators are said to have consulted. Because its vassals also rebelled against the Shang/Yin regime, it would mean that Wu’s circle of advisors included a survivor of the old regime. This reading makes sense and should at the very least be mentioned by anyone using Analects 8.20 to talk about women’s roles in ancient China, even if to be refuted. Cline claims to have relied on the commentarial tradition, but her bibliography is missing standard editions of the Analects that include its commentaries. On top of this, in 2019, archeologists found in Hubei a manuscript collection of sayings attributed to Confucius, the *Kongzi said, in a tomb sealed around 330 B.C. This manuscript indicates that the text of Analects 8.20 was likely erroneous. It merged multiple distinct sayings, hence its incoherent wording. All of this invalidates Cline’s argument that her translation corrects “a number of inaccuracies concerning women and gender.” Errors of this kind would have been avoided if Cline had engaged with the extensive studies of Analects 8.20, scholarship on gender studies, or textual expertise. There are no citations from Chinese sources, nor any references to Anne Behnke Kinney’s 2017 book chapter, “Women in the Analects,” or Li-Hsiang Lisa Rosenlee’s 2006 book, Confucianism and Women. Olivia Milburn’s 2010 study on Nanzi, the only woman named in the Analects, is not cited in either of Cline’s books, even though Cline introduces Nanzi’s story and goes as far as claiming in a recent interview that she is uncovering this story “for the first time.” Consider too the central claim in Cline’s 2022 study: “This book seeks to remedy the absence of literature on the Analects as a sacred text.” According to Cline, there is a lot to lose by not considering the Analects as a sacred text. If this happens, “Confucianism is sometimes not classified as a religion,” which leads to many neglecting “the special status of the text in the Confucian tradition … They also neglect the significance of two very different kinds of literature we find in the Analects: while some passages are records of Kongzi’s conversations with his disciples and contemporaries about how to live, other passages offer descriptions of his conduct and character.” Who are the “many” and the “they” who fail to acknowledge all of this? Cline does not tell us. There are no references to substantiate these claims. Given the existence of a tradition of exegesis of the Analects that spans over two millennia and across multiple cultures, it should come as no surprise that many scholars have, in fact, acknowledged all of this. The 2022 book lacks any reference to scholarship in Chinese on the subject. It also ignores major publications in English, such as Yong Chen’s Confucianism as Religion; A Concise Companion to Confucius; and Sebastien Billioud and Joel Thoraval’s The Sage and The People. As for the Analects as a text that incorporates multiple strands of material—even ignoring once again the wealth of scholarship in Chinese—Scott Cook, Sarah Allan, or Mick Hunter all published on this long before Clein’s book. Cline’s new translation of the Analects claims to reconcile textual issues by creating problems that I am not sure exist. Her work makes the Analects “more accessible to modern readers,” a text that she describes as exhibiting a “high degree of unity and consistency in its themes and ideas,” with no “tension” among passages. The reader is never told what is being measured here. How is the Analects, in its original language or in the many translations available (some of which are freely available online) not accessible? What bars accessibility? How is the degree of unity measured? By what standards? In both works Cline moves from strawman to strawman, regurgitating ideas that are not entirely wrong, but also not original. In Chapter 2 of A Guide, Cline introduces the reader to the historical context in which the Analects was composed. The section on “Authorship and Dating” begins with the following: “There is considerable disagreement about the integrity of the received text of the Analects. … Traditionally, the text has been regarded as an accurate record of Kongzi’s teachings, recorded either during his lifetime or shortly after his death. In the Qing dynasty, this view of the text was called into question, and modern textual critics have shown that the text consists of different chronological strata.” The general claims on “integrity” and “accuracy” are not true. In fact, some statements in the Analects were already so confusing by the first century C.E. that the intellectual and logician Wang Chong dedicated an entire chapter in his philosophical treatise to Confucius’ sayings that were too convoluted to be understood. None of this is taken into consideration by Cline. There is no mention of Tang Minggui’s seminal work, The History of the Study of the Analects (2009), whose painstaking analysis of the reception of the Analects through the centuries makes clear that scholars have doubted whether this material came straight from Confucius’ mouth long before Qing dynasty scholars began in the 17th century. The Analects is a text with a rich and interesting story, one that readers deserve to know. In fairness, in the pages following the above quotation, Cline reviews debates regarding the formation of the Analects, but it is all sourced from secondary scholarship. Cline then acknowledges that “new texts or fragments of existing texts continue to be unearthed” by archeologists, so the process of uncovering the textual history of the Analects remains ongoing. Here, the author is referring to the incredible wealth of artifacts that archeologists have been recovering in China, in particular in the last few decades. These artifacts, often found in tombs sealed in the last few centuries B.C., include manuscripts. These sources offer priceless access into the world at the time, its languages, and its writing habits. However, Cline dismisses the “form-critical work and studies of the textual history” of the Analects as too narrow in focus, with scholars “focusing exclusively on when particular passages and lines were composed … while denying that studies of the ideas and themes in the received text also have merit.” I am one of those scholars who focus on new manuscript evidence recovered by archeologists in China. I have written academic and magazine articles on it, including introductions to anyone interested in textual studies, and have presented my work in East Asia, Europe, and the United States. In all of this, I have yet to encounter a scholar who denies the importance, relevance, and study of transmitted texts because of the new manuscript evidence. Cline gives no references to back up her baffling statement. Studying the transmitted Analects is a perfectly legitimate project. There is still a lot to be said on its commentarial tradition, the reception of the text in different periods, its carving onto steles, and the traditions that it inspired. Yet when discussing and translating the text itself, a proper handling of its formation and its history of circulation is mandatory. It is an essential step towards analyses and interpretations, including philosophical ones. In the same way Cline does not engage with experts of ancient Chinese texts, we experts have not previously engaged with Cline’s work. I cannot find scholarly reviews of either book. I worry that this is because we—experts in increasingly sidelined fields—are conceding too much to the fear that what we have to offer does not matter. The opposite is true. Translations are a matter of interpretation, but interpretations that still build on data (the text itself) and on previous knowledge. More informed participation makes the conversation healthy. It helps the field’s advocacy. Knowledge is meant to grow. It can, and should, be revised according to new evidence, but that ought to be done systematically, organically, building over established foundations. As I have written elsewhere, the popularization of academic topics is necessary and interesting work. Understanding ancient Chinese texts is an important part of understanding Chinese culture and scholarship—something Washington has notably failed at for decades. None of this justifies oversimplifications, a failure to engage with existing work, or misrepresentations of the text and its complexity. The Analects, Confucianism, and other ancient Chinese writers deserve more than to be reduced to simplified fortune cookie messages on how to live meaningfully. Maddalena Poli is a scholar of ancient Chinese manuscripts. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. Subscribe Subscribe Already a subscriber? . item.title: Iceland’s EU Ambitions
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.07
Iceland’s EU Ambitions U.S. threats in the Arctic push Reykjavik to hold a referendum on restarting membership talks. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at an upcoming referendum in Iceland, more potential flooding in Nepal and Tibet, and looming trilateral defensive drills against North Korean threats. Will Iceland Start Fishing in a Larger Pond? Icelanders will head to the polls on Saturday to vote on whether to restart talks to join the European Union. As U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to seize neighboring Greenland loom over Reykjavik, the tiny Nordic nation is considering discarding its genial global reputation to seek European protection from the White House’s imperial-esque ambitions. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at an upcoming referendum in Iceland, more potential flooding in Nepal and Tibet, and looming trilateral defensive drills against North Korean threats. Will Iceland Start Fishing in a Larger Pond? Icelanders will head to the polls on Saturday to vote on whether to restart talks to join the European Union. As U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to seize neighboring Greenland loom over Reykjavik, the tiny Nordic nation is considering discarding its genial global reputation to seek European protection from the White House’s imperial-esque ambitions. Following the 2008 global financial crisis, Iceland applied for EU membership. The process stalled within just a few years amid concerns that it could lead to the country losing sovereignty over its territorial fishing waters. However, accession talks have been brought back to the table as the Arctic transforms into a hotbed of critical mineral competition and a focal point of the Trump administration’s foreign-policy agenda. Trump triggered a NATO crisis in January, when he threatened to take control of resource-rich Greenland either through economic coercion or military force. NATO chief Mark Rutte eventually convinced the White House to back off, negotiating a framework deal that included greater U.S. access to the Danish territory. However, the incident cast light on Europe’s weakening relationship with Washington, and it exposed new vulnerabilities in the Nordic region. “The international system we have lived with since the end of World War II is shaking,” Icelandic Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir wrote in a recent report on the value of European alliances. Those in favor of joining the EU, including Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, argue that membership will not only boost the country’s security but also strengthen its economy. Maintaining the Icelandic krona is “costing us a ton,” Frostadottir told The Rest Is Politics podcast last month, adding that joining the eurozone will bolster investment and foster stability. Those who oppose accession fear that it could cost Iceland both its identity and its sovereignty, including its control over the country’s fisheries. And they maintain that EU membership is not vital for the country’s growth. Iceland already ranks in the top 10 countries globally for GDP per capita; unemployment remains low; and welfare programs provide universal healthcare, preschool, and equal paid family leave. Gallup polling shows a razor-thin margin: 48.4 percent in favor of reopening accession talks and 51.6 percent against, according to a new survey published on Friday. If Saturday’s referendum passes, then the Icelandic government will still need to negotiate the terms of a possible accession deal with the EU. Should such a deal be agreed to, a second national referendum would need to be held on whether to approve it. Today’s Most Read - China’s Success Is Forcing a U.S. AI Rethink by Robert A. Manning and Giulia Neaher - Is Europe Ready for a New Era of Russian Dirty Tricks? by Christian Caryl - Why Iceland Might Finally Join the EU by Gloria Dickie What We’re Following Sweeping devastation. Around 93,000 people in Nepal need assistance after a catastrophic flash flood on Wednesday tore through part of the country along its border with Tibet, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said on Friday. More than 500 people have been killed and at least 1,900 others remain missing in Nepal, according to authorities. In Tibet, Chinese officials have raised the recorded death toll to five people, with 558 others missing, though it is unclear if these numbers overlap with Nepal’s. More than 30,000 Nepali security forces have been deployed for relief missions. However, the destruction of critical infrastructure, including bridges and roads, has made access to rural areas nearly impossible. And fears of new flooding have complicated attempted rescues across the affected zone. In Nepal and Tibet, local authorities temporarily paused rescue operations on Friday after a lake formed by the floodwaters began overflowing into nearby rivers, but operations resumed within just a few hours after the threat eased. Still, Nepal’s disaster management authority urged emergency workers on Friday to immediately evacuate “if risk is observed,” and the head of the United Nations in Nepal warned response teams to be “very, very cautious.” Freedom Edge drills. Japan, South Korea, and the United States will hold trilateral military exercises in international waters next month, Seoul announced on Friday. Dubbed Freedom Edge, the annual five-day defensive drills are intended to test readiness against North Korean nuclear and missile threats. Last week, Washington cut short its Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercise with Seoul, citing Trump’s “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea’s failure to adequately help the United States combat Iran. Then on Monday, the White House canceled a joint amphibious landing drill with U.S. and South Korean troops that was scheduled for September. Some experts believe that the scale-downs were part of a larger strategy to convince Kim to rejoin denuclearization talks. However, Pyongyang’s continued ire over Washington’s involvement in the region—even in a downsized format—suggests that such de-escalation efforts have proved to be ineffective, prompting the White House to go ahead with the Freedom Edge exercise. The deaths of kings. On Friday, Norway mourned the death of King Harald V, who died at age 89 while battling a bacterial blood infection. His son, Prince Haakon, will take the throne. Harald’s 35-year reign was notable for his marriage to a commoner, Sonja Haraldsen; for renovating the Royal Palace in Oslo; and for inspiring patriotic unity after two coordinated terrorist attacks in July 2011 killed 77 people, marking the country’s deadliest peacetime atrocity. As the country’s first Norwegian-born monarch since the 14th century, Harald’s time in power was also riddled with scandal. Documents released by the U.S. Justice Department this year detailed a yearslong friendship between convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and Norwegian Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Harald’s daughter-in-law. The revelation undermined Mette-Marit’s perceived suitability as a future queen and triggered calls for the monarchy’s abolition. Meanwhile, Uganda on Thursday confirmed the death of a tribal monarch, Tooro King Oyo Nyimba, at age 34. Known as the “boy king,” Oyo became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne of the tribal kingdom of Tooro in western Uganda in 1995 at just 3 years old. According to Tooro Prime Minister Calvin Rwomiire Akiiki, the identity of Oyo’s heir will be formally revealed at a later time. Oyo’s death on Thursday shocked Ugandans, who did not know that Oyo was being treated for an unspecified illness abroad. “This is very difficult to comprehend,” Ugandan Deputy Parliament Speaker Thomas Tayebwa said, noting that Tooro authorities had recently maintained that Oyo was in critical condition but alive. The ancient Tooro kingdom has no political authority, but its monarchs wield power as custodians of tribal culture. What in the World? In a video released on Sunday, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella announced he would order the country’s immigration service to begin doing what? A. Draft strict new immigration legislation B. Accept a greater number of refugees from Venezuela C. Receive deported migrants from the United States D. Conduct raids with Colombian police Odds and Ends Ukrainians can’t get enough of President Volodymyr Zelensky’s new four-legged friend. The wartime leader took a step back from his usual schedule on Tuesday to snuggle with a 3-month-old American pit bull terrier, gifted to him by retired U.S. boxer Terence Crawford. Named Freya after Zelensky’s other pet project, Freyja—Ukraine’s proposed missile defense system with Europe—the puppy represents Kyiv’s efforts to win a battle of visuals amid repeated Russian strikes. Notably, Freya’s grandfather survived Russia’s devastating Bucha massacre in 2022. And the Answer Is… D. Conduct raids with Colombian police Recent government data suggests that there are hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans who have fled economic and political crises to Colombia—and now they have to worry about deportation, FP’s Catherine Osborn writes in Latin America Brief. To take the rest of FP’s weekly international news quiz, click here, or sign up to be alerted when a new one is published.
