item.title: These 4 Windows tools helped me regain 16.1GB of storage without deleting a single file
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.68
Running out of storage usually means one thing—hovering over the downloads folder with increasingly desperate intent and looking for anything you can move to an external drive. But unless you’ve genuinely run out of files to delete, the problem likely isn’t what you have; it’s how much space Windows is quietly using behind the scenes. It turns out that a surprising amount of storage is tied to temporary files, recovery data, old updates, and system clutter. The good thing is that you don’t need another PC cleaner because Windows already has a capable cleanup kit built-in. These are the four built-in Windows tools that helped me claw back 16.1GB of storage space that my computer was wasting, and not a single personal file went away in the process. Disk Cleanup The most useful button is the one most people miss Storage Sense and Temporary Files cover the everyday surface layer, but Disk Cleanup goes underneath it. This is a classic utility tool that ships with Windows and one that goes further by surfacing options that aren’t obvious in the Settings panel. Search for Disk Cleanup in the Start menu, select your system drive, and let it scan. The tool displays downloaded program files, temporary internet files, Recycle Bin contents, and other system files. At the bottom of the window is one specific button called “Clean up system files” that most people overlook. It offers deeper cleanup with two additional options—Windows Update Cleanup and, on PCs that have been upgraded, Previous Windows Installation(s). The former removes superseded files from installation packages that the system holds onto after update completion, whereas the latter contains files from previous installations if you want to roll back to that version. Both of these can be an easy source of several gigabytes of storage space. So, unless you want to roll back to a past update or troubleshoot a recent one, they’re dead weight. On my machine, this step returned 8.48GB on its own. Storage Sense Keeps things automatically under control Storage Sense is turned off by default if you have an older PC running an older version of Windows. It is the easiest place to begin because it automatically cleans temporary files, empties the Recycle Bin on schedule, and sweeps out stale files without touching anything you’ve intentionally saved. To use Storage Sense, head to Settings > System > Storage > Storage Sense, and then flip the toggle on. You can set how often you want the tool to run, when the Recycle Bin should be cleared, and how long files can sit in downloads before being removed. For everyday junk that builds up between sessions, Storage Sense runs quietly in the background and handles it without you having to remember. I set mine to run every 14 days, and it freed up 1.86GB the first time I ran it. Temporary files Reveals hidden storage hogs Temporary files, as the name suggests, break down the disposable data Windows has accumulated. This includes cached thumbnails, Delivery Optimization files left over from Windows update downloads, error reports, and residual data from features you may not even use. Go to Settings > System > Storage > Temporary Files, and Windows lays out everything by category with a size estimate beside each entry. That makes it easy to see what's taking up room on your PC. Pay attention to categories such as Downloads before selecting them because the folder can contain files you actually want to keep. I prefer this approach the most instead of blindly running a cleanup utility because I’m informed about what is going away and how much space my PC will reclaim. Storage Sense and Temporary Files cover a lot of the same ground. Don't be surprised if the latter cleans up the system more lightly than expected, because it means that the former has been doing its job. I use Storage Sense for automatic maintenance, while Temporary Files gives me control over what gets removed. System Restore Shrink your safety net instead of deleting it Unlike other tools here, System Restore is basically an undo button for Windows system changes, like when a driver, update, or application causes problems. That makes restore points a sound precaution. However, it becomes far less useful when left unchecked because Windows can reserve a sizable chunk of your drive for them. The good thing is that System Restore lets you control how much space it claims going forward. Search for “Create a restore point” > Open the System Protection tab > Select the system drive > Click Configure. You'll see two figures: Current Usage, which is the amount of space your existing restore points occupy, and Max Usage, which is the space you’re allowing Windows to use. So, here you can put a hard ceiling on how much room restore points can consume. On my PC, the existing restore points were using 17.6GB, after which I lowered the maximum allocation to 5 percent or 11.86GB. So, this gave me 5.76GB of space back. It’s important to note that System Restore doesn’t back up personal files; it is primarily designed to restore the system files, drivers, registry settings, and other parts of Windows to an earlier state. None of these tools delete your personal files or require you to remove them. They simply clear up what Windows quietly accumulated on its own. Run all four on a machine that hasn't seen a cleanup in a year or two, and you might be surprised at how much breathing room you can get back.

item.title: Android's September update finally fixes motion sickness in your car
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.04
Google is rolling out its Android feature drop for September, and it will be ideal if you need help in a store or just get queasy on a road trip. The release notably adds a Motion Assist feature that, like the iPhone's longstanding Vehicle Motion Cues. Motion Assist overlays animated dots that move along with your car or train, reducing motion sickness by ensuring that what happens on-screen matches what your senses are telling you. It can activate automatically, and you can customize it to be as obvious or subtle as you like. You might also appreciate the September Android drop if you want AI to provide pointers. Gemini Live now has Guided Vision that provides audio guidance when you share your camera. If you're looking at a store shelf and can't find what you're looking for, Gemini can tell you. The Find Hub, meanwhile, will soon be useful if you have favorite places for all your things. You can now create an inventory of remembered items using Gemini, so you'll know where you usually put your keys or passport. You won't always need item trackers to keep close tabs on your belongings. Google Messages updates: Keep and chat themes Grocery lists and group chats will never be the same The September feature drop is equally important if you spend much of your time in Google Messages. You can now share Google Keep lists and notes that anyone in a group chat can update, so your grocery list or travel plans will stay current. A long-expected chat theme option is finally coming to Messages. You can now set a custom background wallpaper for chat threads, so you'll know at a glance if you're speaking to your partner or your school group. Many of the new Android features should be available quickly, although Google says Find Hub's remembered items will be available "soon." Don't be surprised if you're waiting a little while to get all the advertised functionality.

item.title: I traveled the world to visit an SSD factory and learned why they keep getting more expensive
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.76
As a tech journalist, it's easy for me to go ahead and criticize RAM and SSD makers for price hikes, and ignore the reasons as to why that might be happening. In reality, there's a ton of stuff that goes in our storage and memory—and I've personally been taking that for granted for too long. Now that I've gone and checked out Lexar's facilities in China by myself, I have a better understanding of why the increased demand from data centers has made all of our everyday tech more expensive all of a sudden. I was invited by Lexar with a group of journalists to visit the company's various facilities in Shanghai, Suzhou, Zhongshan, and Shenzhen, China, from June 8th to June 12th, as part of the company's "Behind the Build" media tour for its 30th anniversary. Lexar had absolutely no input in the content of this article. How is an SSD made? Inside the cleanroom where memory becomes storage Before touring the Longforce Production Line in Suzhou, my group had to change into full cleanroom suits and pass through an air shower designed to blast away any dust or fiber that might contaminate the line. That precaution alone tells you something about how sensitive this process is. Longforce is a joint venture between Longsys, Lexar's parent company, and Taiwan's PTI, and it functions as the manufacturing and packaging arm for both automotive and consumer storage products. Throughout the trip, Lexar was pretty proud to tell us that it's one of the few companies in the world that handles the entire process from when a wafer enters the factory to when an SSD, SD card, or RAM stick is shipped to consumers. That process starts with slicing the wafer into dies, and mounting said dies and a controller chip, which Lexar designs in-house, onto a printed circuit board, followed by wire bonding and encapsulation. What impressed me most wasn't the assembly itself, which is all handled on Longforce's facility in Suzhou, but the testing that follows it. And to see that, the tour continued to Longsys's Zhongshan campus, near Shenzhen, where the company runs its innovation and quality labs. Rather than pulling random samples from a batch, every single unit on this line gets evaluated for sustained write speeds, power consumption, and how it handles sector failures. From there, drives are subjected to thermal extremes, moisture exposure, physical shock, and X-ray inspection before anything ships. This facility is also where new products get validated against real-world devices rather than lab benchmarks alone—the company had a huge room full of pretty much anything users could buy that could take an SSD or an SD card, be it a console, a drone, a smartphone, or even a smart home display. One of the things engineers showed us was a design that combines the controller, NAND chips, and power management into a single unified chip, shrinking a standard M.2 2280 drive down to the far smaller M.2 2230 footprint without sacrificing capacity. That technology has since shipped as the Lexar Play X, a PCIe 4.0 drive rated for read speeds up to 7,400 MB/s and write speeds up to 6,500 MB/s. Seeing this process with my own eyes made it clear that an SSD isn't just a chip in a case. It's the product of sourcing, precision assembly, and exhaustive validation, all of which cost money well before a single unit reaches a store shelf. Why do they keep getting more expensive, then? AI data centers are eating the world's chip supply Touring a factory built for volume made the current price surge feel almost contradictory, until I looked at where that volume is actually going. The core issue isn't a shortage of factories. It's that NAND flash and DRAM production capacity is being redirected toward AI infrastructure at a scale the consumer market simply can't compete with. TrendForce has projected client SSD contract prices to rise at least 40% quarter over quarter in early 2026, with tight supply expected to persist through the full year, and that forecast has already been exceeded in practice. The mechanics behind this are straightforward once you see them laid out. Enterprise SSDs became the single largest NAND flash application segment in 2026, overtaking both client SSDs and smartphones. A single high-end AI GPU can require roughly 16TB of NAND storage to operate efficiently, and a full AI server rack can demand over a thousand terabytes of NAND capacity. Cloud providers buying at that scale simply outbid the consumer channel for the same wafers Manufacturers have responded by chasing the more profitable business. AI infrastructure consumes roughly three times the wafer capacity per gigabyte compared to conventional memory, and every wafer diverted to high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators reduces the supply available for standard DRAM and NAND. Some brands have gone further and wound down consumer SSD lines entirely to focus on enterprise contracts. Remember that the factories building your consumer SSDs are now also the same factories building the hardware for those data centers. Standing on a production floor that was serving both markets, it was easy to see which side of that line is currently winning the allocation fight. Is it getting better anytime soon? Don't expect a price drop before 2027 ... or before the next decade Every person I spoke with in China framed this as a structural shift rather than a passing shortage, and the market data backs that up. Lexar itself wouldn't comment too much on concrete price predictions—the company's representatives stated that semiconductor pricing is cyclical and unpredictable, and that its way of staying competitive was focusing on its own internal R&D. Supply tightness is expected to persist through the rest of the year and into next year, with AI-related demand continuing to grow as a share of total NAND consumption and no incentive for foundries to redirect capacity away from high-bandwidth memory toward standard NAND. That's a meaningfully different situation than the cyclical downturns the memory industry has weathered before, where prices eventually corrected once demand cooled. Part of what makes this cycle stickier is that the biggest buyers have already locked in their access. Cloud giants including Microsoft, Google, and AWS have secured long-term NAND contracts, in some cases already negotiating supply allocations for 2027, which leaves less room for spot-market relief even if demand elsewhere softens. Overall NAND demand is projected to grow 20 to 22 percent year over year while supply grows only 15 to 17 percent, a gap that isn't expected to close in the near term. There is one wildcard worth watching. Chinese domestic NAND producers, particularly YMTC, are expanding their own manufacturing capacity, which could eventually loosen the market from a different direction than the established Korean and American suppliers. But new fab capacity takes years to come online at a meaningful scale, and nothing I saw or heard in Suzhou or Zhongshan suggested that relief is coming within the next few quarters. If you need a drive now, buying sooner rather than later is the more rational move. Waiting for 2024-era pricing to return isn't a strategy anyone in this industry is currently betting on. The real cost of an SSD The way an SSD is made is heavily documented online, but it's one thing to read about it and a different thing to see it by yourself. This trip was an eye-opener in many ways

item.title: Cheap smart LEDs look tacky, here's 3 easy ways to give them more ambient elegance
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.69
LED strip lighting is all the rage, and for good reason. It’s cheap, versatile, easily integrates with smart home platforms, and it’s easier than ever to make your own. But LED strips don’t always look good, and sometimes you need a little help to get that finished look. Hide LEDs for an instant glow-up Do this and you’re 90% of the way there The biggest mistake you can make with LED strip lighting is leaving the LEDs on display. These small, intense beads of light do a great job of illuminating your home, but they’re arguably not much to look at (unless you like them—in which case, you do you). For me, LED strips need some sort of diffusion, and the easiest way of doing this is to simply bounce them off a surface like a wall or countertop. Thankfully, the fix is remarkably easy: hide the LED as best as you can so that you get the benefit of the ambiance, without the harshness of the diodes. One way to achieve this is to place your LED strips strategically. My house is old enough to have picture rails, so I could feasibly hide thin LED strips by attaching them to the top of the picture rail. If you’re using LED lighting to illuminate an area like a kitchen worktop, you can mount them under a cupboard out of view. Sometimes, this isn’t enough. Adding a small lip to any edges where the lights are still visible can do the trick. Do this with a cheap piece of wood and finish or paint it to match whatever it is you’ve attached it to. Hide the LEDs, and you’re mostly there, depending on the density of your strips. Add diffusers to mask LED density Turn harsh light into a warm glow If you can’t avoid having your LED strips on display, or you don’t want to hide them, adding diffusers is a great idea. These sit on top of your LED strips and scatter the light, which can have a transformative effect. The main benefit of a diffuser is that the light is more evenly dispersed, which creates more of a glow. The light will be less harsh and your space more evenly lit. This makes for a gentler light, which works well in spaces like bathrooms, bedrooms, and walk-in wardrobes. The other benefit is that individual LEDs will be much harder (and sometimes impossible) to see. The effect is more pronounced with denser LED strips, where the gap between each diode is shorter. The idea here is to make your LED strip look like one long, neon-like light source. You can get really creative with this effect, especially if your lights are for more than just functional illumination. For example, creating sound-reactive lighting with WLED for your next party, or designing some sort of cyberpunk-esque feature light in a shape of your choice. It’s also worth noting that the diffusion effect is beneficial to LED lighting in general, even if you do a good job of hiding your strips in the first place. For an even glow, consider adding cheap diffusers or more expensive “neonizer” designs. You can even have a go at 3D printing your own. Color-match white temperature for a consistent look Pair strips with each other and the light outside Something else that can really spoil the look of your LED strip setup is mismatched white temperature. This isn’t a problem for lighting that is meant to be moody and colorful, but if you have LED strips and scenes that are designed purely for illumination, getting the white balance right really makes the difference. Thankfully, this is pretty easy. All you need to do is design scenes within your smart home platform of choice that specify the same temperature, which is measured in kelvins (K). You’re probably going to want to match these to existing light sources in your home, like non-smart bulbs. The other way to do this is to use an integration like Adaptive Lighting for Home Assistant. This will change the temperature of select lights automatically, based on the location of the sun. You will see warm hues at the start and end of the day, and more neutral daylight in the middle of the day. Adaptive Lighting is also available in platforms like Apple Home. It works best for lights that are on all day, or that are used to complement natural light sources like skylight windows and solar tubes or sun tunnels. The best way to add LED strips to your home is to use WLED with an ESP32 microcontroller. Check out five WLED-powered projects you can build in a weekend. You can even use WLED to make your own TV Ambilight.

item.title: Claude forgets that my ESP32 isn't a full computer. Here are my 4 fixes
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.31
Most of the vibe coding projects I encounter are written in high-level languages like C, C++, or Python. However, Claude can also write decent MicroPython—you just need to be a little careful. Claude tends to write MicroPython like regular Python, which means the code it produces is often too memory-intensive for many microcontrollers, which only have a few hundred kilobytes of RAM. I've also found that it doesn't always account for the factors that matter when you're trying to build something with a microcontroller. A blinking LED is cool; a blinking LED that prevents you from pushing buttons is really aggravating. These are a few things I've found that guide Claude towards writing more useful MicroPython for ESP32 boards. Do two things at once without freezing Ditch time.sleep() so you can push buttons If you've ever written the basic blinking LED project, you probably used time.sleep(). Claude will usually use it when you vibe code it, and in most common tutorials you'll find use it too. It is fine if you're learning to write code for the first time, but a total pain otherwise. Sleep() tells the board to stop everything for a specified duration. If you push a different button in that time, it is totally ignored. It quickly becomes a problem in real-world projects. Instead, remind Claude that tick_ms() and ticks_diff() can handle a blinking LED without tying up your board. Asyncio is another good one to point Claude towards. Even if you don't specify those commands specifically, be sure to tell Claude that you need to be able to take an input at any time. One button push should only fire once Debouncing is essential When you write a simple script that reads a button press, you'll often find that one push actually registers as multiple hits. That isn't a software bug precisely, it occurs because metal contacts bounce slightly when they make contact, which registers as multiple presses. In order to fix that, Claude will often simply add a sleep after the first press to ensure subsequent presses don't register. However, that can also be a problem if you have multiple buttons you want to press. Make sure to tell Claude to account for debouncing without sleeping so that you don't get any weird pauses. Get reading from your ESP32 to your phone MQTT publishing that reconnects by itself Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) is the best way to get information from an ESP32 board into something like Home Assistant. It is lightweight and is easy to deploy. However, I've found that Claude tends to ignore an important part: reconnecting. Some of my devices run for months without me touching them, and in that time, the router will restart, I'll have a power outage, or something else that interrupts the connection. Some simple scripts you get out of Claude (especially Opus 5, for some reason) don't have a reconnection provision, so once they go offline, they'll stay offline until you intervene. Make sure you prompt Claude to include a retry function that gets your device back online by itself so that you don't have to fiddle with the sensor you stuffed in your attic. Umqtt.robust is a good place to start. Change settings without re-flashing the board Config.json saves you the trouble of reflashing the board If you provide Claude with your Wi-Fi credentials, there is every chance it'll hard code them into whatever script it is writing for your ESP32 board. If the network name or password changes, you have to change the code and then re-flash the board. Absolutely no one wants to do that. Instead, tell Claude that you want your settings to be read from a file stored in the board's flash memory. Config.json is a popular option, but realistically any plain text format will work. The script loads the file when the board boots, which means you only need to tweak your config file if you want to update a password. It also means you can share your code on the internet without providing the world with your Wi-Fi password. Warning: Never hard-code important credentials into your code and then publish it. If you use a separate config file to store credentials, make sure you don't publish that either. This happens way too much with vibe-coded programs. Run for weeks on a battery Learn to use deep sleep well ESP32 projects often need to run for prolonged periods on a battery. If the ESP32 board stays on for the entire time, even a modestly sized battery will be dead in a few days. If you're planning on running your ESP32 project off of a battery, make sure you tell Claude how long you want it to run, what kind of battery you're using, and whether the battery will have any input power (like from a small PV cell). Claude can change how the firmware functions so that the board goes into a deeper sleep and only consumes a few microamps while idle, and only draws a significant amount of power when it briefly powers on to collect sensor data. Note: Some dev-boards have onboard LEDs and USB chips that draw a significant amount of power, which decreases how long a board can run. If you need to maximize your run time, get a bare board. Claude can write great MicroPython, it just needs to be reminded Claude is perfectly capable of writing MicroPython for an ESP32. It just tends not to do so right out of the gate. My experiments with it have consistently found that it seems to approach writing code for microcontrollers the same way that it does code for a regular Linux PC. That can cause problems. If you have a specific use in mind, make sure you include that information in your project or prompt. If you're building for a specific board or family of boards, provide that information to Claude. And, as always, remind it that you're working with a tiny amount of RAM—it may neglect that consideration otherwise.

item.title: ChatGPT got smarter, so I stopped trying to write the perfect prompt
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.69
I used to spend ages crafting ChatGPT prompts, telling it exactly how to behave, what steps to follow, and how to format the answer. But ChatGPT has changed, and so has OpenAI's prompting advice. With the release of GPT-5.6, OpenAI's newest model guidance puts more emphasis on clearly stating your goal and less on micromanaging how ChatGPT gets there. That led me to revisit some of the prompting habits I've picked up over the past couple of years and see where I could simplify the way I use ChatGPT. I'm using Excel examples throughout because it's one of the areas where I've spent the most time using ChatGPT, and it's a good test of how prompting has changed. The same shift applies, though, whether you're asking ChatGPT to write an email, plan a trip, analyze some data, or solve a coding problem. I stopped front-loading my prompts I start with the task instead I used to front-load everything. If I wanted ChatGPT to analyze a spreadsheet, I might give it a long persona, explain the process I wanted it to follow, specify how it should structure its answer, and add a list of things it shouldn't do. For example, previously, after uploading the spreadsheet to ChatGPT, I might have said: You are an expert Excel consultant with 20 years of experience. Analyze the following spreadsheet and identify any errors. Do not make assumptions about the data. Explain each issue clearly, provide a recommended solution for each one, and format your response as a table. Be thorough but concise, and don't make any changes until I've approved your recommendations. But OpenAI's GPT-5.6 developer guidance recommends favoring "leaner prompts," saying that "removing repeated instructions and examples [...] can improve task performance and token efficiency." So, today, I'd start here: Look through this spreadsheet and tell me what looks wrong or needs fixing. The point isn't that I can never give ChatGPT detailed instructions. It's that I no longer feel the need to put every instruction into the opening prompt. I stopped telling ChatGPT how to do the job I just give it the destination For a long time, I assumed that if I knew how I wanted a task completed, I should tell ChatGPT exactly how to do it. For an Excel task, I might have given the spreadsheet to ChatGPT and written: First, create a list of all the unique transaction descriptions in Excel. Then group similar descriptions together and assign each group a category. Create a lookup table containing the descriptions and categories, then add a new Category column to the transaction table and use XLOOKUP to assign each transaction to the appropriate category. Make sure the formula automatically fills down when new transactions are added. However, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 developer guidance says the model can "better infer the user's underlying goal and intended level of work from context, so you often do not need to prescribe every step." It also recommends describing the desired outcome and success criteria. So, I'd write something like this instead: I have a transaction list in Excel with inconsistent descriptions. I want to automatically categorize each transaction, and I need the solution to keep working when I add new transactions. What's the best way to do that? I don't even need to upload the file for this. I'm asking ChatGPT to work out the best approach based on my description of the data, rather than to categorize the actual transactions. That means I'm giving it only the information it needs for this particular question. I'm not saying you should never specify a process. If I'm asking ChatGPT to follow a particular procedure, comply with a legal or technical requirement, or produce something in a specific sequence, I'll tell it exactly what to do. But when how the task gets done isn't important to me, I've stopped micromanaging the route. I tell ChatGPT where I want to end up, give it any constraints that matter, and let it work out the route. I stopped trying to get everything right at once Now I let the conversation do some of the work This is probably the biggest change in how I use ChatGPT. I no longer think of the first answer as the finish line. I use ChatGPT's response to work out what I need to ask next, rather than trying to anticipate the entire solution beforehand. In the past, I might have tried to get everything into the first prompt, especially if I didn't want to upload my Excel file: I have an Excel table containing transaction dates, descriptions, and amounts. I need a formula that identifies duplicate transactions based on the date, description, and amount, ignores blank rows, works inside the table, automatically fills down when new transactions are added, and returns "Duplicate" or "OK". Please explain the formula and any limitations. OpenAI's ChatGPT guidance says, "Treat prompting as a conversation: refine your requests based on initial answers and keep experimenting." That's changed how I think about the first prompt. It doesn't have to contain everything I will eventually want from ChatGPT. I can start with the problem, see what information ChatGPT needs, and use its response to decide what to provide next. See how much shorter this prompt is: My Excel formula is flagging some transactions as duplicates when they aren't. Can you help me work out why? ChatGPT can then ask for the information it needs to diagnose the problem. In my case, it asked for the formula and examples of incorrectly flagged transactions. After I provided those, it identified a possible issue with the underlying date values and suggested some tests to check whether Excel was actually storing the dates as I expected. That's the part I find useful about treating prompting as a conversation. I don't have to guess in advance whether the problem is the formula, the data, or something else. I can give ChatGPT the information it asks for, see what it finds, and then decide what to investigate next. I stopped worrying about the perfect wording I focus on what I'm actually trying to do I've also stopped worrying so much about the wording of my prompts. Previously, I'd rewrite a request, swap words around, add more detail, and try to anticipate how ChatGPT might interpret each sentence. For example, if I wanted a formula to calculate a running total in an Excel table, I might have agonized over something like: I need assistance in creating a formula for the RunningTotal column in an Excel table to calculate a cumulative running total. The formula should reference the Amount column within the same table, use structured references, and automatically extend to newly added rows. Please provide the appropriate formula and a detailed explanation of its construction and operation. But OpenAI's Help Center guidance says, "As ChatGPT grows more intuitive, you can rely more on natural, goal-driven language and less on perfect phrasing." It still recommends being specific about what you want, but the emphasis is on communicating the objective rather than finding the perfect combination of words. There's nothing wrong with the longer prompt, and I'd still include those details if they were important to the result. But these days, I'd probably just write: I have an Excel table with an Amount column. How do I create a running total that keeps working when I add new rows? This isn't carefully engineered. It simply tells ChatGPT what I'm trying to accomplish and gives it the important constraint. In this case, both prompts produced the same formula, even though the second one gave ChatGPT far fewer instructions about how to respond. But the important thing is that I'm giving ChatGPT less micromanagement, not less useful information. OpenAI's guidance still recommends providing the context, constraints, and level of detail a task actually requires. If the answer isn't quite what I need, I can clarify. If it is, I've saved myself the time I would otherwise have spent trying to construct the perfect request before asking the question. The goal matters more than the prompt The biggest change to my ChatGPT prompts is that I spend less time trying to engineer them. Whether I'm building an Excel dashboard, creating a résumé, or building an offline Kanban board, I give ChatGPT the goal and relevant context, then let the conversation do some of the work. That doesn't mean I automatically trust the result—I still check ChatGPT's answers before I rely on them.

item.title: My Pixel phone's camera is hallucinating, and sometimes that's exactly what I want
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.68
Modern phones process the photos they take; that's a fact of life, with the computational photography algorithms being especially busy in photos taken by Pixel phones. Google built its reputation for photo quality in the early years of Pixel phones largely thanks to those algorithms, especially with the advent of Night Sight, which debuted on the Pixel 3. In some situations, AI processing can go overboard, hallucinating details that aren't there and creating photos that have little to do with what was actually captured by the camera sensor. In many cases, though, machine-learning processing can help you take better photos without any intervention on your part, which is why Pixel phones remain regarded as great point-and-shoot camera options. Photos you take with your Pixel can be modified beyond recognition by AI algorithms Sometimes, though, that's just what the doctor ordered Google introduced Pro Zoom (then known as Pro Res Zoom) alongside the Pixel 10 lineup, with the feature kicking in at 30x zoom, when all those machine-learning computational photography algorithms go into overdrive, resulting in photos that are clearly AI-“enhanced.” In most scenes, using Pro Zoom can result in awkward-looking photos that are artificially cleaned up and filled with a bunch of details that simply aren't there in the original photos. But some scenes and subjects can greatly benefit from these hallucinations. A case in point is the photo of the Moon I took a few days ago on my Pixel 10 Pro, on a hot August evening. As you can see below, the original photo (right) is practically unusable. But the AI-enhanced photo doesn't look too shabby, and I wouldn't mind sharing it on social networks. The photo is a perfect example of when AI algorithms can be beneficial. Another example is the photo of a clock tower in my town that I took recently using 80x zoom. While the AI-enhanced photo is too clean for comfort, it looks good enough to share with friends and use on social media, and it shows how AI hallucinations can sometimes be a good thing (although in the vast majority of cases, they're quite the opposite). While I find most Pro Zoom photos to be nothing more than a party trick and a conversation starter, in specific situations, like when taking a shot of the Moon, having AI hallucinate details that aren't really there can give you a photo you can actually use. The Pixel AI processing can help you take better photos But it doesn't always come out ahead The AI processing that's an inescapable part of Pixel photos isn't always as obvious as it is when using Pro Zoom. For instance, I took the two photos below with the Pixel's default camera app (left) and Open Camera (right), which doesn't process photos as much, using the default camera settings and without Night Sight. While quite similar, the photo I took with the Pixel camera app looks a bit better because its HDR processing retains detail on the light pillars on the left, among other things. The machine-learning algorithms also add details to the building in the background and the shrubs encircling the fountain. Note that this time, the Open Camera photo is on the left and the Pixel Camera photo is on the right. But the excessive processing can be detrimental in some scenes. Below, you can see two photos of ivy sprawling across a red brick wall, with the Pixel camera photo on the left and the Open Camera photo on the right. I don't know about you, but I prefer the photo taken with Open Camera. While it's not as sharp and has less contrast, the colors pop more (especially the red bricks), and it looks closer to what my eyes saw when I took it. I've found this to be true for most daylight photos I take with the Open Camera app. They aren't as processed and are closer to what the scene really looks like. While they don't have as much contrast as the photos I take with the Pixel camera, they look more true to life, their colors pop more, and they're more pleasing to my eyes. While far from perfect, Pixel phones are still great point and shoot phones All you need to do is press the shutter button While the Pixel camera app falls short of Open Camera's less processed results in many daylight scenes, the biggest strength of Google's computational photography algorithms is that they deliver very good to great results in an immense number of wildly different conditions. Bright days, overcast days, rainy days, dusk and sunrise, scenes with high and low amounts of contrast, nighttime with less or more ambient light, photos of objects, people, and pets, landscape, nature, and urban photography—the whole nine yards. Thanks to machine-learning algorithms working tirelessly behind the scenes of every photo you take with your Pixel, Pixel phones are still among the best point-and-shoot camera phones around. You don't have to adjust ISO, exposure, or shutter speed; all you have to do is press the shutter button, and your Pixel will handle all those adjustments for you. And in many cases, the results will be among the best on the market. Google Pixel 11 Pro - Brand - SoC - Google Tensor G6 The Google Pixel 11 Pro brings improved cameras, a faster Tensor G6 chip, and the HiLight notification LED to Android's official flagship phone. Pixel phones are not the best in business anymore, but they're still good enough for most people The fact of the matter is that the glory days of Pixels being the undisputed champions of mobile photography are behind us. Google has chosen to focus on software instead of hardware, which has resulted in other high-end phones, especially those ultra-high-end (and ultra-expensive) Chinese camera phones, beating Pixels in the area where they once ruled supreme. But as point-and-shoot phones, Pixels are still a great choice because they don't ask for any input from you and are capable of delivering often admirable results, considering the hardware they're equipped with, in almost any condition imaginable.

item.title: This BIOS setting has been throttling your RAM since day one
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.35
It's 2026. Who on earth is buying RAM right now? Well, you might be tempted to buy some if yours is underperforming, but I'm here to tell you to hold on to those RAM kits a little longer. Not only is RAM massively overpriced right now, but more importantly, you can probably fix yours with one simple BIOS setting. Your RAM may not be running at the speed on the box XMP and EXPO are the missing piece Slow RAM can almost feel like a CPU bottleneck sometimes. It sure isn't the easiest thing to diagnose, and most people will blame their SSD or their CPU before they even consider that the RAM might be the culprit. But just because your RAM isn't delivering on its promises—as in, providing you with the frequencies you've seen on the box—doesn't mean it's broken. Based on my experience, it's probably just fine, and you just forgot to overclock it. It's weird, right? You buy yourself a, let's say, DDR5-6000 kit. Pretty reasonable to assume it'll run at 6,000MT/s out of the box. But a lot of the time, it won't. Many (or most?) enthusiast RAM kits include both standard JEDEC settings and a faster, overclocked memory profile. Guess what ends up on the box? The fastest possible speed, of course. Duh. But those speeds are totally achievable (well, mostly) with the right XMP and/or EXPO profile. Intel XMP and AMD EXPO store predefined settings that tell compatible hardware how to run the memory at the advertised profile. Without enabling XMP or EXPO, chances are your RAM is running at the default speed, which is often a third of its maximum. Your motherboard is just sticking to what's described as safe, and the overclocking is optional, but because of the way RAM is advertised and used, the overclocked state is the default that we've all come to expect. Anything lower than that means you're leaving some performance on the table. The profile changes more than just RAM frequency Speed, timings, and voltage come as a package When you enable the correct XMP or EXPO profile, you essentially tell the RAM to get a move on and kick things up a notch to the frequency you paid for (and you paid a lot if it was in the last year, too). That's the headline benefit, but there's more to it. The profile is, in fact, more like a bundle deal, that includes the data rate, primary timings, and DRAM voltage. When you enable something like a DDR5-6000 CL30 profile, the motherboard will adjust more than just running the full 6,000MT/s. It'll also apply the timings and whatever else is needed to make the RAM kit work properly at its best available level. That's also part of why you shouldn't bother with manually adjusting frequencies in the BIOS. Not only is it arguably harder and more time-consuming, but you're also not achieving the same end result as you do by simply enabling the correct profile for your RAM. Sure, you can tune all those settings by yourself, but honestly, I never bother. It's fun, I guess, if you enjoy manual overclocking or want to try to squeeze out every last bit of performance, but it does get riskier if you try to push harder than the manufacturer intended. Check your memory speed before touching the BIOS Maybe you don't need this after all I'm no stranger to various PC optimizations, both due to my 20-year experience in building the darn things, and also due to the fact that now's not the time to be buying new hardware, so we have to resort to the same tricks we've had to use when we were broke college kids. Still, even I will tell you that there's no need to fix stuff that's doing just fine without your help, so before you start digging through the BIOS, check and make sure your RAM actually does need to be overclocked. Checking is easy: just open the Task Manager on Windows, head to Performance, then Memory, and look at the reported speed. If it's running well below the advertised speed, then yup, BIOS time it is. You can also check the current memory speed from the BIOS itself, and tools like HWiNFO or CPU-Z can give you more detail if you like. Enabling XMP or EXPO is usually a walk in the park You shouldn't need any manual tuning Manufacturers made these XMP/EXPO profiles specifically so that they're easy to toggle and don't require any knowledge of overclocking whatsoever. Once you're certain that your RAM needs to be adjusted, reboot into the BIOS/UEFI, and look for the memory profile setting. Then, select the appropriate XMP or EXPO profile, save your changes, and restart. As is always the case with BIOS settings, the exact location of everything will vary based on your motherboard brand, but these RAM settings are almost never hard to find. Don't be afraid to explore; as long as you don't change any other settings, there's no harm in just having a little look around. All set? Boot up your PC and check memory speed again. If the profile actually took, you're all set, and can start testing your PC. Run a lot of memory-heavy tasks simultaneously, such as a lot of browser tabs as well as a game and some other apps, and see how it all performs. More importantly, monitor PC stability. The advertised speed still isn't guaranteed You're technically overclocking your RAM The thing about RAM overclocking is that it's not guaranteed that you'll have those exact speeds from the box at all times. Even with the right profile enabled, your CPU's memory controller, motherboard, BIOS version, number of DIMMs, and the RAM kit itself all play their own little role in the ultimate performance. And as doing this counts as overclocking, keep an eye out for crashes or memory errors, as they might mean you need to try a lower profile. You paid for faster RAM, so check whether you're making the most of it I'm a big believer in making the most of what you already own. Even older DDR4 RAM can be plenty good enough for just about everyone, but if you're letting it run at half speed, that's bound to feel underwhelming. Check out your XMP/EXPO profiles and see if it helps.

item.title: Don't waste time trying to block Fire TV ads—Amazon has already won
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.34
The Amazon Fire TV series of sticks and (literal) televisions has been popular for years thanks to low price points for decent-quality hardware. However, Fire TVs cost so little because they are at least partly a subsidized ad-delivery system. It's part of the price you pay to not pay the price, so to speak. Naturally, people have used all sorts of methods to block ads and prevent tracking on Fire TVs, but in the end, the way these devices are set up makes this a futile game to play. Fire TV’s privacy settings don’t actually stop the ads or tracking The buttons, they do nothing! My colleague Rich Hein wrote an excellent guide on how to stop your Fire TV from collecting personal information on you. In it, he shows the settings you need to change to disable tracking by Amazon, and you can also turn off personalized ads. Note that you can't turn off ads; all it does is remove the personalization, which means the ads you see may or may not be relevant to you. According to Amazon's developer guidelines, app makers can still use contextual advertising, which isn't affected by your opt-out decision and doesn't rely on your unique advertising ID. Apps are allowed to use alternative identifiers as a fallback, as long as they are in line with Amazon's privacy policy. In 2019, a study titled Watching You Watch: The Tracking Ecosystem of Over-the-Top TV Streaming Devices found that (and I'm paraphrasing) disabling interest-based ads reduced the number transmitting the advertising ID from 35 to 16, but tracker domains fell only from 119 to 115. Apps continued transmitting Android IDs, serial numbers, and MAC addresses. This is an old study, of course, and things might have changed in practice, but it's a good example of how that "opt-out" you're given is more of a pacifier than any sort of effective mitigation of ads and tracking. Apple TV 4K (3rd Gen) - Brand - Apple - Operating System - tvOS You'll get the full Apple experience with this streaming device. The A15 chip provides great hardware for all of your apps, Apple-exclusive or otherwise. - Resolution - 4K - Ports - HDMI Pi-hole can only block the domains it can identify You must know its true name to hold power over it We've written quite a bit about Pi-hole, and it's probably the most popular self-hosted ad-blocking solution. By using Pi-hole as your DNS server, you can block ads before they ever reach any of your devices, and overall it's pretty effective. However, Pi-hole alone won't stop the tracking you think it does. That's because Pi-hole works by managing which domains your network devices can reach. If an ad network's domain isn't on the Pi-hole's block list, it will work as normal. It also doesn't know anything about the content of the data your devices are sending. So a device could be sending thousands of bits of telemetry every day to a home server, and your self-hosted DNS won't know if it should even do something about it, because that's not how it was designed to work. The bottom line is that if ads are being served through a domain not on the Pi-hole (or whatever DNS-based solution you use) block list, or if the same domain for desired content is also being used to serve ads, then you're going to see those ads, and tracking is still technically possible. Amazon can hide unwanted traffic among the traffic Fire TV needs Sneaky, sneaky! Because Amazon controls the cloud infrastructure, your Fire TV's OS, its hardware, and all the first-party services on your device, it can easily bypass your attempts to block ads and tracking. It's basically impossible to know what traffic from your Fire TV is something you want (e.g., pulling show metadata) versus something you don't want (e.g., how you like to watch The Princess Bride at 3 a.m.). It's important that I point out any platform owner can do this. Apple could do it if it liked, but as far as we know, Apple's privacy policy and stance towards tracking and advertising are much more consumer-friendly. At least for now. You can lock down a Fire TV, but eventually it stops being useful If you're going to stick with a Fire TV, you can lock it down to some extent and prevent some degree of tracking and advertising. If you want to get rid of it all, you're going to run into issues. Since tracking and ads can be mixed in with normal legitimate traffic, your device needs to work; at some point you're just turning your Fire TV into a paperweight. If you can't live with that, the best advice I can offer is switching to a different device. A Google TV device gives you more options to stop tracking, at least. As Ars Technica notes, common advice among privacy advocates is to use an Apple TV and disconnect your smart TV or stop using Google, Roku, or Fire TV devices. Apple TV devices do not display ads in the same way as these other devices, and privacy defaults and controls are much stronger. I'd never claim it was perfect, but spending that $100 upfront will save you many headaches and annoyance. Besides, it will be a decade before you need to replace it, if you buy the latest model.

item.title: Eero's silent cloud syncs are turning your router into yet another tracking device
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.18
Your internet router has a very specific job, and it's perfectly reasonable to assume that all it's doing is that job and nothing else. The reality, however, is never that simple. Although it's no secret that your Eero mesh system is a cloud-based product in constant communication with the company's servers, changes in ownership have turned this from a non-problem to a major privacy concern. Because who owns those servers now? Oh, just Amazon, one of the biggest advertising and data companies in the world—no biggie. Your Eero is a very chatty guy "Set-and-forget" actually means "always reporting back" Eero mesh systems have been around for a while now, and their cloud-dependent design has been there since the very beginning. All of the features that make it easy to use, like the in-app management, automatic updates, and seamless device routing, rely on a cloud control plane that stays "in near constant communication" with the company's cloud servers. The company has always been transparent about this, and paired it with a decent privacy policy. But this cloud-dependent design goes deep—even features you'd expect to run locally, like seeing real-time data usage per device, are routed through Eero's cloud rather than served from your local network. This isn't something that needs to be cloud-based, though Eero says it chose to do it this way to prevent misuse from an unsecured local server. Not every feature is cloud-based, however. Eero has also taken steps toward local independence with its "mesh of trust" public key infrastructure, a feature that has been around since 2018 and lets nodes communicate securely over your local network without relying on the wider internet. The point is, there's a lot of data collection going on, and there are no announcements when it happens. Whether your app is open or not, diagnostics, device lists, and telemetry flow continuously in the background. It's easy to forget this kind of thing, and Eero is hardly the only one, since some routers ship with settings that leave your network controls exposed to the wider internet. What it collects (and what it swears it doesn't) It won't collect your browsing data, but it collects plenty of other stuff When the average user hears that their Wi-Fi router is collecting data, the first place their mind will probably go is browsing history. Your router definitely should not be collecting this data—but since it is collecting something, it's a fair question to ask. In Eero's case, the company has told CNET it "does not have the capability to track customer internet browsing activity." This is a good thing, of course, but just because Eero isn't collecting the worst-case-scenario data doesn't mean it isn't collecting anything problematic at all. To be precise, they collect performance statistics, device temperatures, MAC addresses, IP addresses, and the types of devices connected to your network. These things might sound a bit like meaningless numbers that have no tangible connection to you as a person—but when you put it all together, it becomes part of a detailed behavioral fingerprint of the devices you use and how you use them. It can even reveal pretty personal things like when you tend to be home, when you sleep, or when you buy a new device. This is a clear reminder that your router has a privileged view of everything on your network, and it's one of the reasons privacy-minded users split their smart-home gadgets onto a separate network segment to limit what any single device can see. This is why ownership matters so much—when Eero was a small independent company, that mass of data was more likely to stay (from a user's perspective) a garbled mess of numbers only used for diagnostics "or whatever." But Amazon, on the other hand, is one of the most experienced companies out there at building detailed behavioral profiles of its users to fuel advertising, purchases, and various other things. Of course, when Amazon bought Eero, there was an obligatory "don't worry, we won't change the privacy policy" promise. How reassuring that promise sounds to you depends on what you think of Amazon. As for precedents, there are other companies that have made the promise and sneakily gone back on it a couple of years later. A prominent example would be Facebook (now Meta) changing the policy for WhatsApp a few years after acquisition. In this case, however, it's been around seven years since the acquisition, and there haven't been any doomsday-level changes yet. Users do now have the option to link their Amazon account to their Eero device, however, and this opens a data pathway that didn't exist before. Can you opt out of the data collection? Nope Accept your fate, or unplug the mesh system As mentioned already, the cloud-dependent design of Eero mesh systems is purposeful and fundamental. It's basically a no cloud = no product situation, and if you trusted the company with your data, that was okay. If you still trust the company now, it's still okay. Technically, nothing has changed yet. However, you might be wondering if you can limit the data collection a bit. Unfortunately, the answer to that question is a pretty flat "no." Per Eero's own privacy policy, the only way to completely halt collection is to uninstall the app and unplug every Eero device. If you're choosing to stop using your Eero device, you can email the company to request data deletion, but if you do that while still using it, the company warns that it can render the devices inoperable. If that all-or-nothing bargain rubs you the wrong way, it's worth remembering you can always own and control your own router hardware instead of leaning entirely on a cloud-managed ecosystem. So, should you rip your Eero out of the wall? Well, it depends on your stance on data privacy. There's a reason the headline reads "yet another tracking device"—our homes are already full of them. If you're the type to purge any that you don't trust, you probably need to keep a close eye on Eero's privacy policy going forward. On the other hand, if you already own plenty of Amazon home devices and other similar products, you probably won't be bothered by another—even if the privacy policy changes.

item.title: I saved over $1,000 after building this simple Excel subscription tracker
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.70
I realized I didn't have a single place where I could see all my subscriptions, so I built a simple Excel tracker to bring them together. Since I set mine up, it's helped me cut more than $1,000 from my recurring expenses by showing me what I was paying, highlighting overlaps, and giving me time to act before renewals. You can download a free copy of this worksheet. When you click the link, you'll find the download button in the top-right corner of your screen. Then, edit the lookup tables and tracker rows to match your subscriptions. I started with a simple three-column table Entering the information I already know I started by creating an Excel table with three columns: Service, Cost, and Last paid. The "Cost" column uses the Accounting number format, and the "Last paid" column uses a Date format. These are the only pieces of information I need to type manually for each subscription. I know the name of the service, how much it costs, and when I last paid for it. Excel can work out the rest. The subscriptions and figures shown in the worksheet screenshots are illustrative. Putting everything in one place is useful in itself. Instead of searching through emails, bank statements, and my memory, I can see all my recurring payments together. That makes potential overlaps much easier to spot and gives me a clear list of subscriptions to reconsider. In my case, seeing Google One and Dropbox alongside Microsoft 365 showed me I was paying for overlapping storage. Microsoft 365 already gave me 1TB, so I dropped the other two and saved around $140 a year. I added drop-down menus for categories and billing Data validation keeps the information consistent Next, I added Category and Billing columns to the table, both with the General number format applied. The "Category" column lets me group subscriptions such as streaming, software, cloud storage, fitness, and memberships, while the "Billing" column records whether I'm paying monthly, quarterly, or annually. Rather than typing these values manually, I use drop-down lists created with data validation. The main reason for this is to ensure my categories are consistent. If I entered "Cloud storage" for one service and "Cloud" for another, Excel would treat them as different categories, making it harder to see how much I'm spending in each area. Keeping the labels consistent means I can group and compare my spending more reliably. First, I created two small Excel tables beside my main subscription table. One contains the categories, while the other contains the three billing options. I then selected the relevant table column, went to Data > Data Validation, chose List, and pointed the Source to the appropriate lookup table. There's a slightly odd Excel quirk behind the way I've set this up. You can't use a structured table reference directly in the Data Validation dialog box. If you point data validation directly at cells on another worksheet, the range won't automatically expand when you add another item by default. Keeping the lookup tables on the same worksheet avoids that extra complication. This means I can add a new category later without having to rebuild the list. Excel calculates the costs and renewal dates for me Three formulas turn a basic list into a useful tracker The final three columns I added were calculated columns: Annual cost (Accounting), Next renewal (Date), and Alert (General). For the annual cost, I used: =IF([@Cost]="","", IF([@Billing]="Monthly",[@Cost]*12, IF([@Billing]="Quarterly",[@Cost]*4, [@Cost]))) A monthly subscription can look quite different when Excel shows what it adds up to over a year. In my personal tracker, seeing those annual costs prompted me to cancel YouTube Premium, saving me about $200 a year, as well as Adobe Acrobat Pro, which saved around $240. Next, I used EDATE to calculate the next renewal date: =IF([@[Last paid]]="","", EDATE([@[Last paid]], IF([@Billing]="Monthly",1, IF([@Billing]="Quarterly",3, 12)))) EDATE moves a date forward by a specified number of months. The formula therefore adds one month for monthly subscriptions, three months for quarterly subscriptions, and 12 months for annual subscriptions. Then, the alerts tell me when I need to pay attention: =IF([@[Next renewal]]="","", IF([@[Next renewal]]-TODAY()<=3,"Check now", IF([@[Next renewal]]-TODAY()<=7,"Upcoming", "OK"))) This compares the next renewal date with today's date. If the payment is within three days, it says "Check now." If it's within seven days, it says "Upcoming." Otherwise, it says "OK." Finally, I went to Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Text that Contains to format the three alert messages. I used Excel's default green, yellow, and red formatting presets, so the warnings are easy to spot without creating complicated formatting rules. This system is useful because I don't want to find out about a renewal after the money has already left my account. The warning gives me time to compare prices, switch providers, or negotiate before I'm committed to another payment. In my experience, this is where I usually make the biggest savings on automatic renewals like car insurance, roadside assistance, and my internet service. Across those changes, I've cut more than $450 from my annual recurring expenses. I added a slicer to make the list easier to explore This is optional, but useful when the table gets bigger Once the tracker was working, I added a slicer for the "Category" column. I selected the table, headed to Table Design > Insert Slicer, and selected Category. Now I can click a category to see only those subscriptions. For example, selecting "Software" immediately brings my software subscriptions together. It gives me a quick way to compare what I'm spending in that category and spot services I might be able to cut or replace. Place the slicer above your table and arrange it into multiple columns (Slicer > Columns) so it matches the table's width. This keeps the tracker compact and makes the slicer easier to scan. You can also add a "Billing" slicer if you want to filter the tracker by monthly, quarterly, or annual payments, but the "Category" slicer is the one I find most useful for seeing where I'm spending the most and deciding where I can cut back. Excel can be a surprisingly reliable companion Excel isn't just for accountants and analysts. I've found that it's also surprisingly useful for managing everyday life, whether that's spotting patterns in your daily routines or using a spreadsheet as a personal journal. In this case, a few simple formulas helped me take control of recurring expenses and keep more of my money. That's a pretty good use for a spreadsheet.

item.title: These 3 open-source apps do what Windows should have built into the OS years ago
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.65
Microsoft has kept Windows on a steady path for years. Most updates focus on refining and upgrading existing features instead of drastically changing core OS functionality. While Windows’ defaults are perfectly fine for the most part, I decided to revamp a few core parts with open-source tools while keeping the overall Windows 11 look and feel I’ve grown familiar with. Files is the File Explorer replacement Windows should have built More than a worthy replacement For years, File Explorer was a mish-mash of modern UI being added on top of old code that dates back to Windows XP and possibly even older versions. Microsoft has taken many steps in the last few years to modernize File Explorer, and it's a lot better than it used to be. For instance, the Windows 22H2 update introduced browser-style tabs, allowing you to open multiple locations while staying within one window. Well, guess what: Microsoft is still years behind on that feature, as the open-source Files app has featured browser-style tabs for years before Microsoft thought of doing it. And that's actually a good example of the overall theme of the Files app—it's a power-user version of File Explorer that's been built by hundreds of contributors. While some long-standing features that have been available in Files have found their equivalent in File Explorer over the years, there are still a few things that Files does better. One of the coolest features is Dual-Pane View, which allows you to open a folder in a separate horizontal or vertical pane. This makes moving files drastically quicker and more convenient in just a couple of clicks than opening two separate windows or tabs. Another feature people install Files for is the Mac-style column view, which allows you to open folders in a structured horizontal layout that makes large groups of folders easier to navigate. There's also a color-coded tagging system, which allows you to add tags to individual files and folders for easier organization. For instance, if your Documents folder contains a mix of everything, you can use the system to tag your work files, home files, photos, and important files. Additionally, Files lets you create RAR files, eliminating the need to keep a separate third-party app installed. There are a few other minor details I haven't mentioned, but still, perhaps the best thing about Files is that it looks and feels just like File Explorer, completely eliminating any potential learning curve that'd make you stay away from it. System Informer is Task Manager for real power users See what's actually running Windows' built-in Task Manager is an okay tool, and no one can deny that it's gotten more refined over time. However, if you want to do more than just monitor and end background tasks or check memory, CPU, and GPU usage, consider switching to System Informer. It's an open-source system monitoring tool that covers all the same basics as Task Manager, but in far more detail. For starters, all processes are color-coded: green are newly started processes, red are terminated, pink are immersive/UWP processes, blue are core system processes, cyan are Windows background services, and so on. This allows you to easily tell what category a process belongs to without even having to check the username that started it. System Informer also seems to be a lot more capable when you need to terminate a process. While Windows' built-in Task Manager can sometimes hang when you try to terminate a frozen process, System Informer offers more powerful process termination options. It's saved me several times from having to reboot my system because Task Manager refused to shut down a frozen game. But it's really when you start investigating your processes that System Informer makes all the difference. When you open the properties of a process, you get extensive, highly detailed information about it. There are all the usual things like the Process ID (PID), parent process, file path, and the option to open the file location. But System Informer goes into much more depth than Task Manager, as you can see the exact command line used to launch the process, the resources the process consumed over time, environment variables, network details, and a lot more than that. Another neat feature is the ability to identify files used by a process. Whenever Windows doesn't let me delete a file because a process is using it, I can just hop into System Informer, go to Find Handles or DLLs, type in the file name, and immediately identify the process preventing me from deleting it. If you ever need to troubleshoot your system and pinpoint a sketchy background process that's causing trouble, System Informer will get you where Windows Task Manager stops. Windows Search feels painfully limited next to Flow Launcher A search bar for power users Windows' built-in Search has always been kind of lackluster. While it's super easy to access by just hitting the Start key and starting to type, it can't wait to jump at the opportunity to present you with a Bing search. Also, Windows Search is shockingly slow and resource-heavy when running on lower-end machines. Thankfully, Flow Launcher exists. It's a powerful, lightweight alternative to Search that you can bring up with the default Alt+Spacebar hotkey or some other combination of your choosing. It's essentially a floating search bar that looks a little like macOS Spotlight Search. The biggest benefit of Flow Launcher is just how fast it is. Flow Launcher relies on Everything (Voidtools) to search your entire drive instantly, which is a massive improvement over Windows' ultra-slow native indexing system. Some other things Flow Launcher lets you do include running shell commands directly from the search bar by typing > and a space before the command, dragging and dropping photos and documents from search to copy and paste them to a different location, and doing a Google search directly in your preferred browser instead of being forced to use Bing and Microsoft Edge. If you end up enjoying Flow Launcher, you'll be pleased to hear that it offers a surprising level of customization that you can access through the system tray on your taskbar or by searching for "Settings" in the app and selecting the Flow Launcher Settings option. Windows doesn’t have to dictate how you use your PC Look, you don't have to pick between these tools and Windows' built-in features. All of them can work perfectly well alongside Microsoft's default tools, but it's still worth pointing out that some of them let you take things to the next level if you so desire. Files and System Informer can replace File Explorer and Task Manager directly through the registry, while Flow Launcher is powerful enough that you'll quickly forget to even open the Start menu. So go ahead and trick out your Windows installation to make it feel more like your own, without making any major sacrifices.

item.title: 3 Linux phones you can actually buy and use right now (and why you probably shouldn't)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.22
Linux phones have come a long way from the days when that meant installing rough software and hoping for the best. You can now get polished devices that largely work as well as their Android and iPhone counterparts, just with truly open-source code. But where do you start? There are a few solid recommendations if you're determined to run Linux on a phone, including a recognizable brand. With that said, there are still pitfalls that might make you turn to Android (yes, technically based on Linux) if you're uncomfortable with fixing issues yourself. Fairphone 5 Great Linux support, but not so US-friendly The Fairphone 5 is one of the safest picks for a Linux phone. You can flash it to run Canonical's Ubuntu Touch distro very well, with limited voice-over-LTE (VoLTE) one of its few quirks. It's reasonably quick with its Qualcomm Dragonwing processor, offers 128GB of expandable storage, packs 50-megapixel cameras, and is highly repairable. Its ethical construction is in sync with Linux's philosophy, so you can feel better about the workers and ecological impact in addition to the OS. The catch? It's not officially available in the U.S. While the unlocked model should run on T-Mobile's network, you're not guaranteed compatibility with every frequency or feature. You also won't get after-sale help if something breaks, although you can likely source the parts for do-it-yourself repairs. Just be ready to wait for the Fairphone Gen 6+ if you want more robust support, as that's the company's first phone to officially reach American shores. Purism Librem 5 Pure, but not cutting-edge If you want a phone built for Linux, Purism's Librem 5 should be on your short list. PureOS is the definition of free open-source software (FOSS), right down to the drivers. Moreover, it's effectively a desktop platform with enough modifications to run on a handset. If you run Firefox, for instance, you're using the desktop browser rather than a cut-down mobile version. You can run utilities that simply wouldn't be an option with Android or iOS. There are even physical kill switches to disconnect wireless connections and recording components, so you never have to wonder if data is leaking behind your back. However, you'll pay steep prices for that software freedom. In addition to the limited U.S. network compatibility (T-Mobile is once again your pick), it costs $799 for hardware that even the most affordable Android phones can outrun: a nearly decade-old processor, 3GB of RAM, and 32GB of storage. The Librem 5 is more for security mavens and FOSS advocates than everyday users who just want to ditch Apple or Google. Volla Phone Quintus More choice, for a price The Volla Phone Quintus represents one of the few mobile devices with a real choice in software. You can go with its Android-based Volla OS if you want to play it safe with maximum app compatibility, or you can go with Ubuntu Touch. While the fingerprint reader, LTE calling, and dual-SIM support have issues in Linux, you'll get reasonably modern hardware (including a MediaTek Dimensity 7050 chip and 256GB of storage) with little to no setup. However, you're also taking a big chance. The Quintus costs $832, for a start. And like the Fairphone, it's an imported device without stateside support. You'll have to be comfortable leaning on the community (and your own Linux tinkering skills) for help, and there won't be a strong supply of aftermarket parts. It's mainly alluring as a refined device that can come with Linux out of the box. What about AOSP? Open source training wheels There is an alternative if you like the idea of an open-source phone but aren't ready to dabble in full Linux: unofficial firmware based on the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), Google's stripped-down OS without proprietary apps like Gmail and Google Maps.. Custom ROMs like /e/OS and GrapheneOS have more open-source components and are typically more privacy-oriented than regular Android releases. You won't always escape proprietary code, but the experience is typically "de-Googled" if you're worried about Big Tech data collection or an abundance of AI. You can even download Play Store apps on /e/OS without a Google account. You can buy phones with this software preinstalled, such as the Murena Fairphone Gen 6, so you don't need to flash the device yourself. And even if you do, the phones that support these AOSP variants are typically from mainstream brands like Google and (soon) Motorola. You'll get fully up-to-date hardware, not to mention an option to revert to plain Android. Think of AOSP as a bridge. You can edge closer to straightforward Linux without jumping in completely. And when you're ready, there are already some devices waiting for you.

item.title: Proxmox VE turned a $35 Raspberry Pi into my homelab's most powerful machine
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.15
I had a Raspberry Pi 5 lying around and I was not doing much with it. Then Proxmox VE recently announced ARM64 support on 5th of August and that immediately made me think about my Raspberry Pi. Proxmox now provides Proxmox VE for 64-bit ARM platforms, although the Raspberry Pi devices are not officially supported because of their boot and hardware-description architecture. I decided to experiment anyway and installed Proxmox VE on top of Debian on my Raspberry Pi 5. The Pi became my little virtualization lab Small hardware is much more useful when the workloads are isolated The main reason I like this experiment is isolation. When I was using the Pi as a normal Linux machine, anything I installed was part of the host. That is fine for a simple server, but it becomes less attractive when you want to experiment. With Proxmox, I can create a VM or LXC container for a particular task and keep it separate from everything else. If I want to test something on Debian, I can create a Debian guest, run an AlmaLinux environment alongside it, or isolate experimental services that might destroy their own configuration in separate guests. This is where the Raspberry Pi starts punching above its weight. It does not have enough CPU or memory to run large enterprise workloads, but the workloads I actually want to run in a homelab are often small enough that the hardware is perfectly adequate. It can run a small Linux VM with a modest amount of memory. I have also tried several lightweight services and LXC containers really help to keep resource usage low. Just be sure to use the ARM64 versions of the containers. A normal Raspberry Pi server tends to accumulate services over time, with every experiment modifying the same host. I can create a guest for an experiment, give it the resources it needs, take a snapshot before making risky changes, and delete the guest when I am finished. Those lucky enough to own multiple Raspberry Pis might even be able to experiment in a cluster. It is useful precisely because it is small The Pi fills a role that larger machines cannot One not so unexpected advantage of the Raspberry Pi is that it is cheap enough to dedicate to experiments. If I want to try a new Proxmox feature, test an ARM64 image, or build a temporary environment, the Pi gives me somewhere to do it. That makes it a useful complement to a larger homelab server. The bigger machine can handle workloads that need substantial CPU, memory, or storage, while the Pi can remain available for small experiments and services that benefit from being isolated. It also gives you an ARM64 environment that you would otherwise have to emulate or borrow another machine to obtain. There is also something appealing about having a virtualization host that draws very little power and takes up almost no space. You can leave the Pi running continuously without treating it like a full-sized server, while Proxmox gives me the same basic workflow for creating and managing guests that I would expect from a larger virtualization system. There are some big caveats This is a homelab experiment, not a production server There is a reason I keep calling this an experiment.
