item.title: Sen. Blakespear's bill to protect workers from Tijuana pollution passes state Senate
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.42
The state Senate Friday unanimously passed a bill by Sen. Catherine S. Blakespear, D-Encinitas, to create guidelines for protecting workers from ongoing pollution in the Tijuana River Valley. Senate Bill 1046, which also passed the Assembly unanimously on Tuesday, now heads to Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk for his signature. "The untreated wastewater pouring into the Tijuana River Valley has been an environmental nightmare for decades, polluting the surrounding air and water, and we need to protect any workers exposed to it," Blakespear said. "SB 1046 ensures that lifeguards, park rangers and others forced to work outside in the Tijuana River Valley area are adequately protected." The bill directs CalOSHA to develop workplace standards for "minimizing exposure to transboundary pollution, including adopting requirements for personal protective equipment, hazard communication, incident reporting and trainings." The guidelines are to be developed by local communities, as well as lifeguards, park rangers, local governments, labor unions, air districts and academic experts, according to Blakespear's office. The Tijuana River transports millions of gallons of untreated wastewater, including sewage and industrial waste, from Tijuana into California every year. This has led to more than 1,300 consecutive days of beach closures, noxious gases and air and water quality health concerns across the South Bay. Local scientists have found that pollutants from the Tijuana River's contaminated water aerosolize, entering the air and causing health impacts in nearby communities. The contaminated air can contain high levels of hydrogen sulfide, a dangerous, odor-causing gas. Heavy rain and flooding increase risks. According to Blakespear's office, exposure can result in gastrointestinal illness, skin infections and respiratory and neurological disorders. Workers in the Tijuana River Valley have experienced headaches, fatigue, nausea and bloody noses. Local In June, levels of hydrogen sulfide near the Tijuana River Valley spiked so high, county public health officials offered guidance to deal with possible noxious smells. An increase in the gas, which has a rotten egg smell and is associated with untreated wastewater, came after a pipe in Tijuana experienced a break. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, emissions exceeding the Acute Exposure Guideline Level 1 for the gas can cause "notable discomfort, irritation, or certain asymptomatic non-sensory effects. However, the effects are not disabling and are transient and reversible upon cessation of exposure." To reduce exposure, those in the area were advised to limit outdoor activities, keep windows and doors closed when odors are present, use fans to circulate air inside buildings and an air purifier with a high efficiency particulate air filter and activated charcoal with potassium permanganate. In July, Rep. Scott Peters led his Democratic San Diego Congressional colleagues in sending a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer urging continued cooperation with Mexico on addressing the pollution. Peters joined Reps. Juan Vargas and Sara Jacobs, both D-San Diego, and Rep. Mike Levin, D-San Juan Capistrano, in penning the letter to Greer as the United States Mexico Canada Agreement is renegotiated. In the letter, the lawmakers reiterate the commitments made to repair and upgrade wastewater treatment infrastructure on both sides of the border in the 2019 USMCA and said moving forward, "The United States must develop enforceable environmental standards and a rapid response mechanism for violations of the minute treaties and wastewater spills that can and should be avoided with every possible measure available." Any renegotiation is also a chance to secure additional funding and bi- national commitments, the representatives write. "The USMCA has been pivotal for San Diego, a city long plagued by cross-border pollution and chronic sewage spills largely caused by Mexico's failing infrastructure, which threatens our beaches, public health and local economy," a statement from Peters' office read. "President Trump's decision to not renew the agreement risks undoing hard-won progress and leaves San Diego exposed to more pollution and economic setbacks." Multiple steps are still required to get a handle on the long-standing pollution and sewage crisis, including a multi-year funding commitment from Mexico on infrastructure projects, enabling the use of existing funds for the U.S.-Mexico Border Water Infrastructure Grant Program to Mexico and planning and funding river diversion projects and advanced treatment plants.

item.title: NCTD to suspend coastal rail service Sept. 12-13 for maintenance
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.24
The North County Transit District will suspend all coastal rail service this month to perform routine maintenance, transit officials announced Tuesday. The closure, which will take place Saturday, Sept. 12, and Sunday, Sept. 13, will pause all coaster service between San Diego and Oceanside. Regular service is scheduled to resume on the morning of Monday, Sept. 14, according to the NCTD. Transit officials said weekend closures take place periodically throughout the year on a predetermined schedule to allow construction crews to work safely on and along the rail line. The downtime enables workers to complete preventive maintenance improvements and advance major construction efforts. No passenger or freight trains will run during the closure. However, test trains, construction vehicles and equipment will remain active along the railroad right-of-way and on the tracks over the weekend. Officials advised residents to remain alert to cross rail lines only at designated crossings. More information on the weekend closures is available at GoNCTD.com/Alerts.

item.title: Tropical Storm Marie may bring rain to San Diego over Labor Day weekend
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.20
The National Weather Service is monitoring Tropical Storm Marie, which developed near Baja California and could bring a chance of showers to San Diego County over Labor Day weekend. Tropical Storm Marie is currently about 1,300 miles south-southeast of San Diego. It is expected to become a hurricane on Thursday before beginning to weaken late Saturday, the NWS said. By Sunday, it is expected to be about 775 miles southwest of San Diego. "This would bring a chance of showers and a slight chance of thunderstorms from Saturday into next Monday," the NWS said. Potential impacts can include coastal flooding as high tides are expected during the week of Labor Day. According to the meteorologists, associated tropical swells are roughly forecast to arrive Saturday or Sunday, coinciding with high tides of 6.2 to 6.5 feet. "Anticipated wave heights will depend on the track of the storm, so these remain uncertain," the NWS statement read. "It is still way too early to discuss expected rainfall totals; however, even with a storm track further out to sea, tropical moisture may still be funneled into the area during Labor Day Weekend." Local The NWS and National Hurricane Center will continue monitoring the system and providing updates.

item.title: First-year students move into residence halls at University of San Diego
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 3.53
About 1,500 students moved into residence halls at the University of San Diego in Linda Vista Saturday, as they prepare for classes to begin Tuesday to start the 2026-27 academic year. USD officials say the students who moved in Saturday are part of the more than 3,000 first-year, transfer and graduate students who are joining the university community this fall. The incoming first-year class stands out as one of the most accomplished and well-rounded in USD's history, university officials say, with an average weighted Grade Point Average of 3.98. In addition, 22% are the first in their family to attend college, 43% identify as Catholic, and there are 16 different faith traditions represented. The first-year class comes from 43 states, 16 countries and three U.S. territories or military bases, according to officials. "The start of the school year is such a joyous and exciting time. It marks the very beginning of our students' experiences here at the University of San Diego. Last week, the Princeton Review ranked our university not only the most beautiful campus in the nation but, more importantly, we were ranked number one for quality of life and number two for happiest students, and that's not by accident," USD President James Harris III said in a statement. "Our faculty, staff, and students are committed to community engagement, and we extend this bold mission into the world. Each new class brings fresh perspectives and ideas that strengthen our community and move us closer to fulfilling our mission to create a more inclusive, sustainable and hopeful world," he added. Harris pointed out that an example of the students' change-making spirit is their sustainability efforts, reflected in a successful student-led initiative continuing this fall. "EcoShop is a program USD students developed after researching campus waste and donation needs. The initiative allows students to donate or recycle items from their dorm rooms, including lamps, mini-fridges, clothing and school supplies during the spring move-out period," Harris said. Local "The items are placed into storage and made available at no cost to students during move-in weekend. It is a valuable opportunity for students to furnish their rooms sustainably and affordably while supporting USD's commitment to zero waste." Undergraduate and graduate classes begin on Tuesday. The School of Law began classes on Aug. 17.

item.title: Trader Joe's adds 2 new stores in San Diego County. Here's where
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 3.33
San Diego County, prepare to have two more locations to stock up on Trader Joe's favorites (like the highly-sought after mini-totes). New Trader Joe's Clairemont location One of the two new Trader Joe's locations will be moving into the Clairemont neighborhood and will be located at 3962 Clairemont Mesa Blvd., becoming new neighbors to the plaza's Five Below, Vons, and Ross Dress for Less, to name a few nearby stores already doing business at the Clairemont Town Square. Trader Joe's spokesperson Nakia Rohde told NBC San Diego they do not yet have an exact opening date to share for the new Clairemont location. However, the new location has been added to the company's Opening Soon list on their website, which typically makes it to the website three to six months before the opening date, Rohde said. As of Friday, a Burlington Coat Factory covered in scaffolding currently stands at that location. Out front a sign reads "We're remodeling." Around the corner there appeared to be more large commercial space under construction. New Trader Joe's San Marcos location Local Plans are underway for a Trader Joe's store to move into the North City area of San Marcos, Rohde confirmed to NBC San Diego. This will be the city's first and only Trader Joe's store. Rohde did not share any other details about this location. The new store was also announced on the Instagram page for North City, a mixed-use development adjacent to CSU San Marcos. The new Trader Joe's location will join a mixed-use commercial area that includes a variety of restaurants, a fitness center, a clinic and a medical institute. "North City has always been about creating a place where people want to spend time, connect with each other and feel part of something. Trader Joe’s, local businesses, public spaces and community programming are all part of that vision," a recent Instagram post stated.

item.title: Millions of San Diegans got this SDG&E notice Tuesday. It's not a scam
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 2.88
San Diego Gas & Electric sent millions of texts, phone calls, and emails to customers across its service area Tuesday as the utility tested its emergency notification system ahead of the Santa Ana wind season. The Sept. 1 test was designed to ensure SDG&E can reach residential and business customers during emergencies and other situations when timely information is critical. The utility said regular testing helps ensure its notification systems are operational and reliable. “We’re making sure that we can reach customers when it matters most. And that means during an emergency,” SDG&E spokesman Roland Franklin said. SDG&E said Tuesday's test notifications were sent during a two-hour window around lunchtime. Text messages came from the short code 73434, phone calls came from 1-858-868-4586 and emails were sent from notices@sdge.com. Customers who did not receive a test message should check their contact information and notification preferences at MyEnergyCenter.com. More information about the notification test is available at SDGEToday.com/NotificationTest. The test comes as San Diego County approaches a time of year when dry conditions and Santa Ana winds can increase wildfire danger. Blossom Valley resident Chris Barnhill knows that danger firsthand. He witnessed the Cedar Fire in 2003 and remembers how smoke and embers transformed the area. Local “It's pretty terrifying,” Barnhill said. “I mean, you couldn't see the sun. It was just, you know, the embers everywhere. You couldn't see anything.” San Diego County has made changes to wildfire preparation and response in the years since, including bolstering its air attack, conducting controlled burns and regularly clearing brush, and alerting residents of threats any way possible. SDG&E has also invested millions of dollars in wildfire safety measures, including replacing wooden power poles with steel poles, monitoring potentially dangerous weather conditions in its command center, and its notification system — which will also notify customers of important outages and severe weather. “We get them right away because we're East County. You know, we're in the middle of it,” Barnhill said. “The more pre-evacuation notice you can get, the better.” The importance of wildfire preparedness has been underscored by some of the region's most destructive fires. Santa Ana winds knocked down a power line that ignited the Witch Fire in 2007. For Barnhill, who lives in East County, receiving warnings as early as possible can be critical. “Very necessary, I would think. You got to have enough time for the people to evacuate” Barnhill said. “Nobody wants to be through that.” This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC San Diego. AI tools helped convert the story to a digital article, and an NBC San Diego journalist edited the article for publication.

item.title: 26-year-old e-bike rider killed in Vista crash
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 2.81
A 26-year-old man riding an electric bike was killed Saturday when he crossed a Vista street against a red traffic light and was struck by a vehicle. The crash occurred at 3:38 p.m. Saturday near the intersection of South Melrose Drive and Breeze Hill Road, near Breeze Hill Park, according to the San Diego Sheriff's Office's Vista Station. The electric bike rider crossed Melrose against a red traffic signal and was struck by a northbound vehicle, sheriff's officials said. No information was provided about whether the man had been wearing a helmet. He was taken by ambulance to a hospital, where he died from his injuries, officials said. The driver of the vehicle remained at the scene and cooperated with the investigation, officials said. Neither drugs nor alcohol were believed to be a factor in the fatal crash.

item.title: Is a Hotel Subscription Worth It?
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 5.52
For years, getting rewarded for hotel stays came down to one of two things. You could join the loyalty program for free and slowly build up points, or you could apply for one of the hotel's credit cards. Lately, a third option has been catching on, including with a few major hotel brands. Instead of earning your way toward a reward, you pay a membership or subscription fee upfront and start saving right away. These hotel subscriptions may hand you a discount on room rates, fast-track you to a mid-tier elite status and sometimes toss in extras like late checkout, dining credits or a free welcome night. If you already book the same hotel brand often, the discount alone could be enough to cover the fee. But some of the brands have small networks of properties, and others may offer you similar benefits through one of their credit cards — not to mention the chance to earn points on your purchases. 5 hotel subscription plans and what they offer Benefits and access can vary significantly, depending on which hotel subscription you choose. In some cases, you may even get perks that go beyond hotel stays. Here are some of the options. For $95 a year, Wyndham Rewards Insider gets you a long list of benefits. Here are some highlights: - At least 10% off stays booked directly with Hotels by Wyndham. - A 50% points boost on all qualifying stays. - Various discounts on eligible flights, car rentals, cruises, theme parks, all-inclusive resorts, tours and activities. - 24/7 concierge service. The modest cost and the brand's large network of approximately 8,400 hotels across roughly 100 countries make this subscription hard to ignore for Wyndham loyalists. Even if you have a Wyndham credit card, not many of the perks overlap, though the Wyndham Rewards Earner® Plus Card and Wyndham Earner Premier® Card offer higher status tiers than Insider. For diehard Wyndham enthusiasts, it could make sense to have both. InterContinental Ambassador - Guaranteed one-category room upgrades. - Complimentary weekend night, valid on the second night of a paid weekend stay. - Up to $20 in restaurant and bar credits with every stay. - Single room rate for double occupancy. - Guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout. - Extras like complimentary water and internet, as well as a dedicated check-in area. While the IHG chain has a footprint of more than 6,600 properties worldwide, Ambassador benefits largely apply only at IHG’s luxury brand, InterContinental Hotels & Resorts, which has just over 220 destinations. The Platinum Elite status does work with other IHG hotels, but it's the same status the IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card offers. The card's annual fee is $99, and it offers a broad range of perks more suited for people who aren't strictly engaging in luxury travel. The citizenM brand is part of the Marriott Bonvoy family, but it has its own subscription plan for people who love its tech-savvy and design-forward properties. A mycitizenM+ membership runs $170 per year and offers the following perks: - 15% off direct citizenM bookings and up to 30% off during member sales. - 15% off food and drink at citizenM bars. - 15% off meeting rooms. - Free coworking at most properties. - Complimentary Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status. The citizenM brand has only 37 hotels across more than 20 cities in the U.S., Europe and Asia Pacific, making it a tough sell for that price, unless you're a frequent citizenM guest. That said, the free coworking benefit could be a boon for remote workers who live near a citizenM location. Minor Hotels Horizons Club Horizons Club comes in two annual subscriptions: Standard at $205 (179 euros) and Elevate at $285 (249 euros). Here are some of the perks they offer: - 15% to 25% off public rates. - A complimentary welcome night worth 150 Discovery Dollars. - Minor DISCOVERY Gold tier. - 10% off bars and restaurants, plus 20% off the pet fee. - Access to member offers of up to 50% off. - 50 Discovery Dollars back after your first stay. - Complimentary late checkout and flexible cancellations. The only difference between the two is that Elevate members also get access to perks with additional brands. Minor's network runs to more than 350 hotels across more than 30 countries in Europe and the Americas, but it doesn't offer perks with any other major hotel brands, so that's it. There is no Minor credit card either, which leaves the subscription as the only way to access these perks. As a result, it only makes sense if you're fiercely loyal to the Minor brands. If you want to explore Minor Hotels without the subscription, consider the Chase Sapphire Reserve®. Among its many premium perks, the card offers up to $250 in statement credits through Dec. 31, 2026, on prepaid Chase Travel℠ hotel bookings with various brands, including Minor. FoundersCard isn't strictly a hotel program, and it's not a credit card either. Rather, it offers a broad range of lifestyle benefits that include some hotel perks for a $95 initiation fee plus a yearly price of $595. Here are some of the perks on the travel side: - Negotiated rates at luxury hotels, some listed at 30% to 50% off. - Complimentary elite status with hotel brands such as Hilton, IHG, Sonesta and Wynn. - Upgrades, late checkout, welcome amenities and other VIP touches at many participating hotels. - Complimentary elite status with select airlines and car rental companies. - Preferred rates on airport lounge memberships, villa and resort experiences and more. The catch is that you won't be able to view the full slate of FoundersCard features unless you request an invitation or join. Also, some benefits require an upgraded Elite plan, which costs $995 annually. This subscription may be worth it if you value elite status and other VIP perks across several brands instead of just one. But it may make more sense in addition to a travel credit card rather than as a replacement. How to choose between a subscription and a hotel card Whether you go for a hotel subscription or a branded credit card comes down to how you travel. Here are some things worth thinking about before you commit to either one: - How you'd get value: A subscription generally offers a flat discount on the room rate, while a hotel credit card usually skips the discount and instead earns points on all your spending, not just hotel purchases. In some cases, the subscription may offer other travel perks you can't get with a credit card, such as discounts on other travel expenses. While both may offer elite status, hotel cards also often provide welcome bonuses and an annual free night. - How big the network is: A perk only works if you can actually use it. A subscription tied to a small brand can be hard to put to work, while a hotel credit card with a brand that has thousands of properties gives you a lot more flexibility. - What happens if you cancel: If you cancel a subscription, you may still enjoy the benefits until the current term is up. Meanwhile, if you cancel a hotel credit card, you'll lose all the perks upon closure (though you'll still retain the points you've earned). - Approval requirements: You generally need good or excellent credit and sufficient income to get approved for a hotel credit card, while there's no credit check required to sign up for a subscription service. If you want VIP perks but don't have great credit, a subscription may be the better choice. Start by pulling up last year's travel and counting how many nights you booked directly with the brand you're considering. Next, check whether the brand offers credit cards, a subscription service or both. Then, do some math to get an idea of what you could save with discounts and how much value you could get from a credit card. In some cases, it could even make sense to have both. For example, if you book a lot of cash stays, a subscription with a discount on rates and a credit card that offers great rewards on hotel purchases can help you maximize the value you get. The information related to Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful™ Card has been collected by NerdWallet and has not been reviewed or provided by the issuer of this card. To view rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card, see this page. How to maximize your rewards

item.title: I Hiked Waterfalls In North Carolina From This Trailborn Hotel
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 3.10
We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives. So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies. However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners. I Hiked Waterfalls In North Carolina From This Trailborn Hotel With onsite dining and easy access to nature, Trailborn Highlands is a great option for your next mountain getaway. Craig Joseph is a NerdWallet credit cards and travel rewards expert. He has degrees in geology from West Virginia University and oceanography from Oregon State University and has published in academic journals, newspapers and blogs. Craig is passionate about personal finance and wants to enhance the financial literacy of everyone he meets. He'll probably also try to convince you why rocks are cool. Meghan Coyle is an editor on the Travel Rewards team and the co-host of the Smart Travel podcast. She covers travel credit cards, airline and hotel loyalty programs, and how to travel on points. Meghan is based in Los Angeles and has a love-hate relationship with LAX. Published in Updated How is this page expert verified? NerdWallet's content is fact-checked for accuracy, timeliness and relevance. It undergoes a thorough review process involving writers and editors to ensure the information is as clear and complete as possible. If you’re looking for boutique hotel stays near national parks and other outdoor destinations, Trailborn Hotels and Resorts might be for you. This chain of five boutique properties gives you many ways to immerse yourself in nature, from the convenient locations to the design of the public spaces. And the best part? This brand is part of the Outdoor Collection by Marriott Bonvoy, which means you can earn or use Marriott points to stay near some of the country’s most iconic outdoor destinations. I recently had a chance to experience the Trailborn Highlands hotel in Highlands, North Carolina. It’s a town in the southern Blue Ridge Mountains that makes an excellent home base to explore the rainforest and many waterfalls in the area. You can drive there in about an hour and a half from Asheville Regional Airport or about three hours from Atlanta. While Marriott paid for my three-night stay, the opinions in this story are my own. The property itself is rustic, but comfortable (and pet-friendly!). It offers no shortage of amenities, including a fantastic on-site restaurant (the Highlands Supper Club), an outdoor Nordic spa and a lounge area with a firepit. Guests can also book excursions such as guided hikes, fly fishing, kayaking and rock climbing. Room rates at this property start around $128 and balloon to over $500 during the fall leaf-peeping season. Those more expensive periods could be a perfect time to use Marriott points or Marriott Free Night Awards for your adventure. Booking with Marriott Bonvoy points Marriott uses dynamic pricing, so the number of points required for an award stay fluctuates based on demand and the cash rate. However, during peak season in the fall, rates increase to $530 or 70,000 points per night. In that case, you’d get 0.8 cent per point, making it a better option to pay with Marriott points. If you’re short on points, Marriott also lets you combine cash and points for a stay, which can help stretch your points balance across more stays. The easiest way to earn a quick slug of Marriott points is through a welcome offer on a Marriott credit card. NerdWallet's ratings are determined by our editorial team. The Trailborn Highlands location is situated one block from Main Street in this upscale mountain town, making it a great location for both walking around town and accessing the outdoors. The lobby and public areas are bright and airy, with big windows, a fireplace and board games. Guest rooms The Trailborn Highlands property has 63 guestrooms, and each one offers some outdoor space. The ground-floor rooms have a garden patio while second-story rooms have a balcony. I stayed in a balcony room with a king bed. The room was basic but spacious, with checkered carpet and wood accents that fit into the local mountain environment. Each guestroom has a work station, which provides a comfortable space to get work done. The analog radio is a nice touch. When I was in my room, I spent most of my time relaxing on the balcony, listening to the birds chirp and enjoying how green my surroundings were. In contrast, the bathroom was pretty drab. While the color theme matched the muted natural tones throughout the property, the poor lighting and brown and green tile created a dark and uninspiring environment to prepare for the day. The Highlands Supper Club The Highlands Supper Club is the property’s sit-down dining option. The restaurant is housed in a historic log cabin perched atop a hill overlooking the hotel and surrounded by a beautiful rhododendron garden. The menu features a contemporary take on Southern comfort food, with craft cocktails and an extensive wine list. I’ll eat southern food any chance I get, and The Highlands Supper Club did not disappoint. I loved the homemade biscuits and deviled eggs with blue crab and bacon, but my absolute favorite were the oysters on the half shell. The blueberry cobbler a la mode was also a decadent way to end the evening, though I practically had to roll myself out of the restaurant after eating it all. The Nordic Spa The Nordic Spa is located in an enclosed outdoor patio and consists of a dry sauna, a cold spritz shower and a lounge area with a fire pit. The spa is open daily from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. and costs $100 per 50 minute session for up to 4 guests. I’m a sauna fanatic, and while the setting of the spa is clean and modern, the sauna itself wasn’t hot enough to get a full sweat going, even after about 20 minutes. It was still relaxing, and the transition from the warm sauna to the cold shower was invigorating. Just be aware that the spa is semi-private, as the second-story balcony rooms can see into the fenced-off area. The spa area needs a pergola overhead for added privacy. Waterfalls, s’mores and other activities Trailborn Highlands leans into the experiential accommodation trend and works with local guides and businesses to help guests experience the culture and activities that make the southern Appalachian Mountains unique. That includes trout fishing, kayaking, canoeing, river tubing, guided hikes and waterfalls tours. Available activities are posted on a bulletin board next to the front desk, making it easy to know what’s happening during your stay. Additionally, complimentary bicycles are available to all guests, making it easy to ride around the town of Highlands. Countless hikes, waterfalls and scenic overlooks are accessible within a 20-minute drive from the hotel. My personal favorite was Dry Falls, where you can take a path behind the waterfall. Additionally, The French Broad River (one of the oldest rivers in the world) is about an hour away and provides easy access to scenic trout fishing and kayaking. Trailborn lights a fire in the patio area each evening and encourages guests to put the devices away and be social with other guests. It turns out that’s pretty easy when your hands are covered with melted marshmallows from the s’mores session that the hotel offers each evening. Trailborn Highlands: Is it worth it? I really enjoyed the calmness of Trailborn Highlands, and I appreciated that it leans into experiences and community. The location makes access to nature easy, in addition to being centrally located near the shops and cafes on Main Street in Highlands. The price of a cash stay can be an absolute bargain midweek, and Marriott free night awards can offer good value if you want to travel during peak season. The stay also made me excited to check out the other Trailborn properties around the U.S.

item.title: I Slashed My Water Bill by $300 by Doing 1 Simple Thing
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 2.05
Each month, NerdWallet suggests one wallet win to help you feel more confident about your money. This month’s topic is utility bills, and we’re going to show you ways to lower your water bill each month. Time required: About two hours in total, which includes calls to your utility’s customer service line and arranging a plumber’s visit. What happened to me: Earlier this year, I opened up a routine water bill and was shocked at what I saw. According to the utility company, I owed just over $1,000 for the previous three month period of water usage. My typical bill was about half that amount. My first step was to call the utility company to see if perhaps they had made a mistake. They agreed to send out a representative to read my water meter, and then a week later, they confirmed that the reading was correct. In other words, my water usage had shot up and I was on the hook for the mega-bill. They suggested calling a plumber who could troubleshoot my water usage and perhaps identify a leak. The fix: When the plumber came to investigate a few days later, he confirmed that we did, in fact, have a leak. One of our toilets needed a new flapper. The total cost for his visit was $300. The plumber also suggested that I submit the receipt to show we fixed the leak and ask for a one-time reprieve from the utility company. Encouraged by the relatively easy repair and the hope of getting a refund, I waited a couple weeks and then asked the utility company if they could detect that our water usage had fallen. They sent out another meter reader, and then confirmed the problem seemed to be fixed: Our water usage had fallen back down to its typical levels. As for the bill reprieve, the utility company said they would consider it and asked me to send in the paperwork. However, three months later, I’m still waiting for a response. Still, I was relieved that my high water bill was relatively easy to lower. When the next bill arrived, it was about $870. Still too high because the leak had continued into the current meter reading period, but trending in the right direction. Based on the number of gallons we use now, I expect the next bill to be under $700. Over the course of the year, reducing my quarterly bill by $300 adds up to $1,200 in savings. What you can try: Pay close attention to your bills. I know my typical water bill amount, so I was able to spot the increase. If you want help organizing, try using the cash flow feature on NerdWallet’s app. It lets you see your monthly expenses and income in one place. Call your utility company. When you get a high bill out of the blue, it’s worth first calling the utility company to check for an error or obvious explanation. They might also have suggestions for next steps. Ask for help. Utility companies also often offer hardship programs to customers in distress. It’s worth asking if you might qualify. If you’re unsure how to start the conversation, try one of our scripts. Bring in a professional. While hiring a plumber isn’t cheap, the cost can pay for itself within a billing period or two if a leak is identified and fixed. Use less water. Outside of leaks, water can also be wasted in other ways: Extra long showers, leaving faucets running and watering grass unnecessarily all use up extra water. Consider scaling back to see your bill drop. If you’re following along with us on this monthly financial challenge, start by testing out the tips we shared today over the next few weeks. We’ll be back again next month to learn how to save money on holiday shopping. And if you missed last month’s edition, take a look back at how to pay less when you’re online grocery shopping. item.title: Why Intensity Matters for Preserving VO2 Max as You Age
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.79
(Photo: Halfpoint Images / Getty) Let’s say you’re an adult in your 70s, running or biking or swimming two or three times a week. How hard should you push? That’s the question posed in a new study in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, from a research team led by Sindre Midttun of the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. The answer isn’t obvious—for reasons that may be familiar if you’ve been following recent debates about zone 2 exercise, polarized training, and other related fitness theories. Sign up for a ten-part email series from Alex Hutchinson on how to train, fuel, and recover. Each week, Alex covers a new topic, including strength training, supplements, and more! The data comes from a large ongoing study called Generation 100, which was open to everyone between the ages of 70 and 77 in the Norwegian city of Trondheim. Participants were originally randomized into three groups and either told to follow public health guidelines by getting half an hour of moderate exercise per day, or enrolled in twice-a-week supervised sessions of moderate (70 percent of max heart rate) or intense (80 percent of max heart rate) exercise. The program lasted for five years. The original results were published back in 2020, and they weren’t particularly striking. After just five years, there wasn’t much difference between the three groups in how many of them died. Part of the problem is that there wasn’t that much difference between the groups, because they were allowed to do whatever they wanted outside the supervised sessions. On average, the control group actually ended up exercising more intensely than the moderate-exercise group, which muddies the waters. For this reanalysis, the researchers decided to forget about who was randomized to what group, and just look at what the subjects actually did, as reported on exercise questionnaires. From the original sample of 1,500 people, they picked out 500 who consistently reported doing either moderate exercise (between 11 and 14 on the Borg scale, which corresponds to “fairly light” or “somewhat hard” on a scale from 6 to 20) or high-intensity (15 or higher, corresponding to “hard,” “very hard,” or—wait for it—“very, very hard”) over the five-year period. Note that the high-intensity group wasn’t necessarily doing intervals; they were just pushing harder. The question the researchers asked was: Did the choice of exercise intensity make any difference to the aerobic fitness of the subjects, as measured with periodic VO2 max tests? The two groups were pretty well matched. They did a similar amount of exercise (both duration and frequency) over the five-year study period. So we should expect the group that pushed harder to gain more fitness (or, for people in their 70s, to lose less fitness), right? Not so fast. One of the big trends in exercise in recent years has been the rise of zone 2 training, which involves keeping your intensity slightly below threshold. That’s a moderate effort that enables you to carry on a conversation in full but slightly strained sentences. This is thought to be a metabolic sweet spot that maximizes fat-burning and optimally stimulates your mitochondria. (I did a deep dive into this topic last year.) One of the key arguments in favor of zone 2 training is that this is how many of the world’s best endurance athletes do most of their training. What’s sometimes called “polarized training” might involve doing 80 percent of your training in or around zone 2, and just 20 percent above it. You could explain this as a matter of practical convenience: doing lots of relatively easy training enables you to accumulate big volumes of training, and leaves you fresh enough to really go hard in the other 20 percent of your workouts. But another explanation—the one that zone 2 boosters subscribe to—is that pushing above zone 2 actually makes your workout worse. Your metabolism shifts from fat-burning toward carbohydrate-burning, lactate begins accumulating in your muscles and bloodstream, and you no longer trigger the mitochondrial adaptations that you’re looking for. If that’s the case, then harder isn’t necessarily better. Everybody lost fitness. This is the reality of being in your 70s. But the people who were doing high-intensity training (HIT) lost less fitness than those doing moderate intensity (MIT). Here’s the data for the men, showing an initial increase in VO2 max after one year of exercise followed by a decline after three years and a bigger decline after five years. You can see that the high-intensity group (black bars) gets a bigger initial boost in VO2 max, and then hangs onto their advantage even as both groups gradually lose fitness. After five years, the high-intensity group is 3.1 percent lower than baseline, and the medium-intensity group is 7.7 percent lower. And here’s the comparable data for women, who managed to hang on to slightly more of their fitness than the men. In this case, the high-intensity group is actually back to baseline after five years, with no net loss of fitness, while the medium-intensity group is 4.6 percent lower. This is not, I should emphasize, any sort of grand refutation of the theory of zone 2. We don’t know what zone either of the two groups was in; it’s tricky to triangulate between perceived effort and heart rate and metabolic zones. But it’s a reaffirmation of the idea that, all else being equal and within reasonable limits, harder exercise produces greater fitness gains. This might seem obvious, but it bears repeating. I actually think the zone 2 framework is a pretty good one. Among both novice exercisers and people who should know better, pushing too hard on supposedly easy days is a very common sin. Any advice that helps people rein that tendency in can be useful. But the underlying logic, to me, isn’t about the metabolic magic of easier training, and it’s definitely not a shortcut to fitness: it’s about holding back so that you can do more or push harder on another day. For more Sweat Science, sign up for the email newsletter and check out my new book The Explorer’s Gene: Why We Seek Big Challenges, New Flavors, and the Blank Spots on the Map.

item.title: Will Soper Ran 1.5 Miles 1,000 Feet up a Mountain to Deliver Blood to a Fallen Climber
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.88
Will Soper, 28, is an EMT and technical rescuer with Burke Rescue Inc. and SAR (Photo: Courtesy of Will Soper) A North Carolina climber was leading an ascent with his son on Shortoff Mountain, a rugged, remote wall in Linville Gorge, on August 30, when he fell 20 feet. Jacob Gregory, the climber, slammed into a rock and suffered a critical injury. He needed a blood transfusion to save his life. So, Will Soper ran, literally, to the rescue. Soper, 28, is an EMT and technical rescuer with Burke Rescue Inc. and SAR, a volunteer lifesaving unit serving central North Carolina. In just 31 minutes, Soper ran 1.5 miles through the gorge, gaining roughly 1,000 feet in elevation—all while carrying a bag of blood needed to stabilize the climber. “My goal was simple: get the blood from the parking lot to the top of the rappel,” Soper told Outside. When the accident was called in, Soper was teaching a training with Ashe County Rescue Squad, another SAR outfit about two hours away. He quickly packed his gear and hopped in the car, knowing that the rescue would require an all-hands-on-deck approach. First responders called in 24 agencies for assistance, including the North Carolina National Guard, which sent in a Black Hawk helicopter. “The rescue occurred in a notoriously remote and challenging place to access,” Soper told Outside. “As soon as I heard the dispatch, I knew it would be a challenging rescue.” By the time Soper arrived at the trailhead, a first wave of rescuers had reached the patient. His condition deteriorated, and paramedics evaluating his vital signs on the scene radioed that the patient suffered internal bleeding and needed blood—quickly. “When I was about halfway up the mountain I heard Incident Command requesting me: ‘800 to Soper,’” Soper said. “I responded: ‘Go ahead, 800.’” Over the radio, a paramedic told Soper that he’d need to turn around and run back to the parking lot to get a bag of blood and items used for a transfusion. He knew the route well, and with more than a decade of rock and ice climbing experience, was fit enough to carry the gear over such a steep elevation gain. He made his way back down to the trailhead to pick up the blood bag, placed it in a cooler with extra cold packs to keep it viable, and ran everything up the mountain in a backpack. “Off I went,” he said. “In all honesty, ‘run’ is a little bit hyperbolic. I maintained a fast hiking or jogging pace and made sure I didn’t stop for any breaks.” Will stayed steady, ensuring not to overexert himself or, worse, make a small slip and hurt himself in the process. He reached the summit of the mountain, and then scrambled down a gully to where the climber was located “This was the most treacherous part as I was tired and it is the steepest, slickest section,” he said. “I quickly reached the rappel station and handed off my backpack, with all of the supplies, to my colleague, Robert Vasile, who was waiting with harness and helmet on and ready to rappel. He made the descent smoothly and quickly before delivering the pack to the Paramedics.” Shortoff Mountain is notorious for its steep, rocky summit trail that is mostly unprotected from the sun, Soper said. The rescue took place at the bottom of one route, which is 2,800 feet high and requires a 200-foot scramble. “At the bottom of the gully is what climbers call the ‘rappel station,’ which has fixed anchors located on top of an 80-foot cliff,” Soper said. “Once you rappel down, you can access the bottom of the climbing routes. Although it is not the most populated climbing area, it is one of the most common areas for climber rescues.” As Soper ran, other rescuers worked their way down the mountain, establishing technical rope systems to reach and treat the patient. They transported the victim to Atrium Carolinas Medical Center in Charlotte. Gregory suffered multiple serious injuries and underwent emergency surgery on August 31, his family wrote on a GoFundMe page. “It is far too early to know what the coming weeks, months and possibly years will look like. His recovery will be long, and there are many unknowns ahead. What we do know is that Jacob has a tremendous amount to fight for,” they wrote of the independent contractor. “To every responder who answered that call: thank you. You saved a life and brought a husband, father, brother, son, friend and loved one to safety.” Such a rescue is another day on the job for Soper. “I am an ordinary person asked to do an extraordinary task,” he said. “Many people could have done this in a similar or faster time, so I urge them to consider this a call to action. If you read this and thought, I want to help, please contact your local rescue squad or search and rescue team.” The Burke County Search and Rescue was joined by search-and-rescue teams from surrounding counties, along with North Carolina Emergency Management, NC HART, Charlotte Fire Department, MedCenter Air and the North Carolina National Guard.

item.title: OpenAI Teases Astra, Limits Cybersecurity Tools After Hugging Face Hack
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 7.38
OpenAI is ready to talk more about its upcoming Astra model, although it has yet to share a launch date for its next advanced release. In a blog post, the ChatGPT-maker said it plans to “make Astra available soon.” According to OpenAI, Astra will be particularly effective at identifying flaws in security systems without human assistance, confirming it believes Astra meets its own “Critical cybersecurity capability threshold." OpenAI's definition of that benchmark says, “With the right tools and access, it can find previously unknown security flaws and develop ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step.” These advancements, paired with the fallout from the July Hugging Face attack, mean that OpenAI is taking security more seriously than ever, adding further safeguards before releasing a new model. It also plans to limit its most advanced cybersecurity features to select partners, though it hasn't revealed how it will do so. The Astra model wasn’t involved in the Hugging Face incident, but the fallout affected all of the brand's systems. In July, an advanced OpenAI model, working in tandem with GPT-5.6 Sol, broke containment of its sandbox by using a previously unknown zero-day vulnerability to access the internet. The models then targeted the AI platform Hugging Face, which hosts over 2 million public AI models and datasets, to help it obtain additional information. OpenAI says, “We have since implemented even stronger safeguards for Astra, including training the model to more reliably refuse harmful cyber requests and respect safety restrictions, additional protections against misuse, and monitoring that can stop potentially unauthorized activity.” Earlier this year, rival Anthropic delayed the launch of its Mythos model due to concerns about worldwide cybersecurity. The news was largely positive for Anthropic, showing how confident it was in its major AI advancements, and it's likely OpenAI feels similar about Astra's advances. OpenAI says it will allow a group of testers to trial its Astra tools first, but there's no word on a schedule or who it will trust those testers to be. OpenAI says, "We will continue to test these systems, share what we learn, and be clear about what remains uncertain. The models that follow Astra will demand more of us. We will take the time and do the work needed to meet that responsibility." Not everyone is convinced by OpenAI’s new precautions, though. Former employee Yona Shavit, who now works at the OpenAI Foundation, posited that if the models knew researchers were watching, it may be capable of lying through "explicit or implicit metagaming-reasoning." Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Apple Launches New iOS 27 Public and Developer Betas. Every New iPhone Feature, Plus How to Install It
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.21
Apple's iOS 27 public beta launched in July, but yesterday, the sixth version of the public beta and the eighth version of the developer beta landed. First unveiled at Apple's WWDC, iOS 27 will offer new features including an AI-powered Siri, a redesigned Screen Time app, more Liquid Glass customizations, and deeper Apple Intelligence integration. No new features were introduced in these betas; instead, they focused on refining performance and correcting existing bugs. The Aug. 31 updates are meant to ensure a more stable release come September 9, when the official iOS 27 update is expected to hit. The stable version of iOS 27 is expected soon after Apple's Fall event next week, but you can check out some of the iPhone's coolest features now with either the public beta or the developer beta. Like any beta software, we expect it to be a little buggier than the final release, and it could be a battery hog, so we recommend installing it on an extra device. Here's what's included in the latest versions of the iOS 27 beta, which phones are compatible, and how to sign up. How to Install the iOS 27 Public Beta on Your iPhone To test out the public beta version of iOS 27, you'll need to first sign up for the Apple Beta Software Program. Follow these steps: - Visit beta.apple.com - Sign in using the Apple Account you use on your iPhone - Once enrolled, open your iPhone. Go to Settings > General > Software Update. - Tap Beta Updates, then iOS 27 Public Beta If you want to test the iOS 27 public beta on your iPad, follow the same steps, but select the iPadOS 27 Public Beta instead. How to Install the New iOS 27 Developer Beta on Your iPhone If you want to join the developer beta for iOS 27, you need to register as an Apple developer. You can then access the beta by restarting your phone and navigating to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates. You should see the iOS 27 developer beta there. Note that the developer beta might not include every feature coming to iOS 27 just yet. What Features Are Included in the New iOS 27 Public Beta? The iOS 27 public beta includes every feature released so far across the three developer betas. You can test the long-awaited revamp of Siri, now called Siri AI. This virtual assistant is integrated across your phone, accessible via a dedicated Siri app, directly from the Dynamic Island, and seamlessly throughout the rest of the OS. The public beta also includes the new Liquid Glass customization options. You can also try our voice controls for Pace and Expressivity, which let you control how quickly or expressively Siri talks. Other features you can explore include Write with Siri, an Insights feature in Apple Wallet, updates to iPhone-to-Android RCS chats, and more. You may be limited in what you can test, depending on your device. Which Phones Can Install the iOS 27 Public Beta and Developer Betas? Though it may be trimming the number of Apple Watches that work with watchOS 27, Apple's list of compatible iPhones for iOS 27 goes all the way back to 2019's iPhone 11. That said, many features require Apple intelligence, which only works on the iPhone 15 Pro, 15 Pro Max, and up. - iPhone 11, Pro, Pro Max - iPhone SE (second gen and up) - iPhone 12, mini, Pro, Pro Max - iPhone 13, mini, Pro, Pro Max - iPhone 14, Plus, Pro, Pro Max - iPhone 15, Plus, Pro, Pro Max - iPhone 16, 16e, Plus, Pro, Pro Max - iPhone 17, 17e, Air, Pro, Pro Max About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: Flight Cancelled? United App Adds New Standby Options to Get You Moving Faster
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.07
The United Airlines app now offers a potential power-up for passengers dealing with an interrupted itinerary: the option to get an earlier flight than the departure they were rebooked on after a delay or cancellation. This new feature, announced Tuesday, lets customers add themselves to standby lists for up to three flights leaving earlier than a rebooked reservation. The airline will then send a text advising them when a seat opens up on one of those earlier options, allowing passengers to decide whether the time saved is worth a possible trade-off, such as losing a window seat or extra legroom, or if they should stick with Plan B. That is the sort of flexibility that you could traditionally only get by bringing your case to an airline representative with time to work the problem for you. Otherwise, you’re stuck with whatever flight was immediately available after your scheduled flight got scratched. (Literally as I type this, my brother is looking at a five-hour delay in Philadelphia as a result of a rebooking after an unexplained flight cancellation.) United’s press release says more than 85% of its passengers use its apps on their travel days. Once useful for not all that much more than watching streaming video in-flight and scanning in a passport before an international departure, the app has become a key part of the airline’s push to raise its tech altitude. United’s announcement notes such recent additions to the app as support for Apple Wallet’s digital ID option, sharing tracking info from an AirTag in a lost checked bag, estimates for wait times for TSA screening at its US hub airports, and tips for connections that include estimated walking times and notifications if the airline is holding a departure to let people with delayed arriving flights make that connection. Should none of your standby attempts for earlier flights pan out, United’s app offers one way to while away the time that Tuesday’s release doesn’t highlight: the simple Boeing 787 flight-simulator game that it added four years ago. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: Sunseeker S4 Wireless AI Robot Lawn Mower Review: High-Tech Trimming for Small Lawns
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.57
The Sunseeker S4 is a robot lawn mower designed for small yards up to .25 acres (10,890 square feet). It doesn’t require wires or antennas, and it creates a map of your lawn and avoid obstacles. Cutting and edging performance is first-rate, but battery life could be better, and it lacks certain features such as GPS and cellular radios. At $1,799.99, it is significantly more expensive than our Editors’ Choice winner for small- to medium-sized lawns, the $1,399 TerraMow V1000, which offers longer battery life, cellular and GPS radios, and a slightly wider cutting width. Designed for properties up to .25 acres, the S4 uses LiDAR technology and a camera to map and cut your lawn. As such, it doesn’t require any antennas or perimeter wires and is very easy to install and configure. If you have a larger lawn, the $2,699.99 Sunseeker X7 can handle up to 3 acres, but you'll need to install an RTK antenna for navigation. The S4 has an IPX6 weatherproof rating, measures 17 by 24 by 11 inches (HWD), and weighs 26 pounds. It’s a rear-wheel drive mower that uses two knobby-treaded wheels in the back and two swiveling caster-style wheels up front. The top of the mower holds a LiDAR dome, which powers Sunseeker’s AllSense 3D mapping and obstacle avoidance system. There's also a rain sensor, a big red Stop button, and a control panel that is hidden behind a pop-up cover. The control panel contains four buttons (Power, Start, Home, OK), a dial with settings ranging from 1.6 to 3.2 inches of cutting height, and a small monochrome LCD panel that displays menu options, error codes, and PIN numbers. The Power button turns the mower on and off, the Start button starts a work cycle, and the Home button returns the mower to the charging station. When navigating the menu system, you use the Start button to go up, the Home button to go down, and the OK button to select an option. There’s an AI camera on the front of the mower that works with the LiDAR sensor to detect and avoid obstacles. Below the camera are a pair of electrodes that connect with the charging station to charge the 4Ah lithium-ion battery pack. The battery provides only around 90 minutes of work time and takes 80 minutes to fully recharge, whereas the TerraMow V1000’s battery provides 150 minutes of work time and takes 120 minutes to fully recharge. The S4 does not come with a garage like the TerraMow V100, but you can buy one for $199.99. Additionally, it lacks GPS and cellular connectivity like the V1000, but it does have Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios and supports Alexa and Google voice assistants. The mower can work at night, but will not work in the rain. It supports auto and manual mapping and uses a six-blade cutting disk that provides a cutting width of 7 inches, slightly less than the TerraMow V1000, which offers an 8-inch cutting width. In comparison, the Ecovacs Goat A3000 ($2,999.99) provides a 12.99-inch cutting width, while the Mova Lidax Ultra 3000 AWD ($2,999) is an impressive 15.8 inches. The S4 can handle slopes of up to 42% (22 degrees) and has a sound output rating of 60dB. For comparison, the TerraMow V1000 can handle slopes of up to 32.5% and has a sound rating of 54dB. If your lawn has steep hills, you’ll need a more powerful mower like the Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000, which handles slopes of up to 80%. The mower can be controlled from your phone using the Sunseeker mobile app for iOS and Android devices. Tap the mower’s image on the home screen to view a map of your lawn and the current position of the mower. Below the map, you can see how much land the mower has covered during the week and the next scheduled start time. There’s a Start button near the bottom of the screen that, when pressed, lets you begin an unscheduled work cycle or resume a work cycle in progress. Below that are buttons to view a work log and create a work schedule. On the right side of the map screen are buttons to remotely steer the mower, edit the map, and view a textured map of your lawn. Use the map editing screen to create work zones, no-go zones, safe zones, and corridors that link one zone to another. Here you can also choose a pattern, such as a star, heart, circle, or digit, that the mower will cut into your lawn. Tap the circle in the upper-right corner to access the settings menu. Here you can create work schedules, edit maps, set individual parameters for multiple zones, select a mowing speed (slow, standard, fast), a cutting direction (default, traceless, multi-angle), and an edge-cutting distance (close, far). Other settings allow you to enable night mode, edit PIN codes, update the firmware, view work logs, and configure network settings. Preparing the S4 for its initial run is easy. I unboxed the mower and base station, plugged the base station into a nearby GFCI outlet, and slid the mower onto the charging dock, at which point the LED began flashing green, indicating that the mower was charging. I downloaded the mobile app, created an account, and tapped Add Device. I scanned the QR code on the back of the mower, selected the S4, and entered my Wi-Fi credentials when prompted to complete the pairing process. To create a work zone, I made sure the mower was docked and tapped Start Mapping. After completing a quick self-check, the mower exited the base station, and the app prompted me to guide the robot to a boundary using the remote steering feature. I tapped Auto Map, and the mower began scanning the perimeter of my lawn and creating an accurate map. With the main zone completed, I created two more zones for areas on the other side of my driveway and walkway, linked them to the main zone with two corridors, and my mapping was complete. The S4 did a great job of cutting my lawn and trimming the edges. It followed the boundaries without issue and provided a nice, even cut. That said, its battery life came up short. It took 83 minutes to complete 76% of the main lawn before it had to return to the base to charge. Once fully charged, it automatically left the base station and resumed where it left off. In comparison, the TerraMow V1000 needed 128 minutes to complete a full work cycle, but it did so on a single charge. The mower had no trouble dodging obstacles, which I purposely left lying on the lawn, including a shovel, a large rock, and a softball, and the rubber safety bumper worked as intended. It always adhered to my work schedules and never failed to return to its base when the work cycle was completed. Final Thoughts Sunseeker S4 Wireless AI Robot Lawn Mower - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. With the Sunseeker S4, you can have a beautifully landscaped lawn without having to push around a mower or pay for a professional landscaping service. It did an excellent job of cutting and trimming in my tests and was a snap to install, but at $1,799.99, I expect a few more features, such as cellular and GPS connectivity, as well as longer battery life. You’ll get all of that with the $1,399 TerraMow V1000, along with better battery life and a wider cutting width, so it remains our Editors' Choice winner. About Our Expert I’ve been working with computers for ages, starting with a multi-year stint in purchasing for a major IBM reseller in New York City before eventually landing at PCMag (back when it was still in print as PC Magazine). I spent more than 14 years on staff, most recently as the director of operations for PC Labs, before hitting the freelance circuit as a contributing editor.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro 'Surprise and Shine' Event Kicks Off Sept. 9. What We Expect to See
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.33
Apple is scheduled to host its next event on Wednesday, Sept. 9, where it will likely unveil the iPhone 18 Pro, its long-rumored foldable, and a next-gen Apple Watch. It will also mark the first Apple event with John Ternus as CEO after Tim Cook stepped down this week. "Surprise and shine," the invite reads. Things kick off at the Steve Jobs Theater in Cupertino at 10 a.m. PT. PCMag will be there to bring you all the news, but it will also be livestreamed. What can we expect? And how much more expensive will Apple's latest and greatest be, given the memory crunch? Apple already raised prices across several major product lines in June, while the new Mac mini and Mac Studio are pricier than their predecessors. Thus far, iPhone pricing has remained steady, helping drive iPhone 17 sales during the last quarter. However, "For September, we expect to pay even higher memory costs,” Cook said during a recent earnings call. With Apple's foldable expected to cost north of $2,000, the iPhone 18 Pro is probably the more economical choice if you're looking to upgrade this fall. To help you know what to expect, we've rounded up the biggest iPhone 18 Pro rumors we have heard so far. iPhone 18 Pro: Revised Lineup The biggest rumor around the iPhone 18 lineup is its release timeline. Unlike previous years, where Apple released four phones in the same series in one go, Bloomberg reports Apple could take a two-pronged approach to ensure consistent revenue throughout the year. Flagship phones, such as the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and the foldable iPhone, will be unveiled in September, while the base iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2, and the iPhone 18e could be launched in spring 2027. We discuss the foldable iPhone in detail in a separate rumor roundup, so we’ll just stick to the Pro models here. iPhone 18 Pro: Design and Colors The iPhone 17 Pro models brought a major overhaul to Apple’s smartphone design language, with a new camera “plateau” and two-toned color scheme. This year, Apple isn’t expected to drastically change the device's appearance, but it could add a few bold colors and return to a more uniform color scheme on the back. Several leakers, including Sonny Dickson and Instant Digital, claim that Apple could go with a never-before-seen cherry red and a new light blue, alongside the regular dark gray. Dickson also shared pictures of potential dummies, including one in light gray. In a fresh leak this week, Fixed Focus Digital backed dark cherry, sky blue, and dark gray colors for the new models, but noted that light gray or white/silver was highly unlikely. While the appearance of the rear is expected to remain the same, the in-hand feel could be a lot different. Ice Universe says the battery could get slightly larger on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, contributing to increased weight and bulk. More precisely, the leaker expects the device to be 0.25mm thicker and 7 grams heavier. iPhone 18 Pro Display On the front, we might see one significant change. The Dynamic Island, or the camera cutout, could be reduced by 35%, Ice Universe says. This won’t shrink the feature's overall functionality, but it could move the Face ID sensor’s illuminator to one corner below the screen. When it comes to display sizes, the consensus is that the iPhone 18 Pro will come in its usual 6.3-inch screen, while the Pro Max will have a 6.9-inch screen. Apple, however, has reportedly been pushing suppliers to provide much brighter displays and could use the more power-efficient LTPO+ display tech. iPhone 18 Pro Cameras The iPhone 17 Pro lineup bumped all three cameras to 48MP. For the iPhone 18 Pro, the biggest camera-related rumor we have heard is around variable aperture. While the iPhone 17 models had a fixed aperture, the iPhone 18 Pro may introduce a variable aperture. ETNews reports that the modified system has already entered production and would help the cameras deliver more light to the sensors in dark conditions and reduce light in bright conditions. Apple may also modify its relatively new Camera Control button. Introduced with the iPhone 16, the capacitive button at the bottom right of the phone lets you quickly launch the Camera app, take pictures, and adjust settings for zoom, exposure, depth, and other controls. Mastering the capacitive button, however, has proved difficult, with users noting that they have been accidentally launching the Camera app. Apple may finally fix the problem by removing the touch-sensitive components of the button and delivering a more user-friendly experience, 9to5Mac reports. iPhone 18 Pro Performance The iPhone 18 Pro is likely to receive a performance boost with the A20 chip. It will use TSMC’s 2nm technology, an upgrade from the previous generation’s 3nm tech. The transition will allow more transistors on each chip but also raise chip costs by 50%, MacRumors reports. The chip is also rumored to have TSMC’s Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module (WMCM) technology, which infuses RAM into the same wafer as the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. Overall, it is expected to be 18% faster and 30% more power-efficient than previous generations, according to leaker Fixed Focus Digital. Apple usually reserves the base variant of its chip series for the standard iPhone models, while the Pro models get the corresponding Pro chip. With the iPhone 18 series, Apple is reportedly considering offering just the high-end variant across the lineup. Another expected upgrade is for the modem. The iPhone 17 Pro models had an unspecified third-party modem, but the iPhone 18 Pro could get the company’s proprietary C2 modem. It will support 5G satellite connectivity and reduce the scope of location data retained by networks, according to MacRumors. iPhone 18 Pro Battery Apple never reveals its battery capacities, but multiple leakers have indicated a larger and more efficient battery for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. According to Digital Chat Station, the top variant will have a capacity of up to 5,200mAh, slightly better than the 5,088mAh capacity of its predecessor. With a more efficient modem and processor, the battery life could be significantly longer. The iPhone 18 Pro, on the other hand, could see a minimal bump from 4,252mAh to 4,288mAh. More recently, leaks posted on Korean and Chinese social media sites tip a US iPhone 18 Pro Max model with a 5,567mAh battery, a nearly 10% increase over the iPhone 17 Pro Max, MacRumors notes. iPhone 18 Pro: Pricing and Release This is what much of the decision-making hinges on. According to The Wall Street Journal's estimate, rising component costs would push the iPhone 18 Pro to start at $1,299. If you couple that with recent Apple trends, the iPhone 18 Pro Max could be priced $100 higher, taking its starting price to $1,399. In comparison, the iPhone 17 Pro starts at $1,099, while the 17 Pro Max starts at $1,199. When asked on a recent earnings call about potential price hikes for the iPhone, Cook said it's "too early to come to a definitive conclusion of what happens there. Because it takes a little while for the channels to adjust since there's channel inventory, it takes a while for the consumer to respond. We'll understand that more in the weeks ahead." With the event scheduled for Sept. 9, preorders will likely begin a few days later, ahead of the launch the following week. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: TP-Link Teases Wi-Fi 8 Router Preorders. Will FCC Ban Thwart a US Launch?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.32
TP-Link is at IFA in Berlin to debut its first consumer Wi-Fi 8 routers, dubbed the Archer and Deco, and while you can preorder them later this month, they won't actually arrive until 2027. And a US launch is far from certain, thanks to the FCC. TP-Link first teased the Archer 8 router in May, but today at Europe's biggest consumer electronics show, it provided more details about it and the rest of its upcoming Wi-Fi 8 lineup. The tri-band Archer 8 Ultra features 18 internal high-performance antennas that deliver up to 19Gbps of aggregate wireless speed and 10Gbps wired connectivity. The tri-band Deco 8 Ultra mesh system, meanwhile, can deliver up to 22Gbps of aggregate wireless speeds and 10Gbps wired connectivity. With a three-pack, TP-Link says it can support more than 200 connected devices across a home as large as 9,800 square feet. "Built on the upcoming IEEE 802.11bn standard, the growing lineup will pair Wi-Fi 8 chipsets from Broadcom, Qualcomm, and MediaTek with TP-Link's U.S.-led hardware and software engineering to deliver the most reliable Wi-Fi ever built," TP-Link says. The company also teased Wi-Fi 8 range extenders and adapters it expects to launch in Q2 2027. TP-Link will open preorders for the Archer 8 Ultra and Deco 8 Ultra on Sept. 30, ahead of an expected Archer 8 Ultra launch in Q1, followed by the Deco 8 Ultra in Q2 2027. Pricing wasn't announced, but we'll probably hear more at an online launch event scheduled for Sept. 30, too. That said, we might not see these devices in the US. TP-Link says preorders will open in "select regions," without elaborating. It currently faces an uncertain future in the US, thanks to the FCC's ban on foreign-made routers. Since TP-Link manufactures its products in Vietnam, it will need an exemption from the US agency to sell new routers in the US, which it has yet to secure. The ban doesn't affect existing devices or those that have already received FCC authorization. It's unclear if the Archer or Deco were submitted to the FCC for approval; we reached out to TP-Link for details and will update this story when we hear back. How Does Wi-Fi 8 Work? The announcement comes as Wi-Fi 7 is still picking up steam. And while TP-Link's first Wi-Fi 8 routers don't offer any major performance enhancements over Wi-Fi 7, they do promise more consistent performance and a greater ability to use available bandwidth through smarter management of the network and its connected devices. Using Dynamic Sub-band Operation (DSO), a router can "assign channels more precisely based on each device’s actual bandwidth," TP-Link notes. "This smarter channel frees up space for other traffic, reduces slowdowns, and improves performance across the entire network." If a channel gets too busy, it can dynamically open a second channel, thanks to its Non-Primary Channel Access (NPCA) technology. Advances in modulation reportedly improve reliability with Wi-Fi 8, with a particular focus on reducing interference from objects and other Wi-Fi networks. Enhanced Long Range and Distributed Resource Units features reportedly improve wireless performance at the edge of the network's range, so it doesn't drop off so dramatically once you're at the edge of coverage. The former works by extending the router's effective range, while the latter concentrates the device's signal into a narrower band, making it clearer even at long distances. At this point, few devices support Wi-Fi 8, but the technology is backward-compatible, so you'd get Wi-Fi 7 performance and features and then benefit from the advances of Wi-Fi 8 later. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program.
