He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Were You Inundated With X Password Reset Requests Today? You're Not Alone
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.18
UPDATE 9/2: US Attorney General Todd Blanche today attributed the password-reset spree to "sophisticated cybercriminals" who targeted hundreds of X accounts. "X disrupted the attack to prevent user accounts from being captured," Blanche tweeted. "We are working closely with X to track down the criminals behind this week’s attack. There is no refuge for those [who] perpetrate their criminal schemes from behind computer screens." Original Story 9/1: Did you wake up this morning to multiple password reset requests from X? Dozens of users took to the social network this morning to report receiving at least 10 emails around 9:30 a.m. ET. The messages, which appeared in the inboxes of at least one PCMag staffer, looked legit; they came from [email protected] and included the six-digit confirmation code required to complete a password reset. "If you didn't make this request, ignore this email," it said. Easier said than done. The messages sparked a wave of concerned posts on X from people worried they had been hacked or targeted by a phishing campaign. X Product Engineer Mridul Singhai said the company is "actively investigating the issue and, so far, [has] found no evidence of any breaches. We apologize for the multiple emails and appreciate your patience as we work to resolve this.” Singhai attributes the concerning emails to X Money, Musk’s payment platform for X Premium subscribers that became publicly available in July. "Attackers appear to believe that, now that @XMoney is widely available, they can gain unauthorized access to accounts." How to Secure Your X Account If you’ve received suspicious emails, don’t click on any links. Go directly to the X mobile or web app to check your account status. If you don't have secondary security set up on your account, do that ASAP, whether it's two-factor authentication (2FA) or a passkey. Also consider enabling Password reset protect via Settings > Security and account access > Security > Password reset protect. "If you check this box, you will be prompted to enter either your email address or phone number, or your email address, then phone number if both are associated with your account, to send a reset password link or confirmation code if you ever forget it," X says. The same Security page is also where you'd go to set up 2FA or a passkey. For 2FA, you can use an authenticator app or a security key. To receive codes via text messages, you'll need to be a Premium subscriber, but we don't recommend using SMS for 2FA codes anyway. For more on passkeys, check out our explainer. About Our Expert I’m a New York-based writer currently serving as PCMag’s Editorial Intern. I cover the impact of technology and internet culture on our daily lives, with a specialization in video games and cultural criticism. I have written for Kotaku, The A.V. Club, Unwinnable, Aftermath, and more. In addition, I have a formal background in video game development and visual design. You can find all of my work on my website.

item.title: Want to Help Fund an 80,000-Year Journey? Nonprofit Wants to Send Space Probe to Alpha Centauri
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.94
A team of entrepreneurs has created a nonprofit to send a spacecraft over four light-years away to Alpha Centauri, the nearest star system to Earth. The team announced the Fermi Explorer mission today; it's seeking donations to build, launch, and operate a space probe costing under $15 million that's also capable of interstellar travel. The project will be mainly led by executives at US startup Starcloud, which is also working to build a constellation of orbital data centers. Other advisors include former Blue Origin President Rob Meyerson and Jeff Thornburg, a former SpaceX executive. The plan is to send a craft carrying at least a 1-kilogram (2.2-pound) payload, such as sensors and scientific instruments, to the neighboring star system, which consists of three stars. The project is relatively small and modest compared with other space flights, but the larger goal is to inspire humanity and push it to colonize the stars. “The mission is intended to make the idea of interstellar travel real, and to encourage more people to confront one of humanity’s biggest unanswered questions when we look beyond our planet: ‘Where is everybody?’” tweeted Starcloud CEO Philip Johnston. The project tackles the Fermi Paradox, or why we’ve found no strong evidence for extraterrestrial civilizations, despite the high likelihood of their existence. “There is a concept called a Fermi Great Filter, which says that the Fermi Paradox is explained by the existence of a great filter that is extremely hard for life to pass through,” the nonprofit said, later adding: “After the Fermi Explorer mission, we will have more confidence both that it is possible for intelligent species to leave for their nearest star in a way that isn’t resource prohibitive, and that there are at least some species that try to do it (namely us!).” The mission will appeal to sci-fi and space travel fans. But if you donate, you won’t see an immediate return on your investment, since it’ll take up to 80,000 years for the space probe to reach Alpha Centauri. That's because we lack a sci-fi warp drive or hyperspace engine to easily traverse the stars; instead, the nonprofit plans to use solar-electric propulsion and possible "gravity assist" orbits from Earth or Jupiter to accelerate the craft and launch it toward Alpha Centauri. In an FAQ, the nonprofit also claims there’s only a 50% chance of success, which seems optimistic, given that the craft will need to remain functional over the eons. In addition, the nonprofit has published a video about its mission that subtly concedes that sending the probe to Alpha Centauri might be pointless. The video shows the probe arriving at the star, only to be greeted by a fleet of sci-fi spaceships created by future humans. Still, the nonprofit is hopeful the project will excite the public. The team wants to launch the probe before the end of 2029 and plans to outsource its manufacturing to a satellite maker through an open tender. "We already have one proposal from a US satellite bus manufacturer, that has completed more than 50 successful missions, for less than $15M to complete the mission," the nonprofit added. "The board members, program manager, and advisors of the Fermi Explorer Mission will make the selection over the coming months, and we will consider track record, price, and schedule in making the award." About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Claude vs. Gemini: Smarter Brains or Better Features?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.78
Table of Contents AI chatbots are now a mature technology with impressive performance across the board and a large variety of features, so you might struggle to decide on which to use. Even if you narrow it down to Claude and Gemini, you will still find some notable distinctions. For instance, Claude specializes in exceptional model intelligence, while Gemini provides seamless features across nearly every Google app. I’ve spent countless hours testing both chatbots, so I've compared them across key categories, such as deep research, value, and vibe coding, to help you pick the best one for your needs. Full Specs | Claude | Google Gemini | | |---|---|---| | Free Version | | | | Free Version | | | | AI Model | | | | AI Model | Fable 5, Haiku 4.5, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5 | 3.7 Flash and 3.1 Pro | | Cites Sources | | | | Cites Sources | | | | Ability to Browse Web | | | | Ability to Browse Web | | | | Can Resume Prior Conversations | | | | Can Resume Prior Conversations | | | | Image Generator | | | | Image Generator | | | Price: Gemini's Free Tier and $5 Plan Leave Claude in the Dust You can use both Claude and Gemini for free, or you can opt for a paid subscription. Free versions for both come with significant feature and usage limitations. However, you still get a lot more from Gemini for free, such as access to deep research, Google Drive storage, image generation, and video generation. Outside of deep research, which Claude offers on paid plans, Claude doesn’t support any of the other features above across its plans. Paid versions start at $17 per month (billed annually) for Claude and $5 per month for Gemini. Both have plans that cost $200 per month; these unlock higher usage limits and more features, such as access to Claude Design or Google’s Antigravity coding app. The right plan for you depends on what you plan to do, but Gemini's base paid tier is far more affordable. And, as mentioned, Gemini’s plans also come with varying amounts of cloud storage, which can justify the subscription cost on its own. Winner: Gemini Platforms and User Experience: Claude’s Browser Ecosystem vs. Deep Google Integrations You can use Claude and Gemini on the web or via their desktop apps (macOS and Windows) and mobile apps (Android and iOS). Claude’s coding capabilities are a part of its desktop app, while Gemini maintains the separate Antigravity app. Claude has a Chrome extension for AI agent and assistant features in your browser, while Google integrates Gemini directly into Chrome. Of course, Google pushes Gemini in its Chromebook Plus lineup and presumably will do the same with Google Books. Anthropic doesn't provide any type of similar hardware integration. Claude’s and Gemini’s models are accessible across various online services, with Claude available on Perplexity and Gemini via Google’s partnership with Apple. You can also access Gemini across Google apps, such as Calendar, Docs, Drive, Gmail, Maps, Notebook, Keep, Photos, Sheets, and YouTube Music. However, I recommend sticking to their official apps and websites to access most of their features. The interfaces of Claude and Gemini are generally consistent and straightforward across platforms. Minor differences exist depending on the feature in question, but you can expect central text fields with sidebar menus on both. You can give both instructions to follow when chatting, but neither supports ChatGPT’s level of personality and tone customization. Winner: Tie AI Models: Claude's Four Intelligence Tiers vs. Gemini's Flash and Pro Claude’s lineup of AI models has four primary entries: Fable, Haiku, Opus, and Sonnet. Fable is Claude’s flagship model, and Anthropic says it's capable of the toughest challenges you have. However, expect to pay a hefty usage price to access it. Claude’s complex reasoning model, Opus, matches or surpasses Fable 5 in most areas and is much more efficient. Sonnet is Claude’s balanced, midrange model, whereas Haiku is Claude’s fastest, lightweight model, ideal for simpler tasks. It's possible to change the intelligence level of each Claude model. Gemini has Flash and Pro models. Flash is fast and suitable for daily use across most tasks, while Pro is Gemini’s complex reasoning model for tougher prompts. You can’t adjust the intelligence of Gemini’s models outside of its Antigravity app, though you can enable extended thinking. The latest model from Claude is Opus 5, while Gemini’s most recent is 3.7 Flash. Gemini also features image- and video-generation models, including Nano Banana, Nano Banana Pro, Omni, and Veo. Winner: Tie Web Search: Claude Goes Deeper With Prompts Both Claude and Gemini can search the web without issue and adequately source their findings. However, if you use Claude’s most capable models, especially at their highest intelligence settings, you can get better answers than what’s possible with Gemini’s 3.1 Pro model, even with extended thinking enabled. For example, I asked both bots about the current meta for The Finals, and Gemini’s answer lacked important details that Claude's included. Gemini has a dedicated shopping interface, complete with clickable tiles that make it easy to see product information and quickly open links to retailers. It also has a unique feature that lets you visualize how clothes will look on you. However, it doesn’t tell you anything about fit. Claude doesn’t have any meaningful shopping features. Nonetheless, I don’t recommend using AI as your only source of information when deciding what to buy. Winner: Claude Deep Research: Gemini’s Reports Are More Accessible and Detailed You can generate well-sourced reports on any topic with both Claude and Gemini. However, the quality of Gemini’s reports usually outshines Claude’s. For example, while troubleshooting a stuttering issue with my multi-monitor setup, Gemini’s report included helpful equations, tables, and a clear conclusion with steps to take. Claude’s report, on the other hand, was a lengthy block of text that concluded with a list of caveats and questions. Both interfaces have their strengths. Gemini lets me export reports to Google Docs with a single click and displays them in a large central window. Claude relegates reports to a sidebar for comparison. However, Claude provides a clearer visualization of its sources, making it easier to see how many pages from a particular site it accessed during the research. Claude doesn’t list the sources it ultimately cites, unlike Gemini. Winner: Gemini Image Editing and Generation: Claude Doesn’t Support Either Gemini’s AI image generation (and AI image editing) capabilities are top-notch, courtesy of its excellent Nano Banana series of models. Whether you want to make complicated diagrams, narrative-focused comics, or render scenes of any kind, Gemini can handle just about anything with minimal errors and distortion. Just keep in mind that editing images with Gemini can introduce some blurriness. Claude doesn’t support AI image editing or generation. However, you can make HTML-based visualizations with it. Below are some sample images I generated with Gemini’s Nano Banana Pro model: Winner: Gemini Video Generation: Gemini Wins by Default Video generation is another strength of Gemini, thanks to its best-in-class Omni and Veo models. Not only is Gemini capable of generating realistic video with audio, but you can also create videos from images or prompts. It's possible to extend clips with AI or even tap into some movie magic with Google’s AI filmmaking Flow tool. Since OpenAI killed Sora, Gemini and Grok are the only mainstream AI chatbots that support video generation, including Claude. Below is my favorite video clip generated with Gemini, courtesy of its Veo model: Winner: Gemini File Processing: Claude Identifies Fine Details That Gemini Misses In general, file processing doesn’t cause either chatbot to break a sweat. Both have large context windows, which is great for chewing through larger files, such as manuals or textbooks. Of course, that doesn’t mean Claude and Gemini will always answer every question about documents correctly, so make sure to verify anything critical. Although Gemini can understand images reasonably well, Claude’s image recognition is often more capable. For example, I presented both with an image of my computer's internals and a request to identify as many components as possible. Claude provided more specifics, such as correctly identifying my case and watercooling pump. Gemini’s identifications were far more vague. Winner: Claude Creative Writing: Both Deliver Competent But Cliche-Prone Writing Creative writing is a fairly trivial task for modern chatbots. From speeches to poems, you can prompt Claude and Gemini for pretty much any kind of writing. Just keep in mind that AI writing tends to have a distinct feel due to repetitive phrasings, topics, and word choices. For example, I asked Claude and Gemini for poems, and both focused on imagery seen during a walk: Winner: Tie Complex Reasoning: Claude’s Models Are Clearly Smarter Claude and Gemini can help with homework, whether you’re in high school or tackling a graduate-level course. Just don't assume they give you the correct answer every time. However, even Gemini’s Pro model with extended thinking enabled can't quite match Claude’s top models at their highest intelligence settings. For example, even with a relatively simple query about when Nioh 3’s final DLC will launch, Claude’s complex reasoning models gave a better answer. It included helpful details, such as the earlier-than-expected release of the first DLC, which Gemini didn't. You might not notice such a big difference with every prompt, though. Winner: Claude Coding: Gemini Just Isn’t a Great Coding Tool The AI coding market is fiercely competitive, with great options for both super-intelligent models and incredibly efficient ones. Gemini doesn’t stand out. It's impressively fast, but its intelligence pales in comparison to that of Claude’s models, such as Opus 5. Without careful prompt calibration, Gemini can and will mess up simple tasks that Claude handles easily. Although you might be able to incorporate Gemini into your workflows in some ways, Claude is a better choice for any hobbyist vibe coding projects. Winner: Claude Integrations: Gemini’s First-Party Support Is Peerless Claude supports a ton of integrations with a range of apps for both consumers and professionals, from Google Drive to Monday. The usefulness of these integrations depends on the apps you use and the available features, but they mostly just give you more ways to prompt Claude. For example, you can connect your Gmail and then ask Claude to tell you about your unread emails, among other things. Google embeds Gemini directly within Google apps. So, while you can open up Claude and ask it questions about your email, you could simply open up Gmail and prompt Gemini from the sidebar. This goes beyond email insights into upgrading your YouTube watching experience and much more. Furthermore, Gemini’s Personal Intelligence feature spans Google’s apps, allowing it to dynamically reference whatever information it needs to answer prompts. Claude doesn't offer anything similar. Winner: Gemini Agents: Claude Has No Answer for Gemini Spark Gemini Spark is my favorite AI agent, thanks to its generally competent performance, fast speeds, and impressive leverage of Personal Intelligence. For example, you can task Spark with finding you jobs, and it will automatically pull the resume you sent from your Gmail to match you with gigs that fit your experience. Claude doesn’t have an AI agent that competes with Spark in a meaningful way, and ChatGPT recently killed off its agent, so Gemini is one of the only chatbots worth using if you need regular AI agent access. Winner: Gemini Context Windows and Usage Caps: 1,000,000 Tokens on Both Claude and Gemini both have up to 1,000,000-token context windows, which is about as large as I've seen. This means both perform well when ingesting complex codebases, large documents, or anything else that might benefit from ample context. Both Claude and Gemini have five-hour and weekly usage limits that depend on your particular plan, but if you aren’t coding, you won’t have to pay much attention to those. Free users are likely to run into usage caps even if they aren't coding, however. For coders, Claude and Gemini (like other AI chatbots) may require more expensive plans, as usage can disappear quickly on both, depending on the task at hand. Winner: Tie Privacy: Neither Cares About Keeping You Safe Claude and Gemini collect a wide variety of data, and both use it to train their models by default. However, you can turn training off, and Google doesn’t use Workspace data for training by default, at least. Gemini feels particularly invasive with features like Personal Intelligence, though the functionality is unique. Neither chatbot has a history free of hacks or leaks, so I don't consider either of them especially reliable for safeguarding user data. You shouldn't share anything too sensitive with any AI chatbot. Winner: Tie And The Winner Is... Claude Both Claude and Gemini are impressive chatbots, but Claude wins this comparison because it excels in the area I consider most important: model intelligence. That makes it superior for everything from complex reasoning tasks to file processing to vibe coding. I’m much less interested in generating AI images and videos (which you can do to a limited extent for free with Gemini). However, if you care about media generation, frequently use Google apps, or want the best value in AI chatbots, Gemini is easy to recommend.

item.title: Roku Is Making OLED TVs Now, and I'm Here for It
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.68
Roku just unveiled new Pro Series OLED TVs, its first to use OLED panel technology instead of LED-backlit LCD. I can't say whether they're actually good TVs until I get them into the lab for testing, but this news is promising for a few reasons that go beyond the TVs themselves. The Roku Pro Series OLED TVs are available in two tiers: the standard Pro Series OLED and the higher-end Pro Series LX OLED. They both sit above the Editors' Choice Roku Pro Series Mini-LED in price and status, with the LX OLED as Roku's newest flagship TV. The Pro Series is available now, starts at $999 for a 55-inch screen, features a 120Hz panel, and includes an enhanced Roku Voice Remote with backlit buttons and remote finder. The Pro Series LX begins shipping in October, starts at $1,299 for 55 inches, has a brighter panel with a 144Hz refresh rate, and comes with a Roku Voice Remote Pro with hands-free voice control and a rechargeable battery. Potentially Premium Performance for the Price OLED technology is generally superior to LED TVs, offering per-pixel control of light output for excellent contrast, without the light bloom that comes with mini-LED TVs with backlight zones that can brighten or dim, or the awful black levels of LED backlights with no local dimming at all. They also tend to show excellent color that's wide and accurate, and as a bonus, they can be made extremely thin because they don't require a separate backlight system like LED TVs do. These benefits come with two trade-offs. First, OLED TVs are almost always more expensive than LED TVs—even most high-end mini-LED TVs. Second, OLED panels generally can't get as bright as their LED-lit counterparts. Roku clearly addresses OLED pricing with its new models. At $1,000, the Pro Series OLED is $600 less than the 55-inch version of the Editors' Choice LG Evo C6, and $300 less than its usual $1,300 price. It's also $300 less than the step-down LG B6E OLED TV, which I haven't tested. Even the higher-end OLED LX model only costs as much as the discounted Evo C6. For OLEDs, that's dirt-cheap. As for brightness, don't expect miracles. You get what you pay for, and based on the price of both Roku OLED TVs, I suspect the standard and LX models will perform similarly to the LG B6 and C6, respectively. Again, I haven't measured the B6's light output, but the C6 passes the 1,000-nit threshold (with an HDR10 signal and an 18% white window, hitting over 1,500 nits at 10%). That means it really does high dynamic range (HDR) content justice, and it's why it earned our Editors' Choice, along with most of LG's C-series of OLED TVs. If the LX can hit similar numbers for a similar price, that's stellar. Even if the regular Roku OLED and LG B6 can consistently reach 700 nits at 18%, I'd say that's pretty good for a "budget" OLED. To put those numbers into context, the single OLED TV Vizio released, 2020's OLED-H1, put out just over 500 nits with a 10% window. That's unacceptably dim now, but I still awarded it an Editors' Choice because at $1,300 for 55 inches, it was by far the most affordable OLED I'd ever tested. On the other end, the top-of-the-line Editors' Choice Samsung S95H and LG Evo G6 blast out over 1,500 nits with an 18% field and more than 2,200 nits with a 10% field, competing with many high-end LED TVs in brightness. But you won't find either of them for less than $2,000 for 55 inches, and close to $3,000 for 65 inches. Flagship price and performance are very much on a spectrum, depending on the brand. Seeing more OLED TVs at lower prices is good news, because unless the manufacturer somehow completely botches their implementation, it's reasonable to expect they'll meet at least a modest performance floor. Unlike cheap LED TVs, I've never seen an OLED TV I would consider "bad." Of course, that doesn't mean Roku's OLEDs are good, but I'm looking forward to finding out with my extensive tests in the lab Making OLEDs More Accessible Among all the smart TV platforms out there, I recommend Roku OS the most to older users and anyone who isn't tech-savvy. Even with recent changes that add more algorithmic recommendations to its top-level screens, it's by far the easiest to use and least intrusive TV interface. It doesn't push a huge, multi-section home screen filled with different flavors of recommendations and ads aggregated across multiple services into your face. When you press the Home button, it shows a few suggestions and otherwise provides a simple list of tiles to access the service you want. It doesn't try to bundle everything together into a mish-mash of feeds or turn your TV into an AI hub. Is it technically less advanced, from a features perspective? Sure. But it's simple, and that's really appealing if you aren't the most tech-headed person. There aren't many good options for OLED TVs with Roku. Philips apparently makes a model, but I haven't gotten a look at it. LG and Samsung make excellent OLEDs, but their respective webOS and Tizen OS platforms are less than intuitive (Samsung's platform, especially, which I note in every review of its otherwise technically very impressive TVs). Sony makes OLED TVs like the Bravia 8 II that use Google TV, and Panasonic uses Amazon's Fire TV operating system for its excellent Z95B OLED (currently unavailable but will return to shelves sometime this fall). But they're also pretty visually crowded and place a heavy emphasis on their AI assistants, Gemini and Alexa. As the first first-party OLEDs to use Roku OS, the Pro Series OLED and Pro Series OLED LX could be great ways to offer OLED performance to people who don't want to have conversations with their TV and dive through multiple screens to watch what they want. It's Not RGB LED The newest trend in high-end TVs isn't OLED, but RGB LED, a technology I once thought could be the future of premium TVs, but have become very skeptical about. They're like regular LED TVs, using an LCD panel with an array of LEDs to light it, but instead of just white (or blue, for QLED) lights, they use clusters of red, green, and blue LEDs that can individually brighten or dim each color to push the range of color of the TV further than what the panel alone can show. On paper, it's brilliant, which is why Hisense, Samsung, Sony, and virtually all other major TV makers have launched RGB LED TVs as their top-of-the-line models. When I heard that Roku was stepping into a new TV category separate from its standard LED TVs, I feared it was next. Every RGB LED TV I've tested, including the Hisense UR9, the Samsung R95H, and the Sony Bravia 9 II, has shown some significant flaws that might be fundamental to the technology itself. They show incredibly wide color gamuts in testing because those numbers are measured by analyzing light from large, flat fields of color, which lets their RGB LEDs go all out in boosting those hues. When showing complex video with many different colors, though, the LEDs can't be pushed to those extremes without risking screen-tinting color bleed, so they effectively look much less vibrant than the tests would indicate for most content. RGB LED TVs also universally have significant light bloom and poor off-angle viewing, showing large hazy clouds where very dark parts of the picture meet very bright parts when you slightly move away from the center of the screen. These are problems with every RGB LED TV, and they're completely absent on OLEDs. Oh, and did I mention that RGB LED TVs are almost always very expensive? The Sony Bravia 9 II has the best effective color performance with video, but even it pales next to OLED or very good QLED TVs like the TCL QM8L, and it's $3,599 for 65 inches, its smallest option. The tech might overcome its problems in the future, but I don't see it happening quickly, which means that, in choosing OLED over RGB LED, Roku dodged a bullet. The Review's Coming! Despite my optimism about a new company rolling out a new line of OLED TVs, we won't really know how the Roku Pro Series OLED and Pro Series OLED LX perform until I get them in the lab, so keep an eye on PCMag for reviews in the coming weeks. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s home theater and AR/VR expert, and your go-to source of information and recommendations for game consoles and accessories, smart displays, smart glasses, smart speakers, soundbars, TVs, and VR headsets. I’m an ISF-certified TV calibrator and THX-certified home theater technician, I've served as a CES Innovation Awards judge, and while Bandai hasn’t officially certified me, I’m also proficient at building Gundam plastic models up to MG-class. I also enjoy genre fiction writing, and my urban fantasy novel, Alex Norton, Paranormal Technical Support, is currently available on Amazon.

item.title: Apple TV Review: A Pricey and Limited Streamer With Some Gems
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.56
Years after debuting in a crowded video streaming market, Apple TV has found its niche by prioritizing quality over quantity. Just as Apple makes premium hardware and software, Apple TV offers premium original entertainment, including acclaimed shows, Oscar-winning films, and sophisticated sports offerings. Apple TV also has impressive premium features: Subscribers can stream shows in 4K, download content for offline viewing on iOS, and enjoy ad-free viewing. Still, its library is far more limited than you'd expect from an industry heavyweight, a problem that has become more noticeable as the service has grown more expensive. Editors' Choice winners Hulu, Netflix, and Peacock offer far more variety with their paid subscriptions. After its most recent price increase, Apple TV—not to be confused with the Apple TV 4K media hub—now costs $14.99 per month (you can save money by signing up for an annual subscription at $119.99). Apple offers a seven-day trial, but you must provide a payment method. Purchasers of new Apple devices get a year of free access. See our story on how to cancel your Apple TV subscription for detailed info on the cancellation process. You can also get Apple TV through one of several Apple One subscription bundles. The Individual plan includes Apple Arcade, Apple Music, Apple TV, and 50GB of iCloud storage for $21.95 per month. The $27.95-per-month Family tier boosts the iCloud storage to 200GB, and you can share the service with up to six family members. The $39.95-per-month Premier option has Apple Fitness+, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud storage. Other video streaming services offer bundles, too. For example, you can pay $21.99 per month to get ESPN Select and the ad-supported versions of Disney+ and Hulu. Apple TV is now more expensive than many other top streaming services. Peacock starts at $8.99 per month, and Netflix starts at $8.99 per month. However, those are for the ad-supported tiers. Apple TV lacks commercials. Hulu and HBO Max's ad-supported plans are less expensive than Apple's, at $11.99 and $10.99 per month, respectively. If you don't want to pay anything for your entertainment, our roundup of the best free video streaming services has options worth checking out. Our top free pick, Tubi, includes popular and offbeat network shows and movies. For a rundown on how to get started with the service, see how to get and use Apple TV. In addition to hosting Apple TV originals, the app lets you subscribe to other services, which it designates as channels. These include on-demand services, such as Hulu, Paramount+, and Prime Video, as well as DirecTV Stream and other live TV services. You can also rent and buy movies and shows from the app. Note that Apple TV channels are not the same as subscribing to the services directly; if you subscribe to them via Apple TV, you can only watch them on devices that support the Apple TV app. You can subscribe to Apple TV on iPhones, iPads, and Macs, as well as via tv.apple.com in your web browser. Support extends to select LG, Samsung, and Sony smart TVs, as well as media streaming devices that support the Apple TV app, such as Roku units. Apple now offers Apple TV apps for video game consoles and Android devices. Apple TV's original catalog includes Central Park, an animated musical series about a family who lives in the famous park; Little Voice, a romantic comedy; Mythic Quest, a video game-themed workplace comedy; Tehran, a co-produced spy-thriller revolving around the Israeli-Iranian conflict; Tiny World, a nature documentary series; and real-life tech drama WeCrashed. Apple promises new shows every month and new episodes every week. However, the total number of exclusive titles (shows and movies) is approximately 300. Netflix, on the other hand, has thousands of originals. You won't find fan favorites from broadcast networks or older shows to bolster Apple TV's offerings. Disney+, on the other hand, debuted with a staggering number of shows and movies from its vast catalog and a trove of 21st Century Fox content, in addition to the promise of new originals, such as Daredevil: Born Again. None of the other services we've reviewed depend entirely on brand-new original shows. HBO Max, Netflix, and Prime Video are the current leaders in producing original content. Among Amazon Prime's most notable shows are The Boys, Invincible, and Undone. HBO Max is highly regarded for its original shows, both past and present, including Game of Thrones, Lanterns, and The Wire. Netflix's blockbuster originals include Ozark, Squid Game, and Tiger King. All these services also offer non-original shows and movies. There's a clear value in the third-party content that pads out the vast catalogs of services like Hulu and Prime Video. Apple certainly has the resources to build up its library, but you should weigh the show and movie reviews before subscribing. For what it's worth, though, Apple TV originals like Ted Lasso and Severance have become acclaimed hits and genuine parts of current pop culture. Apple TV's library includes several documentaries and feature-length films, such as Beastie Boys Story, a documentary about the band directed by Spike Jonze; Greyhound, a WWII thriller starring Tom Hanks; and the comedy On The Rocks, which stars Bill Murray, Rashida Jones, and Marlon Wayans. Coda was the first streaming-funded film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture. Cinephiles should check out our roundup of the best movie streaming services for a more comprehensive selection. Look to The Criterion Channel, Filmatique, Mubi, or Ovid for good selections of classic and independent films. The service also offers sports. With Apple TV, you can stream F1 and Friday night MLB games, which are included with your existing subscription. Multiview lets you watch multiple live games at once on Apple TV devices. I tested Apple TV on an iPhone. Apple TV's interface is clear and easy to navigate, with buttons for Watch Now, Library, and Search at the bottom. In the app, Apple Originals live in your Watch Now and Library tabs alongside HBO, Showtime, and Starz content. Note that you can't sort shows by network unless you are a subscriber. Tapping the standard cloud-plus-down-arrow icon next to an episode listing lets you download a show for offline viewing. Downloading a show may take several minutes, given the large file sizes. I watched an episode of The Morning Show over Wi-Fi, and the stream was generally sharp. I didn't like that you had to back out of the playback screen to the show listing to play the next episode. Note that Apple TV integrates with iOS's built-in parental control options, which makes things simple. Although Apple's marketing primarily highlights the Apple TV streaming service on devices that support the Apple TV app, you can still sign up for the service and watch shows in a web browser. In testing, Apple TV's web interface seems less polished than the Apple TV app. For instance, you can browse and watch only Apple TV content—none of the other services that you can subscribe to via the Apple TV app appear here. The Apple TV website is elegant, but, like many of the service's shows, the experience is only surface-deep. All the shows appear in a wide list. Selecting a show brings you to a description page with the show's available episodes, cast information, and other Apple TV recommendations. You can also search for shows and add them to your Up Next list. Want to access account settings? Click the profile icon in the upper-right corner of the screen to view your billing information and change your subscription. Likewise, you can set up parental control restrictions, but note that these limitations are not profile-based; whatever settings you choose apply to everyone using that account on the web. I watched several episodes from The Morning Show, See, and For All Mankind in Chrome and Edge on a 1080p monitor, and the shows looked and sounded excellent. Playback controls are standard, with a draggable progress bar, forward and rewind buttons, a volume slider, and accessibility options in the lower-right corner. Apple TV offers many languages and closed-caption options, too. In addition, you can tweak the size and position of the text on the screen to make it more readable or fire up clearly labeled audio descriptions. Apple TV's technical features are impressive. As noted, subscribers can download content for offline viewing on iOS devices via the Apple TV app. HBO Max, Netflix, Prime Video, and Showtime also offer offline viewing. Hulu only offers this capability to subscribers of its premium ad-free tier. Apple TV users can share a subscription and stream with up to six people via Apple's Family Sharing feature. Apple says that Originals are "subtitled and/or dubbed in nearly 40 languages, including Subtitles for the Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (SDH) or closed captions," and that they support audio descriptions in eight languages. Netflix and Prime Video also support Audio Descriptions. This accessibility feature adds vocal narration to scenes to explain character movements, settings, and other on-screen actions that are not discernible from character dialogue. These accessibility options outclass those found in competitors. 4K streaming, HDR, Dolby Atmos, and Dolby Vision support round out the list of Apple TV's tech specs. Only select devices, such as the Apple TV 4K, support all these capabilities. Netflix and Prime Video offer some original shows in 4K, with sporadic support for Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision. Since most launch shows support these high-end standards, the service, combined with the Apple TV 4K, could be very attractive to home theater enthusiasts. You should use a VPN to protect your internet traffic from nosy ISPs and malicious actors on a network. Many video streaming services block VPN traffic because a VPN can also let you spoof your location and potentially access location-restricted content. Apple plans to offer Apple TV in over 100 countries with the same content, so that shouldn't be an issue. I streamed content from Apple TV via the web with a desktop connected to a US-based Mullvad VPN server. Even if you do find a VPN that works with your video streaming service, you might eventually get blocked, as video streaming services actively work to block VPN connections. I recommend selecting a VPN based on additional factors, such as its privacy policy, performance, and features. Final Thoughts Apple TV - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Apple TV competes with the front-runners in the video streaming category based on technical features alone. However, its catalog isn't quite intriguing enough to draw interest away from other services. Its high price makes it a tough sell, too, and I'd like to see improvements to its interface and support for more devices. For now, I suggest holding off on Apple TV unless it offers a wide range of shows you enjoy. Hulu, Netflix, and Peacock remain our Editors' Choice winners for on-demand video streaming thanks to their larger libraries and greater platform support. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert My PCMag career began in 2013 as an intern. Now, I'm a senior writer, using the skills I acquired at Northwestern University to write about dating apps, meal kits, programming software, website builders, video streaming services, and video games. I was previously a senior editor at Geek.com and have written for The A.V. Club, Kotaku, and Paste Magazine. I'm the author of the gaming history book Video Game of the Year: A Year-by-Year Guide to the Best, Boldest, and Most Bizarre Games from Every Year Since 1977, and the reason everything you know about Street Sharks is a lie.
