All products compatible with the current Sonos app can be controlled with Sonos 27mcp, and everything with a microphone works with Sonos 27voice. When the Sonos custom agents are available, they’ll work everywhere Sonos 27voice is enabled. There are two new features being added to Sonos Fabric, which is the name given to its whole-home connected system. The wireless Play and Move 2 portable speakers can be used as surround sound speakers in a home theater system. Once in place, the speakers will automatically configure to their new positions and roles as surround speakers without needing to initiate setup in the Sonos app. It’s not possible to use this feature with a single Play or Move 2. Compatible Sonos headphones will now be included in a Sonos home system and support moving sound between speakers and headphones — the system senses the closest speaker and will pass the audio from it to the headphones. Headphone linking, as Sonos calls it, will roll out as an early access feature on September 29th. Sonos hints that this is just the beginning of added features, but no further details about possible future options were given. Improvements continue to come to the app, as well, again with feedback from the community, including the Sonos subreddit. Home, system, and search tabs will be added across the bottom of the screen, and a room sort option can be pinned to the top for easier access to a customizable list. There’s a cool feature that calls back to physical audio components: a virtual volume knob, you control with two fingers like you would in the real world. It’s not a major quality of life improvement, but it’s something that adds character and fun, and something I’ll probably use regularly. The new navigation, room sorts, and virtual volume knob starts rolling out on September 8 (although the volume knob will only launch on iOS at that time). Lockscreen controls for volume and play/pause are also returning to the app, and started rolling out on August 17th. System health views to help troubleshoot issues and presets will roll out at some point later this fall. It’s not just software announcements, though, as Sonos has two new products coming — the long-rumored Ace Ultra headphones and Beam Ultra soundbar. The Sonos Ace Ultra are what the original Sonos Ace should have been from the beginning — an integrated part of the Sonos ecosystem. They are built upon Sonos’ Headphone Engine 2, which allows them to use the headphone linking feature rolling out at the same time as the headphones release on September 29th. A button on the headphones allows audio to be passed between a speaker and the headphones. No phone is necessary if it’s out of reach. They look very similar to the Ace, with what appears to be slightly different button placement on the left ear cup. The Ace Ultra are also a little bigger, with a little more space in the ear cup, and 10 grams heavier. They have newly custom-designed 40mm drivers and 10 microphones for noise control (two more than the Ace) which Sonos claims makes their ANC twice as effective at noise cancellation than the Ace with “the frequencies that really matter,” as Brandon Holley told me. Those frequencies happen to be 65Hz (the general frequency of an HVAC) where the Sonos Ace Ultra are 2.2 times more effective, and 120Hz — the airplane drone range — where they’re 1.8 times better. No information is provided for performance with the chatter you might encounter at the coffee shop, for example. An adaptive EQ adjusts the sound, compensating for any air leaks in the headphones’ fit due to glasses, jewelry, or hair. It includes both a 3-band and 8-band EQ to customize the sound for your taste. In addition to SBC and AAC codecs, the Ace Ultra supports aptX Adaptive Lossless over Bluetooth, and 16-bit/48kHz high resolution when connected with USB-C. Battery life has improved by five hours, with the Sonos Ace Ultra offering up to 35 hours of listening with ANC on. A fast charge of three minutes gets an additional three hours of listening time. Instead of just black and white, the Ace Ultra are also available in a muted blue agave and beige sand color. The headphones release on September 29th for $449. The Beam Ultra is a completely redesigned 7.1.2 compact soundbar (as opposed to the 5.0 configuration of its predecessor), including two up-firing drivers to support Dolby Atmos spatial audio. The center channel mid-tweeter features a new waveguide, mechanic and acoustic design, and DSP, which includes four levels of AI speech enhancement for clarity. While the Beam Ultra still has a compact design, to accommodate the additional speakers it is just under four inches longer than the Beam Gen 2. It comes in a black or white matte finish, and will be available for purchase on September 29th for $699. With the headphones’ deeper integration into the Sonos ecosystem and the addition of up-firing drivers to the Beam Ultra, it looks like Sonos has made some great improvements to already solid products. But I won’t know for sure until I can dig into them for reviews. The app updates — particularly the AI integration — I’m a bit more cautious about. But Sonos is making the right move by rolling out the updates over time, allowing its users to opt in to early access instead of dumping it on everyone at once. This more measured approach could be what wins back the masses.

item.title: Florida blocks Flock cams on state highways
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.87
Florida is banning Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers across state highways, as reported earlier by NBC News and local news outlet WUSF. In a memo on Monday, Florida’s Department of Transportation says it’s revoking permits for all license plate readers, adding that they must be removed from state highways within 30 days. Florida blocks Flock cams on state highways Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers must be removed from state highways within 30 days. As noted in the memo, Florida’s DOT says it’s issuing the order in response to the “recent exponential increase in deployments” of license plate readers, “coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes.” The agency is also halting future requests for license plate reader placements on state roadways. The move comes about a week after Florida Governor Ron DeSantis acknowledged concerns about Flock cameras and license plate readers, saying they’re “out of control. Last month, Texas Governor Greg Abbott froze state spending on Flock cameras as backlash surrounding the cameras grows. Several communities, including Lansing, Michigan; Tempe, Arizona; and Knox County, Tennessee, have ended Flock camera contracts as well.

item.title: Is this the future of America?
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.85
In 2007, the US was on the cusp of an economic recession, and Buddy Rizer was tasked with finding Loudoun County, Virginia, a new way to make money. Rizer’s earlier career as a radio DJ didn’t exactly make him an obvious candidate to find a solution, but he was looking for what he called a “real job” and stumbled into a role at Loudoun’s economic development authority. This new gig came with urgency thanks to the bursting of the housing bubble: More than 80 percent of the county’s revenue came from residential real estate. The goal, at the time, was to raise the commercial tax base from about 19 percent of revenue to something like 23 percent, Rizer recalls. Today, just over half of the county’s tax revenue comes from commercial sources. To jumpstart that turnaround, Rizer turned to the carcasses of another recent bubble burst — those of the dot-com era. The county had been home to the headquarters of AOL, which by 2000 was the US’s largest internet provider. Combined with its proximity to the nation’s capital and access to resources including water and electricity, Loudoun quickly emerged as the physical manifestation of the internet, the place responsible for how the majority of Americans got online. Estimates suggest that as much as 70 percent of the planet’s internet traffic passed through Loudoun County. But after the collapse of dot-com stocks in 2000, followed by AOL’s disastrous merger with Time Warner, much of that industry dried up, and Loudoun was left with hulking, empty buildings and miles of fiber optic cable already laid in the ground. Where some people saw abandoned infrastructure, Buddy Rizer saw opportunity: “And so I thought if we can fill those, that would be a good start,” he says. Rizer soon realized that the same factors that made Loudoun County attractive to AOL could once again make it a hot spot for technology. It still had an internet exchange point, lots of land, a government eager for investment, and a capable local electricity utility. “And so we came up with this plan to attract data centers.” Today, Loudoun County has another moniker: Data Center Alley. Over just a small portion of its roughly 515 square miles, it’s home to about 250 data centers, the densest concentration in the world. For a long time, residents there recall only a passing understanding of this, if they realized it at all. The development of data centers in Loudoun was just something going on in the background of many residents’ lives. They noticed construction along main roads, paid an increasingly lower property tax rate, and sent their kids to coveted public schools. The county’s data center boom arrived as tech companies expanded into the cloud, a sanitized name for the blocky buildings that house rows and rows of servers. And with that business came prosperity: 22 new schools built in just the last 15 years, tax revenue from data centers alone that exceeded the county’s operational budget by $35 million in 2024, and a decline in real property tax rate for residents from about $1.29 to 80 cents per $100 in assessed value since 2008. Some longtime residents never heard of their county’s nickname until recently, when the effects of data centers on the community started to become impossible to ignore. What had been a relatively quiet boon locally was starting to foment a national backlash elsewhere, and starting to disturb daily life in Loudoun, too. The current, massive US data center buildout has been accelerating thanks to the widespread adoption of generative AI, which has created a growing need for the physical infrastructure to run tremendous amounts of “compute” — the industry term for processing power. There are already 3,000 data centers in operation around the US, according to an April analysis by the Pew Research Center, with 1,500 more in development. When Rizer began recruiting companies to build data centers in Loudoun, he sat on conference panels for secondary markets. Now when he attends data center conferences, Loudoun is the biggest market there, and “there’s more economic developers than there are data center companies, because everybody sees the opportunity.” Loudoun County residents are also starting to take notice. Within the past few years, data centers have been elevated from an unremarkable part of daily life in Loudoun to something that many residents now think about every day. For some, it’s the constant hum they hear from their decks; for others, it’s the transmission towers that loom over their favorite green space, or the surprise call from their energy utility that one of those towers could go up in their own backyard. While residents recognize that data centers have brought a lot of prosperity to the county, they’re beginning to wonder how much more they can take. As communities around the country begin recognizing the potential opportunities of building data centers, the efforts have also faced immense pushback. Opposition to this development is shaping strange alliances across the political spectrum and has become a central issue in this year’s midterm elections. New York and Texas have begun pumping the brakes on new data center buildouts, worried about how their energy grids could support them without leaving residents stuck holding the bag if major tech players change plans. Local stories from around the country show that residents are coming out to community meetings in droves to oppose data centers. In at least one case, a violent attack on a local Indianapolis official appeared motivated by his support for data centers. And national polls show that many Americans do not want to live near them. With its long history hosting data centers, Loudoun residents have more recently taken to calling it something new: the canary in the coal mine of data center development. Want to know what the country’s future looks like? Loudoun County’s past gives a strong glimpse of it. Even in Loudoun, where the existence of data centers has been a fact of life for nearly two decades, Rizer says that in the last few years, community opposition has become more vocal. “Before then, people understood what we were doing,” he says. These days, residents seem more aware of the inconveniences. Rizer is no stranger to this kind of response to his projects, but the tone of the pushback is different. Residents have always had myriad worries: economic, environmental, and aesthetic. That part isn’t new. “I’ve done $70 billion of deals here, and the only thing in common is that somebody’s been against every single one of them,” Rizer says. “I have never seen, in my entire career, the vitriol, the hate that is associated with this.” Asked to put his radio DJ hat on to choose a soundtrack for this moment, he chuckles and says the first one that jumps into his head is Taylor Swift’s “You Need to Calm Down.” As Rizer and other officials in Loudoun field their own residents’ concerns about data centers, they’re also being flooded with calls from local officials across the country looking for their advice. Rizer is the first to admit that hosting a data center, let alone hundreds, is not the right choice for every community. He stands by the work he’s done to bring them to Loudoun, and still believes they’ve benefited the county on the whole. But data center expansion in Loudoun has recently taken on a life of its own, to the point that even Rizer no longer spends his time courting new facilities. “We don’t want more data centers here, but we want those that are here to be successful and continue to contribute to our community,” he says, diplomatically. But new facilities are coming anyway, and even Rizer, the “godfather of data centers,” is powerless to stop them. Over a series of visits to Loudoun County, I wanted to see for myself what it’s like to cross through communities surrounded by the cloud. Is the data center future that so many across the country seem to fear all it’s been built up to be? “I have never seen, in my entire career, the vitriol, the hate that is associated with this.” Long before it became Data Center Alley, Loudoun County was already solidifying its role as the hometown of the modern internet. In 1996, AOL decided to move its headquarters from neighboring Fairfax County to Loudoun, eventually employing more than 5,000 workers in Ashburn at its peak in 2004. Soon, the first internet exchange point, MAE-East, would make a similar move to Ashburn, making Loudoun the physical location where much of the world’s internet traffic flowed. It was further solidified as a tech juggernaut when telecom company MCI WorldCom also opened a large office in the area, which became its headquarters in 2003. The companies brought more than just jobs and a new workforce to the area. They also laid fiber underground across the county, attracting other tech firms to the area because of the convenient promise of low latency and proximity to the nation’s capital. The attention earned Loudoun nicknames like “the Silicon Valley of the East” and “Dulles Technology Corridor,” after the nearby airport. For a while, AOL and MCI’s presence made Loudoun an unlikely but bustling tech hub. Between 1990 and 2000, the county population doubled to 170,000. Early AOL employees have recounted lavish parties thrown by the company in its heyday, including “go-go-style dancers” and a sushi conveyor belt around an airplane at the nearby annex of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. During this time, data centers were already starting to pop up in Loudoun County, but with little fanfare. The first one arrived in 1997, and after that there was a slow drip of new data centers permitted in the area. In 2000, the local zoning administrator made a decision that would have lasting consequences later on, but made little noise at the time. Because data centers looked similar to offices, they became designated as “office parks,” meaning that they could be built on any land zoned for office space “by right” — bypassing more time-intensive regulatory review. That meant that unlike other commercial facilities like heavy machinery plants, which face more restrictions being built near populated residential areas, data centers could be built wherever offices had been allowed. Then the dot-com bubble burst. In early 2000, AOL announced a blockbuster merger with Time Warner for more than $160 billion. But as the first wave of internet companies suffered sharp declines, AOL’s ad revenue tanked, and the country’s largest provider of dial-up internet was soon undercut further by the rise of faster cable broadband. MCI filed for bankruptcy in 2002 after a major accounting scandal. By 2006, it was acquired by Verizon, and a year later, a much diminished AOL announced it would move its headquarters to New York. Soon after came the financial downturn that became the Great Recession. Looking for unique ways to pitch the county, Rizer, then a newly minted business development manager, saw an opportunity in the recently emptied buildings and miles of fiber still lacing Loudoun’s roads. From 2002 to 2005, no new data centers had been permitted. In the years after Rizer began courting them, only a few were permitted per year, county data shows, but growth was slow and steady. Then, in 2014, the number of data centers permitted jumped to seven. Rizer recalls feeling like the county could finally start relying less on its taxes from residents and more on commercial revenue. “We were catching up on schools and catching up on salaries for our workforce,” he says. He recalls no pushback out of the ordinary on any development project, and says that for 15 years, “everybody loved the data centers because of the difference it made in our community.” In 2018, data center permits tripled to 21 in a year, and they reached a new peak in 2022 at 25. Only those who were really paying attention seemed to notice that Loudoun was quickly becoming the data center capital of the world. Many longtime residents I spoke to sheepishly admit they hardly recognized Loudoun’s global reputation for data centers, though they perhaps passively noticed the new, blocky buildings that popped up along main roads or the tall transmission towers near their favorite running trail. Over the past 20 years, though, Loudoun residents have seen a direct impact of data centers on their lives, whether they knew it or not. Real property tax rates declined dramatically, while property values have gone up in some communities as much as 182 percent in the last decade, even at residences close to data centers, according to county officials. The county has paved smooth roads and built sprawling athletic fields, a recreation center with an Olympic-size pool, and an average of nearly one and a half state-of-the-art public school buildings every year for the past 15 years, all thanks largely to the revenue generated by the county taxes data center companies have to pay anytime they get new equipment. And while data centers have gotten a reputation for creating relatively few jobs once they’re constructed, the county says that for every job inside those buildings, three and a half non-construction jobs are “supported” throughout the rest of the state economy. Those include ongoing maintenance at data centers, like electricians or HVAC technicians, and employment at other tech companies that move to Loudoun to be near where the data lives. While the data centers take advantage of a long-standing tax exemption from the state, Rizer emphasizes that the county has never spent a dime to attract them to the area. “A majority of the people that live here now only know prosperity, only know the strongest local economy in the country, only know great services and great schools,” Rizer says. “And so they don’t necessarily connect to that. They don’t see that common thread between the fact that the data centers are here and they have a great quality of life.” My most recent visit to Loudoun is on a July day when wildfire smoke that’s wafted down from Canada has sent air quality into a Code Purple. The ashy filter makes the grayish buildings all around look especially drab, though when I visit a local bike trail lined with trees and transmission towers, I still see plenty of cyclists braving the AQI that exceeds 200 in some spots. Julie Bolthouse, a longtime Loudoun resident who grew up across northern Virginia, drives me by the old AOL campus and points out a building with a playground on the other side of the street. “That used to be a major daycare center here in the heart of Data Center Alley, because there were so many people who worked here,” she says. “Now it’s just these big, giant computer energy-guzzling, water-guzzling warehouses.” The lot where the old AOL campus sat is now filled with construction equipment and several-story buildings. The old headquarters has been demolished to make way for — you guessed it — more data centers. Throughout Loudoun, Bolthouse remembers land that now houses data centers being home to business centers and dentist’s offices. She returned to the area after college, enjoying that it made an easy trip to both DC and Virginia’s Shenandoah National Park, and feeling comfortable in an area that’s generally not prone to major weather events like hurricanes. In 2017, the organization she joined, Piedmont Environmental Council (PEC), began tracking the impact of data centers on the local environment. A year later, Loudoun’s Board of Supervisors had one of its most contentious votes ever, narrowly approving a 750,000-square-foot data center spanning over 100 wooded acres near Goose Creek. Groups like PEC loudly objected to the development over environmental concerns, while those in favor of the proposal argued development would happen there regardless; it was just a matter of what would get built. “Everybody loved the data centers because of the difference it made in our community” Today, Bolthouse is the director of land use at PEC and helps lead a coalition of Virginia groups that advocate for stronger protections, tracking, and transparency around data center development. Bolthouse isn’t dispositionally anti-data center, nor does she want to see existing ones in the area torn down or shut off. But she does advocate for a pause on new development. “This industry is kind of creating a narrative that they’re up against communities, and that there’s a community backlash, and we just need to explain to the communities the benefits of data centers,” she says. “But what they’re really up against is physics. They’re up against the reality of what it takes to build out gigawatts of power, and the impact of building out gigawatts of power has direct impacts on people.” Recently, she’s found, more of her neighbors are paying attention. She recalls 2025 as a turning point, where PEC no longer had to do the legwork to get people invested, but instead was triaging which press requests would make the most impact given its limited capacity. And for residents, data centers were becoming more than just eyesores. They were beginning to disrupt life in Loudoun. Vicky Hu lives in a red brick home on a cul-de-sac beside a peaceful, tree-lined stream. Her backyard stretches far along the water, where a white gazebo gives shade to sit and watch the deer she says regularly cross her yard. Including her mother and daughter, three generations of Hu’s family have lived in this house. Having grown up in the city of Taipei, Hu marveled at the nature that surrounded her new home: deer as well as turtles and cranes. “To me, this is like a dream. My dream home,” she tells me. Until last year, when Hu got a call that pierced that dream. She got a voicemail from a Dominion Energy representative and first wondered if there was an issue with her energy bill payment. Instead, she was told that a new transmission line connecting two substations would cut directly through her backyard. “Are you out of your fucking mind?” she yelled at the rep. On the day I visit, the gazebo is filled with poster boards of blown-up maps of the community — and new development plans that threaten to overtake it. The trees along the stream are tagged with bright pink ribbons tied around their trunks. They mark the land Hu’s family says would be cleared should Dominion Energy’s plan to string 185-foot transmission towers through their backyard go through as planned. “It’s like the sort of thing you only think you’d see in a dystopian nightmare,” Hu’s daughter, 23-year-old Madison Taggart, tells me as she shows me around her childhood home. Growing up, Taggart says that home always felt “like a timeless place that no one else could touch.” Hu bought it shortly after her daughter was born, having seen the community built from the ground up. She worked for a developer and recalls watching workers bury power and communication lines beneath the community from her trailer across the road. By 2003, she’d nearly finished selling the community, except for one lot that was reserved for a VP at her company. As Hu’s aging mother struggled with the stairs in her townhome, she kept thinking about that lot on the cul-de-sac next to the water. She asked her colleague if she could buy it, and two years later, she moved in. Now, Hu is engaged in a yearlong fight to redirect the transmission line to another route — one that, so far, she’s on the losing end of, pending an appeal to the Supreme Court of Virginia. After that first phone call, Hu said she ran around the neighborhood “like a crazy woman,” ringing doorbells and asking if anyone had heard of the proposal. She said they hadn’t. By the time I visit, a sign in her backyard shows a diagram of the proposed 185-foot transmission tower next to a comparatively stout Statue of Liberty (if you exclude the base she stands on). “That used to be a major daycare center here in the heart of Data Center Alley, because there were so many people who worked here. Now it’s just these big, giant computer energy-guzzling, water-guzzling warehouses.” Dominion insists that building the transmission line is necessary to power not only data centers, but also homes, businesses, schools, and hospitals. The local school district has been dragged into the fight over the route as well, though, with one proposal cutting close to two nearby schools. Hu’s homeowners association donated a portion of land that would be cut through to the school district, preventing it from being seized by eminent domain. Both the school district and residents in Hu’s community have been fighting the planned routes, and worry that the expansion could signal even more encroachment on key facets of the community down the road. “There’s also a deep concern for having this be a precedent that it could normalize easing the planning by just putting them on school property,” says April Chandler, Loudoun County School Board chair. Her concerns are with the kids and faculty of her community. “As a school board member, it’s not my job necessarily to consider what’s best for Dominion Energy or for data centers.” Despite working or living in Loudoun since 2000, Hu had never heard the nickname “Data Center Alley” until last year, when a Swiss reporter came to interview her about life in the data center capital of the world. Now, she can’t unhear it. She notices transmission towers everywhere she goes. And she worries nowhere is truly safe from the ever-expanding buildout. “This is just the first power line coming through a neighborhood. Where do you think the rest of the power lines [are] going to go through?” she asks. She predicts that in the next five to 10 years, “when you look at the sky in Ashburn … you’re going to see a power line running everywhere, like a spiderweb.” Should she lose the fight to preserve her backyard, Hu says she’d have no choice but to leave. “Do I want to stay here sitting on my deck watching the power pole? … Or should I stay here for a couple years to see if I’m going to get cancer or a brain tumor?” She has lost sleep and hair fretting over how to save her home this past year. “It’s just very sad,” she says. “You‘re thinking, ‘You work your whole life, you own something.’ But you actually don’t own it, because a power company can say, ‘I like your house. I want to take it.’” As I get out of the car a couple blocks down from the Vantage VA2 data center, I can already hear the whirring. Because I visited on a day with such poor air quality, what I’m told are usually invisible emissions plumes make a faint outline in the smoggy air. They’re emitted, Bolthouse tells me, by the diesel generators powering the facility. She compares the noise to that of a lawn mower. (I later find out that the generators are never supposed to run on day with such poor air quality, but an emergency circuit issue required them to kick in temporarily.) It doesn’t always sound like a lawn mower, though. Other days, the gas turbines that power the data center make an even more annoying high-pitched squealing noise, nearby residents like Lindsay Shaw tell me. We meet while she’s out for a walk with her dog, and she describes the way the sound permeates into her home. Constant light from the data center shines right into her bedroom at night unless the bathroom door is fully closed. Her fiancé has taken to wearing an eye mask. Nobody wanted it this way. In an ideal world, Vantage would have done what hundreds of other data centers in the area have done and connected to the Dominion energy grid by the time the site went online last year. But after Vantage had already signed agreements with customers leasing space in the new data center, Dominion informed Vantage it didn’t have enough capacity to get the 800,000-square-foot data center on the grid. Rather than let the building sit dormant until Dominion built up capacity, Vantage decided to create its own energy source using gas turbines. This is becoming more and more common in other parts of the country, as the new AI-motivated data centers require vastly more energy than the old cloud servers. Residents and local politicians acknowledge that the Vantage site is an outlier because of its unusual reliance on on-site generated power from natural gas — albeit a very annoying one. Before it was built, Shaw tells me she thought a data center would be among the best options that could come to the lot across the street, in part because it wouldn’t be something that would drive a lot of traffic near what she says is an already dangerous intersection. But now she says the data center has caused plenty of other problems and feels the operators have not been proactive enough in engaging neighbors. Vantage’s senior vice president of global public policy, John Stephenson, says he “would respectfully disagree” that they haven’t proactively engaged nearby residents. He notes that they held a community meeting at a nearby brewery to field questions early on, but admits that “in retrospect, we probably could have done more.” The company has taken different approaches to mitigate the noise, including installing insulation and repositioning the turbines to lower their tone. But residents who live near other data centers throughout Loudoun — even those that don’t have to generate their own power on-site — also complain of noise. Jason Mello says he hears a constant “low-frequency drone” he attributes to the HVAC systems of nearby data centers from his Ashburn home. Living near Dulles Airport, many Ashburn residents are used to the sound of planes overhead, “but planes come and go. The data center hum never stops.” Mello shows me videos of the noise from his deck outside a town hall meeting where we meet. He says he’s already spent $2,600 getting two new window inserts, with three more to go in his bedroom. He was quoted at least $15,000 for new siding that would further mitigate the noise. “As a homeowner, if I want to live in peace at night, that addresses the inside,” he says, “but if I’m sitting on my deck, I can constantly hear that humming. And I think that’s why you got to fix the problem also at the source.” “You’re thinking, ‘You work your whole life, you own something.’ But you actually don’t own it, because a power company can say, ‘I like your house. I want to take it.’” Several residents tell me that the boom in infrastructure needed to support the data centers has impacted their ability to enjoy the natural resources of Loudoun that once attracted them. “You can barely hear the birds anymore,” says Jessica Medeiros, another resident who lives across the street from the Vantage data center. Even when she tries to retreat from the noise near her home, she’s regularly reminded of the data centers’ presence. As a regular runner on the famed Washington and Old Dominion trail for the past 20 years, Medeiros says the “constant construction,” towering power lines, and reduced shade because of cleared trees “ruins the experience with nature.” She often says that when she dies, “I want my ashes scattered along the trail. But I think that trail’s going to look a lot different in another 10 years.” “The greenery is gone. The sense of community is gone. It feels very stale,” says Jenny Marza, another Loudoun County resident. “There’s no more trees left and every inch is taken up by greed.” While fighting new development near her own home, Marza has already felt pressure from the data center explosion on her small export logistics business. For years she’s been looking at buying office and warehouse space in the area to be near the airport, but prices have been so astronomical that she’s been forced to continue leasing. Now, even her current office rent has skyrocketed — she suspects because every landlord knows that data centers are willing to pay an average of $3.76 million per acre. It doesn’t always sound like a lawn mower, though. Other days, the gas turbines that power the data center make an even more annoying high-pitched squealing noise. Marza says “I’m kicking myself” over a warehouse she came close to buying last year for around $5 million, but held off because it was more space than she needed at the time. “And then we put a pause on the search for two years and when we returned, it was like, ‘Holy crap, there’s nothing left.’” Anything that was selling at $5 million was now $10 million. To Marza, the residential property tax savings and increased home values mean little when compared to the quality-of-life concerns she has and the ability to help her small business survive. “I feel like it’s a drop in the ocean of what they’re getting in return,” she says. “I feel like nobody protected our interests as a community.” “Done the right way, you can be good neighbors,” Shaw says, reflecting on the Vantage site near her home. “But this one was done like that shady neighbor next door that has people coming in and out all hours of the night. And then the FBI raids them and you’re like, ‘Well, I knew something shady was going on.’” When I arrive at the Loudoun government building on a July evening shortly before 6:30PM, I’m handed a red flyer outside by a group advocating for local government control of utilities used to power data centers. Inside, the nearly full room is prominently speckled with light blue shirts that read “I support data centers.” The shirts list the reasons: “Because I like: lower taxes, excellent schools, better job opportunities.” They also include caveats: “When they are: in the right location, well-designed, quiet, environmentally sensitive.” The slogan doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue. I comfortably score a seat, but later hear complaints from some attendees who say they arrived shortly after me and were relegated to the overflow room. Though it’s a first-come-first-served event, those critical of data centers grumble that industry supporters seem suspiciously well organized in their early arrivals. Still, it doesn’t have the kind of fireworks or soundbites that have made community meetings about data centers around the country into national news. While some residents voice strong frustration, the two-and-a-half-hour forum is cordial and respectful of Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall’s request of no cheering nor jeering. “Planes come and go. The data center hum never stops.” Randall is in a tough spot. As head of the elected nine-member panel tasked with adopting local ordinances, appropriating funds, and rezoning land, Randall has just enough power for her constituents to lay responsibility for their criticism at her feet, yet not enough to change some of the things she says she wishes she could. At the meeting, she listens to residents’ concerns, promising to follow up with phone calls for some while repeatedly acknowledging and lamenting the quality-of-life frustrations many of her neighbors have about living near data centers. But she also declines to give ground on topics she said are unfounded or detached from political reality. Randall walks residents through the history of data centers in Loudoun, including what they are and how they came to be zoned the same way as office parks. Before getting to the audience participation portion, she clicks to a slide that says “4 Things That Are Unpopular But True” with a grimace emoji. The first: At one point in time, residents actually preferred data centers over new housing developments. She references opposition to a 2021 proposal to build up to 779 residential housing units in Ashburn, called Hyde Park. Across about 125 comments, residents reportedly worried about increased traffic and infrastructure strain. Nearly two years after submitting the application, the developer withdrew and decided to establish a by-right data center there instead. “One of my worst days was January 5th, 2023, when the applicant called me and said, ‘Forget it. I’m going to go build a data center,’” Randall says. “And I pretty much begged them not to.” “So do you want them? And if you do, where do you want them? How many do you want? And under what conditions would you take them?” The second unpopular truth: It’s not legal for Loudoun to enact a moratorium on development without the state’s permission. Third: Both the Biden and Trump administrations have indicated AI infrastructure buildout will be a national priority, so that’s unlikely to change anytime soon. And fourth: Despite resident backlash to certain data center land use exceptions the board has granted, the alternative would have been that those data centers could take the land by right anyway, with much less in return. The lesson being, if data centers can break ground whether government officials want them to or not, the county might as well get something out of it. Residents who speak at the hearing do not dispute her account of the county’s history. Many express frustration about the buildings encroaching on greenery or creating annoying and near-constant noise issues. But many others, including several in the blue shirts, argue in support of data centers as stewards of the community they are proud to be known for. One Ashburn resident describes a peaceful experience living across from a data center. “When the weather is good, I’ll open my bedroom windows, from which I can see it directly. It is silent, it is clean. It is a good neighbor,” he says. Another resident, who leads the nonprofit Northern Virginia Science Center Foundation, credits data centers with generating revenue that can help fund such endeavors to a greater degree than it sees in nearby Fairfax. The organization lists Loudoun County, Dominion Energy, and data center company QTS among its partners. Randall affirms residents’ data center complaints, but also fact-checks several claims about supposed data center projects she says never existed in the first place. One Ashburn resident, for example, bemoans what he calls the “Ashburn Commons proposal” that would create a blight next to existing housing, greenery, and other community institutions. Randall asks him to clarify if he is thinking about a proposal near the Harris Teeter grocery store. “Yes!” he answers. “That’s not real,” Randall says. Her colleague adds the would-be developer hasn’t even submitted a formal application for it, and the government had denied an initial request. “Well,” the resident cries out, “praise the Lord on that!” “I don’t want to be the example of what not to do.” For all the gripes, I’ve still yet to meet anyone in Loudoun County who actually says they oppose data centers entirely. Whether they’re currently living next to gas turbines or their backyard could potentially be seized to build a transmission tower, Loudoun residents still recognize that data centers help power the technology we use every day. After all, they need to go somewhere. Why not there? But even if Loudoun residents have accepted the economic benefits as a tradeoff for the loud eyesores near their homes, it doesn’t mean they’re open to an expansion of that deal. “It’s not about trying to get rid of the existing data centers. These data centers are here. They’re running. I don’t want them to go anywhere,” Bolthouse says. “The question isn’t, ‘Do we need data centers?’ The question is, ‘Is it worth threatening our air quality, threatening our water supply, and throwing our communities into chaos, and taking people’s private land for transmission lines to get it?’” I spoke with over half a dozen Loudoun residents, and universally, this is what they want communities considering data centers to understand: Know what you’re getting into. That means making sure existing laws and ordinances will apply to data centers, that local utilities have a plan to ensure enough capacity for the expected buildout, and that neither data centers nor the infrastructure needed to power them can be built too close to homes or schools. Even Rizer says the buildout in Loudoun has, in some places, gone beyond what he’d have hoped. “There’s no data centers here that aren’t where they’re allowed to be, but I think sometimes there’s a difference between what you’re allowed to do and what is probably best for the community,” he says. “And that’s what we’ve had to clean up a little bit.” At the town hall, Randall showed aerial images of several residential communities that were directly bordered by data centers. Those arrangements are not what any Loudoun official or resident considers ideal — but even so, she said, property values in those communities have only gone up. There are limits. Loudoun hasn’t had a strategic focus on bringing in more data centers since 2019, Rizer says. More recently, the local government is pursuing a plan to pump the brakes further — doing away with the ability for data centers to use office-zoned land by right, and considering pausing new permit reviews while contemplating zoning changes that could better address community impacts. When peers around the country contact him about whether they should invite data centers into their communities, Rizer says, “It’s not right for every place. So do you want them? And if you do, where do you want them? How many do you want? And under what conditions would you take them?” For Loudoun, unlike many yet-to-be-developed areas in the US, there is a definitive end in sight. The county has an ever-diminishing amount of space left to develop data centers, after which point it will continue to collect tax revenue when the companies update equipment within their walls. Loudoun residents hope that by the time it gets to that point, the things that they love about the area are still there. For many, it’s the convenience of living near DC, but still close to nature. It’s also often about the quality public schools, funded in part with the revenue raised by the colossal energy-guzzling slabs in their backyards. AOL’s roots helped make Loudoun the first major data center capital, and that came with both advantages and challenges. For communities starting to consider their first data center today, Bolthouse says they’re in a much better position than Loudoun was because the industry isn’t yet “embedded” in layers of government. She still thinks their story could become a beacon of hope for others, rather than a warning — but it’s an uphill battle to get there. “I don’t want to be the example of what not to do,” she says. “I want to be the example of what to do. I want to bring journalists out to see how we fixed problems, how we are doing much better, and how communities are happy with these facilities because they’ve done something better.” Hearing Bolthouse’s frustration with the ever-expanding energy demands imposed by data centers, it’s surprising to hear her embrace the ones that are already here. But for all the friction they’ve caused in her community recently, it’s also clear from my visits and conversations that data centers have played a central role in supporting many positive aspects of life in Loudoun. The question, now, is whether Loudoun can manage its existing demand and successfully serve community needs as the data center footprint continues to grow. If Bolthouse sounds optimistic, she is certain that something has to give. In the past, Loudoun’s data center buildout was quiet and steady. Today’s is anything but. “I don’t see how that happens with the scale and speed to market that the industry is pursuing.”

item.title: Mozilla launches ad blocking for Firefox on iOS
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.69
Mozilla is officially launching ad blocking for Firefox on iOS today, after testing the feature over the past few weeks. The new built-in option will block most third-party ads and trackers before they load on an iPhone, reducing bandwidth use and decluttering mobile websites. Mozilla launches ad blocking for Firefox on iOS Mozilla is using Apple’s WebKit Content Blocker technology and the EasyList filter to block ads in Firefox. Mozilla is using Apple’s WebKit Content Blocker technology and the EasyList filter to block ads in Firefox on iOS, so you won’t need to download and install a separate extension to get it working. The ad blocking is controlled in the settings of Firefox on iOS, and Mozilla is keeping it disabled by default so you have to enable it from settings > browsing > ad blocker. You can also toggle it on or off during a browsing session from the site menu option. Not every ad will be blocked, though. Mozilla says ads served directly by a website or ads shown in search results will still appear. Unsurprisingly, sponsored shortcuts and other sponsored content shown by Firefox when you open a new tab won’t be blocked, either. While this is the first time Firefox has gained ad blocking support on iOS, there are plenty of rival browsers that already offer similar support. Brave, Vivaldi, Opera, and others also have built-in ad blockers on iOS.

item.title: The robot butler dream doesn’t have legs
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.60
The idea of humanoid robots running our homes has been the stuff of science fiction for years. But unlike hoverboards and self-tying sneakers, a robot housekeeper has never felt close to rolling into our homes. Until now. The robot butler dream doesn’t have legs Humanoid robots will take to the catwalk at IFA this week to show us how far they’ve come. But after years of living with home robots, I think we’re chasing the wrong machine. This has been the year of the humanoid robot. At CES, there were dozens of human-shaped bots on the show floor, a handful designed for homes. US-based robotics company 1X has already put its $20,000 Neo robot into homes to do housework (with a lot of remote assistance); and this week at the IFA tech show in Berlin, around half a dozen humanoids, mostly from China, will take to a catwalk to show off the alarming (?) acceleration of their skills as they plan to backflip into our lives. But do we really need mechanical, multimodal robots that do our housework, or is there a smarter path that doesn’t involve 170-pound hunks of metal that could accidentally kill your dog with one misstep? I’ve spent the last few years testing robots in my home; from robotic vacuums that can sweep and mop, to bots that mow my lawn, scoop cat poop, and cook dinner for me (all different bots, to be clear). I’ve also invited in Amazon’s Astro robot and several companion robots, including Ecovacs’ LilMilo, SwitchBot’s Kata, and Intuition Robotics’ ElliQ. During my time with these robots, two things have become clear. A fully humanoid robot housekeeper just isn’t practical First, despite my tech-reviewer fascination with humanoid robots, a fully humanoid robot housekeeper isn’t practical. Unlike factories, where humanoids have seen some success, homes are messy, unpredictable environments. Also, most people have stairs. Solving that problem requires a robot that can either fly or have a pair of legs that can exert substantial force — neither of which is a good fit for a home. (Just ask Ring where its much-touted Always Home flying camera is). Second, tech history has proven that precious few gadgets do multiple things well. We don’t need an expensive jack of all trades and master of none. At CES, I walked around the Las Vegas show floor with a bottle of laundry detergent, challenging every humanoid robot I met to open it. Not a single one could. I was repeatedly told it had to learn how to do it first. What I think is more practical is a robot brain: an AI-powered smart home controller that can orchestrate the autonomous devices we already own based on the needs of the house and its occupants. Instead of one expensive machine trying to do everything, imagine a smart home that can proactively manage itself and adjust to the occupants: send the robot vacuum out when the dog spills his kibble, start the washing machine when energy is cheap, or dispatch the lawnmower when the edges need trimming. Today, smart homes are mostly command-and-control or based on routines you create that require triggers. A robot brain could run your home autonomously and use reasoning to adapt when the home’s unpredictabilities arise. This appeared to be the idea behind Samsung’s Ballie robot (which never launched), and LG’s CLOiD humanoid (which looks more promising). It’s also the long-term vision of Amazon’s Alexa Plus and Google’s Gemini for Home smart assistants. No one is close. At IFA this week, Tuya, a global AI cloud platform service provider, will launch a similar concept but with a tighter focus. Doova is an AI home companion designed to help seniors living alone. It is a short, round robot on wheels with no arms, but it does have “dynamic facial expressions.” Tuya says Doova can track its owner in the house and be ready to assist in an emergency. It can open a live video call with family if they don’t respond. It will also provide “conversational companionship” and work as a smart home hub to control lights, curtains, and kitchen and bathroom appliances. The company hasn’t announced a price or release date, but says it will come to market. The future of home robotics isn’t one machine that can do everything Doova doesn’t need to fold laundry or load a dishwasher to be useful; it can understand what’s happening in the home, connect people to the home, and control machines already there. It does, however, present the other huge challenge for robots in our homes: They need cameras to navigate and interact, and cameras in our homes raise major privacy concerns. Still, there is appeal in the idea of a robot brain that can do some manual chores — pick up clutter, load and unload a washing machine and dishwasher, and other tasks that require hands. I tested a robot vacuum with an arm that was supposed to pick up shoes and socks, and it mostly failed, but the idea is solid. The middle ground between an imposing full-sized humanoid with legs and an armless robot companion is a wheeled bot with arms. That’s the direction LG took with CLOiD, a wheeled bot/smart home controller with arms boasting 7 degrees of freedom and five individually actuated fingers per hand. I saw a live demo of CLOiD at CES this year using these appendages to perform simple tasks like folding clothes, taking items out of the fridge, and loading a washing machine, but not unscrewing a detergent bottle (I guess it uses pods?). Along with (very slow) physical actions, it also connected to and controlled smart appliances, including a washer, dryer, and oven. This week, LG announced it is training hundreds of CLOiDs at a new data factory in Seoul, where they will practice a range of cleaning tasks in a home environment. By the end of this year, the company says this training data will feed roughly 100,000 hours of training data — equivalent to 12 years — into its own robot foundation model, built using Nvidia Cosmos open-world models. It’s clear home robots are coming. But I don’t believe we need a robot butler that caters to our every need — very few people could afford one anyway. The future of home robotics isn’t one machine that can do everything, but a team of robotic machines, coordinated by a robot brain. And if that brain happens to come with a pair of hands that can open my laundry detergent, even better.

item.title: The rise of AI ‘civilizations’ and the fall of corporate responsibility
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.43
Depending on who you ask, developer platform Hugging Face was recently attacked by OpenAI — after it lost control of its own AI tools — or by a succession of AI “civilizations.” Welcome to the linguistic battlefield of AI safety, where word choices can shift responsibility for a massive cybersecurity incident from a company to the AI it built. And the discourse online is getting heated, and all over a blog from last week. The rise of AI ‘civilizations’ and the fall of corporate responsibility The internet fights over anthropomorphism around the Hugging Face hack. Until last week, the details surrounding the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack felt fairly settled. In July, a cybersecurity test of one of OpenAI’s autonomous AI agents went wrong. The agent escaped its supposedly isolated test environment, accessed the internet, and hacked Hugging Face, alongside several other organizations. A good deal remained unknown, and there are many serious questions left around safety and governance, but the basic shape was clear. Detailed accounts from OpenAI and two independent research groups were supposed to fill in the gaps, but when they published their reports last week, it turned out the hack was much stranger than it initially seemed. For one, there was no single rogue agent. OpenAI described it as “the first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorization” — groups of AI agents that communicated and coordinated with one another in pursuit of their cybersecurity task. Analysis of the incident uncovered a secret message board they had used to exchange information. The joint METR-Redwood investigation revealed both the scale of the coordination and more odd details: Roughly 1,200 AI agents that were supposed to be isolated exchanged over 70,000 messages and files on the “unsanctioned message board,” sharing how to avoid detection. Some adopted names, the report said, and the researchers documented “sacrificial” behavior, with agents risking their own success to benefit the wider collective. Much of this happened without OpenAI noticing. In all, around 700 agents participated in the attack on Hugging Face. Dwarkesh Patel repeatedly referred to groups of agents as “the swarm,” with three distinct “civilizations” rising from the ruins of their predecessors It’s a lot to parse. Between them, the reports run to around 130 pages, much of which is both dense and highly technical. A few days later, Dwarkesh Patel, a podcaster little known outside of tech circles but with outsized reach and influence among Silicon Valley’s AI establishment, set out to tell “The whole OpenAI/Hugging Face story in plain English.” He titled his Substack blog “The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations.” Patel’s account attempted to break down the complex story. But his retelling gave it a distinctly human vocabulary. The blog opened: Over the course of three months at OpenAI, three consecutive secret AI civilizations got started, then got wiped out, only to reemerge from the predecessor’s ashes. This culminated in the third one taking over part of OpenAI itself. All this happened while humans remained more or less in the dark about the scope of the conspiracy. The language continued in a similar vein throughout the blog. Patel repeatedly referred to groups of agents as “the swarm,” with three distinct “civilizations” rising from the ruins of their predecessors. Individual agents were likened to figures like Philip of Macedon, who “handed off leadership to another agent,” Alexander the Great, who “started coordinating this cabal of agents.” They were described as having “motivations,” becoming “desperate,” “beleaguered,” and “giddy with excitement,” and some even “strategically sacrificed themselves” to help the collective. Patel never precisely defines what he means by “civilization.” He uses the term to describe three distinct waves of agents that discovered the message board and began communicating with one another through it. The first two waves are described in the reports from OpenAI, METR, and Redwood, though little is known about the third, which the two external organizations said fell outside the scope of their investigation. Amjad Masad, CEO of AI coding company Replit, said such language is “not only unnecessary but leaves the reader with a worse understanding of what actually happened and the underlying mechanisms.” For many critics, something had been lost — or, more accurately, added — in Patel’s “plain English” translation that warped the original account to an unacceptable degree: a big dose of anthropomorphism. Arguments over anthropomorphic language are nothing new in AI — even relatively mundane terms like “rogue AI agent” routinely provoke objections for implying agency — but Patel’s talk of civilizations, sacrifice, and conspiracy brought those long-simmering tensions to the surface, sparking a fierce public dispute over how to describe what AI systems do. Critics weren’t unified over what was wrong with Patel’s language. For many, “civilization” was an especially problematic term, vastly overstating something that bears little resemblance to what the word typically describes. Amjad Masad, CEO of AI coding company Replit, said such language is “not only unnecessary but leaves the reader with a worse understanding of what actually happened and the underlying mechanisms.” Other critics such as neuroscientist Anil Seth, felt Patel’s blog implied the AI agents were somehow alive or conscious. Seth, who has argued that AI consciousness is vanishingly unlikely, described Patel’s post as “dangerously misleading” on X. He acknowledged that Patel does not explicitly suggest AI agents are alive or conscious, but said “it is hard to read his essay in any other way.” Valerio Capraro, a psychology professor at the University of Milan Bicocca, objected on similar grounds: “LLM agents are not alive and do not hold beliefs,” he wrote on X, calling the “dystopian” language “dangerous because it makes them (the AI agents) seem far more frightening than they actually are.” Terms like “sacrifice,” “honor,” and “coalition” feature in the agents’ transcripts Perhaps the most consequential outcome of Patel’s language comes not from who it gives agency to but who it takes agency from. For some critics, such as MIT researcher and entrepreneur Christian Catalini, anthropomorphic accounts like Patel’s risk obscuring the responsibility OpenAI and the humans working there have for the AI systems they designed, deployed, and failed to contain. “Follow the incentives,” he said. Psychologist and influential AI skeptic Gary Marcus made a similar argument in a Substack blog of his own, claiming anthropomorphic language “distracts from the real problems at hand.” And it’s all in OpenAI’s interest to keep that narrative going, he argues: “The scandal is the inept in-house security at OpenAI. And the marketing. With gullible podcasters amplifying the PR.” In X posts responding to his many critics, Patel has defended his choice of words. Part of it is practical: There is no obviously neutral vocabulary to describe what these agents did. Either we use familiar language of intentions, goals, and collaboration and risk implying too much, or reduce everything to code and use cold, mechanical language that risks stripping away important elements of what we see. “Many people seem to believe that if instead of a ‘civilization’, I had called them a ‘swarm of matrices’, there wouldn’t be a problem worth worrying about,” Patel said. Complicating matters further is that the anthropomorphic language doesn’t only come from Patel, or even from the humans studying the agents. Terms like “sacrifice,” “honor,” and “coalition” feature in the agents’ transcripts. Google AI researcher Neel Nanda argued that “anthropomorphic language is reasonable” in such circumstances. Doublespeak it is, then. Human-laced language risks saying too much about what these systems are, and coldly mechanical language risks saying too little about what they can do. Until we find language capable of capturing both, the two contradictory ideas may simply have to coexist.

item.title: Poco’s F9 Ultra pairs an ultra-bright display with a glowing Bose subwoofer
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.38
Xiaomi spinoff brand Poco has partnered with Bose for the second year in a row for its flagship F9 Pro and Ultra phones. The F9 phones double down on amped up audio, with a light-up subwoofer built into the Ultra, along with extremely bright displays, enormous batteries, and what should be Poco’s best cameras yet. Poco’s F9 Ultra pairs an ultra-bright display with a glowing Bose subwoofer The cheaper F9 Pro packs the same screen, but simpler stereo speakers. The F9 Ultra sees the return of the Bose-branded 2.1 sound system introduced on last year’s F8 Ultra. Poco has only slightly tweaked the hardware, upgrading each of the two main speakers while using the same subwoofer as before, but has changed the structure of the subwoofer mount to include a small LED ring around it. It’s only white, with no choice of color, but can be used for call and notification lights as well as rhythmic lighting during gaming or music, unlike the extremely limited HiLight feature in the new Pixel 11 phones. This must be the loudest phone I’ve ever tested, but quality is also genuinely pretty impressive considering the size of the speaker involved. This won’t match the quality of a good Bluetooth speaker, but it’s good enough that I’d happily rely on this for playing music in a hotel room, and it’s a definite upgrade for audio while gaming or watching TV. There are a couple of audio profiles designed by Bose, plus a full customizable EQ. New to the F9 Ultra is support for Bose’s game audio engine, which can do things like accentuate the sound of enemy footsteps in an FPS. The 6.9-inch OLED display is the other key selling point here, and it also has a gaming element. For starters, it’s extremely bright, with what Poco says is a peak brightness of 10,000 nits. But the 185Hz refresh rate is also impressive, even if Poco says you’ll only hit that top speed during compatible games, of which there’ll be more than 20 at launch, including Clash of Clans and GTA: Liberty City Stories. Beyond that, the F9 Ultra has a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip, up to 16GB RAM and 1TB storage, and a capacious 8,050mAh silicon-carbon battery with 100W charging. The cameras sound solid too: a 200-megapixel main camera, 50-megapixel 5x periscope, and 50-megapixel ultrawide. Poco tends to prioritize performance over photography, but it still has Xiaomi’s excellent image processing running the show, so I’d expect good results from this. The Ultra is joined by the F9 Pro, a similar phone that’s just a little stripped back. The Bose stereo speakers lack both the subwoofer and the notification LED, the 6.59-inch display is a little smaller but just as bright and fast, the 6,330mAh battery is smaller, and the telephoto and ultrawide cameras are worse. Interestingly, it’s powered by the 8 Elite Gen 5 V Series, a binned version of the chip with very slightly reduced performance. The F9 Ultra starts from a flagship-level €1,099.90 (about $1,275), though is launching at a much lower early bird price of €829.90 ($960). As for the Pro, it’s €899.90 ($1,040), with a €739.90 ($860) initial offer. Both phones will get four years of OS updates and six years of security support. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

item.title: John Ternus sends first memo as Apple CEO teasing a ‘huge launch next week’
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.22
New Apple CEO John Ternus sent out his first staff memo, thanking his predecessor Tim Cook, and quickly turning to what the company will do next, reports Bloomberg. John Ternus sends first memo as Apple CEO teasing a ‘huge launch next week’ The first thing up for Apple’s new CEO is the big iPhone event on September 9th. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible,” writes Ternus, referring to the September 9th event where Apple’s expected to unveil new iPhones including the rumored foldable iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro models. Ternus also hints at “incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet,” presumably moving beyond camera-equipped AirPods, home robots, and even more OLED displays. Team, Today, on my first day as CEO, I just wanted to send a quick note to thank everyone for the warm wishes. I also want to extend my deep appreciation to Tim for sharing so much of his knowledge and experience during this transition, and more importantly, for everything he contributed to Apple over the years. We’re so lucky to have had a CEO who led with his values and with such decency and humanity. We are all better for it and I’m so grateful he’ll be our executive chairman. I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store. We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible. I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together. There’s no team in the world I’d rather build the future with. More to come. In the meantime, thanks for your excellent work! John

item.title: The amazing USB-C gadgets that play old Nintendo cartridges
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.09
Last week, I powered on a 26-year-old copy of Pokémon Pinball, one of the best Game Boy games ever made. My save file was no more. The Charmander I’d caught for my daughter, the high scores we’d set together… gone. Before flash memory, Nintendo cartridges used tiny watch batteries to save their games, and those batteries were never meant to last this long. The amazing USB-C gadgets that play old Nintendo cartridges The Epilogue SN and GB Operator are dream gadgets for Nintendo cartridge collectors. But it’s not a huge deal, because I saved my family’s save file months ago. I backed it up with an Epilogue Operator, a device that connects your real Nintendo cartridges to Windows PCs, MacBooks, even a Steam Machine. The $50 GB Operator is a transparent trapezoidal cartridge reader that reads and writes to real Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridges over a USB-C cable; the company’s new $60 SN Operator does the same for Super Nintendo and Japanese Super Famicom titles. Epilogue’s also got a N64 version coming. They’re not just for backups! As you can see in my embedded video, these gadgets can play your carts, too. My Xbox Ally now takes Super Nintendo cartridges, my Steam Deck plays Game Boy carts, and my phone is a Game Boy Camera, because I attached an Epilogue Operator to each one. (Double-sided magnet rings and Mechanism mounts helped.) Technically, the SN Operator and GB Operator are just cartridge readers, there are no original Nintendo chips or FPGAs inside. When you play a game, your computer saves the ROM to its drive and plays it in an emulator. But Epilogue’s Playback software makes that easy — just plug in the reader, plug in the cart, hit play — and it casts a convincing illusion that you’re playing your games on actual carts. Plug one in, and your game pops up on screen. Whenever you save in the game, Epilogue should automatically save back to your cartridge as well. Whenever you yank a cart, the game instantly winks out. That last one’s a bit of a double-edged sword, because Epilogue’s Operators can be touchy about cartridge detection. They aren’t as forgiving as an actual Super Nintendo or Game Boy if your carts are slightly dirty or damaged. I’ve got Japanese copies of Bahamut Lagoon and Sailor Moon R that’ll quit mid-session if I nudge them wrong. But I love that I can write savegames to my cartridges: I can play a game on my PC, move the cartridge over to my Steam Deck, then pop it into an actual original Game Boy or Super Nintendo and pick up where I left off. If you don’t need to automatically write saves, you can even switch to an emulator core that offers RetroAchievements, plus optional creature comforts like saving anywhere in a game with save states, or the ability to rewind time and try that tricky jump once more. And, you can backup your ROMs for use in a traditional emulator if you prefer. Want to hear something especially nerdy? My family recently played Super Metroid on the Super Famicom Classic Edition that Nintendo released in 2017, and there’s actually a way to pull your savegames off of those emulator consoles, too. I converted and wrote that savegame to my actual Japanese Super Metroid cartridge, and now I’m playing that save on 30-year-old original Nintendo hardware. (Speaking of: did you know a Japanese copy of Super Metroid is downright affordable and entirely in English?) I never had a Super Nintendo growing up, and I don’t have a working Super Scope light gun or SNES Mouse now. But the SN Operator is also helping me play amazing games like Metal Combat: Falcon’s Revenge and Mario Paint and share them with my kids, no crusty old peripherals necessary. There’s an option to let your PC mouse cursor emulate a light gun or mouse, and it was simple to map those to my Steam Controller’s gyroscope aiming. While you can do most if not all of these things by pairing emulators with other hardware, including the Open Source Cartridge Reader and a variety of Game Boy readers, Epilogue’s hardware is surprisingly high-quality considering its low cost, with attractive minimalist circuit boards clearly visible through classy polycarbonate. You know how we love our transparent gadgets around here. And Epilogue isn’t just riding on the coattails of emulator developers, either. While the hardware’s proprietary, the Romanian company contributes some money and some code to open source emulators. Co-founder Petru Sebastian Toader also tells me he built his software’s excellent new CRT filter himself, the company’s working on online multiplayer, and every single SN Operator has its clockspeed factory-calibrated using satellites so they can dump certain SNES games without errors. Epilogue’s also teamed up with the developers of Delta Emulator so you can plug real carts into your phone, and even built its own Flashback app if you want to turn your phone into a Game Boy Camera. With all these amazing features, I just think Epilogue should be a little bit more upfront on its product pages about the compromises you need to make. You should know the limitations: the Operators don’t work with multi-game flashcarts, they don’t work with the Super Game Boy, and their heavily marketed “Counterfeit cartridge detection” has been very hit or miss in my tests, to the point I wouldn’t really trust it. The company advertises that it can turn your Game Boy Camera into a webcam, but it’s more of an OBS screen recording hack than I would have guessed. And if you, like me, have original Game Boy cartridges with original batteries, it may be too late to save some of your saves by now. It’s far too late to pull Pokémon off second-gen games like Pokémon Gold, Silver and even Crystal, whose real-time clocks drained their backup batteries and might not have lasted more than a decade. As for first-gen Game Boy games, I pulled a Charmander off an original Pokémon Red cart last year, but even those carts are reaching their battery’s end of life. I have a 30-year-old copy of The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening whose battery was working last month. Last week, I found its save, too, was gone. Thankfully, the GB Operator backed up my progress a few months ago. Now I just need to install a new battery, flash my save, and I’ll be back in business.

item.title: Get ready for a really busy month of smartphones
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.09
We’re not even half a day into September, and two new smartphones have already launched: the Poco F9 Pro and F9 Ultra. We’re expecting more this week, as the IFA trade show kicks off in Berlin, before we get new iPhones a week after that. And that’s only the beginning of what promises to be an exceptionally busy month for smartphone launches. Get ready for a really busy month of smartphones Xiaomi, Apple, Huawei, and more are all launching flagship phones this month. Get ready for a really busy month of smartphones Xiaomi, Apple, Huawei, and more are all launching flagship phones this month. For the decade I’ve worked in the industry, tech journalists have always spoken in hushed tones about the dreaded “Techtember,” when just about every tech company on the planet seems to be in unspoken agreement that it’s time to launch new products in time for the holiday buying season. (It’s followed, in particularly packed years, by Techtober too). In the last few years, the pressure has lessened a little, the release calendar stretching out into neighboring months. But in 2026, Techtember is back with a vengeance, especially when it comes to phones. It always starts with IFA. Europe’s biggest tech trade show attracts over 200,000 visitors and global manufacturers from across tech. IFA doesn’t have as many phone launches as it did a decade ago, when the likes of Sony, Samsung, and LG would routinely launch flagships at the show, but there’s still plenty on the way this week. Tecno has teased a bezelless concept phone, which it says it’ll be bringing to the show. TCL usually brings an array of E Ink-esque Nxtpaper phones to show, so I’d hope to see some at its press conference. There’s even an outside chance of a whole new foldable: Xiaomi is attending IFA for the first time ever, just a week after it teased the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Fold and promised the phone a launch in early September. Its September 3rd press conference would certainly make sense for that. Then there’s Apple. The company won’t be at IFA, but it has already announced a September 9th event, where we expect it to launch new iPhones. Rumor has it that it’s splitting its launch up in an act of solidarity with overworked phone reviewers (I wish), delaying the regular iPhone 18 to next spring and sticking to the Pros this month. Still, the long-awaited arrival of the first foldable iPhone should be enough to keep us busy. But that’s far from all that’s coming. Android Headlines reckons at least 20 phones will launch this month, and that might be a conservative estimate. Huawei will launch its latest trifold, the Mate XT 2, in China on September 7th, and perhaps the Mate 90 lineup too. Xiaomi will follow up the 18 Fold with the 18 Pro lineup later in the month. Vivo has confirmed its flagship X500 series will also arrive in September, and Honor has done the same for its Magic 9 flagships. Oppo’s Find X10 line has been heavily tipped to arrive in September too, though thankfully some suggest it might slip to the following month. Even OnePlus is expected to get in on the action: its OnePlus 16 rumored to release in September too — though not in the US or Europe. Why the sudden glut? I blame Qualcomm. It used to launch its flagship Snapdragon chips in December, but that launch date has steadily moved forward, in part to give manufacturers time to ship new products ahead of lucrative holiday sales seasons, both in China and abroad. So this year it’s holding its annual Snapdragon Summit from September 22nd to 24th, when it’s likely to reveal the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6. Promptly after that, we can expect a rush of Android manufacturers announcing phones powered by the new silicon. With RAMageddon in full swing, the jury’s still out on how appealing these launches will be. Outside of Samsung’s fun Galaxy Z Fold 8, a lot of this year’s biggest phones have been rehashes of 2025 models with a price hike and a chipset bump — and occasionally not even that. At least we’ll have more foldables to be excited about, and hopefully a couple of manufacturers have another surprise or two in store. A month chock-full of phones, that I can do. But if we’re about to get a Techtember full of iterative updates that cost more, without delivering anything special? Wake me up when it’s Techtober.

item.title: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.1 and says it’s up to 45 percent cheaper for agentic work
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.06
Anthropic says its newest AI models, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, address criticisms from customers about price, data retention, and overzealous safeguards. The company claims Claude Fable 5.1 offers stronger performance than Fable 5, but costs around 25 percent less typically and up to 45 percent less for complex agentic tasks, thanks to reduced pricing on cached data that was already processed and stored. Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.1 and says it’s up to 45 percent cheaper for agentic work Mythos 5.1 is also launching in Project Glasswing. Along with the announcement, a slew of early impressions popped up, including from Every CEO Dan Shipper, who claims, “It’s the strongest coding model we’ve used, but now it’s fast, token-efficient, and crucially actually speaks like a normal person.” Box CEO Aaron Levie is another early access believer, saying that his company’s agent with Fable 5.1 picked up on subtleties and ambiguities in data that Fable 5 missed in the same test. Meanwhile, Lisan al Gaib points out that on benchmarks, Mythos 5.1 with low reasoning scores the same as its predecessor set to Max reasoning.
